input: A 38-year-old man presented to the First Department of Orthopaedics at the University of Athens in June, 2013, with a 4-year history of an enlarging left shoulder mass. He reported minor recurrent injury during athletic activity. Medical and family history were unremarkable. Clinical examination showed a firm, painless mass. Radiography showed calcifications posterior to the left scapula (figure, A). CT scan showed multiple calcified nodules, without scapular erosion (figure, B). MRI showed heterogeneous signal intensity (figure, C). Serum calcium, phosphate, vitamin D, and amounts of parathyroid hormone were within normal limits. Differential diagnosis included tumoral calcinosis, myositis ossificans, synovial chondromatosis, and synovial sarcoma. Tumoral calcinosis consists of lobulated, well-demarked calcifications, generally at the extensor surfaces of large joints. Myositis ossificans consists of bone and cartilage formation within muscle; rapid evolution and absence of lobular morphology are typical features. Synovial chondromatosis consists of intrasynovial proliferation of cartilage, with typical rings-and-arcs calcifications and intra-articular location. Synovial sarcomas are poorly defined and infiltrative, with punctuate calcifications occurring sporadically. Because of the absence of family history of tumoral calcinosis and biochemical abnormalities in this patient, and to avoid potential diagnostic pitfalls, a needle biopsy was done. Histology was consistent with tumoral calcinosis showing amorphous calcium nodules surrounded by histiocytic and giant cell reaction. The lesion was completely surgically excised, without any recurrence at the 3-year follow-up in September, 2016. Follow-up is ongoing.

A 61-year-old man presented with bilateral, asymptomatic, indurated non-pitting verrucous plaques and nodules on his extremities and buttocks. He was diagnosed with Graves' disease 20 years ago. The patient developed hypothyroidism secondary to radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid 4 years prior to presenting to us and received levothyroxine replacement therapy, after which he attained a sustained euthyroid state. However, he developed an asymptomatic rash over his extremities and buttock, which worsened gradually. On physical examination, several plaques that were leathery in texture and nodules were observed on his extremities and buttock (figure A–D). The results of thyroid-function tests were normal (free tri-iodothyronine [T3] 3·83 pg/mL, local reference 1·80–4·10; free thyroxine [T4] 1·23 ng/dL, local reference 0·81–1·89) except for a thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of 0·094 μIU/mL (local reference 0·38–4·34) and thyrotrophin receptor antibody concentration of 280·51 IU/L (local reference <13). Results of liver and kidney function tests were normal, and concentrations of calcium, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3, 25-hydroxyvitamin D3, parathyroid hormone, urinary calcium, and urine phosphorus were within normal limits. On histological examination of skin lesion biopsy specimens stained with haematoxylin and eosin and alcian blue, abundant deposition of mucin was seen in the dermis (figure E, F). The final diagnosis according to the pathology report was myxedema. Despite application of potent topical corticosteroids, occlusive or compressive therapy, and multipoint subcutaneous injection of long-acting glucocorticoid, the skin lesions showed no obvious signs of remission after 6 months of treatment.Myxedema results from the accumulation in the dermis of glycosaminoglycan secreted by fibroblasts. The pathogenesis of the extrathyroidal manifestations of myxedema involves fibroblast activation and increased glycosaminoglycan production. Some studies postulate that the destruction of the thyroid gland by therapeutic drugs (especially iodine-131) results in the release of an antigen from thyroid cells that then stimulates the production of the thyrotrophin receptor antibody. The fibroblast in the orbital area and pretibial dermis share antigenic sites that underlie the autoimmune process that causes Graves' disease. Thereby crossreaction contributes to the development of myxedema occurring long after euthyroid status is achieved through treatment. Although myxedema does not seem to be related to the concentrations of T3 and T4, only four cases of euthyroid patients being diagnosed with myxedema have been reported in the literature.

A 60-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve and dilatation of the ascending aorta had surgical bioprosthesis implantation with aortic repair. 6 weeks after the sternotomy scar had completely healed, several soft nodules appeared progressively along the scar without pus or grains (figure, A). He had no fever, pain, or erythema on the sternal area. Laboratory tests showed normal leucocytosis, and C-reactive protein was 190·48 nmol/L. Cultures of cutaneous swabs and biopsy samples grew meticillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA). Mycobacterial and fungal cultures were negative. Investigation of skin biopsy samples showed a dermal polymorphic infiltrate with epithelioid and giant cell granulomas without necrosis or grains (figure, B). Periodic-acid Schiff, Gram, Grocott, and Zielh stains were negative. Thoracic CT revealed a sternum osteolysis with periosteal reaction and bone disjunction (figure, C). Sternum osteitis was confirmed by surgical findings and cultures of bone sample, positive for MSSA. The treatment combined surgical drainage and antibiotic therapy with 1 week of intravenous cefamandole followed by oral ofloxacine and rifampicin for 3 months. The patient did not relapse during more than 15 months of follow-up.Botryomycosis is a rare, chronic, and granulomatous cutaneous bacterial infection mostly due to Staphylococcus aureus, presenting as nodules typically characterised by the formation of grains. However, lesions can be atypical, similar to pyogenic granulomas. Cutaneous lesions usually reveal underlying, chronic soft tissue, muscle, or bone staphylococcal infection, as in our case. Pathophysiology of botryomycosis involves a balance between a low virulence of the bacteria and host resistance.
When presented with such lesions, clinicians should look for an underlying bone or soft tissue staphylococcal infection, especially in patients who have had recent surgery.
output: Botryomycosis with underlying sternum osteitis due to meticillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA)

A 27-year-old Asian man presented with erythematous, violaceous, and photosensitive lesions on the face, upper chest, and scalp, which had developed over 6 months (figure A). The patient had previously consulted a private practitioner for malar and heliotrope rash with photosensitivity and periorbital puffiness, who prescribed him methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine. However, the lesions progressed with ulceration over bilateral malar areas and the left mandibular angle (figure B–C), associated with non-scarring alopecia, oral ulcers, and violaceous papules on the dorsal aspect of metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints (Gottron's papules). There were no other comorbidities. On examination, the patient's blood pressure was 146/96 mm Hg and he had facial ulcers, as described (figure B–C). Investigations revealed he had mild elevation of alanine aminotransferase and gamma-glutamyl transferase, both elevated up to 2 × the upper limit of normal.
Based on the patient's history and symptoms, a number of differential diagnoses were considered, including dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus, lupus vulgaris (tuberculosis), granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and sarcoidosis. Buruli ulcer, which might also have a similar presentation, has yet to be reported in India. He had no clinical, radiological, or laboratory evidence of myositis, interstitial lung disease, neuropathy, nephritis, or arthritis. Serum creatine kinase, nerve conduction study results, and urine analysis were within normal limits and a high-resolution chest CT showed no abnormalities. Histopathological examination of a skin biopsy sample from the ulcer edge from the left mandibular angle revealed perivascular and periadnexal lymphoid infiltrates, vacuolar interface dermatitis, and basement membrane zone thickening (figure D). Direct immunofluorescence was negative for IgA, IgG, IgM, C1q, and C3. Ziehl–Neelsen staining was negative for acid-fast bacillus, and there was no evidence of malignancy. Serology for antinuclear antibody (Hep-2 cell by indirect immunofluorescence assay) was negative; although, an immunoblot was strongly positive for anti-MDA5. A diagnosis of anti-MDA5 amyopathic dermatomyositis was made.
Treatment with a combination of oral prednisolone (30 mg per day for 2 weeks, tapered over 2 months), mycophenolate mofetil (2 g per day), and topical tacrolimus healed his facial ulcers completely and dramatically reduced facial erythema, oral ulcers, heliotrope rash, and Gottron's papules over 7 months (figure E–F). The patient was followed up initially on a monthly basis for 3 months and then once every 3 months subsequently. Residual post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation was noted at 1 year after starting mycophenolate mofetil and prednisolone (figure E–F). The patient also remained hypertensive during the first 2 months of treatment, which was managed and controlled with lifestyle modifications alone. The patient has been under follow-up for 18 months with no additional symptoms, and continues to be treated with mycophenolate mofetil.
Anti-MDA5, a myositis-specific antibody, is typically associated with ulcers on the digits and extensor surfaces and facial ulcerations have not been reported previously. Progressive facial ulcers without accompanying myositis make for a diagnostic challenge.

The patient had previously consulted a private practitioner for malar and heliotrope rash with photosensitivity and periorbital puffiness, who prescribed him methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine. However, the lesions progressed with ulceration over bilateral malar areas and the left mandibular angle (figure B–C), associated with non-scarring alopecia, oral ulcers, and violaceous papules on the dorsal aspect of metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints (Gottron's papules). There were no other comorbidities. On examination, the patient's blood pressure was 146/96 mm Hg and he had facial ulcers, as described (figure B–C). Investigations revealed he had mild elevation of alanine aminotransferase and gamma-glutamyl transferase, both elevated up to 2 × the upper limit of normal.
Based on the patient's history and symptoms, a number of differential diagnoses were considered, including dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus, lupus vulgaris (tuberculosis), granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and sarcoidosis. Buruli ulcer, which might also have a similar presentation, has yet to be reported in India. He had no clinical, radiological, or laboratory evidence of myositis, interstitial lung disease, neuropathy, nephritis, or arthritis. Serum creatine kinase, nerve conduction study results, and urine analysis were within normal limits and a high-resolution chest CT showed no abnormalities. Histopathological examination of a skin biopsy sample from the ulcer edge from the left mandibular angle revealed perivascular and periadnexal lymphoid infiltrates, vacuolar interface dermatitis, and basement membrane zone thickening (figure D). Direct immunofluorescence was negative for IgA, IgG, IgM, C1q, and C3. Ziehl–Neelsen staining was negative for acid-fast bacillus, and there was no evidence of malignancy. Serology for antinuclear antibody (Hep-2 cell by indirect immunofluorescence assay) was negative; although, an immunoblot was strongly positive for anti-MDA5. A diagnosis of anti-MDA5 amyopathic dermatomyositis was made.
Treatment with a combination of oral prednisolone (30 mg per day for 2 weeks, tapered over 2 months), mycophenolate mofetil (2 g per day), and topical tacrolimus healed his facial ulcers completely and dramatically reduced facial erythema, oral ulcers, heliotrope rash, and Gottron's papules over 7 months (figure E–F). The patient was followed up initially on a monthly basis for 3 months and then once every 3 months subsequently. Residual post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation was noted at 1 year after starting mycophenolate mofetil and prednisolone (figure E–F). The patient also remained hypertensive during the first 2 months of treatment, which was managed and controlled with lifestyle modifications alone. The patient has been under follow-up for 18 months with no additional symptoms, and continues to be treated with mycophenolate mofetil.
Anti-MDA5, a myositis-specific antibody, is typically associated with ulcers on the digits and extensor surfaces and facial ulcerations have not been reported previously. Progressive facial ulcers without accompanying myositis make for a diagnostic challenge.

A 12-year-old boy with a 3-week history of abdominal pain, was referred to our emergency room. The patient had been diagnosed with acute pancreatitis at another hospital before he came to see us. Notably after treatment, he went into remission, but relapsed after he started eating again, prompting the referral to our department.
On examination he was generally well but in pain; pulse rate 90 beats per min, blood pressure 97/64 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 99%. He had marfanoid habitus: height 167 cm and arm length 172 cm, with long thin fingers (figure). The patient had a history of lens dislocation and had intraocular lens implantation. He also had a history of poor academic performance.Laboratory investigations showed serum amylase concentration of 98 U/L (normal range 40–132) and serum lipase concentration of 143 U/L (normal range 0–60). Liver function tests and blood triglyceride concentrations were within normal range. An abdominal CT showed signs indicative of pancreatitis and intestinal wall oedema (figure).
We put the patient in a fasting state (nil by mouth); he was given intravenous fluid therapy, antibiotics, omeprazole, and somatostatin.
An MRI, done after admission, showed multiple cystic lesions of the pancreas—possibly encapsulated necrosis—and a small amount of ascites. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography showed that the common bile duct was slightly wider locally, and the pancreatic duct was segmentary. After a radiology and surgical consultation, we decided there was no indication for either angiography or endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography—although we concluded the decision could be re-visited at any time, if necessary.
Importantly, the patient reported that his abdominal pain had reduced; the amylase concentration had decreased to 91 U/L and the lipase concentration had decreased to 91 U/L. Enteral nutrition, through a nasal jejunal feeding tube—with low-fat semi-fluid—was started.
Two days later, the patient said that the abdominal pain had gradually increased again; the amylase concentration was 324 U/L and the lipase concentration was 337 U/L, D-dimer concentration was greater than 20 mg/L (typical range 0–0·5), and fibrinogen degradation products concentration was 88 ug/mL (typical range 0–5). We re-commenced treatment, again based on a diagnosis of pancreatitis, with the addition of anticoagulant therapy. During the admission, an ophthalmologist examined the patient, and he was again found to be short-sighted and to have relaxed suspensory ligaments in his eye.
Combining the patient's case in the round, we suspected for hyperhomocysteinemia, which was confirmed by a raised total homocysteine (tHcy) concentration of 351 μmol/L (typical level ≤15) and a raised methionine concentration of 220 μmol/L (typical range 10–80). After consultation with paediatric endocrinology colleagues, we prescribed the patient vitamin B6 and oral betaine; folic acid and vitamin B12 were also prescribed because levels were also found to be low. One week later, the tHcy concentration had decreased to 137 μmol/L.
Whole exon sequencing showed a mutation of the cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS) gene (c.719 T>C, c.1126 G>A). As the patient made only a partial response to vitamin B6 treatment, the doses of vitamin B6 and betaine were increased; a protein-restricted diet was commenced because the level of tHcy was still high. The patient's condition improved, and he was allowed home after 100 days in hospital. A regimen of oral vitamin B6, betaine, folic acid, and vitamin B12 was continued, along with a protein-restricted diet; because the child had significant weight loss, he was also given a diet supplemented with methionine-free formula milk to supplement nutrition.
At regular follow-up appointments, the concentration of tHcy remained between 100–110 μmol/L. An abdominal CT showed no inflammation of the pancreas or intestine.
Acute pancreatitis—commonly caused by gallstones and alcohol abuse—has been reported in cases of hyperhomocysteinemia. Clinical features of hyperhomocysteinemia caused by cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency include dislocation of the optic lenses, osteoporosis, a marfanoid habitus, learning difficulties, and a predisposition to thromboembolism.
output: Homocystinuria due to cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency

Our 17-year-old male patient, with a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vEDS), presented to the UK Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome National Diagnostic Service for specialist advice and support, following the sudden death of his brother, who was also affected by vEDS. The patient and his brother were heterozygous for the familial COL3A1 (c.547G>A p.[Gly183Ser]) variant, identified following predictive testing in childhood. Despite having a molecular diagnosis in childhood (done locally), the patient only presented to our specialist service after the death of his brother.
Our patient had easy bruising and translucent skin with prominent superficial veins, particularly around the chest and forehead, and subtle facial features consistent with vEDS (figure). He had an initial left, then subsequent right, recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax requiring pleurodesis (figure). He is now receiving magnetic resonance angiography screening locally and has recently commenced losartan, in order to reduce vascular events.
His brother's medical history comprised an intra-abdominal bleed following a fall from a skateboard, (managed conservatively), and bypass surgery for a ruptured right subclavian artery aneurysm at age 19 years (figure). At age 20 years, he presented to hospital with loss of sensation in the right arm and severe, acute-onset chest pain. He deteriorated quickly and went into cardiac arrest, with no response to resuscitation efforts. Post-mortem examination confirmed the cause of death was aortic dissection. Magnetic resonance angiography screening was planned following his initial vascular event, but did not occur before death. He was not on medical therapy.
This diagnosis was first identified in the father of our patient, who suffered an intestinal arterial rupture at age 16 years, had previous joint dislocations (thumb and shoulder), and early-onset varicose veins (figure), which prompted the genetic testing in the two children when they were young to screen for vEDS. He was also referred to our specialist service following the death of his son. He had also been managed elsewhere (locally), but was not on treatment.
vEDS is a rare type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and accounts for less than 5% of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome diagnoses, with an estimated prevalence of between 1 in 50 000 to 1 in 200 000. This autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder is characterised by fragile connective tissues due to altered type III collagen. Potentially fatal consequences include blood vessel dissection and rupture, tension pneumothorax, and hollow organ rupture (primarily sigmoid colon). Musculoskeletal manifestations, in addition to those described in this family, can include small-joint hypermobility and distal contractures (including talipes).
In an emergency, the diagnosis of vEDS must be considered to guide medical care or intervention due to increased tissue fragility and the risk of bleeding. Longitudinal management comprises regular vascular screening, although vessel dissection can occur spontaneously. β blockers, angiotensin II receptor blockers, and lifestyle modifications have been shown to reduce vascular events. Multidisciplinary involvement is recommended for planned procedures.

The patient, who had been born at 39 weeks of gestation, also had feeding difficulties, nasal obstruction, and a reduced ability to open her mouth; she had developed progressive macrocephaly in the first few months of life (appendix).

Additionally, the patient had mixed hearing loss due to blockage of the ossicular chain with ossification of the petrous bone and cochlear nerve compression. She did not pronounce words and could only make hissing sounds.

After HSCT, we observed a halt in disease progression and a significant improvement in the patient's condition; no additional procedures or surgical interventions were required.
Imaging showed a significant reduction in hyperostosis and no novel bone thickening (figure 2), and slowing down of macrocephaly progression (figure 3). Furthermore, the patient's neurosensory status remained stable; her respiration improved significantly, and nocturnal polysomnography was normal. No progression of the optic nerve atrophy or the facial nerve paralysis, as evidenced by normal electromyography, occurred.At the last clinical assessment, 5 years and 6 months post HSCT, the patient aged 8 years and 8 months had neither abnormal fractures, arthropathies, bone pain, nor headaches—the common features of autosomal dominant CMD. She had acquired speech and was attending school; her parents described an overall significant improvement in her quality of life.
Autosomal dominant CMD is a rare skeletal disorder characterised by progressive thickening of craniofacial bones leading to dysmorphic features and severe visual and hearing impairment due to compression of cranial nerves.
To date, medical management had been limited to symptomatic measures—including invasive decompressive surgeries of obstructed cranial foramina to relieve symptoms. Additionally, as osteoblasts, unlike osteoclasts, are not derived from the haematopoietic stem cell, it was unclear whether allogeneic HSCT could restore the bone phenotype (appendix).
However, it has been suggested that as ANK protein plays a regulatory role in bone formation and resorption, it may directly affect osteoblast and osteoclast differentiation and function. Furthermore, experimental bone marrow transplantation has been shown to reduce hyperossification in homozygous Ank knockin mice with a CMD phenotype, implying that allogeneic HSCT may also be beneficial in human autosomal dominant CMD; our results are proof of concept that allogeneic HSCT may mitigate osteocondensation, thereby preserving neurosensory function and improving quality of life. Prompt diagnosis and management—before onset of skull hyperostosis and cranial nerve compression—may further improve outcomes.

A 51-year-old woman presented to our department with a 5-year history of a loud clicking sound in her left ear. The patient said that the clicking was persistent and distressing; it disappeared during eating and talking, and she could suppress it at will for a few minutes.On examination, we found no abnormalities of the cranial nerves; eye examination was normal with no exophthalmos or conjunctival congestion. She had no involuntary movements of her mouth, face, jaw, or tongue. Fundoscopy was normal.
Laboratory investigations found no abnormalities. Otorhinolaryngological studies and tympanometry also showed no abnormalities.
However, we did find a constant, semirhythmic movement of the patient's soft palate—which had not been noticed previously—that disappeared when the patient was distracted by asking her to clap her hands (figure; video).
MRI showed no abnormalities, and we made a diagnosis of isolated palatal myoclonus—also known as essential palatal tremor or myoclonus. We treated her with 3 mg of clonazepam orally per day and her symptoms partially improved over the next 2 months.
Palatal myoclonus is an uncommon clinical finding characterised by a rhythmic contraction of the palatal muscles—including the levator veli palatini and the tensor palatini muscles. The contractions lead to the rapid opening and shutting of the Eustachian tube, which produces a clicking tinnitus that is usually audible to the examiner. Secondary or symptomatic palatal tremor is caused by lesions involving the connections between the ipsilateral red nucleus in the midbrain, the inferior olive in the medulla, and the contralateral dentate nucleus in the cerebellum—the three nuclei together being referred to as the Guillain–Mollaret triangle forming the dentato-rubro-olivary pathway (figure). In approximately 70% of cases the lesion is a vascular infarct; other causes include glial fibrillary acidic protein or mitochondrial DNA polymerase γ mutations, neuroferritinopathy, or progressive ataxia and palatal tremor.
Patients with no apparent structural lesions are considered to have isolated palatal tremor. Notably, the tensor veli palatini—innervated by the trigeminal nerve—is mostly involved in cases of isolated palatal tremor, whereas in symptomatic or secondary palatal tremor it is the levator veli palatini muscle—innervated mainly by the vagus nerve—that is affected.
Some cases of isolated palatal tremor may be considered as functional neurological disorders. Some patients report being able to suppress the clicking sound either at will or while being distracted, suggesting a functional origin.
Palatal tremor should be distinguished from middle ear myoclonus—another form of objective tinnitus. In middle ear myoclonus, the sound of the tinnitus is reported to be a buzzing rather than a clicking, and movement of the tympanic membrane rather than the palate is seen on otoscopy.
Treatment options are limited, but phenytoin, carbamazepine, clonazepam, sumatriptan, and botulinum toxin have been found to be useful in some patients.

Secondary or symptomatic palatal tremor is caused by lesions involving the connections between the ipsilateral red nucleus in the midbrain, the inferior olive in the medulla, and the contralateral dentate nucleus in the cerebellum—the three nuclei together being referred to as the Guillain–Mollaret triangle forming the dentato-rubro-olivary pathway (figure). In approximately 70% of cases the lesion is a vascular infarct; other causes include glial fibrillary acidic protein or mitochondrial DNA polymerase γ mutations, neuroferritinopathy, or progressive ataxia and palatal tremor.
Patients with no apparent structural lesions are considered to have isolated palatal tremor. Notably, the tensor veli palatini—innervated by the trigeminal nerve—is mostly involved in cases of isolated palatal tremor, whereas in symptomatic or secondary palatal tremor it is the levator veli palatini muscle—innervated mainly by the vagus nerve—that is affected.
Some cases of isolated palatal tremor may be considered as functional neurological disorders. Some patients report being able to suppress the clicking sound either at will or while being distracted, suggesting a functional origin.
Palatal tremor should be distinguished from middle ear myoclonus—another form of objective tinnitus. In middle ear myoclonus, the sound of the tinnitus is reported to be a buzzing rather than a clicking, and movement of the tympanic membrane rather than the palate is seen on otoscopy.
Treatment options are limited, but phenytoin, carbamazepine, clonazepam, sumatriptan, and botulinum toxin have been found to be useful in some patients.

A 44-year-old man attended our hospital reporting reduced vision in his left eye. 10 days earlier he had been started on treatment with supplemental oxygen, intravenous antibiotics, and corticosteroids because of a moderately severe pneumonia caused by SARS-CoV-2. The patient explained that a blackish patch—extending from just below his left eye to the left side of his face to the level of his mouth—had also developed 2 days earlier (figure).The patient was a known diabetic; he had no history of malignancy.
On examination his temperature was 37°C, pulse was 84 beats per min, blood pressure was 118/82 mm Hg, and respiratory rate was 16 breaths per min; pulse oximetry showed an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. The patient had exophthalmos, ophthalmoplegia, and chemosis of his left eye. Best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in his right eye, but he reported no perception of light in his left eye.
Laboratory investigations showed a random blood sugar concentration of 298 mg/dL (normal 140 or below), glycated haemoglobin A1c of 9·8% (normal 4–5·6), arterial blood pH 7·4 (normal 7·35–7·45), serum bicarbonate concentration 24 mEq/L (normal 23–30), and a mild neutropenia (1510 neutrophils per μL; normal 1800–6300).
Examination of a potassium hydroxide mount of nasal scrapings showed broad, pauci-septate hyphae; and Sabouraud dextrose agar culture and lactophenol cotton blue mount were suggestive of Rhizopus arrhizus (figure).
Contrast-enhanced MRI showed non-enhancement of the bilateral middle and inferior turbinate: the characteristic so-called black turbinate sign (figure). Contiguous extension of non-enhancing soft tissue into the left middle and ethmoidal air cells, with a breach in the cribriform plate to involve the basal frontal region was noted (figure). T2-hyperintense diffuse inflammatory changes were seen in the soft tissues of the left orbital region—involving the pre-septal, post-septal, and intraconal and extraconal compartments with orbital fat stranding (figure). Heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue inflammatory changes were noted on the left side of the face involving the premaxillary region, buccal fat pad, and infra-temporal fossa (figure). Together—the clinical picture and the radiological findings—indicated mucormycosis.
The patient was started on intravenous liposomal amphotericin B at a dose of 5 mg/kg per day; an insulin infusion was also continued because of persistent hyperglycaemia. Extensive debridement, a left total maxillectomy, and orbital exenteration were done under a general anaesthetic; however, the patient died 6 days later.
During the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic in India, an unprecedented surge in cases of mucormycosis was observed: immune dysregulation caused by the SARS-CoV-2 and the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics and corticosteroids—particularly in patients with poorly controlled diabetes with ketoacidosis—is likely to have contributed to the rise.
COVID-19 followed by mucormycosis carries a very high mortality rate and timely detection, antifungal therapy, and aggressive surgical debridement remain key factors in the management (video).
output: Triazole—fluconazole, voriconazole, and itraconazole—class of anti-fungal agents is the drug of choice for primary treatment of mucormycosis.

input: A 68-year-old woman living in Japan presented to the clinic with a 5-day history of fevers, myalgias, and petechial rash spreading on her arms, trunk, palms, and soles. On exam, there was also an eschar on the right medial ankle. Laboratory studies showed thrombocytopenia, elevated inflammatory markers, and elevated liver transaminases. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
output:
Doxycycline

The clinical presentation is consistent with **Japanese spotted fever** (or scrub typhus), a rickettsial infection:

**Key findings:**
- Fever, myalgias
- Petechial rash involving palms and soles
- Eschar (inoculation site from tick/mite bite)
- Thrombocytopenia
- Elevated liver transaminases
- Geographic location (Japan)

**The characteristic triad of rickettsial infections:**
1. Fever
2. Rash (often petechial, involving palms/soles)
3. Eschar at bite site

**Treatment:** Doxycycline is the first-line antibiotic for all rickettsial infections, including:
- Rocky Mountain spotted fever
- Japanese spotted fever
- Scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi)
- Mediterranean spotted fever

Treatment should be initiated empirically based on clinical suspicion without waiting for confirmatory testing, as delay can lead to severe complications.

A 64-year-old man hospitalised for observation after treatment with chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cells targeting the B-cell maturation antigen reported a 4-day history of indentations developing over the top of his head; he had not been involved in any recent trauma and he did not have any pain (figure).The patient had a history of refractory high-risk κ light chain multiple myeloma with known bone plasmacytomas in his skull and spine: 5 years ago, he was diagnosed with multiple myeloma, presenting with back pain. Imaging had shown compression fractures of T4, L3, and L5. Laboratory investigations had shown hypercalcaemia (14·4 mg/dL; normal range 8·8–10·2) and renal failure (serum creatinine concentration 2·04 mg/dL; normal range 0·74–1·35). A urine protein electrophoresis showed 623 mg per 24 h of urine with a monoclonal band (M-spike); serum free light chain ratio was greater than 1000 (normal range 0·26–1·65), and his baseline bone marrow biopsy showed 55% involvement by κ light chain restricted plasma cells with the presence of t(11;14) seen by fluorescent in-situ hybridisation. Since the initial presentation, the patient had received more than 4 lines of systemic therapy, which included a failed autologous stem-cell transplantation. We therefore felt he was a good candidate for autologous CAR T-cells.
On examination, we found the patient to be well; his vital signs were within normal limits. Over his calvarium, we found 2 depressions—one on the left frontal skull and the other on the right parietal skull—each approximately 20 mm × 30 mm. They were soft and non-pulsatile. While monitoring the depressions, we noticed that his myeloma-related laboratory tests improved.
A CT scan of the patient's head showed 2 lesions over the calvarium (figure), corresponding to the lesions previously noted at the time he was diagnosed with multiple myeloma. No intracranial extension, mass effect, or midline shift were seen; no new or enlarging lytic lesions had developed.
At follow-up 4 months post CAR T-cells, the patient reported continued improvement of his calvarium lesions with connective tissue. We plan to continue to monitor the patient periodically, hoping for additional clinical and radiographic improvement. Laboratory investigations have shown improvement of serological markers—including normal creatinine and calcium concentrations.
We believe that the soft tissue and bony component of the multiple myeloma lesions had reduced in size due to effective treatment of the myeloma, as the skull indentations developed shortly after the CAR T-cells were infused, which correlated with serological evidence of improvement in the myeloma markers.
As multiple myeloma is known to have a predilection to affect bone structures and novel cellular therapies are becoming more available, clinicians need to be aware of the potential effect of CAR T-cells in patients with skeletal involvement, as abnormalities may represent response to therapy instead of progression of disease.
output: Resolving skull plasmacytomas following CAR T-cell therapy

Tinea capitis (ringworm of the scalp)

1. The annular morphology with raised papular/pustular borders
2. Central hyperkeratotic/scaly areas
3. Mother with similar lesions (indicating person-to-person transmission)
4. Location on the scalp of a neonate

This presentation is consistent with **Tinea capitis** caused by dermatophyte infection, likely transmitted from the mother who has tinea corporis. This is particularly common with anthropophilic dermatophytes such as *Trichophyton tonsurans* or *Microsporum audouinii*, which are more prevalent in certain populations including those from African regions.

A 61-year-old woman with a 4-day history of asthenia, fever, and a rash was seen by our team in the hospital intensive care unit.
The patient had clear cell renal cell carcinoma with tumoral thrombosis of the right renal vein and inferior vena cava. She was being treated with a checkpoint inhibitor, pembrolizumab—a PD-1 inhibitor—and the endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGF-R) tyrosine kinase inhibitor, axitinib, before re-assessment for surgery, in the oncology day hospital unit. 3 days after the third infusion of pembrolizumab, the patient had been admitted to the intensive care unit because she had become haemodynamically unstable; she had developed heart failure, and purpura fulminans (figure; appendix) over her arms and legs, which had initially appeared as livedo racemose a few hours before. She had also been found to have an ascending sensory motor deficit of her lower limbs.
On examination, we found the patient to be unwell; her blood pressure was 90/60 mm Hg, pulse 30 beats per min, oxygen saturation was 100% on 15 L/min oxygen, and temperature was 32°C. She was confused, with a Glasgow Coma Score of 8 (eye opening response 2, verbal response 2, and motor response 4). She needed both noradrenaline and dobutamine because of her cardiac failure. Additionally, the patient was being treated with meropenem and amikacin; axitinib had been stopped at the point of admission to the intensive care unit.
Laboratory investigations showed high concentrations of N-terminal-pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (10 518 pg/mL; typical level <125 in people younger than 75 years) and troponin (109 ng/L; typical level <14). Concentrations of liver enzymes and thyroid-stimulating hormone were elevated; C-reactive protein concentration was 36 mg/L (typical range 8–10). Analysis of a sample of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed an elevated protein concentration (0·52 g/L; typical level <0·4) and a normal white blood cell count; cultures of blood, CSF, urine, and skin showed no abnormalities.
PCR skin swab testing was negative for Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae, resulting in the cessation of antibiotics treatment.
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed diffuse thickening of the wall of the colon; echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 25% (normal range 50–70). MRIs of brain and spinal cord showed no abnormalities. An electromyogram showed severe sensory-motor neurogenic damage compatible with axonal length-dependent processes without demyelination.
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a skin biopsy showed thrombosis with leukocytoclastic vasculitis, which, considering the patient's presentation, investigations, and history in the round, led us to conclude she had developed an immune-induced myocarditis, acute motor and sensory axonal polyneuropathy, colitis, hypothyroidism, hepatitis, and purpura fulminans.
The patient was commenced on pulse methylprednisolone (1 g per day for 5 days) and intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g per kg over 4 days), which resulted in the improvement of her general condition. She had three separate plasma exchanges to clear the pembrolizumab and surgery of the deepest wounds with skin grafts.
The corticosteroids were gradually tapered down over the next 4 months, and at follow-up 6 months later the skin lesions had completely healed. The patient's neoplastic disease was under control—despite discontinuation of the pembrolizumab and axitinib.
Immune checkpoint inhibitors have become established treatments for several cancers including malignant melanoma and renal cell carcinoma. Such developments have, in some patients resulted, in treatment-related adverse effects of variable severity. Immune-related purpura fulminans associated with pembrolizumab has been reported previously in a patient treated for lung carcinoma.

A 2-year-old boy presented to our unit with swelling of the left side of his face and mouth. He had been investigated before we saw him, and imaging was consistent with recurrence of a giant cell tumour in the left maxilla. 2 months earlier, the patient had a subtotal resection of the mass; he had initially presented aged 1 year and 11 months with a painless swelling of the left side of his mouth. On examination the patient was generally well; he had a 2 cm × 2 cm reddish purple bulging lesion on the left palate.A CT scan, with contrast, of the maxillofacial region showed that the tumour had invaded the left nasal cavity, maxillary and ethmoid sinuses, and raised the floor of the left orbit.
We started the patient on high-dose denosumab— 1·7 mg/kg given subcutaneously every 4 weeks—which was continued after he had been allowed home. The size of the tumour reduced substantially.
After 7 months of treatment, the boy developed pain in his left knee; an x-ray showed dense sclerosis about the distal femoral, proximal tibial, and fibular metaphyses along with two atypical stress fractures (figure). An x-ray of his left hand showed diffuse sclerosis with an asymptomatic atypical stress fracture of the metaphysis of the distal ulna (figure).
Because of propitious response seen on the tumour by the treatment, together with the observed metaphyseal sclerosis and concern for atypical stress fractures, we decided to stop the denosumab and do a further surgical resection of the lesion.
Follow-up will involve the patient being seen every 3 months with serial imaging to monitor for tumour recurrence.
Giant cell tumours are rare benign primary bone neoplasms composed of neoplastic primitive mesenchymal stromal cells that overexpress receptor activator of nuclear factor-kappa β ligand (RANKL) which promotes formation of osteoclast-like giant cells that create osteolytic lesions. Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL that suppresses osteoclastogenesis and inhibits bone resorption. In neoplastic disorders such as giant cell tumours of bone, denosumab may also promote osteoblastic differentiation resulting in mineralisation of the lesion. Sclerotic bands are a manifestation of antiresorptive therapy in children before closure of the epiphyseal growth plates, and result from disruption in osteoclastic resorption of growth plate cartilage. The extent of sclerosis varies depending on the patient's age, growth rate, and antiresorptive regimen. Denosumab has potent anti-osteoclastic effects, and oncologic doses may result in bone turnover suppression—particularly in young children with rapid skeletal growth—which may result in stress fractures, as seen in our patient. Children treated with denosumab should undergo clinical monitoring for potential adverse metaphyseal effects. Radiographic assessment may be helpful in evaluating metaphyseal changes and should be done in any patient presenting with bone pain (video).
output: Denosumab-induced metaphyseal sclerosis with atypical stress fractures

A 17-year-old boy came to our hospital with a wound infection 5 days after urological surgery. CT scan done to assess the depth of the infection showed multiple well circumscribed, ovoid, radiodense bony lesions in the pelvis and proximal femurs, consistent with the diagnosis of osteopoikilosis. Osteopoikilosis or “spotted bone disease” is a rare, benign, autosomal dominant disorder characterised by sclerotic bone lesions most commonly involving the hands, feet, pelvis, and ends of long bones.1,2 Lesions are typically found incidentally on imaging studies done for unrelated complaints.3 The symmetric distribution, lack of bone destruction, and location differentiates osteopoikilosis from metastatic disease, which tends to be seen more often in ribs, vertebral bodies, and the diaphysis of long bones.4 Bone scintigraphy is normal in patients with osteopoikilosis.2,4 Early recognition is essential to prevent unnecessary emotional distress and invasive testing.3 No routine follow-up or studies are necessary.

output:
Based on the clinical history of a 66-year-old man with shortness of breath, leg swelling, weight loss, and the gross pathological finding of multiple dark-red, hemorrhagic nodules infiltrating the pericardium and myocardium, the diagnosis is a primary malignant vascular tumor of the heart. A 68-year-old woman with a 20-day history of exertional dyspnoea, acrocyanosis, and critical ischaemia—dry gangrene—of her fingers, presented to our rheumatology clinic (figure); she also reported the recent onset of pain in the small joints of her hands and wrists, Raynaud's phenomenon in her fingers and toes, and a feeling of general fatigue. The patient, a farmer, had been unable to carry out her daily tasks for the past 1 month. She had a medical history of well controlled hypertension treated with nebivolol; she had never smoked cigarettes.
On examination, the patient was distressed and tachypnoeic; pulse was 75 beats per min, blood pressure was 125/75 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 92% on 21% fraction of inspired oxygen; respiratory rate was 25 breaths per min. Her temperature was 36·0°C. Inspiratory crackles were heard on auscultation of the chest; neurological examination showed no abnormalities and proximal muscle strength of her arms and legs was within typical limits.
Laboratory investigations found antinuclear antibodies were positive with a 1:160 titre (normal range <1:80) in a speckled pattern. Anti-Jo-1 antibodies were positive and anti-Ro52 antibodies were strongly positive (range from negative to borderline to positive, and strongly positive) identified through immunoblotting. Anti-phospholipid antibodies were negative. Acute phase proteins were increased—including concentration of C-reactive protein, which was 1·7 mg/dL (normal level <0·3).
Chest CT showed a fibrotic non-specific interstitial pneumonia pattern (figure). Additionally, ulnar artery pulses were clinically absent with severely diminished blood flow observed during doppler ultrasound; CT angiography showed occlusion of the ulnar arteries bilaterally.
Considering the patient's presentation and laboratory findings, we diagnosed rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease due to antisynthetase syndrome complicated by critical ischaemia in her fingers. She was treated with three doses of pulse methylprednisolone (500 mg) followed by high dose intravenous prednisolone (1 mg/kg) and rituximab (2 × 1 g intravenous infusions, each separated by 15 days). The patient was also anticoagulated with subcutaneous enoxaparin 8000 IU/0·8 mL twice daily and aspirin 100 mg daily; intravenous iloprost—as a vasodilator—to counteract the ischaemia and to aid reperfusion was started.
The patient's condition stabilised with no further deterioration of the ischaemia in her fingers or her pulmonary function, and she was allowed home 42 days after her initial presentation. She was prescribed supplemental oxygen to use at home at a flow rate of 2 L/min.
At her last follow-up, 3 months after her initial presentation, the patient reported some progression of the digital ischaemia with gangrene up to the distal interphalangeal joints; her lung function had not changed, and a follow-up vascular ultrasound showed improved blood blow of the previously diminished pulses. The patient reported no fatigue but nevertheless still required home oxygen therapy.
Antisynthetase syndrome is one of a group of immune-mediated idiopathic inflammatory myopathies which primarily affect skeletal muscle but may also involve other organs such as the lungs, skin, and joints—as in our patient. Multimodality immunosuppressive therapy may be required to control both the muscle and pulmonary manifestations of the disease; more recently CAR T-cell treatment has been used. Early diagnosis and appropriate treatment improve outcomes.
output: Antisynthetase syndrome with rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease and digital ischemia

A 46-year-old woman attended our emergency department reporting a 3-month history of dyspnoea and, in the last 2 weeks, lower limb oedema. The patient had a history of rheumatoid arthritis, which had been diagnosed 13 years before, and had been treated with oral hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice a day. 1 year earlier, she had presented with syncope; an electrocardiogram (ECG) had showed paroxysmal third-degree atrioventricular block, and a dual-chamber pacemaker had been fitted. An echocardiogram had shown normal biventricular systolic function and mild to moderate left ventricular hypertrophy with an interventricular septum diameter of 13 mm (normal range 6–9); no further investigations were done.
On examination, at our hospital, the patient was generally unwell; her blood pressure was 80/40 mm Hg, she had peripheral oedema, jugular venous distension, pulmonary crackles, and cold extremities. An ECG showed atrial fibrillation with ventricular pacing at 69 beats per min (appendix). Laboratory tests showed a significantly raised N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide concentration of 31 255 ng/L (normal range 0–86) and high-sensitivity cardiac troponin concentration of 543 ng/L (normal range 0–14); and signs of hepatic injury with alanine aminotransferase concentration of 126 U/L (normal range 3–45), aspartate aminotransferase concentration of 92 U/L (normal range 0–40), total bilirubin concentration of 2·51 mg/dL (normal range 0·25–1). Echocardiography showed severe biventricular systolic dysfunction—left ventricular ejection fraction of 20%—and a restrictive filling pattern. Severe concentric hypertrophy was evident with an interventricular septum diameter of 17 mm and heterogeneous myocardial texture (figure).
The differential diagnoses we considered included inflammatory and infiltrative cardiomyopathies—specifically reactive systemic (AA) amyloidosis related to the long-lasting autoimmune disorder—or a hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy.
Inotropic support was immediately started, the hydroxychloroquine was discontinued, and the patient was admitted to our intensive care unit. Despite all these measures, 3 days after admission, the patient developed cardiogenic shock and required haemodynamic support with venous-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.
An endomyocardial biopsy was done with the patient on temporary mechanical support; we hoped the results would inform ongoing treatment. Histopathological examination of a sample obtained at biopsy showed vacuolisation of multiple cardiomyocytes with no inflammatory infiltrate; no amyloid was found (figure). Transmission electron microscopy showed lamellar lysosomal structures—myeloid bodies—and curvilinear inclusions consistent with drug-induced myocardial toxicity. Considering these classic findings, a diagnosis of hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy was made.
8 days after admission, despite maximal pharmacological and mechanical support, the patient died due to refractory cardiogenic shock while heart transplantation screening was ongoing. The results of metabolic testing, available after the patient's death, showed no evidence of lysosomal storage disorders—including Fabry's disease and mucopolysaccharidoses. Additionally, the heart post-mortem showed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy: septal thickness 16 mm (normal value 13·6 mm [SD 2·0 mm]) and an increased thickness of the right ventricle free wall of 8 mm (normal value 3·8 mm [SD 0·9 mm]). The cardiac mass was also increased (weight 500 g; typical range 190–360; figure).
Chronic use of hydroxychloroquine can result in a drug-induced cardiomyopathy characterised by concentric hypertrophy and conduction abnormalities. Early clinical suspicion is essential, since the condition is potentially reversible. Delay in discontinuation of the drug may not improve the pathology, especially in patients—as in this case—with advanced heart failure.

A 37-year-old man attended our hospital with a 1-week history of fever, chills, headaches, sore throat, generalised malaise, and a rash on his arms, legs, trunk, and in his groin. The patient also reported significant pain and discomfort in his rectum when defecating. He had a history of HIV and metastatic Kaposi sarcoma; secondary syphilis, which had been treated; and hypertension. He was prescribed the following medications: emtricitabine-tenofovir, doravarine, darunavir-cobicistat, and hydrochlorothiazide.The patient reported no recent travel or contact with human or animal with a similar rash or illnesses. He reported no history of varicella zoster virus infection as a child and said he had received all childhood vaccinations. The patient reported no sexual activity for the past 6 months.
On examination, the patient was afebrile: temperature 37·3°C. He appeared uncomfortable and had several scattered, pink, umbilicated papules, vesicles, and pustules on the trunk, upper and lower extremities, groin, and peri-anal region (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 12·7 g/dL (normal 13·3–16·3), CD4+ T-helper cell count of 262 cells per mcL (normal 490–1740), HIV-1 RNA PCR less than 20 copies per mL, and an absolute lymphocyte count of 3·01 per uL (normal 1·1–2·7). Serology was negative for Bartonella henselae, Aspergillus spp, hepatitis A, B, and C, cryptococcal antigen, herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), and (1→3)-β-D-glucan.
Immunohistochemical analysis of a biopsy sample of one of the truncal papules was negative for HSV-1, HSV-2, and Treponema pallidum. Warthin-Starry staining was negative for spirochetes and periodic-acid-Schiff staining was negative for fungal organisms. Histopathological analysis of the biopsy sample showed focal epidermal necrosis with underlying acute inflammation in the superficial dermis and individually necrotic keratinocytes at the periphery. A Dacron swab of one of the truncal lesions was positive for human monkeypox virus.
Considering our patient's history of immunosuppression, we prescribed doxycycline, ceftriaxone, and valacyclovir; we subsequently gave him a 2-week course of 600 mg of tecovirimat twice a day. He reported no significant adverse effects and the skin lesions healed rapidly. At follow-up one month later, the patient reported areas of hyperpigmentation at the sites of the healed lesions and said he was doing well.
Monkeypox is caused by the monkeypox virus, a member of the Poxviridae family and Orthopoxvirus genus. The virus is transmitted via large respiratory droplets, direct or indirect contact with bodily fluids or lesion material, or contact with fomites—including bedding or towels. Malaise, lymphadenopathy, headache, myalgia, and cutaneous symptoms can occur within 1–3 days of the onset of fever. Lesions may initially appear as macules progressing to papules, vesicles, and pustules that dry up and fall off. The development of skin lesions, in addition to viral prodromal symptoms, in immunocompromised patients should raise the possibility of other diagnosis, such as primary or secondary infection with varicella zoster virus or other organisms such as Cryptococcus neoformans, Histoplasma capsulatum, or Bartonella henselae; we considered this unlikely in our patient given his presentation. Molluscum contagiosum also presents with umbilicated papules, but usually without systemic symptoms. Notably, proctitis has recently been recognised as being associated with a human monkeypox infection. Tecovirimat is approved for treating human smallpox disease. Treatment in cases of human monkeypox should be considered in severe cases, immunocompromised patients, paediatric populations, pregnant or breastfeeding women, and people with concurrent disease or other comorbidities.

input: A 32-year-old man presented with a 6-week history of tingling in his arms and legs and a 2-week history of inability to walk. A positive Romberg test, sensory ataxia, impaired proprioception and vibratory sensation, and preserved nociception were noted. Magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine showed hyperintensity in the posterior spinal cord from C1 to T12 and hyperintense lesions in the dorsal column on T2-weighted images. A vitamin B12 level was 107 pg per ml (reference value, >231) without macrocytic anemia. Toxicity of which of the following is the most likely cause of this presentation?
output:
Nitrous oxide (N2O) toxicity

The clinical presentation and imaging findings are classic for subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord due to functional vitamin B12 deficiency. The key findings include:

1. **Clinical features**: Sensory ataxia, positive Romberg test, impaired proprioception and vibratory sense with preserved pain sensation - indicating posterior column dysfunction

2. **MRI findings**: "Inverted V" or dorsal column hyperintensity pattern on T2-weighted imaging, extending from C1-T12

3. **Low vitamin B12** without macrocytic anemia in a young patient

In a 32-year-old with this presentation, nitrous oxide abuse is the most likely cause. N2O irreversibly oxidizes the cobalt ion in vitamin B12, inactivating it and causing functional B12 deficiency even when serum levels may be only mildly reduced. This is increasingly common, particularly with recreational "whippet" use. The absence of macrocytic anemia is typical in N2O-induced B12 deficiency because the onset is often rapid, not allowing time for hematologic changes to develop.

A 70-year-old man presented to our clinic in April, 2014, with a 4 month history of painful, pruritic rash involving the scalp, face, chest, and back. He had a history of colon cancer and deep venous thrombosis. A biopsy sample of the rash had been interpreted as eczema, but he had had only minimum improvement with short courses of both topical and systemic corticosteroids and antibiotics. Examination showed a healthy-looking man with erythematous papules and plaques displaying cornflake-like scale in a seborrheic distribution (figure). Oral and ocular mucosae were normal. Previous serological studies, including antinuclear antibody (ANA), complement, and serum protein electrophoresis, were normal. We did lesional punch biopsy for routine histology (appendix) and perilesional punch biopsy for direct immunofluorescence (figure). Clinicopathological findings were diagnostic of pemphigus foliaceus.Pemphigus foliaceus is a rare autoimmune bullous disease characterised by pathogenic autoantibodies against desmoglein-1 (a desmosomal protein) that cause disruption of intercellular adhesion between keratinocytes in the epidermal granular layer (acantholysis). This results in fragile bullae that rupture easily to form erosions with characteristic scale crust. Pemphigus foliaceus often begins on the upper body in a seborrheic distribution, but progresses to widespread involvement or erythroderma if not appropriately treated. Pruritus and burning are common and can be exacerbated by UV exposure. Unlike pemphigus vulgaris, pemphigus foliaceus is rarely associated with mucosal involvement. Diagnosis is made with biopsies for routine histology and direct immunofluorescence. Pemphigus foliaceus typically arises in middle age and can be drug-induced, such as by penicillamine and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors. An endemic form, Fogo Sevelagem (“wild fire”), occurs in South America and has been linked with exposure to black flies.
Before effective treatment was available pemphigus foliaceus fatality reached 60% due to dehydration and sepsis. Rituximab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, has recently gained favour as treatment of choice for pemphigus foliaceus and other autoimmune bullous diseases because of relatively high rates of induced remission compared with classic treatments. We prescribed 30 mg prednisolone daily and rituximab (375 mg/m2 intravenously once weekly for 4 weeks) for our patient, and triamcinolone 0·1% cream twice daily. At follow-up 2 months after treatment with rituximab most skin lesions were healed and we could reduce prednisolone to 20 mg daily (appendix). He will be followed up every 3 months until prednisolone is tapered off completely.

input: A 62-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of dyspnea. output:
Propofol

The green discoloration of urine in this intubated ICU patient is a well-known side effect of **propofol**, a commonly used sedative agent for mechanically ventilated patients.

Propofol is metabolized to phenolic metabolites that are conjugated in the liver and excreted in the urine. These metabolites can cause a characteristic green discoloration of urine, which is benign and resolves after discontinuation of the medication. This phenomenon is more commonly seen with prolonged infusions.

output:
Purpura fulminans

This is a classic presentation of **purpura fulminans** secondary to meningococcal septicemia (meningococcemia).

The image shows the characteristic findings:
- Large, irregular purpuric lesions with dark necrotic centers
- Hemorrhagic bullae with surrounding erythema
- Geographic/stellate borders typical of purpura fulminans

This condition results from disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and microvascular thrombosis associated with severe meningococcal infection, leading to skin necrosis and potentially limb-threatening ischemia.

A 29-year-old woman presented with a 23-year history of multiple joint swelling and intermittent pain. Physical examination showed large, soft, and fluctuant soft tissue swelling of the hands, wrists, elbows, knees, and ankles, bilaterally (figure A; appendix p 2). Symmetric tense knee effusions restricted her range of motion. She had previously had multiple recurrences of panuveitis, cataract, and secondary glaucoma in both eyes for 7 years, with retinal detachment leading to blindness in her left eye. 9 years earlier, she had undergone knee synovectomy, and histopathological examination showed extensive infiltration of mature adipose tissue, consistent with lipoma arborescens. Noncaseating granulomas were also observed at higher magnification (figure B). MRI of the knee at that time showed diffuse villous and frond-like intra-articular fatty masses in the suprapatellar bursa, with associated marked joint effusion (appendix p 3). Her father had displayed almost identical symptoms and had died 19 years previously, at the age of 34 years.
Immunological tests showed no abnormalities. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was slightly elevated, at 34 mm/h. MRI of the right hand revealed multiple lobulations along the tendons, with joint effusions (figures C and D, appendix p 4); the signal intensity of the frond-like lobules was high on T1-weighted images (figure C) and very low on fat-saturated T2-weighted images (figure D), indicating their fatty composition. Whole-exome sequencing revealed a novel heterozygous missense frameshift mutation in NOD2 (1066G>C [Glu356Gln]), which was predicted to be damaging by in silico analysis (appendix p 5). The patient recalled having scaly erythematous lesions in childhood. A diagnosis of Blau syndrome was made. Genetic analysis could not be done on the father, but, given his medical history, it is highly probable that he had a severe form of Blau syndrome.

Joint manifestations are chronic and symmetrical polyarthritis, which usually start within the first decade of life, with marked soft-tissue swelling, especially in the wrists and ankles, due to synovial granulomatous inflammation. Ocular involvement usually occurs later than other symptoms but accounts for the highest morbidity.
Lipoma arborescens is a rare disorder that results in the growth of fatty tissue within the joint linings, often leading to swelling, pain, and restricted movement, primarily affecting the knee, although it can involve multiple joints. Hand involvement, early childhood onset, and familial inheritance in lipoma arborescens are very rare, suggesting a possible misdiagnosis. Joint involvement in Blau syndrome presenting as lipoma arborescens has only been documented once but cases might be underestimated due to the lack of genetic confirmation. Hence, Blau syndrome should be looked for in lipoma arborescens cases with uveitis, familial history, hand joint involvement, or early onset.
If the condition had been identified sooner, blindness might have been averted in the patient, highlighting the importance of early recognition and treatment. In this case, the patient was treated with glucocorticoids and thalidomide, resulting in pain relief and stabilisation. Glucocorticoids were tapered gradually, with the addition of tofacitinib.

A 40-year-old man attended our ophthalmology department reporting a gradual worsening of vision in both eyes over the previous few months.The patient had a history of sensorineural hearing loss and he had received a kidney transplant at age 19 years; he had previously been diagnosed with X-linked Alport syndrome. Genetic testing, at the time, showed a mutation in the COL4A5 gene. The kidney was donated by the patient's healthy father; the patient has one healthy brother and no children. His mother was identified as the carrier and she was also affected by the disease. The patient was prescribed sirolimus 3 mg daily and prednisolone 5 mg daily.
On general examination, he was well. Regarding his eyes, a slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment showed a clear crystalline lens with an anterior lenticonus—a subtle protrusion of the anterior surface—in both eyes (figure); the protrusion was clearly visible on anterior segment swept-source optical coherence tomography (OCT; figure) and was also detected as an oil-droplet sign with retro-illumination (figure).
Additionally, the patient showed the typical retinal findings of Alport syndrome: central fleck retinopathy—seen as scattered pigmentation irregularities around the macula, which were more obvious on red free images (figure)—temporal retinal thinning on retinal OCT (figure), and peripheral retinopathy. His best corrected vision was reduced to 20/40 (typical 20/20) in both eyes.
We implanted a toric intraocular lens with extended depth of focus in both eyes after lens removal, which improved his vision to 20/25 bilaterally. At 3 months follow-up, the patient had a full corrected distance visual acuity of 20/20.
Alport syndrome is a rare, progressive, hereditary glomerular disease characterised by haematuria, proteinuria, and progressive impairment of kidney function caused by mutations in the COL4A5, usually inherited as X-linked—as in our patient—and COL4A3 and COL4A4 genes, which are transmitted in either an autosomal recessive or dominant pattern. The mutations disrupt collagen type IV synthesis, which is a crucial component of the basal membrane in the renal glomerulus, cochlea, cornea, lens capsule, retina, and skin.
Visual impairment is mostly caused by anterior lenticonus—even if there is no cataract present; it is diagnostic for Alport syndrome, seen in 50% of patients, and can be treated effectively with lens replacement. Central and peripheral retinopathy is seen in 70% and 80% of patients, respectively, and usually does not affect vision. Lenticonus and central retinopathy are predictive for sensorineural hearing loss and renal failure before the age of 30 years. Therefore, in young men with hearing loss and haematuria, an eye examination can give helpful information in confirming the diagnosis of Alport syndrome.
output: Alport syndrome with anterior lenticonus and central fleck retinopathy

After 8 years of levothyroxine therapy, a male patient who underwent thyroidectomy at the age of 47 years for Graves' disease developed a 3 cm mass on his left hallux. The lesion was removed and diagnosed as localised myxoedema. Two years later, at the age of 57 years, the patient presented to our sarcoma service with a local recurrence. On physical examination, he had orbitopathy and no sign of pretibial myxoedema; the recurrence presented as a soft, mobile lump of the dorsal aspect of the hallux (figure). MRI showed a suprafascial mass with hyperintense T2-weighted signal and poorly defined margins (figure). To confirm the dermopathy and to exclude a soft tissue neoplasm, tissue slides of the previous surgery were reviewed. Haematoxylin and eosin stain showed a diffuse widening of the reticular dermis by a faintly basophilic acellular material, associated with isolated lymphocytes, that was dissecting collagen fibres and diffusing in perivascular and periadnexal spaces (figure). These microscopic features were consistent with an extracellular mucopolysaccharides deposit (ie, myxoedema). The original diagnosis was thus confirmed, the present lesion considered a recurrence, and the patient referred for conservative management.Graves' disease manifests with infiltrative orbitopathy in around 25% of patients, and with thyroid dermopathy in less than 5% of patients. Although usually located on the anterolateral aspect of the lower leg (pretibial myxoedema), it can occur elsewhere, especially after trauma. Dermopathy and orbitopathy can also occur after thyroid surgery, radioiodine therapy, or in clinically euthyroid patients. Myxoedema usually does not require treatment, and surgical excision is not advised due to recurrence (as in this patient). In case of cosmetic issues or interference with shoe fitting, topical glucocorticoids under occlusive dressing might be beneficial. Localised nodular myxoedema is a rare form of Graves' dermopathy, and although this mass-forming condition might cause concern about a soft tissue neoplasm, clinical presentation and histology warrant a conservative approach.

A 5-year-old girl presented to her primary care physician with swellings on both sides of her neck. She was referred directly to the Center for Oncology, in Minsk, because she had been living 70 miles away from the Chernobyl Power Plant at the time of the accident, in the Gomel District of Belarus. An ultrasound scan of the area showed a suspicious nodule of more than 2 cm in diameter in her thyroid gland as well as multiple bilaterally enlarged lymph nodes in the neck. She had a thyroidectomy and bilateral lymphadenectomy. Histology showed an invasive papillary thyroid cancer over 2 cm in diameter and bilateral lymph node metastases (pathological stage T4N1bM0). The girl was given levothyroxine postoperatively to prevent hypothyroidism and to suppress TSH. However, because of the low quality of the drug available at that time, TSH suppression was not permanent and 2 years later, tumour recurred in a lymph node on the right side of the girl's neck and was removed during a unilateral dissection. She was then given a course of radioiodine therapy (RIT). A scan done after treatment showed intense uptake of iodine-131 (131I) in both lungs; a chest x-ray was normal. The RIT was repeated three times at intervals of 4–6 months (cumulative activity 5·3 GBq of 131I). However, because no change occurred in the level of 131I uptake in the lungs, it was thought that the metastases were not responding to the RIT, and five courses of chemotherapy with bleomycin were given, again without any clear metastatic response.The patient's clinical course and the small amounts of poor-quality—selenium-75-contaminated—131I available in Belarus resulted in her being selected for treatment at the University of Essen, Germany, where she had her fifth course of 3 GBq of 131I, given in hypothyroidism—to ensure a high uptake of 131I—with a raised TSH concentration (>80 mU/L). The patient's parathormone and serum calcium concentrations were both low, leading us to treat her for postoperative hypoparathyroidism. A post-therapy scan showed intense 131I uptake in the lungs (figure) and a correspondingly high serum concentration of the thyroid-specific tumour marker thyroglobulin of 3750 ng/mL, which should be undetectable after thyroidectomy if all benign or malignant thyroid tissue is removed.
The RIT was repeated five more times and 131I uptake in the lung metastases finally disappeared (figure). At her last follow-up examination, in the Gomel District, in September, 2019, no scintigraphic or radiological remnants of pulmonary metastases were seen. The patient's thyroglobulin concentration had decreased considerably to 17 ng/mL (classed as a stable partial response), mild pulmonary fibrosis was seen on a lung CT, and pulmonary function was reduced. The patient trained as a kindergarten teacher. 1 year after marrying, she gave birth to a healthy son, in 2007 (figure). Both patient and son are doing well and living in the Gomel District.
Treating differentiated thyroid cancers in children with RIT has short and long term side-effects—including thyroiditis due to irradiation, gastritis, nausea, bone marrow suppression, secondary primary malignancies (leukaemia and solid tumours), and—as in our patient—pulmonary fibrosis.

A 42-year-old woman was reviewed by our team after a right femoral artery endarterectomy for acute ischaemia of her leg which developed following coronary angiography using femoral access. The patient had a history of type 1 diabetes—managed by insulin pump therapy—and diabetic-hypertensive kidney disease which had required maintenance haemodialysis for the previous 9 months.
Post-surgery, the patient's blood glucose concentration had increased to 21·7 mmol/L (typical range 3·9–5·6) or 391 mg/dL (typical range 70–100); capillary blood ketones were so high that they were unmeasurable (>8 mmol/L; typical level <0·6). An arterial blood gas showed metabolic acidosis with pH at 7·26 (typical range 7·35−7·45), pCO2 23·8 mm Hg (typical range 35−45), bicarbonates 10·05 mmol/L (typical range 22−26), lactate 2·55 mmol/L (typical range <2), and an anion gap of 28·1 mmol/L (typical range 5−12). The insulin pump was functioning well. We concluded the findings compatible with a diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).
Haemodialysis and intravenous insulin, plus glucose supplementation, were started with careful monitoring of potassium and glucose levels; ketone levels reduced within 24 h.
A review of data from the patient's continuous glucose monitoring system showed chronically elevated monthly mean blood glucose concentrations, between 13·95−17·25 mmol/L (251–311 mg/dL); with low glycaemic levels and frequent hypoglycaemias on days the patient had dialysis and elevated glycaemic levels on days she did not have dialysis (figure; appendix). Additionally, we noticed a surprisingly high level of bicarbonate on the routine protocol of chronic haemodialysis; it had progressively increased from 30 mmol/L to 38 mmol/L over the previous 9 months to maintain a normal (>22 mmol/L) pre-dialysis serum bicarbonate concentration, as recommended by the latest guidelines (appendix).
Furthermore, we found the anion gap to be surprisingly high, which we thought unlikely to be caused by chronic kidney disease alone. Therefore, given the high level of ketones before and after dialysis, we concluded that the excessive need for bicarbonates was due to the DKA.
We excluded lactic acidosis since the lactate was only slightly increased at 2·55 mmol/L (typical level ≤2). And based on clinical history, we also ruled out salicylate intoxication, ingestion of toxic substances, and small intestine bacterial overgrowth.
The duration of the DKA was indicated by the progressive increase in bicarbonate in the dialysate, which, combined with the high glucose clearance during haemodialysis, had been responsible for maintaining metabolic stability without marked acidosis (appendix). However, ketones had increased to high levels because of limited clearance during successive haemodialysis sessions.
In conclusion then, the high ketonaemia with an exceptionally high anion gap—despite partial clearance—together with relatively moderate decreases in bicarbonate and pH, in a patient with end-stage kidney disease, suggested chronic DKA partially masked by alkalinisation of the dialysis baths.
In cases of high anion gap metabolic acidosis with end-stage kidney disease, necessitating bicarbonate-enriched dialysate, physicians must search for a cause of metabolic acidosis. In diabetic patients, the diagnosis of DKA should be considered first, especially with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes under pump therapy.Diagnosing DKA in dialysis patients is challenging. Relying solely on glycated haemoglobin or blood glucose levels during dialysis is insufficient to assess glucose control. As patients with end-stage kidney disease present with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, both the anion gap and the bicarbonate may not be the most reliable diagnostic parameters for DKA; therefore, the measurement of plasma β-hydroxybutyrate is key.
Although the optimal concentration of bicarbonate in dialysate for haemodialysis is uncertain, the presence of a high dialysate bicarbonate concentration (≥38 mmol/L) has been reported to be associated with poorer outcomes: all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalisation (appendix).
Regarding glucose variation in patients having dialysis, the lowest glycaemic level—on days of dialysis—is due to glucose loss to the dialysate and diffusion of glucose into erythrocytes. After dialysis, a paradoxical rebound hyperglycaemia occurs due to increased secretion of counter-regulatory hormones—specifically glucagon, adrenocorticotropic hormone, and cortisol—and partial clearance of negligible amounts of insulin during dialysis, even though the insulin resistance is diminished after dialysis (appendix). The lack of glucose clearance then maintains hyperglycaemia on days between dialysis.

input: An 80-year-old man presented with this lesion on the bottom of his left foot, which had been growing for the past 2 years. It had become ulcerated and bled intermittently. What is the diagnosis?
output:
Based on the clinical presentation of an 80-year-old man with a solitary, growing, ulcerated, and intermittently bleeding erythematous nodule on the plantar surface of the foot, and the visual appearance of a reddish, fleshy, amelanotic mass, the diagnosis is **amelanotic melanoma** (specifically, an amelanotic acral melanoma). This condition is frequently misdiagnosed clinically as pyogenic granuloma or a benign ulcer due to the lack of pigmentation.

A 55-year-old man with a history of aortic valve replacement was admitted because of pelvic pain. He had been treated with antibiotics over the past 4 weeks for a presumed lower urinary tract infection with fever. Treatment had been unsuccessful. Both urine and blood cultures grew Enterobacter cloacae. Abdominal radiography showed a thin line of air within the bladder wall, outlining its perimeter (figure). A bacteraemic emphysematous cystitis complicated by prosthetic valve endocarditis was diagnosed, and effective antibiotic treatment was initiated. Emphysematous cystitis is a potentially life-threatening condition caused by gas-producing pathogens. This rare form of urinary tract infection typically occurs in middle-aged diabetic women. Contrary to radiological findings, clinical features are non-specific (irritative bladder symptoms, pyuria, haematuria, and, rarely, pneumaturia). Plain abdominal radiography, as well as ultrasonography, may lead to the diagnosis but CT scan is regarded as the procedure of choice, particularly to rule out a vesicocolic fistula. Early diagnosis and management consists of antibiotic therapy, bladder drainage, and sometimes surgery.
