A 41-year-old man presented to our rheumatology clinic with a 2-month history of symmetric inflammatory polyarthralgia and pleuritic chest pain. 1 year before, he had visited another hospital reporting a dry cough; 2 months later he returned to the same institution complaining of breathlessness and fatigue; at that time, pulmonary tuberculosis and heart failure had been ruled out.Notably, in his occupational history, 11 years before his current health difficulties, he had finished 6 years of employment in a factory producing glass and fibreglass, in Medellin, Colombia. The patient's main tasks had been in the blending process: mixing sand and soda ash, cutting, polishing, and repairing flat glass and fibreglass. He worked 9-h days in a poorly ventilated workspace and used personal protection equipment for less than 30 min per h. The patient had smoked one to two cigarettes daily for the past 26 years and stopped 4 months before his current presentation.
On examination he was well looking and not distressed; he had bilateral effusions in his wrist, metacarpophalangeal, and knee joints. Crackles were audible at the apex of his right lung.
Laboratory investigations showed positive antinuclear antibodies—at a titre of 1:320, homogeneous pattern—and raised anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies (ACPAs; 37 UI/ml; reference value <5). Rheumatoid factor was negative.
A digital chest x-ray showed scattered and tiny lung nodules, cavitation in the right upper lobe, and consolidation at the left upper lobe (figure). A CT scan showed cavitation and numerous nodules between 1 mm and 5 mm in size, with some confluent areas, randomly distributed throughout the lungs (figure).
Ziehl-Neelsen staining, nucleic acid amplification test, and culture for Mycobacterium tuberculosis of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid were negative. Histopathological analysis of a sample obtained by thoracoscopically guided open lung biopsy showed multiple granulomas with a central necrotic area, surrounded by layers of crystal silica and mononuclear infiltrate, without neoplasm or acid-fast bacteria (appendix). Considering the patient's occupational history, signs, and symptoms, and findings on investigation, we diagnosed accelerated silicosis complicated by Caplan syndrome—mimicking a miliary pattern and cavitary disease. At 6 months’ follow-up, spirometry testing showed FEV1/FVC (%) 95% (0,77), FVC 145·0% (7,14 L), and FEV1 138% (5,5 L).
At 12 months’ follow-up, the patient continued to report a dry cough and dyspnoea on exertion; original x-ray findings remained unchanged. However, treatment with rituximab, methotrexate, and prednisolone had improved the condition of the patient's painful, swollen knee and hand joints.
Caplan syndrome is a rare complication of silicosis—incidence between 0·75% and 0·89%—characterised by pulmonary nodules and rheumatoid arthritis in patients with pneumoconiosis.
The relationship between silicosis and rheumatoid arthritis development has been the subject of much debate. Disease development begins when respirable crystalline silica dust is engulfed by macrophages producing lysosomal dysfunction. Cell death results in exposure of sequestered antigens, NALP3 inflammasome activation, production of proinflammatory cytokines (eg, IL-1β and TNF-α), and activation of T and B cells (eg, T-reg with production of IL-10 and TGF-β which produces fibrosis, and T-helper CD4+ cell responses). These changes lead to the formation of autoantibodies and immune complexes—including rheumatoid factor and ACPAs—which ultimately lead to synovial cell activation, infiltration, inflammation, neoangiogenesis, and joint tissue destruction.
Tuberculosis and lung cancer—at high risk in patients with silicosis—need to be excluded before diagnosing Caplan syndrome since all three can produce cavity lung lesions and miliary pattern on imaging.

A 34-year-old man, from sub-Saharan Africa, was referred to our hospital for short stature, when he came to France, as an actor, to play the part of a child. The patient reported that at birth he required incubator support and that his growth was blunted from early childhood.At our first evaluation, his height was 137 cm, weight was 26·4 kg, and body-mass index 14 kg/m2. He had long extremities compared to his trunk and he had signs of hypogonadism—including small intrascrotal testes (0·5 mL; typical 12–30 in adult males), absent pubic and axillary hair, micro-penis (2 cm), and a high-pitched voice.
Hormone assays showed combined pituitary hormone deficiencies with low serum morning cortisol and undetectable dehydroepiandrosterone-sulphate with low adrenocorticotropin; low thyroxine and triiodothyronine; undetectable testosterone and oestradiol; low inhibin B and low gonadotrophins; low prolactin; and growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 were both below detectable limits (appendix).
Brain MRI showed marked pituitary gland hypoplasia, absence of pituitary stalk and ectopic posterior hypophysis, and no extra-pituitary abnormalities.
The patient's bone age was 13 years, and knee MRI showed persistent growth plates at the distal femoral or proximal tibial epiphysis. Genetic testing did not identify pathogenic variants in any of the genes responsible for congenital hypopituitarism.
We commenced treatment with hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, and recombinant human growth hormone replacement for 2 months before the patient had to return to his country as his visa had expired; he was provided with growth hormone cartridges for an additional 3 months.
Figure Congenital hypopituitarism treated in adulthood
Show full caption
Figure viewer
The patient returned to France 3 years later; his height was 142 cm, but otherwise, his clinical state was unchanged. We commenced stepwise replacement with hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, growth hormone, and gonadotropins for the next 4 years. His height increased to 161 cm—an increase of 24 cm—and he achieved normal pubertal development (appendix). During the increase in height, the patient developed scoliosis which necessitated surgical correction and an arthrodesis at T2-L1 (appendix).
At baseline, cardiac MRI showed a small heart—but well-proportioned to the patient's body size—with normal contractile function; hormone treatment resulted in linear, uniform growth of the heart with a progressive increase in ventricular mass and volume. Concomitant decrease in the extracellular space indicated that the cardiac growth resulted from cardiomyocyte correction of hypotrophy; the initial rapid decrease in extracellular space, after levothyroxine and hydrocortisone were started, was mostly attributed to resorption of myxoedematous infiltration, and possibly due to inflammation.
Growth hormone—given prior to puberty induction—transiently increased ventricular contractility to supraphysiologic values, with the ejection fraction reaching 78%; it normalised during gonadotrophin therapy. Left ventricular stroke volume increased proportionally compared to end-diastolic volume, reflecting the heart's ability to enhance its contractile strength in response to increased venous return—Frank-Starling law.
We further observed a uniform increase of the cross-sectional area of the patient's femoral muscles during treatment accompanied by a progressive decrease of intramuscular fat fraction. Growth hormone induced transient glucose intolerance, which resolved during further therapy.
Congenital hypopituitarism is usually diagnosed and treated during childhood or adolescence to correct blunted growth and lack of pubertal development. Rarely is hormone replacement initiated in adulthood, and results of such cases are limited. Regarding the heart, the capacity to generate cardiomyocytes during adult life has been the subject of much debate; cardiomyogenesis is minimal in healthy humans after birth. Metachronous heart growth—as seen in our patient—from size of a child to a normal adult, has not previously been reported. In conclusion, hormone replacement, administered gradually, in an adult patient with congenital hypopituitarism can safely induce heart growth normalisation proportionate to linear growth (video).
output: Congenital hypopituitarism with combined pituitary hormone deficiencies

Furthermore, serum chitotriosidase activity was elevated (1036 nmol/h per mL; typical range 0–195), indicating possible increased macrophage activity or any of several lysosomal storage disorders. Neuropsychiatric assessment showed the patient had impairments of both short-term memory and executive functioning.
Brain MRI with contrast showed diffuse dural thickening and enhancement without any focal pathology of the brain (figure 2). Histopathologic examination of a sample obtained from dural biopsy indicated clusters of CD68-positive macrophages (figure 2); analyses of samples of biopsies from the skin and of biopsies obtained during a gastroscopy were normal.

input: A previously healthy 26-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 5-day history of an asymptomatic rash, sore throat, fevers, chills, and malaise. On physical examination, scattered, erythematous papules and macules could be seen across the upper chest and anterior neck (left). In the mouth, palatal petechiae, buccal mucosal ulcerations, and pharyngeal erythema were observed (right). The patient reported having had condomless sex with a new partner 2 weeks before presentation. A diagnosis of acute Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) infection was made. Which of the following is the first to become positive after a patient is infected with HIV?
output:
Based on the case description and images provided, the patient has been diagnosed with **Acute Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) infection** (also known as Acute Retroviral Syndrome). The text explicitly states this diagnosis and asks a specific medical knowledge question at the end: "Which of the following is the first to become positive after a patient is infected with HIV?"

The order of appearance for HIV markers after infection is:
1.  **HIV RNA** (Viral Load): Detectable approx. 10–12 days post-infection.
2.  **HIV p24 Antigen**: Detectable approx. 14–20 days post-infection.
3.  **HIV Antibodies (IgM/IgG)**: Detectable approx. 20–90 days post-infection.

Therefore, the first marker to become positive is **HIV RNA**.

diagnostic result:
**HIV RNA**

input: A 28-year-old woman came to our clinic saying she had blurred vision in her right eye. 22 h earlier, she had noticed areas of darkness in the lower half of her right visual field. Her medical history was unremarkable apart from her reporting that she had recurrent tonsillitis as a child. Corrected visual acuity was 20/80 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. Slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment showed no abnormalities, with normal pupillary reactions. However, slit lamp biomicroscopy and fundus examination in the right eye showed intra-retinal oedema with retinal whitening in the superior area (figure). Fluorescein angiography showed an arterial filling defect along the superotemporal arcade (figure). A diagnosis of right eye superotemporal branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) was made. A cardiology review was sought as part of the mandatory systemic investigations required in such cases. Our cardiology colleagues reported that the patient's electrocardiogram was normal but that her echocardiogram showed moderate mitral stenosis. An analysis of her urine found no abnormalities. Her fasting blood glucose, blood cholesterol, and serum triglyceride concentrations were normal, and a full blood count showed values within the normal range. Also, both her erythrocyte sedimentation rate and serum C-reactive protein concentration were normal. The patient was treated with acetyl salicylate 75 mg once a day and spironolactone 25 mg once a day. She was seen again 12 months later, and her visual fields had improved and she had no further problems.The incidence of retinal arterial obstruction in patients under the age of 30 years has been estimated at less than one in 50 000 outpatients. The causes of retinal arterial occlusion in young adults—different from those in older individuals—include systemic vasculitis, migraine, sickle-cell haemoglobinopathy, myeloproliferative disorders, hypercoagulable states, use of oral contraceptives, and intravenous drug abuse. Valvular heart disease—originating from rheumatic fever—remains an important cause of BRAO that should be borne in mind, although rates are declining in developed countries.

A 13-year-old boy presented to the paediatrics outpatient department with recurrent fever and abdominal pain that started 8 months before presentation. He was admitted to the paediatric nephrology unit for evaluation following a generalised seizure, persistent stage 2 hypertension, and melaena for one week requiring packed red cell transfusion. Significant examination findings included severe thinness (BMI-for-age –5·2 standard deviation score), stage 2 hypertension (blood pressure 136/110 mm Hg), pallor, and generalised muscle tenderness. Investigations identified normocytic normochromic anaemia (haemoglobin 85 g/L), acute kidney injury (serum creatinine 353·6 μmol/L), and elevated inflammatory markers (serum ferritin 3312 pmol/L, serum C-reactive protein 146 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 50 mm/h). Urinalysis revealed proteinuria (2+ on dipstick) and haematuria (4–5 red blood cells per high power field).
On diagnostic evaluation, serum antinuclear antibodies and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative and C3 and C4 complement protein concentrations were normal. Serum hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus, and HIV antibodies were also absent. A non-reactive tuberculin skin test excluded tuberculosis infection. Malignant lesions were excluded after a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen. Worsening gastrointestinal bleeding prompted a CT angiogram. The beaded appearance of medium-sized arteries, alternating stenosis and dilatation, and microaneurysms, particularly along the coeliac–mesenteric axis, was consistent with polyarteritis nodosa (figure 1A, B, C). MRI with angiography showed similar abnormalities in intracranial vessels (figure 1D). Vasculitis-induced end-organ ischaemia was evident in both scans. Considering the characteristic angiographic findings, multisystem presentation (fever, myalgia, hypertension, and central nervous system, gastrointestinal, and renal involvement) and laboratory features of inflammation, the patient was diagnosed with childhood-onset polyarteritis nodosa. Clinical exome sequencing excluded inherited deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2 (DADA2 mutation).
Therapy with intravenous methylprednisolone pulses (30 mg/kg per day for 3 days) was followed by oral prednisolone at 1 mg/kg per day for 4 weeks, gradually tapered to 5 mg/day over the next 16 weeks. The day after finishing the three methylprednisolone pulses, intravenous cyclophosphamide pulses (500 mg/m2 per dose) were started once a month for 6 months. Vasculitis-induced ischemia resulted in generalised myalgia, anuric acute kidney injury requiring maintenance haemodialysis, stage 2 hypertension that was controlled on concomitant therapy with five oral antihypertensive medications (amlodipine, 0·6 mg/kg per day; prazocin, 0·6 mg/kg per day; enalapril, 0·6 mg/kg per day; metoprolol, 3·0 mg/kg per day; and clonidine, 5·0 mcg/kg per day), and nervous system involvement with seizures requiring two oral antiseizure medications (initially phenytoin, 5·0 mg/kg per day; which was changed to levetiracetam, 20·0 mg/kg per day). During treatment initiation with intravenous methylprednisolone pulses and the first cyclophosphamide pulse, mesenteric ischaemia deteriorated into gut perforation, requiring bowel resection and re-anastomosis. Post-operative peritonitis and septicaemia required intravenous broad-spectrum antimicrobials (renal-modified doses; piperacillin–tazobactam, 210 mg/kg per day; teicoplanin, 5 mg/kg per day; metronidazole, 30 mg/kg per day; and caspofungin, 50 mg/m2 per day) and intravenous vasopressors (adrenaline and noradrenaline, titrated to 1 μg/kg per min). The overall disease was severe, reflected by a Factor-Five Score of 3. Discharged under multidisciplinary follow-up, the patient was receiving oral prednisolone (0·5 mg/kg per day, on tapering), oral mycophenolate mofetil (500 mg/m2 per day), and maintenance haemodialysis (done locally) at the last teleconsultation.
Childhood-onset polyarteritis nodosa is a rare, severe condition that requires prompt recognition and management. Patients with Factor-Five Scores exceeding 2 have a fulminant course of polyarteritis nodosa with a high risk of mortality and long-term morbidities. This case illustrates the role of early diagnosis and treatment in preventing mortality and improving outcomes.

A 34-year-old woman with a 2-year history of progressively worsening difficulties in walking, eating and swallowing, presented to our department. Additionally, the patient's sister reported observing unusual behaviours over the past 6 months: she said her sister had been taking her meals to eat alone in the bathroom and had crafted a doll from leaves gathered from local trees, referring to it as her son (figure). The patient had no previous medical history or family history of similar difficulties.
On examination, the patient was cachectic, drooling her saliva, and had multiple injuries and scars on her tongue, lower lips, and arms caused by self-biting (figure); she had abnormal—primarily choreatic—movements of her trunk and oromandibular region, involuntary vocalisations, and vocal tics (video 1). She also had involuntary jaw opening and dystonia—particularly during feeding (video 2). Limb examination showed mild bradykinesia, hypotonia, mild motor weakness, and reduced reflexes in all extremities.
Laboratory investigations found urea and electrolyte levels within normal range; liver enzymes were slightly elevated with alanine aminotransferase at 43 U/L (normal range 4–36 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase at 74 U/L (normal range 8–33 U/L). Thyroid function was normal. Haemoglobin concentration was within the normal range at 12·1 g/dL (normal 11·0–14·0). The serum creatinine kinase level was elevated at 1 344 U/L (normal range for a woman is 26–192), and lactate dehydrogenase was raised at 269 UI/L (normal range for a woman is 100–240 UI/L). A blood smear showed that 15% of the red blood cells were acanthocytes (normal < 3%) (figure).
An MRI brain showed bilateral atrophy in the caudate nucleus and cortical atrophy in the frontal-parietal and occipital regions (figure). Nerve conduction studies showed axonal neuropathy affecting both sensory and motor neurons. Whole exome sequencing showed the patient to be a compound heterozygous carrier of two novel pathogenic loss-of-function variants in the VPS13A gene, namely: NM_033305.3(VPS13A): c.2425C>T (p. Gln809*) and NM_033305.3(VPS13A): c.5072delA (p.Asp1691fs). No other pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were found in any genes previously associated with adult-onset dystonia, chorea, or related movement disorders. Considering the findings together, we diagnosed VPS13A disease. Initially, we prescribed oral haloperidol with no response; she was switched to oral risperidone and tetrabenazine resulting in some improvement in both psychiatric and motor symptoms.
After 1 month, the patient was allowed home and followed up every 4 weeks as an outpatient. The patient's condition continued to deteriorate, with significant weight loss and worsening of both motor and psychiatric symptoms. At last review, she was receiving palliative care.
VPS13A disease—previously known as Chorea-acanthocytosis—is an autosomal recessive condition resulting from mutations in the VPS13A gene, which encodes a lipid transfer protein. Patients typically have progressive symptoms of chorea, oromandibular dyskinesia, Parkinsonism, neuropsychiatric issues, diminished or absent tendon deep reflexes and seizures. Symptoms usually begin around 30 years of age. Prognosis is poor, and the disease is ultimately fatal. Additional features indicative of VSP13A disease include elevated creatinine kinase levels, transaminitis, acanthocytocytosis, and caudate atrophy. The differential diagnoses include XK disease—also known as McLeod syndrome. Both VSP13A and XK disease fall under the umbrella of neuroacanthocytosis syndrome: XK disease is an X-linked disorder predominantly affecting middle-aged men.
Huntington's disease, Huntington's disease-like 2, Wilson's disease, and other rare adult-onset choreatic disorders, including neuroferritinopathy, aceruloplasminaemia, and c9orf72-related disorders, should also be considered as other possible differential diagnoses.
In Africa, choreatic movement disorders—seen in our patient, which we believe is the first genetically confirmed case of VPS13A disease in a black patient from sub-Saharan Africa—are often underdiagnosed; many cases are referred to traditional healers and customary medicine.

An 85-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of fever. At another hospital, treatment with cefditoren had been ineffective. 55 years earlier, she had been diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and given a 2-year course of antituberculosis drugs, including isoniazid, streptomycin, and paraaminosalicylic acid. On physical examination, ulcerative inflammation involved the left auricle and completely spared the left earlobe (figure), which suggested chondritis rather than dermatitis. Tender left cervical lymphadenopathy was noticed (figure). Whole-body CT showed enlarged left cervical lymph nodes, stippled and nodular calcification in both lungs, and lymph node calcification in the mediastinum, which suggested old healed pulmonary tuberculosis. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT showed abnormal fluorodeoxyglucose accumulation in the left auricle and left cervical lymph nodes (figure) with no arthritis or vasculitis. Incisional biopsy specimens of the affected cervical lymph nodes showed epithelioid granulomatous inflammation with Langhans giant cells and caseous necrosis on haematoxylin and eosin stain, which were consistent with tuberculosis. Biopsy specimens of the cartilage and skin in the inflamed auricle identified chondritis with no granulomatous inflammation on haematoxylin and eosin stain. In both specimens, Ziehl Neelsen stain results, mycobacterial culture result, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR were negative. Treatment with antituberculous drugs, including 2-month course of isoniazid (200 mg/day), rifampicin (450 mg/day), and ethambutol (500 mg/day), and 7-month course of isoniazid (200 mg/day) and rifampicin (450 mg/day), resolved fever, auricular chondritis, and cervical lymphadenitis. At the 2-year follow-up, the patient did not have recurrence of lymphadenitis and auricular chondritis, and chest x-ray showed no recurrence of pulmonary tuberculosis.M tuberculosis can be an immunological trigger for onset of various connective tissue diseases. Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis, Henoch-Schonlein purpura, and cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa have been reported to develop concomitantly with tuberculous infection and respond to antituberculosis drugs.
Auricular chondritis is a typical sign of relapsing polychondlitis, but is rarely seen in patients with various connective tissue diseases, such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis, systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjogren's syndrome, Behcet's disease, and ulcerative colitis. In this case, tuberculous lymphadenitis, with no other sites of active tuberculous involvement, was diagnosed on the basis of the specific pathophysiological findings because the sensitivity of mycobacterial culture and M tuberculosis PCR for tuberculous lymphadenitis is low and biopsy is the most reliable method. Auricular chondritis is probably not a tuberculous infection on grounds of the non-contiguousness, pathophysiological findings, and microbiological examination results. Therefore, cervical tuberculous lymphadenopathy is considered to induce autoimmune inflammation of the auricular cartilage based on the coincidence and response to antituberculosis drugs.
output: Auricular chondritis associated with cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis

A baby girl delivered vaginally at full-term at a local hospital was found to have a global decrease in tone which was predominately in her arms. She had been born after an induction of labour because of decreased movements and oligohydramnios seen at 39 weeks of gestation on ultrasound.An ultrasound of the baby's head soon after birth demonstrated no obvious abnormalities. However, a T1-gadolinium enhanced MRI of the brain and spine showed an enhancing, intramedullary lesion extending from the medulla down to the upper thoracic spinal cord—indicating a possible high-grade neoplasm (figure). The patient was transferred to our quaternary referral hospital and comprehensive cancer centre.
On examination, the baby was awake and alert, with a flat fontanelle, normal head circumference, and global hypotonia. Over the next 2 weeks, her quadriparesis became progressively worse—the cervical spine showed signs of compression because of the expansile tumour in the spinal canal. We decompressed the cervical spine by doing a laminoplasty; we used electrostimulation, neuromonitoring, and intraoperative ultrasound to locate a safe midline entry point to obtain a biopsy and partially debulk the tumour. Histopathological analysis of a biopsy sample confirmed the suspected diagnosis of congenital spinal cord glioblastoma WHO grade IV.
Next generation sequencing showed a gene fusion involving the neurotrophin tropomyosin receptor kinase (NTRK) 1 gene: an inversion on chromosome 1q. No other pathogenic mutations, amplifications, deletions, or rearrangements were identified. Additionally, the tumour showed diffuse tropomyosin receptor kinase (TRK) positivity; she was treated with induction chemotherapy and the oral TRK inhibitor, larotrectinib, starting at a 50% dose of 50 mg/m2 twice a day for the first week to monitor for possible signs of toxicity because of the concurrent chemotherapy. The full dose of 100 mg/m2 twice a day was started in week 2 and continued. The patient tolerated the treatment well, and following cycle 1 of only conventional chemotherapy, a small reduction in size of the spinal cord tumour was seen.
2 weeks after the addition of larotrectinib, we observed a significant decrease in the size and enhancement on MRI of the lesion, with improvement in the patient's quadriparesis.
8 weeks into treatment with the oral TRK inhibitor and 4 cycles of carboplatin and etoposide, the tumour had completely regressed and was no longer visible with imaging (figure). 17 months after starting treatment, the patient was crawling and progressing toward walking; she continues treatment on the oral TRK inhibitor only, and there was no evidence of recurrence of the tumour.
The NTRK genes—NTRK1, NTRK2, and NTRK3 which produce TRK proteins—are affected by oncogenic fusions leading to a wide range of both paediatric and adult neoplasms. Small molecule TRK inhibitors have shown efficacy in treating a diverse array of TRK-positive tumours. In clinical trials of TRK inhibitors for tumours—in both adult and paediatric patients with a variety of different primary tumour types with NTRK gene fusions—response rates ranged from 75–93%. The first generation TRK inhibitors appear, on the whole, to be well tolerated in terms of adverse events: most are low grade—including neurotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, anaemia and neutropenia, and nausea and vomiting.
Aided by histopathological examination findings, next generation sequencing can uncover NTRK fusions that may change the clinical course for patients with many primary tumours. While we could not entirely rule out a response to chemotherapy alone resulting in the improvement seen in our patient, the prognosis for congenital glioblastomas treated with chemotherapy alone remains very poor (video).
output: High grade, primary tumours of the brain and spine in infants do not harbour druggable oncogenic targets.

input: A 53-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer receiving 3-week cycles of vinorelbine (30 mg/m2 on days 1 and 8) plus capecitabine 2000 mg/m2 (days 1–14) at the All India Institute of Medical Science (New Delhi, India) developed a large erythematous lesion at the chemotherapy port site on her left chest after day 4 of vinorelbine therapy (figure). The lesion was slowly progressive with ulceration and bullae formation. A dye study showed that the catheter was intact and it was in position. She was managed with antibiotics (oral amoxicillin–clavulanic acid 625 mg three-times daily for 7 days), subcutaneous injection of hyaluronidase 900 IU, and warm compression and showed signs of recovery. At 4 months (May 17, 2016), she was recovering with a firm scar over the left chest wall. The chemotherapy port was excised surgically in view of partial thrombosis.

A 69-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the ophthalmology clinic for a routine ocular examination. He had a history of cataract surgery 3 years ago for a retinal detachment in the right eye. Clinical examination of the right eye showed a white substance covering the upper third of the iris. Visual acuity was 20/400 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye. What is the diagnosis?
output:
Silicone oil emulsification in the anterior chamber

This image shows silicone oil that has migrated into the anterior chamber and accumulated in the superior portion (appearing as the white/milky substance covering the upper third of the iris). This is a known complication following vitreoretinal surgery where silicone oil was used as a tamponade agent for retinal detachment repair. The emulsified silicone oil droplets rise to the top of the anterior chamber due to their lower specific gravity compared to aqueous humor.

A 25-year-old man presented to our department with a 5-year history of an insidious, progressive weakness in his right hand. Despite being right-handed, he had recently become reliant on his left hand to carry out tasks needing manual dexterity. A CT of the patient's abdomen and pelvis showed no abnormalities or extra-thoracic lymphadenopathy. Laboratory investigations showed a raised high-sensitive cardiac troponin-I (hs-TNI) concentration (60·6 ng/L; normal range 2·0–19·9), brain natriuretic peptide concentration (380; normal range 0–100), and C-reactive protein concentration (55 mg/l; normal 0–0·5).
Viral serology ruled out recent viral infection; HIV serology, serum angiotensin-converting-enzyme, autoimmune screen, and TB ELISpot were negative. Transthoracic echocardiography and cardiovascular MRI (CMRI) confirmed a global pericardial effusion with thickened basal—mid-inferior and inferior-lateral—left ventricular walls and mild biventricular dysfunction. Histopathology and immunohistochemistry ruled out lymphoma, malignant histiocytosis, and amyloidosis; Ziehl-Neelsen stains were negative for mycobacteria.

However, the atypical cardiac features prompted us to seek further tissue samples prior to starting a glucocorticoid: a biopsy of the right inguinal lymph node showed necrotising granulomatous inflammation, and PCR showed Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Based on the serum hs-TNI, the extensive pericardial and myocardial inflammation on PET and CMRI, and confirmation with PCR, we revised the diagnosis to tuberculous perimyocarditis. A 52-year-old builder with a 6-year history of neck pain and dysphagia was referred to our rheumatology unit by a spinal neurosurgeon who was concerned the patient might have axial spondyloarthritis.
A review of the patient's history found that at age 45 years, he had been referred to the spinal surgeons; an x-ray and CT scan of the cervical spine showed osteophytosis at C5-C7 (figure). The radiologist had noted elongation of the styloid processes and calcification of the stylohyoid ligaments, suggestive of Eagle's syndrome.
Aged 47 years, new osteophytosis within mid and lower cervical spine were noted after the patient had a work-related injury.
Aged 50 years, the patient had been referred to both the neurosurgeons due to persistent neck symptoms, and to the Ear, Nose, and Throat (ENT) department because of ongoing dysphagia. The conclusion at that time was that the main reason for his dysphagia was laryngospasm and that his cervical osteophytosis was unlikely to be a contributing factor.
Additionally, the patient had a history of long-standing rosacea and folliculitis, a metallic heart valve, hypertension, a stroke, and gout; he was prescribed medication which included warfarin, atorvastatin, bisoprolol, allopurinol, and isotretinoin. The prescription of isotretinoin, which had been started 13 years earlier to treat the rosacea, necessitated the patient remaining under the care of the dermatology department. He was an ex-smoker.
On examination, we found the patient to be well; his BMI was 29·0 kg/m2 (typical range 18·5–24·9), his blood pressure was 142/82 mm Hg, and he had limited movement in his cervical spine, brisk reflexes, and some paraesthesia, which we considered to be related to his previous stroke. The patient had reduced movement in his left hip—consistent with advanced osteoarthritis. He had no skin rashes or peripheral synovitis.
Laboratory investigations found a typical C-reactive protein concentration (<0·5 mg/dL; normal range 0·3–1·0), total vitamin D concentration of 85 nmol/L (typical range 50–100), alkaline phosphatase concentration of 79 IU/L (typical range 30–130), parathyroid hormone concentration of 7·2 pmol/L (typical range 1·5–7·6), HbA1c concentration of 35 mmol/mol (typical range 20–41), estimated glomerular filtration rate of 82 mL/min/1·73 m2, and triglycerides concentration of 1·2 mmol/L (typical range <2·3). Testing for HLA-B27 was negative.
A review of previous x-rays showed progressive ossification of the patient's cervical spine, which impinged on adjacent soft-tissue structures—including the oesophagus (figure). An MRI confirmed multi-level spinal ossification consistent with a degenerative, rather than an inflammatory process; no evidence of axial spondyloarthritis or radiographic axial spondyloarthritis—which is also termed ankylosing spondylitis—was seen.
Furthermore, even though our patient had features of the metabolic syndrome—associated with diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis—the relatively young age at which his symptoms began, and the speed of progression of the symptoms indicated an alternative diagnosis. Considering the x-ray and MRI findings together with the absence of any markers of inflammation—ruling out diagnoses of axial spondyloarthritis or any other inflammatory arthropathies—and the history of isotretinoin treatment, we concluded the patient had retinoid-induced diffuse skeletal hyperostosis. We recommended that the isotretinoin was stopped, and the patient was again referred to the spinal surgeons for consideration of surgery to improve his dysphagia. At follow-up aged 53 years the patient was seen again by the ENT and spinal neurosurgeons and was listed for excision of his cervical osteophytosis.
Arthralgia and new bone formation have been recognised as side-effects of isotretinoin since it was first licensed for treatment of disorders of keratinisation—including severe cystic acne. Osteophytes involving the anterior margin of the cervical vertebrae may cause dysphonia, dyspnoea, or dysphagia. Clinicians need to be aware that the effects of retinoid-associated skeletal toxicity can be seen within 6 months of initiating treatment—although prompt withdrawal of the drug can prevent irreversible ossification.

A preterm baby—delivered by caesarean section at 36 weeks and 5 days due to pathological trace on cardiotocography—presented immediately after birth with tachypnoea, and sternal, intercostal, and subcostal recessions.The pregnancy had been normal, the baby's birthweight was 2825 g and the Apgar scores were 7, 8, and 9 at 1, 5, and 10 min.
The baby was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit and after he was initially stabilised using continuous positive airway pressure, he required nasal continuous positive airway pressure of 7 mbar. During the first day of life, the fraction of inspired oxygen increased from 0·3 to 0·6.
At this stage, we thought the most likely diagnosis was respiratory distress syndrome, transient tachypnoea of the newborn, neonatal sepsis, or pneumothorax.
Laboratory investigations found normal C-reactive protein (0·5 mg/dL; normal <1·5) and interleukin-6 concentrations (90·1 pg/mL; normal <100); there was no leukopenia or leukocytosis. A raised bilirubin concentration (16·48 mg/L; normal 0·0–14·6) was effectively treated with light emitting diode phototherapy using a fibre optic phototherapy blanket for 14 h.
A lung ultrasound showed no signs of respiratory distress syndrome, transient tachypnoea of the newborn, or pneumothorax. However, in the parasternal view—usually a helpful window for the assessment of the tracheal tube position and where the great vessels are visible below the thymus in the healthy infant—a stairway-like set of horizontal hyperechogenic reflections was seen instead of the great vessels indicating the presence of trapped air below the thymus (figure; video).
A chest x-ray confirmed that the patient did not have respiratory distress syndrome or a pneumothorax, and showed a large, clearly defined radiolucent structure above the heart—known as the spinnaker sign—indicative of pneumomediastinum and affirming the findings and diagnosis made using the lung ultrasound (figure).
The patient was successfully weaned off respiratory support within 5 days and was allowed home after 8 days; no drainage was necessary.
We believe that—based upon the current literature and our findings in this case—a lung ultrasound can differentiate between some of the key causes of acute respiratory conditions in the neonate—namely, respiratory distress syndrome, transient tachypnoea of the newborn, pneumonia, pneumothorax, and pneumomediastinum. We would like to propose that the distinctive finding of a set of horizontal hyperechogenic reflections below the thymus—indicating pneumomediastinum—be known as the stairway sign.
Pneumomediastinum after birth is an uncommon condition—defined as air trapped in the mediastinum—presenting with signs of respiratory distress, uneven chest expansion, and muffling of cardiac sounds. Resolution usually occurs within 1–2 days and, in most cases, no specific treatment is needed. Risk factors associated with pneumomediastinum include prematurity, the need for positive pressure ventilation, pneumonia, and meconium aspiration. Patients need to be closely observed—depending upon the severity of the air leak and the ability of the infant to compensate for the respiratory distress—due to the risk of further deterioration, and possible pneumothorax or emphysema.

A 57-year-old native English-speaking man attended our department with a 5-week history of progressively becoming unable to understand words—despite hearing them. Much to his distress, he also reported hearing a constant noise which he said sounded “like trucks”.18 months earlier, the patient had presented with dysphagia due to an inoperable adenocarcinoma in the oesophagogastric junction which had been treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy; he had no other relevant medical history and no previous hearing difficulties.
On examination we found the patient to be healthy with normal vital signs. Left and right external auditory canals were normal with intact and mobile tympanic membranes. We found he could identify and distinguish syllables, rhythms, voices, musical instruments, and individual environmental sounds even without visual cues, but he could not discern their content or structure, describing what he heard as being “all mushed together”. He reported no difficulties with reading, writing, or cognition. He also had vertical diplopia on downward gaze and to either side—indicating mild bilateral fourth nerve palsies; he had normal pupils, eyelids, convergence, and vertical eye movements.
While pure-tone audiometry showed only a mild to moderate bilaterally, almost symmetrical, sensorineural hearing loss (figure), he was unable to understand speech in either ear, even at 100 decibels hearing level (dB HL)—which is as loud as a nightclub (figure). T1-weighted sagittal MRI showed a contrast-enhancing 20 mm mass in the quadrigeminal cistern compressing the midbrain tectum and including both inferior colliculi (figure). The lesion—which we assumed to be metastatic—was treated with stereotactic radiotherapy.
Since his pure-tone audiometric abnormalities—a mild to moderate pure-tone hearing loss—could not account for his profound speech comprehension impairment, we made the diagnosis of word deafness due to the mass compressing the inferior colliculi. We were able to teach the patient and his family to communicate using a smartphone voice-to-text translator.
3 months later, a repeat MRI showed that the mass had reduced in size and enhancement. We repeated the pure-tone audiometry which was essentially unchanged: speech comprehension was now normal with his left ear and mildly impaired in his right at 40 db HL—like in a quiet library (figure). The patient died 2 months later.
Pure tones used in audiometry are simple sounds without the complex structure of speech, which has rapid, unpredictable fluctuations in frequency, amplitude, and timing. The cochlea converts sound into neural signals that ascend from the cochlear nuclei, via the lateral lemnisci, to the inferior colliculi and then to the medial geniculate nuclei and on to the auditory cortex.
The auditory pathway processes sound timing and frequency extracting features that indicate what and where the sound is. The inferior colliculi begin to integrate the features that create an auditory object: the assignment of a sound to a specific source.
A general inability to perceive and identify the nature of any sounds is called auditory agnosia; although patients can hear pure tones, all complex sounds lose meaning, such that they cannot recognise or understand speech, music, or environmental sounds. The usual cause is bilateral temporal lobe lesions. A specific inability to understand speech, despite intact hearing of pure tones and intact language comprehension, is called verbal auditory agnosia (or word deafness); only speech sounds lose meaning, probably due to impaired processing of their rapidly changing acoustic content. The usual cause is bilateral lesions of the superior temporal gyrus or their projections, or—like our case—a single brainstem lesion of the inferior colliculi.
Testing hearing with speech, as well as with pure tones, evaluates the full bandwidth of the auditory pathway. It is important to bear in mind that if patients complain that they can’t hear, sometimes the problem is not in the ear (video).

A 66-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 5-year history of recurrent episodes of epigastric burning pain, bloating, and constipation. In the past 3 months, the patient reported that his symptoms had resulted in him losing 4·5 kg in weight.He had a medical history of hypertension, but reported he was not taking any medications—specifically aspirin or any non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
On examination the patient was generally well; his blood pressure was 147/91 mm Hg, and his pulse rate was 95 beats per min. The patient had mild epigastric and right upper quadrant abdominal distention; hypoactive bowel sounds were heard in the right upper quadrant region.
Laboratory investigations found a positive test for Helicobacter pylori using the 13C-urea breath test.
CT of the patient's abdomen showed gastric dilation above the junction between the gastric antrum and the duodenum where the calibre of the gastric antrum reduced substantially in diameter (figure).
The patient initially underwent gastric decompression using a nasogastric tube; he was then prescribed a 14-day course of H pylori triple therapy—consisting of a proton pump inhibitor (pantoprazole), and the antibiotics clarithromycin and amoxicillin.
An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, done for further diagnostic evaluation, showed gastric stenosis and chronic gastritis. Immunohistopathological examination of a sample of biopsied tissue section confirmed the presence of H pylori with no evidence of gastric dysplasia.
The patient's symptoms were alleviated within 2 days, and after a successful oral food challenge with a regular diet, he was allowed home.
At 3-month follow-up, the patient remained asymptomatic; a repeat upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed stenotic gastric regions—without any visible obstruction—and chronic inactive gastritis; further immunohistopathological examination of a sample of biopsied tissue was negative for H pylori, indicating successful eradication. The patient will be followed up episodically for the foreseeable future primarily to monitor for signs of gastric outlet obstruction recurrence.
Gastric outlet obstruction occurs in both acute and chronic peptic ulcer disease. Repeated episodes of acute peptic ulcer disease can cause progressive stenosis of the gastric antrum—as probably occurred in our patient—and subsequent gastric outlet obstruction.
Risk factors for peptic ulcer disease include poor diet and hygiene, reduced physical activity, use of NSAIDs and infection with H pylori. Notably, recurrent rates of obstruction due to peptic ulcer disease are variable; and interestingly, rates appear reduced in cases associated with H pylori. Endoscopic balloon dilation of the pylorus or more invasive surgical intervention is reserved for cases of gastric outlet obstruction that are not resolved with medical treatments.
Gastric outlet obstruction is a rare, but important, complication of peptic ulcer disease and identification of any risk factors—specifically infection with H pylori—aids diagnosis and treatment regimens.
output: Gastric outlet obstruction secondary to Helicobacter pylori-associated peptic ulcer disease

input: A 70-year-old man presented to his primary care physician with postprandial epigastric pain. He was prescribed antacids, which were ineffective; his weight then decreased by 11 kg in 3 months. Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy showed a mass in the antrum; histopathological analysis of a biopsy sample established that the mass was a signet-ring adenocarcinoma. Even before the biopsy was analysed, examination of the neck supported the diagnosis of cancer: the left supraclavicular lymph node was firm and enlarged (figure). The left supraclavicular lymph node is near the junction of the thoracic duct and the left subclavian vein, where the lymph from much of the body drains into the systemic circulation. An enlarged node can be the first sign of gastric cancer—and is often called Virchow's node, because the association between left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy and gastric cancer was first described by the German pathologist Rudolf Virchow (1821–1902). Virchow lectured and practised at the Charité Medical School of the Humboldt University of Berlin, where he discovered several facts fundamental to modern medicine.
output: Gastric adenocarcinoma with Virchow's node metastasis

He complained of polyuria and polydipsia for several days before admission, had an altered mental status, and extreme dehydration of both skin and mucous membranes with a prolonged capillary refill (>2 sec). The initial blood count was 6 130 000 red cells per mL, haemoglobin 18·8 g/dL, haematocrit 54·5%, and 555 000 platelets per mL. Blood biochemistry analyses showed ketoacidosis (pH 7·07, HCO3 9·7 mmol/L, and blood ketones >7 mg/dL) and stage 3 prerenal acute kidney injury. Inflammatory indexes and blood toxicology screening were negative. His clinical condition was rapidly deteriorating and he was extremely dehydrated, in shock, tachycardic, unresponsive to verbal stimuli, and developed Kussmaul breathing. Soon after massive haematemesis episodes, blood tests showed severe normochromic anaemia (haemoglobin 7·4 g/dL [reference 13–16 g/dL]).
The endoscopic examination after removal of abundant blood residues showed circumferential black oesophagus appearance, sparing only the first proximal 3–4 cm (figure A). The stomach was filled with blood material and several mobile clots. After thorough cleansing, no sources of active or recent bleeding were found in the stomach or the duodenum. No biopsy samples were collected to avoid the risk of perforation. A CT angiogram showed oesophageal wall thickening and millimetric gaseous microareolas in pneumomediastinum (gas bubbles smaller than 1 cm, indicating esophageal microperforation).
The patient was treated with exclusive parenteral nutrition with continuous insulin infusion and monitoring of glycaemia, proton-pump inhibitors infusion, oral sucralfate, intravenous fluconazole, and broad antibiotic intravenous coverage. Within 4 weeks, the epigastric pain had resolved and the patient was able to feed orally safely. A repeated oesophagogastroduodenoscopy 1 month after admission showed complete recovery of the oesophageal mucosa, except for the presence of mild circumferential scar striae (figure B; green arrow). Findings on CT angiogram of the chest and abdomen were normal.

Men are four times more affected than women and the peak incidence occurs at an average age of 67 years. A mortality rate of 7% has been reported, mainly linked to underlying diseases. To the best of our knowledge, this case is the first instance of so-called black oesophagus in paediatric age, perhaps an intriguing complication of childhood-onset diabetes. From the possible comorbidities, our patient had only diabetic ketoacidosis. Therefore, we hypothesise that blood hypo—perfusion due to the extreme dehydration linked with ketoacidosis was the main factor leading to oesophageal ischaemia. He had developed non-autoimmune diabetes (glutamate decarboxylase antibodies, islet tyrosine phosphatase 2 antibodies, insulin autoantibodies, and Zinc Transporter 8 antibodies were absent); HbA1c 14·5% at the age of 10 years, having multiple paternal inheritance. Although known to have a bulimic behaviour, his medical history was negative for gastrointestinal disorders and for gastrointestinal toxic drugs or caustic consumption.At admission, he had very poor metabolic control (glycaemia 840 mg/dL, HbA1c higher than 13%) because he had voluntarily withdrawn insulin and refused metformin. He complained of polyuria and polydipsia for several days before admission, had an altered mental status, and extreme dehydration of both skin and mucous membranes with a prolonged capillary refill (>2 sec). The initial blood count was 6 130 000 red cells per mL, haemoglobin 18·8 g/dL, haematocrit 54·5%, and 555 000 platelets per mL. Blood biochemistry analyses showed ketoacidosis (pH 7·07, HCO3 9·7 mmol/L, and blood ketones >7 mg/dL) and stage 3 prerenal acute kidney injury. Inflammatory indexes and blood toxicology screening were negative. His clinical condition was rapidly deteriorating and he was extremely dehydrated, in shock, tachycardic, unresponsive to verbal stimuli, and developed Kussmaul breathing. Soon after massive haematemesis episodes, blood tests showed severe normochromic anaemia (haemoglobin 7·4 g/dL [reference 13–16 g/dL]).
The endoscopic examination after removal of abundant blood residues showed circumferential black oesophagus appearance, sparing only the first proximal 3–4 cm (figure A). The stomach was filled with blood material and several mobile clots. After thorough cleansing, no sources of active or recent bleeding were found in the stomach or the duodenum. No biopsy samples were collected to avoid the risk of perforation. A CT angiogram showed oesophageal wall thickening and millimetric gaseous microareolas in pneumomediastinum (gas bubbles smaller than 1 cm, indicating esophageal microperforation).
The patient was treated with exclusive parenteral nutrition with continuous insulin infusion and monitoring of glycaemia, proton-pump inhibitors infusion, oral sucralfate, intravenous fluconazole, and broad antibiotic intravenous coverage. Within 4 weeks, the epigastric pain had resolved and the patient was able to feed orally safely. A repeated oesophagogastroduodenoscopy 1 month after admission showed complete recovery of the oesophageal mucosa, except for the presence of mild circumferential scar striae (figure B; green arrow). Findings on CT angiogram of the chest and abdomen were normal.

Men are four times more affected than women and the peak incidence occurs at an average age of 67 years. A mortality rate of 7% has been reported, mainly linked to underlying diseases. From the possible comorbidities, our patient had only diabetic ketoacidosis. input:
An 86-year-old woman with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis—reporting progressive dyspnoea, rated as Class II on the New York Heart Association Functional Classification, for the previous few months—had a transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) in our unit. The patient's valve was replaced with an aortic valve bio prosthesis (Evolut PRO/PRO+ 29 mm [Medtronic Evolut™]).
Immediately after the valve had been replaced, continuous electrocardiogram monitoring showed ST-segment elevation in all antero-septal leads. A coronary angiogram showed complete occlusion of the distal part of the left anterior descending artery (figure 1).We then did a mechanical embolectomy—using a stent retriever (enVast 4·5 × 37 mm [enVast™]) combined with vacuum-assisted aspiration—which resulted in the immediate restoration of blood flow in the blocked artery; no residual material was seen in the vessel on repeat angiography (figure 1).
The extracted material was amber-coloured, calcified, and 2 mm in size; histopathological examination showed that it was mostly composed of collagen, proteoglycans, and extracellular matrix—compatible with a fragment of a leaflet from the patient's original aortic valve (figure 2). Additionally, substrates appeared non-birefringent under polarised light, confirming the absence of polymer-coated device fragments.The patient's chest pain promptly resolved; concentration of high-sensitivity troponin peaked at 24 h (202 ng/L; normal value <14). The patient remained asymptomatic for 1 day after the operation.
On day 2 postoperatively, she developed severe abdominal pain; an abdominal CT scan showed patency of both the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries with radiological signs of intestinal ischaemia. The patient had abdominal surgery which was complicated by multiple-organ failure; she died 4 days after the index TAVR.
Embolisation of aortic valve debris is a feared complication during TAVR, typically resulting in cerebrovascular accidents, and mesenteric or peripheral ischaemia. Histological analysis of captured material from cerebral protective devices has previously been done.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report showing that embolisation of aortic valve debris—confirmed by histological examination—into coronary circulation can be extracted with a stent retriever. Coronary embolisation during TAVR is unpredictable and no effective preventive measures exist; conventional angioplasty is often unsuccessful because of the presence of the calcified, non-friable material inside the vessel.

A 69-year-old man with chronic renal impairment and tophaceous gout, who had recently taken traditional Chinese medicines, presented to our hospital after 4 days of right forearm redness and swelling. A well demarcated, erythematous, indurated, mildly tender plaque was present, extending from the dorsum of the right hand to the elbow (figure). He had a white blood cell count of 8·4 × 109 cells per L, haemoglobin concentration of 11·5 g/dL, platelet count of 146 × 109 per L, sodium concentration of 141 mmol/L, potassium concentration of 4·4 mmol/L, and creatinine concentration of 246 μmol/L.
He was given intravenous cefazolin, 2 g every 8 h, for presumed bacterial cellulitis. However, the rash progressed and blisters developed after 2 days (figure). A skin biopsy was done and a mucinous substance was observed. Histological results showed encapsulated yeast forms that stained positive with periodic acid-Schiff stain and Gomori methenamine silver stains, and mucoid capsules staining strongly with mucicarmine and Alcian blue (figure). Fungal cultures were positive for Cryptococcus gattii.
Blood fungal cultures, lumbar puncture, and unenhanced CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis did not reveal disseminated disease. Serum cryptococcal antigen was positive at a titre of 1:320. The patient started oral fluconazole 400 mg daily, dose adjusted for his renal function.
Further assessment for an underlying immunodeficiency was negative for HIV, anti-IFN-γ, and anti-granulocyte-macrophage colony stimulating factor antibodies. His peripheral blood mononuclear cells responded appropriately to BCG with or without IFN-γ and IL-12 stimulation. He had normal lymphocyte subsets. His IgG, IgA, and IgM were low initially but recovered when traditional Chinese medicines were discontinued.
Despite being on antifungal therapy, the patient's wound worsened, developing ulcerations and myositis (figure). He required surgical debridement and intraoperative tissue also showed C gattii. He was treated for 5 days with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B 200 mg daily and transited back to oral fluconazole therapy 400 mg daily. After 6 months of antifungal therapy, the skin had just begun to re-epithelise (figure).
Severe ulcerative cryptoccocal cellulitis is unusual and can occur in apparently immuncompetent hosts. We believe the patient's renal disease and use of traditional Chinese medicines (suspected to be adulterated with steroids, although these medicines were unavailable for testing) might have contributed to this infection.
output: Ulcerative cryptococcal cellulitis caused by Cryptococcus gattii

An 80-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with chest pain and shortness of breath.The patient had a long medical history of diabetes, ischaemic heart disease, and end-stage kidney disease requiring regular haemodialysis.
On examination we found him to be in acute distress, with bilateral ankle oedema, and basal lung crackles. An electrocardiogram showed ST segment depression over leads V2-V6 and a Q wave in lead III. Laboratory investigations showed a serum cardiac troponin T concentration of 1297 ng/L (normal <14) with an unaffected creatinine phosphate kinase level.
We made a diagnosis of an acute non-ST elevation myocardial infarction.
1 day after a percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stent insertion into the right coronary artery and mid-left anterior descending artery, he began to repeatedly vomit; he also developed a low-grade fever with a temperature of 37·8°C. An urgent chest x-ray (figure) showed a radio-opaque nodule—not seen in previous x-rays—in the right lower lung field. We initially wondered whether the patient had aspirated his denture but on review of the lesion we were unconvinced. However, on closer inspection using magnification, we found the radio-opaque object had a complex internal structure consisting of a microchip, a battery, and an electronic circuit (figure). Before the film was sent for reporting, our physician examined the patient and found a subcutaneous continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) transmitter device (FreeStyle Libre Flash Glucose Monitoring System, Abbott Laboratories, Chicago, IL) which had been displaced from deltoid muscle to the patient's back. We treated the patient as if he had a diagnosis of a nosocomial infection and his condition improved with intravenous piperacillin and tazobactam.
He was allowed home after 14 days and at follow-up 2 weeks later the patient was well with no angina or chest symptoms. However, the patient died 6 months later with a recurrent myocardial infarction.
In patients with a history of heart disease, unidentified electronic gadgets seen on chest x-ray might well be cardiac related—specifically pacemakers. Although CGM devices are typically located on the upper arm, they may slip—especially in semiconscious patients and those requiring frequent transfers—to other body parts. CGM devices may look like unexpected foreign objects on limited resolution x-rays. As CGM gains in popularity, health-care professionals should be able to identify CGM devices and be aware of their potential to move to unexpected positions where they may cause consternation on x-ray interpretation. Using appropriate magnification of x-rays may be necessary for recognising CGM devices.
output: Displaced subcutaneous continuous glucose monitoring device

A 69-year-old man with chronic renal impairment and tophaceous gout, who had recently taken traditional Chinese medicines, presented to our hospital after 4 days of right forearm redness and swelling. A well demarcated, erythematous, indurated, mildly tender plaque was present, extending from the dorsum of the right hand to the elbow (figure). He had a white blood cell count of 8·4 × 109 cells per L, haemoglobin concentration of 11·5 g/dL, platelet count of 146 × 109 per L, sodium concentration of 141 mmol/L, potassium concentration of 4·4 mmol/L, and creatinine concentration of 246 μmol/L.
He was given intravenous cefazolin, 2 g every 8 h, for presumed bacterial cellulitis. However, the rash progressed and blisters developed after 2 days (figure). A skin biopsy was done and a mucinous substance was observed. Histological results showed encapsulated yeast forms that stained positive with periodic acid-Schiff stain and Gomori methenamine silver stains, and mucoid capsules staining strongly with mucicarmine and Alcian blue (figure). Fungal cultures were positive for Cryptococcus gattii.
Blood fungal cultures, lumbar puncture, and unenhanced CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis did not reveal disseminated disease. Serum cryptococcal antigen was positive at a titre of 1:320. The patient started oral fluconazole 400 mg daily, dose adjusted for his renal function.
Further assessment for an underlying immunodeficiency was negative for HIV, anti-IFN-γ, and anti-granulocyte-macrophage colony stimulating factor antibodies. His peripheral blood mononuclear cells responded appropriately to BCG with or without IFN-γ and IL-12 stimulation. He had normal lymphocyte subsets. His IgG, IgA, and IgM were low initially but recovered when traditional Chinese medicines were discontinued.
Despite being on antifungal therapy, the patient's wound worsened, developing ulcerations and myositis (figure). He required surgical debridement and intraoperative tissue also showed C gattii. He was treated for 5 days with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B 200 mg daily and transited back to oral fluconazole therapy 400 mg daily. After 6 months of antifungal therapy, the skin had just begun to re-epithelise (figure).
Severe ulcerative cryptoccocal cellulitis is unusual and can occur in apparently immuncompetent hosts. We believe the patient's renal disease and use of traditional Chinese medicines (suspected to be adulterated with steroids, although these medicines were unavailable for testing) might have contributed to this infection.
output: Severe ulcerative cryptococcal cellulitis caused by Cryptococcus gattii

A 50-year-old man with a 2-year history of a dry cough and mild exertional dyspnoea was referred to our lung disease clinic. The patient—who was originally from Turkey—had a significant cigarette smoking history but no relevant occupational exposures.Physical examination was unremarkable. A chest x-ray was normal and lung function testing showed a moderate reduction in diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide: 72% predicted. A high-resolution CT scan of the patient's chest demonstrated extensive septal thickening and ground glass abnormalities in a crazy-paving pattern (figure; appendix).
Differential diagnoses we considered at this stage included organising pneumonia, lymphangitic spread of a tumour, lipoid pneumonia, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and atypical infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii.
A bronchoscopy and transbronchial biopsies were performed. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was normal in appearance and no pathogens were identified. Transbronchial biopsy showed architecturally preserved alveoli filled with amorphous material positive for periodic acid-Schiff, granular material, and foamy alveolar macrophages (figure).
Immunohistochemistry showed surfactant protein B proprotein in the intra-alveolar material and cytoplasmic staining in the adjacent alveolar epithelial type II pneumocytes (appendix). Surfactant protein C proprotein was also expressed in alveolar epithelial type II pneumocytes but absent in the intra-alveolar material (appendix).
Taken together, the findings were consistent with a diagnosis of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) syndrome. Serum concentration of antibodies to granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) was raised at 33 μg/mL (normal <5), confirming the diagnosis. Over the subsequent 12 months, the patient reported increasing dyspnoea on exertion and his pulmonary function tests declined. He is under consideration for whole lung lavage or inhaled recombinant GM-CSF therapy.
PAP is a rare syndrome characterised by alveolar surfactant accumulation resulting in progressive dyspnoea and hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Autoimmune PAP accounts for 90–95% of cases; notably dust exposure, infection, and myelodysplastic syndrome are among several secondary causes of PAP.
An important clinical feature of PAP is a discrepancy between the severity of chest CT findings and patients' symptoms—as seen in our patient whose symptoms were mild despite a markedly abnormal chest CT. GM-CSF autoantibody levels in serum are reported to be close to 100% sensitive and specific for autoimmune PAP, and their measurement can prevent delay in the diagnosis. A 71-year-old woman attended our hospital with a 2-week history of fluctuating confusion.
The patient, who lived in the German state of Bavaria, close to agricultural areas, had no medical history; she was prescribed no regular medications.
On examination at admission, the patient was well and orientated; her vital signs were within typical range. Neurology examination was within normal limits.
Laboratory investigations on admission for systemic infection, liver function, and kidney function were within typical range.
A chest x-ray showed no abnormalities; an electrocardiogram showed a right bundle branch block and electroencephalography showed no epileptiform discharges.
2 days after admission, the patient rapidly became increasingly encephalopathic; she developed aphasia, atactic movements, and fluctuating vigilance resulting in a state of unresponsive wakefulness syndrome on day 16 after admission.
Brain MRIs on days 2, 5, and 14 after admission showed no abnormalities (figure 1).Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) on days 2, 5, and 20 after admission showed repeatedly raised total protein concentration ranging from 0·41 to 0·57 g/L (typical range 0·15–0·45); all other measurements were within normal range or unclear with regard to diagnosis (appendix; table 1).
Since MRIs and further tests were not conclusive, 18fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT of the brain was done on day 8 which showed marked hypermetabolism in the basal ganglia, the temporomesial lobes, and the cerebellum; frontal and parietal lateral cortex showed distinct hypometabolism (figure 2).
On day 19 after admission, a whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT showed progression of the abnormalities found in the initial scan (figure 2).
Considering a probable autoimmune pathology, the patient was treated with high-dose glucocorticoids—increasing to a maximum of 4 g methylprednisolone after 5 days and then tapering down—and intravenous immunoglobulins (2 g/kg of bodyweight) without any clinical response.
On day 34 after admission, T2 FLAIR and diffusion-weighted MRIs showed hyperintensities in the basal ganglia and head of the caudate nucleus (figure 1) indicating possible Borna disease virus 1 (BoDV-1) encephalitis.
Retrospective analysis, done on day 37 after admission, of CSF taken on days 5 and 20 after admission using reverse-transcription quantitative polymerase-chain-reaction (RT-qPCR) was positive for BoDV-1 RNA with quantification cycle values of 34·3 and 32·5, respectively.
Testing for BoDV-1-antibodies was negative until day 35 after admission; seroconversion occurred on day 42 (indirect immunofluorescence antibody test 1:1280, line blot BoDV-1-phosphoprotein 14 arbitrary units [AU], BoDV-1-nucleoprotein 22 AU; appendix, table 2).
On day 49 after admission, the patient died. Post-mortem histology, BoDV-1-specific immunohistochemistry (appendix, figure 2), and RT-qPCR on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue confirmed BoDV-1 encephalitis. A timeline was constructed of the patient's case (appendix, figure 1).
18F-FDG PET/CT findings may aid the diagnosis of patients with unexplained encephalitis and may—as in our patient—precede MRI changes. In Rasmussen encephalitis and anti-leucine glioma-inactivated protein 1 autoimmune encephalitis, for example, brain MRI has been reported as being less sensitive when compared to 18F-FDG PET/CT. In herpes simplex virus encephalitis, temporal lobe, ventral striatal, and septal abnormalities have been described on 18F-FDG PET/CT. And in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, 18F-FDG PET/CT may show hypometabolism in the basal ganglia, the occipital, frontal and parietal lobes, and in regions of the brain specifically related to clinical signs.
BoDV-1 infection is a potentially lethal zoonosis in endemic regions with reported spillover infections in horses and sheep. BoDV-1 infection can result in fatal encephalitis; all severe encephalitis cases of unknown cause should be tested for bornaviruses—especially in endemic regions.

A 37-year-old man presented to our emergency room with a sudden onset of partial loss of vision and diplopia while driving home 2 h earlier. The patient was previously fit and well and had no medical history.On examination we found him to be alert and oriented. Temperature was 37·6°C, pulse was 93 beats per min, and blood pressure was 130/89 mm Hg supine and 120/75 mm Hg erect. Neurological examination showed the patient to have decreased visual acuity in both eyes with a bitemporal hemianopia; we observed no oculomotor palsies and no sensory or motor deficits.
Laboratory investigations showed no abnormalities.
Brain MRI showed a partially cystic sellar and suprasellar mass that was hyperintense on T1-weighted images and hypointense on T2-weighted images without clear contrast enhancement. The optic chiasm was compressed and displaced by the lesion (figure).
Endocrinological work-up showed a slightly elevated serum prolactin concentration of 30 ng/mL (normal <20 in men); all other pituitary function studies—including thyroid-stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, adrenocorticotropic hormone, cortisol, insulin-like growth factor 1, testosterone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and luteinising hormone—were within normal ranges.
We then embarked upon a transsphenoidal endoscopic resection of what we thought was a pituitary adenoma in a patient with pituitary apoplexy. However, on removal of the sella floor, the classic white-greyish discolouration of the dura was not evident: the sella had a more purplish appearance—and although this might have been attributable to intrasellar haemorrhage, a small scratch of this layer produced a mass with yellow crystalline-like fluid. Progressive resection was performed using sharp dissection and curettes, and no evidence of haemorrhage was found; after near complete resection, a dural layer came, surprisingly, into view. A 4 mm 45° endoscope was inserted for verification and this confirmed that the dural layer was intact with no intraoperative cerebrospinal fluid leakage. Further, we observed no cavernous sinus invasion or mass remnant. Postoperatively, the patient had complete resolution of his diplopia and visual deficit and no evidence of diabetes insipidus.
Histopathological examination showed the tumour consisted of fibrous tissue with cholesterol clefts, lympho-plasma-cellular infiltrates, marked haemosiderin deposits, multinucleated giant cells, granular necrotic debris, and accumulations of foamy macrophages; no epithelial cells positive for epithelial membrane antigen or cytokeratin were observed in any part of the tumour. A xanthogranuloma was therefore confirmed.
The patient was well with no neurological deficits or evidence of disease recurrence 12 months postoperatively.
Pituitary apoplexy—a clinical syndrome secondary to sudden haemorrhage or infarction—occurs in approximately 7% of pituitary adenomas; a severe headache, often accompanied by visual disturbances, is commonly the presenting complaint. Xanthogranulomas of the sellar region are extremely rare and might be misdiagnosed as macroadenomas presenting with pituitary apoplexy if—as in our case—the lesion is an intrasellar, extradural xanthogranuloma with suprasellar extension (video).

A 37-year-old man presented to our emergency room with a sudden onset of partial loss of vision and diplopia while driving home 2 h earlier. The patient was previously fit and well and had no medical history.On examination we found him to be alert and oriented. Temperature was 37·6°C, pulse was 93 beats per min, and blood pressure was 130/89 mm Hg supine and 120/75 mm Hg erect. Neurological examination showed the patient to have decreased visual acuity in both eyes with a bitemporal hemianopia; we observed no oculomotor palsies and no sensory or motor deficits.
Laboratory investigations showed no abnormalities.
Brain MRI showed a partially cystic sellar and suprasellar mass that was hyperintense on T1-weighted images and hypointense on T2-weighted images without clear contrast enhancement. The optic chiasm was compressed and displaced by the lesion (figure).
Endocrinological work-up showed a slightly elevated serum prolactin concentration of 30 ng/mL (normal <20 in men); all other pituitary function studies—including thyroid-stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, adrenocorticotropic hormone, cortisol, insulin-like growth factor 1, testosterone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and luteinising hormone—were within normal ranges.
We then embarked upon a transsphenoidal endoscopic resection of what we thought was a pituitary adenoma in a patient with pituitary apoplexy. However, on removal of the sella floor, the classic white-greyish discolouration of the dura was not evident: the sella had a more purplish appearance—and although this might have been attributable to intrasellar haemorrhage, a small scratch of this layer produced a mass with yellow crystalline-like fluid. Progressive resection was performed using sharp dissection and curettes, and no evidence of haemorrhage was found; after near complete resection, a dural layer came, surprisingly, into view. A 4 mm 45° endoscope was inserted for verification and this confirmed that the dural layer was intact with no intraoperative cerebrospinal fluid leakage. Further, we observed no cavernous sinus invasion or mass remnant. Postoperatively, the patient had complete resolution of his diplopia and visual deficit and no evidence of diabetes insipidus.
Histopathological examination showed the tumour consisted of fibrous tissue with cholesterol clefts, lympho-plasma-cellular infiltrates, marked haemosiderin deposits, multinucleated giant cells, granular necrotic debris, and accumulations of foamy macrophages; no epithelial cells positive for epithelial membrane antigen or cytokeratin were observed in any part of the tumour. A xanthogranuloma was therefore confirmed.
The patient was well with no neurological deficits or evidence of disease recurrence 12 months postoperatively.
Pituitary apoplexy—a clinical syndrome secondary to sudden haemorrhage or infarction—occurs in approximately 7% of pituitary adenomas; a severe headache, often accompanied by visual disturbances, is commonly the presenting complaint. Xanthogranulomas of the sellar region are extremely rare and might be misdiagnosed as macroadenomas presenting with pituitary apoplexy if—as in our case—the lesion is an intrasellar, extradural xanthogranuloma with suprasellar extension (video).

**Mycoplasma pneumoniae serologic testing (IgM antibodies) and/or PCR testing, along with initiation of supportive care and macrolide antibiotic therapy (azithromycin or erythromycin)**
