On examination, hyperpigmented plaques were observed on the dorsa of both hands at the sites of previous intravenous access. The darkened skin extended up the arms in a linear pattern along the network of superficial veins; the lesions were palpable but non-tender. What is the most likely diagnosis?
output: Superficial thrombophlebitis with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (chemotherapy-induced phlebitis/hyperpigmentation)

A 58-year-old woman presented as an emergency with a 4-month history of intermittent upper abdominal pain, distension, and vomiting.She had a history of a hernia which had been repaired and augmented with prosthetic mesh 4 years earlier.
On examination, we found the patient to be apyrexial but not distressed. Her abdomen was slightly distended; she had normal bowel sounds with a non-tender fullness at the umbilicus—at the site of the earlier hernia repair—with no discharge.
Laboratory investigations showed a normal white cell count of 11·3 × 109 per L with a haemoglobin concentration of 14·6 g/dL (normal 13·0–16·5); her serum C-reactive protein concentration and renal function were both normal. An initial unprepared contrast enhanced CT showed gallstones and it also raised the possibility of a fistula between the small bowel and the mesh, because the mesh appeared adjacent to the slightly distended gut (figure). We managed the patient conservatively with intravenous fluids and kept her nil by mouth and her symptoms settled within 12 h.
However, 2 months later, at an outpatient appointment review, she continued to report pain and abdominal distention; a fully prepared CT suggested a stricture in the distal transverse colon. We carried out a colonoscopy and a biopsy which indicated that the lesion was malignant. We then did an open extended right hemicolectomy, cholecystectomy, and a segmental small bowel resection when we found the mesh from the earlier hernial repair intra-luminal (figure). Histopathological examination of a sample of the excised lesion showed a T4aN2a adenocarcinoma; the patient was then given adjuvant chemotherapy. At 12 months’ follow-up she remains symptom free.
Repairs of abdominal wall hernias are currently frequently augmented with prosthetic biomaterials—such as mesh—and this has resulted in minimal tension reconstruction and a lower later recurrence rate. However, the use of such prostheses, irrespective of type or size, may be associated with various complications including migration and visceral fistulation to the bladder, colon, or small bowel. The incidence of such fistulation—albeit clinically uncommon—remains uncertain, as not all cases give rise to symptoms. It is likely that many cases go unreported for a variety of reasons—including the possibility of litigation.
In the radiological report of our patient's initial CT scan, the presence of the mesh was considered incidental as she was not systemically unwell, she had few local symptoms, and the scan had shown gallstones. However, if symptoms persist—even causing only minimal discomfort, as in our patient—careful re-imaging is essential. Finally, although the migration of mesh into the gut lumen may be more common than is appreciated, it is crucial to consider that it might obscure more significant intra-abdominal pathologies, such as adenocarcinomas of the gut (video).
output: Colonic adenocarcinoma with mesh migration and entero-colonic fistula

A 67-year-old man presented with progressive dysphagia, weight loss, regurgitation, and halitosis. A barium swallow examination showed stasis of barium in the upper esophagus with an outpouching lesion anterior to the C5 and C6 vertebrae. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a Zenker’s diverticulum. These diverticula pass through which muscular defect?
output:
Killian's dehiscence (Killian's triangle)

This is the triangular area of weakness in the posterior pharyngeal wall located between the inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscle (specifically the thyropharyngeal muscle) superiorly and the cricopharyngeus muscle inferiorly. Zenker's diverticulum is a false diverticulum (pulsion diverticulum) that herniates through this muscular defect due to increased intraluminal pressure during swallowing against a poorly relaxing or hypertonic cricopharyngeus muscle.

A 62-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol abuse was admitted to our hospital with chronic diarrhoea, confusion, and weakness in both legs. Initial physical examination showed marked cachexia and decreased strength in both lower limbs. His sensation was intact. Laboratory testing showed several electrolyte abnormalities—presumed to be due to his diarrhoea—including hyponatraemia (130 mmol/L); this was gradually corrected over the course of 4 days, using 0·9% sodium chloride. At the end of this period, the sodium was 140 mmol/L (normal range 135–145 mmol/L). Over the next few days, he continued to be encephalopathic and eventually lost motor function of his arms and legs; his pupils continued to be reactive to light and the function of his extraocular muscles remained intact. An MRI scan of his brain showed restricted diffusion and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) showed a corresponding abnormality in the central pons that was consistent with a diagnosis of central pontine demyelination (figure). Sadly, the patient died in the intensive care unit after his family decided to pursue palliative care.
Osmotic demyelination syndrome—also known as central pontine myelinolysis or extrapontine myelinolysis—usually occurs after rapid correction of sodium abnormalities, although it might be seen secondary to chronic alcohol use, other severe electrolyte disturbances, and malnutrition. According to one theory, the lack of sufficient energy in malnourished patients leads to suboptimal functioning of the Na+/K+ATPase pump, which subsequently results in imbalances in sodium homoeostasis in the brain. A high degree of clinical suspicion that it is likely to occur in patients with chronic alcohol use and those who are malnourished might help to prevent the development of osmotic demyelination syndrome. Treatment is usually just supportive management. However, there have been some case reports of successful treatment with plasma exchange, methylprednisone, and immunoglobulins. MRI usually confirms the diagnosis, and the FLAIR sequence is used to suppress the effects of cerebrospinal fluid on the image—this is especially helpful in showing subtle changes at the periphery of the cerebral hemispheres and in the periventricular region.

A 64-year-old man presented with high fever (38–39°C oral temperature), severe joint pains with explosive onset, and substantial weight loss (4 kg in 1 month). On examination, he had dorsal oedema on the hands (figure) and symmetrically tender and swollen joints (ie, proximal interphalangeal joints, metacarpophalangeal joints, wrists, elbows, and knees). Additionally, he had generalised lymphadenopathy (bilateral upper cervical, left lower cervical, right supraclavicular, bilateral inguinal) and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory investigations were notable for anaemia (haemoglobin 8 g/dL), hypoalbuminaemia (2·8 g/dL), hyperglobulinaemia (5·2 g/dL), increased erythrocyte sedimentation (35 mm/h), and increased concentrations of C-reactive protein (11·3 mg/dL). Tests for antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and anticyclic citrullinated peptide were negative. PET scanning with 18-fluorodeoxyglucose showed avid lymph nodes on both sides of the diaphragm and uptake in both shoulders and the right wrist (figure). A cervical lymph node was excised for haematoxylin and eosin staining that showed architectural effacement by lymphoid cells (positive for PD-1 and CD3) surrounding an arborising network of high endothelial venules, which was suggestive of angio-immunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (figure). The patient was transferred to the haematology unit where chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (known as the CHOP regimen) was initiated, which resolved the fever and arthritis.Many aetiologies can cause fever with polyarthritis: infections (viral infections, infective endocarditis, Lyme disease), para-infections (rheumatic fever, reactive arthritis), true arthritis (adult-onset Still's disease), connective-tissue diseases (systemic lupus erythematosus), vasculitis (giant-cell arteritis, ANCA-associated vasculitis), and paraneoplastic arthritis. Paraneoplastic arthritis is arthritis secondary to solid-organ (particularly carcinomas) or lympho-reticular malignancy, which is not due to direct tumour infiltration. Important clues for paraneoplastic arthritis include advanced age, explosive onset, severe pain disproportionate to the pathological findings on examination, unresponsiveness to disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), substantial weight loss, highly increased acute-phase reactants, and seronegativity for rheumatoid factor, anticyclic citrullinated peptide, and antinuclear antibodies. Specific patterns such as asymmetric arthritis, lower-limb predominance, sparing of small joints, palmar fasciitis, and remitting seronegative symmetric synovitis with pitting oedema should alert the clinician to investigate for an underlying malignancy.
In this man's case, the underlying malignancy was angio-immunoblastic T-cell lymphoma. Although an uncommon non-Hodgkin lymphoma overall (1–2% of all patients diagnosed with lymphoma globally), it is common in patients with peripheral T-cell lymphomas (18% prevalence) and typically occurs in older people (median age 65 years). Angio-immunoblastic T-cell lymphoma is notorious for immune-activation features such as rash, arthritis, cytopenia, polychondritis, hypergammaglobulinaemia, and even positive autoantibodies. These symptoms are thought to be secondary to increased serum concentrations of pro-inflammatory cytokines, notably TNFα and interleukin-6 secreted by the tumour cells. The case highlights the importance of clues such as disease onset at an older age, explosive-onset joint pain, weight loss, and a thorough general examination (to detect lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly) to make an accurate diagnosis of paraneoplastic arthritis.

A 13-year-old girl presented with a 2-week history of mild pain in her right knee. She reported no recent injury. x-rays showed a high-density linear abnormality with a periosteal reaction in the proximal right tibia (figure), which medical staff, at the hospital where she was first seen, thought might have been a tumour of the bone.On examination in our hospital, we found the patient to have some tenderness in the proximal right tibia with no swelling, ecchymosis, or any obvious deformity. The patient had normal range of movement of the knee and no restriction in squatting.
MRI showed a rough hypointense fracture line surrounded by an extensive hyperintense area of bone marrow oedema in the T2-weighted image (figure) clearly indicating a fracture of the tibia. Further, on closer questioning, the patient remembered that she had recently fallen on her knees while walking. After 4 weeks of rest and restricted weight bearing, the patient had no further trouble with pain during daily activity.
An x-ray repeated 4 weeks after the initial presentation showed a healed fracture with obvious bone callus formation (figure); the repeat MRI showed that the bone marrow oedema had receded (figure).
An occult fracture—often known as a bone contusion or bone bruising—is defined as a fracture that cannot be seen on conventional x-ray or radiographically shows subtle abnormalities which are prone to be overlooked or misdiagnosed at initial presentation. In most cases the bone marrow oedema will completely disappear after 6–12 weeks. For most occult fractures without severe ligament or articular cartilage injury, conservative therapy is the first-line treatment—including analgesia treatment and weight-bearing restriction.
In children with symptoms of swelling, pain, or redness, and a fracture of the bone—particularly either side of the knee or in the upper arm—the diagnosis must be considered to be a malignancy until proven otherwise.

Based on the MRI image and the clinical history, the diagnosis is a **Giant intracranial aneurysm**.

**Analysis:**
The MRI image (T2-weighted axial view) displays a very large, well-circumscribed, round mass in the left middle cranial fossa (left temporal lobe region). The lesion shows a characteristic mixed signal intensity with a "swirling" or "onion-skin" pattern, which represents concentric layers of thrombus within the aneurysm sac. There is also a distinct dark rim and areas of signal void (black), indicating rapid blood flow in the patent portion of the lumen. The mass is causing significant mass effect, compressing the left lateral ventricle, shifting the midline to the right, and causing dilation of the contralateral ventricle (hydrocephalus). The clinical presentation of gradual neurological decline (confusion, memory loss, imbalance) is consistent with the mass effect exerted by this giant space-occupying lesion, a phenomenon sometimes referred to as a "tumor-like" presentation of a giant aneurysm.

**Diagnosis:**
Giant intracranial aneurysm

A 41-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 1-month history of worsening abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The patient gave no history of recent travel, previous abdominal surgery, or adverse reactions to any allergens. She had no past medical problems. However, 2 days before we saw her, the patient had a gastrointestinal endoscopy which found no abnormalities; gastroduodenal and colonic mucosal biopsies had also been reported as healthy.On examination we found the patient to be generally well; heart rate was 92 beats per min, blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 98%. She was afebrile. Her abdomen was tender and distended with bulging flanks and shifting dullness: indicative of ascites.
Laboratory investigations showed leukocytosis (19·54 × 109 per L; normal 4·5–11·0) associated with a significant eosinophilia of 8·94 × 109 per L (normal 0–0·5), a raised IgE concentration (208 IU/mL; normal 1·5–144), and a slightly elevated C-reactive protein concentration (43 mg/L; normal <3·1). CA125 concentration was elevated (83 units/mL; normal 0–35); no other tumour marker was positive. Serum tryptase concentration was normal and tests screening for autoimmune diseases—including antinuclear antibodies for systemic lupus erythematosus or scleroderma—found nothing abnormal.
A CT scan excluded any visceral lesions. A diagnostic paracentesis showed eosinophilic ascites (figure). Blood, stool, and ascites analyses, including specific serological examinations and cultures, excluded viral, bacterial, and parasitic infections. That some parasitic infections, such as Strongyloides stercoralis, can be hard to diagnose based on one stool sample, led us to do repeated parasitological examinations of different stool samples, which all showed no positive results.
Lymphocytic and myeloproliferative forms of hypereosinophilic syndrome were excluded: a bone marrow biopsy showed no abnormalities. Using RT-PCR, no FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion gene was found, and T-cell-receptor gene rearrangement testing of the patient's peripheral blood was negative. A QuantiFERON-TB test was also negative.
We suspected a case of eosinophilic gastroenteritis, but to rule out any intra-abdominal neoplasm and to collect biopsies from the caecum serosa, we did a laparoscopy. Histopathological analysis of biopsy specimens confirmed our suspicions: significant eosinophilic infiltration with greater than 20 eosinophiles per high-power field; the small vessels were not involved, ruling out an associated vasculitis (figure). The patient was started on oral methylprednisolone and her symptoms rapidly improved; the serum eosinophilia returned to a typical level.
Three patterns of eosinophilic gastroenteritis are described: mucosal, mural, and serosal. Diagnosis of the serosal form is often considered a challenge as clinical and radiological presentations can be atypical. Likewise, histological findings can be misleading, as mucosal biopsies in the serosal form of eosinophilic gastroenteritis may appear normal, unlike those of the serosal layers which can confirm the diagnosis.
The diagnosis is usually made based on the combined biological, radiological, and histological findings. Finally, a good response to oral corticosteroids—as happened in our patient—adds weight to making a correct diagnosis of eosinophilic gastroenteritis.

A previously healthy 2-year-old boy was brought to clinic with a 1-week history of itchy, red spots. Three days before the onset of the rash, the child had had an upper respiratory infection for which he had been given ibuprofen. On physical examination, tense vesicles and edematous pink plaques with central erosions and crust were seen on the patient’s legs, arms, and back. Dense clustering of skin lesions was observed in the axillae and inguinal folds. No mucosal involvement was noted. Histopathological analysis of a skin-biopsy sample obtained from the right lower back showed a subepidermal blister with robust neutrophilic infiltration. Direct immunofluorescence revealed a linear band of IgA along the dermoepidermal junction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
target: Linear IgA bullous dermatosis of childhood

A 71-year-old woman with a 3-month history of nausea, 5 kg weight loss, and a hypochromic microcytic anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 8·9 g/dL) was referred to our hospital by her family doctor for further investigation.On examination the patient was pale and had a palpable, non-tender epigastric mass.
Apart from the anaemia, laboratory investigations showed mild thrombocytosis (platelet count 589 × 109 per L) and elevated liver enzymes with a gamma glutamyl transferase concentration of 96 U/L and alkaline phosphatase concentration of 358 U/L.
Gastroscopy showed an ulcerating mucosal lesion on the lesser curve of the stomach which was biopsied and confirmed histologically as a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma; the tumour was human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) positive with an average HER2 gene copy number of 7·25 (normal <4·0), and an average chromosome 17 enumeration copy probe (CEP) number of 1·45 (normal <3·0), giving an elevated HER2: CEP17 ratio of 5·0 (a ratio of less than 2·0 indicates a negative result).
CT scan showed extensive epigastric, porta hepatis, and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy with several hypodense liver lesions, consistent with multiple metastases (figure). The clinical diagnosis was stage 4: non-curable gastric carcinoma.
Following oncology assessment, the patient was deemed suitable for chemotherapy—accepting the target of the treatment was at best a short-term extension of a predicted median survival of approximately 12 months. Trastuzumab—a humanised IgG1 monoclonal antibody that binds HER2-receptors in certain cancer cells inhibiting tumour cell growth—was prescribed in combination with cisplatin and capecitabine. She tolerated the chemotherapy well apart from some initial nausea; at follow-up 6 weeks after commencing treatment, she reported feeling well with no further nausea. At the 3-month review, the patient was clinically stable, and CT imaging showed that her cancer had resolved macroscopically; accordingly, cytotoxic chemotherapy was stopped at 18 weeks, but she continued trastuzumab therapy every 3 weeks for the next 7 years. At review, 21 months after stopping trastuzumab, the patient was still in complete remission, with no evidence on CT scan of malignant disease (figure).
In the Trastuzumab for Gastric Cancer (also known as ToGA) Trial, none of the HER2-positive randomly assigned patients with advanced gastric or oesophago-gastric cancer were alive at 36 months’ follow-up. However, as our case shows, some patients with HER2 receptor-positive gastric adenocarcinoma can experience complete long-term remission with good quality of life from protracted trastuzumab therapy.

The headache worsened with upright positioning and improved with lying flat. Physical examination, including fundoscopy, was normal. It also showed protrusion of the cerebellar tonsils (arrow) into the foramen magnum, flattening of the pons with effacement of the prepontine cistern (arrowhead), and enlargement of the pituitary gland owing to increased blood flow (asterisk; right image, T1 sequence without contrast). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
output:
Spontaneous intracranial hypotension
# Medical Knowledge for Beginners: Understanding Intracranial Hypotension

## Introduction

Intracranial hypotension is a condition characterized by reduced pressure within the skull. The "pop" sensation in the patient's back, followed by a positional headache that worsens when upright and improves when lying down, is a classic presentation. Let's understand what's happening here.

## Key Clinical Features

1. **Positional Headache**: The hallmark symptom - headache that:
   - Worsens when sitting or standing
   - Improves when lying flat
   - Often described as throbbing

2. **Triggering Event**: The "pop" in the back suggests a spontaneous cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak, likely from a dural tear in the spine.

## Understanding the Imaging Findings

The MRI shows several characteristic signs of low CSF pressure:

### 1. Diffuse Pachymeningeal Enhancement
- The thick outer covering of the brain (dura mater) shows abnormal enhancement with contrast
- This occurs because when CSF pressure drops, the blood vessels in the meninges dilate to compensate

### 2. Brain Sagging
- The cerebellar tonsils protrude downward into the foramen magnum
- This happens because reduced CSF "buoyancy" allows the brain to sink

### 3. Flattening of the Pons
- The brainstem appears compressed against the skull base
- Another consequence of the brain "slumping" downward

### 4. Pituitary Enlargement
- Increased blood flow to the pituitary gland
- A compensatory mechanism for the reduced CSF volume

## The Diagnosis

**Spontaneous Intracranial Hypotension (SIH)**

This condition occurs when CSF leaks from the spinal canal, reducing the pressure and volume of fluid surrounding the brain. The combination of the clinical history (sudden onset with positional component) and characteristic MRI findings confirms this diagnosis.

A 58-year-old man attended our hospital with a 3-month history of bloody diarrhoea, proctalgia, arthralgia, and weight loss. The patient said that when his symptoms began, he had noticed a rash that had recently become more conspicuous. Accompanying the change in the rash, he said he had developed a high fever.3 weeks before we saw him, the patient had been admitted to the surgical ward for treatment of an anal fistula; he was given oral antibiotics and the fistula was surgically debrided.
Additionally, in his medical history, he had type 2 diabetes, arterial hypertension, and dyslipidaemia: he was prescribed metformin, gliclazide, enalapril, a thiazide diuretic, and simvastatin.
On examination, the patient looked unwell: he had pale mucous membranes and a temperature of 37·5°C. He had extensive, well-delineated, erythematous, and mildly tender plaques on the upper part of his back, arms, and hands (figure); he had multiple non-tender mouth ulcers. His abdomen was generally mildly tender with no specific area of localisation. We found no other atypicalities.
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 7·6 g/dL (normal 13·0–16·5), white blood cell count of 7·6 × 109 per L (normal 4·5–11·0), neutrophil count of 6·0 × 109 per L (normal 2·0–7·0), and elevated acute phase reactants: ferritin concentration was 533 ng/mL (normal 25–400), erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 120 mm/h (normal 1–10), and C-reactive protein concentration was 15 mg/dL (normal <5).
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a skin biopsy showed a rich, diffuse, predominantly neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate (figure). At colonoscopy we found multiple star-shaped ulcers scattered throughout the colon with areas of preserved mucosa between them (figure); histological analysis showed active chronic colitis with crypt inflammatory destruction and abscesses.
Considering the myriad of clinical and histopathological findings, we concluded that the patient had Crohn's disease with an acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis—also known as Sweet's syndrome. The patient was given systemic corticosteroids and his gastrointestinal symptoms improved. His skin lesions significantly improved over the next 14 days, at which point he was started on adalimumab and allowed to go home.
Bloody stools and significant unintentional weight loss should raise the possibility of a serious systemic disease. The presence of a fever and skin lesions suggests an inflammatory, infectious, or paraneoplastic disorder. Mouth ulcers and a recent history of a perianal pathology—as seen in our patient—would suggest an inflammatory bowel disease: Crohn's disease. Sweet's syndrome should be considered in the case of a fever and neutrophilic dermal nodular plaques with a neutrophilia.
Sweet's syndrome represents a group of autoinflammatory skin lesions or neutrophilic dermatoses, associated with a wide variety of infections, haematological malignancies, and autoimmune and inflammatory disorders. The concurrence of Sweet's syndrome and Crohn's disease is rare. And in reality, Sweet's syndrome should be considered as an extraintestinal manifestation of Crohn's disease. Differentiation from the other inflammatory diseases accompanying Crohn's disease—including erythema nodosum and pyoderma gangrenosum—is key.

A 48-year-old Chinese man with a 12-month history of increasing shortness of breath on exertion was admitted to our hospital. He was a heavy smoker and had been diagnosed with Child-Pugh class C alcoholic cirrhosis 5 years earlier, which was complicated by oesophageal varices that haemorrhaged 1 month before this admission; he had an urgent gastroscopy and the varices were banded.On physical examination, he was asymptomatic while lying supine but dyspnoeic while sitting up. He had clubbing of his fingers (figure), clear lung fields, and pitting ankle oedema. An arterial blood gas while supine and breathing room air showed a partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) of 57 mm Hg with a widened alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient (Grad[A–a] O2) of 66 mm Hg (normal gradient for a 40-year-old man is less than 14 mm Hg). However, when the PaO2 was retaken while the patient was sitting upright, it dropped to 43 mm Hg. His chest x-ray was unremarkable.
Looking at these clinical features in the round, we suspected that our patient had hepatopulmonary syndrome. To confirm the diagnosis and to investigate the patient's pathophysiology further, we did a contrast-enhanced transthoracic echocardiography, which, with saline bubbles appearing in the left side of the heart, indicated intrapulmonary right-to-left shunting (figure). An intravenous injection of agitated saline in a healthy person will only show bubbles in the right side of the heart because they would be trapped by the pulmonary capillaries as they travel through the lung.
Hepatopulmonary syndrome is an important diagnostic consideration in patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension who present with respiratory symptoms and digital clubbing. The pathogenesis is poorly understood but leads to pulmonary vascular angiogenesis and intrapulmonary vascular dilatation: this causes a ventilation–perfusion mismatch, reduced oxygen diffusion, and intrapulmonary shunting. The symptoms of a gravity-dependent hypoxaemia—namely, dyspnoea, platypnoea (dyspnoea in an upright position), and orthodeoxia—are characteristic but not pathognomonic. A consensus group has defined a clinically relevant Grad(A–a) O2 in patients with the disease as at least 15 mm Hg (>20 mm Hg in those older than 64 years of age). The additional presence of digital clubbing and cyanosis would strongly suggest a diagnosis of hepatopulmonary syndrome. Additional investigations—including respiratory function tests and a chest CT—are non-specific but useful to exclude other causes of dyspnoea such as a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation. A technetium-99m-labelled macroaggregated albumin scan—where radioactively labelled particles are usually prevented from passing through the pulmonary veins—may help in the diagnosis of hepatopulmonary syndrome. However, the test also shows positive results in patients with intracardiac shunts. Long-term oxygen therapy provides symptomatic relief for patients with hepatopulmonary syndrome, but liver transplantation is the only definitive cure. Our patient was discharged home with continuous oxygen therapy at 4 L per min and is awaiting orthotopic liver transplantation.

A 60-year-old man was brought to our emergency room after he collapsed while working out in a gym. He was unable to speak to his personal trainer or move his right side after he fell. He had a history of uncontrolled hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and a previous left occipital stroke. When we saw him, his blood pressure was 205/115 mm Hg, which we controlled with intravenous nicardipine. He was not on any anticoagulation or antiplatelet medication. Physical examination showed the man had a profound right-sided hemiplegia, expressive aphasia, and leftward gaze deviation. A non-contrast CT scan (figure) of the man's head showed a 44 mL intracerebral haemorrhage in the left basal ganglia without intraventricular extension. CT angiography of the head showed a fusiform aneurysm characterised by a 1 cm dilatation of the left supraclinoid internal carotid artery distant from the haemorrhage site and no evidence of vascular malformation. A repeat non-contrast head CT, performed 6 h after the first, found that the clot had not increased in size. MRI of the patient's brain showed scattered small cerebellar and occipital infarcts, diffuse white matter disease, and subcortical small vessel disease.The following day, 36·5 h after symptom onset, we performed a left frontal minimally invasive endoscopic intracerebral haemorrhage evacuation with the Artemis aspiration device (Penumbra, Alameda, CA, USA) in our angiography suite. A non-contrast CT scan (figure) of the patient's head, performed on postoperative day 1, demonstrated that the haemorrhage had almost completely been evacuated, with just 1 mL remaining, and a small cavity in the place where the haematoma had been. After 2 weeks in the neurosurgical intensive care unit, the patient was discharged to an acute rehabilitation facility, where he regained movement in his right side and the ability to speak short phrases. 1 year after his haemorrhage, he was living independently with home nursing care and he was able to walk with a walker for assistance. A CT scan at that time showed a residual haematoma cavity (figure).
Minimally invasive intracerebral haemorrhage evacuation is an increasingly common surgical technique used to treat spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage. A study in The Lancet, evaluating a different minimally invasive evacuation technique—stereotactic catheter placement with aspiration and thrombolysis—showed that the intervention did not improve functional outcome in patients with intracerebral haemorrhage. However, the results did show that in a prespecified secondary analysis—when no more than 15 mL of haematoma remained at the end of the treatment—patients had improved functional outcome at 1 year compared to medically managed controls. Endoscopic intracerebral haemorrhage evacuation, as we have shown here, is an alternative type of minimally invasive evacuation technique, with some evidence suggesting that it can reliably meet established surgical goals.
Even though endoscopic intracerebral haemorrhage evacuation may be achievable in patients—as in our case—they may still be left with functional impairment. Further, it is worth noting that although minimally invasive evacuation can be technically successful, several other factors impact long-term clinical outcome in intracerebral haemorrhage, including baseline functional status, patient age, the presence or absence of intraventricular haemorrhage, severity of white matter disease, subsequent hospital complications, and other confounders: the true effect of this procedure remains unknown.

A 37-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 1-week history of pain and swelling in the left upper arm that had started after blunt trauma during soccer practice. The heart rate was 120 beats per minute, the blood pressure 96/54 mm Hg, and the body temperature 37.9°C. Examination of the left upper arm was notable for swelling, tenderness, and crepitus. The overlying skin was red and warm to the touch. An initial radiograph is shown. Which of the following factors is most associated with increased mortality in this diagnosis?
output:
Based on the clinical presentation and radiograph, this patient has **gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis)** of the left upper arm.

The radiograph shows characteristic findings of gas within the soft tissues of the upper arm, appearing as multiple lucent areas tracking along the muscle planes. Combined with the clinical presentation of:
- Rapid onset after trauma
- Pain, swelling, and crepitus
- Skin changes (erythema, warmth)
- Systemic signs (tachycardia, hypotension, low-grade fever)

The factor most associated with increased mortality in gas gangrene is:

**Delay in surgical debridement/treatment**

Other factors associated with increased mortality include:
- Truncal/proximal involvement (as opposed to distal extremity)
- Underlying malignancy or immunocompromised state
- Septic shock at presentation
- Clostridium septicum species (often associated with occult GI malignancy)
- Spontaneous (non-traumatic) gas gangrene

However, the **delay in surgical intervention** is consistently the most critical modifiable factor affecting mortality, as this condition progresses rapidly and requires emergent surgical debridement along with antibiotics and often hyperbaric oxygen therapy.

A 41-year-old woman presented to our hospital complaining of breathlessness and pain in the right side of her chest. She said that the problem was not new and that it happened every time she had her period: she had begun menstruating 24 h earlier.On examination she had reduced breath sounds and dullness to percussion on the right side of her chest. In her medical history, it was noted that she had been diagnosed with catamenial pneumothorax 9 years earlier for which she was treated with the gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist buserelin 1200 μg/day; she stopped taking it after 6 months.
A CT scan of her chest showed a moderately sized pneumothorax on the right side. A blood test showed a serum concentration of the tumour marker cancer antigen 125 of 2219 U/mL (normal level <35·0 U/mL). Considering the history and the current presentation, we concluded that our patient had again had a catamenial pneumothorax. We therefore decided to do a thoracoscopy, during which a red lesion was seen in the pleura of the superior segment of the right lower lobe (figure) and two black lesions were seen in the pleura of the right middle lobe: the lesions were resected. Additionally, several small defects—known as blueberry spots—ranging between 2-3 mm in diameter, were seen on the right side of the diaphragm (figure), through which the liver was visible. Histopathological examination of both the diaphragmatic and the pulmonary lesions showed endometrial stroma, which was oestrogen and progesterone receptor positive and CD10 positive.
The lesions were cut out and resected areas were covered with sheets of polyglycolic acid and fibrin glue. The patient recovered well postoperatively, and no further lesions were identified; however, 72 days after the surgery, she had a further pneumothorax. She was re-started on buserelin.
Catamenial pneumothorax is a rare condition and has a mean age of onset of 32–35 years. The pneumothorax usually occurs within 72 h before or after the start of menstruation. The lesions are classically on the right side and endometriosis might also be present. The actual cause is unknown, but three theories have been proposed as underlying mechanisms: retrograde regurgitation of endometrial cells through the ovarian duct into the pelvis and then into the diaphragm; metastatic spread of endometrial cells through lymphatic or venous dissemination; and müllerian cell metaplasia of the coelomic epithelium.
Menstruation has a clear association with the worsening of several other diseases including migraine, epilepsy, and some psychological disorders. Questions about the relationship of any symptoms to the menstrual cycle can sometimes provide an important clue to the precise diagnosis.

input: A 26-year-old man was referred to our orthopaedics department with left thigh pain. Radiography and CT revealed a cortical mass unilaterally on the medial side of the distal femoral diaphysis (figure A, B). The lesion extended with osteoblastic and osteolytic changes that accompany a periosteal reaction. MRI revealed a contrast-enhanced soft tissue mass surrounding the cortical lesion (figure C–E). No major blood vessel or bone marrow infiltration was observed. Our primary differential diagnosis was malignancy, particularly periosteal osteosarcoma, followed by fracture, osteomyelitis, or periostitis. A periosteal biopsy did not show malignancy but did reveal neutrophilic inflammation (figure F, G). Additional testing showed elevated inflammatory markers and arterial wall thickening in the aortic arch and its common branches (figure H) but not in the left femoral artery. At follow-up 2 months after the first visit, the patient reported general fatigue. Carotid bruits and blood pressure differences between the arms were observed. The patient was diagnosed with Takayasu arteritis based on the American College of Rheumatology–European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology classification criteria. Treatment of Takayasu arteritis was initiated using daily oral prednisolone (initial dose of 80 mg followed by decreasing dose thereafter) followed by subcutaneous tocilizumab (162 mg/week), after which the left thigh pain disappeared and periostitis subsided on imaging (figure I–K). The patient's Indian Takayasu Clinical Activity Score decreased from 6 to 2. We concluded that the femoral lesions were associated with Takayasu arteritis. Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis that presents with non-specific symptoms and signs, but periostitis is a rare manifestation. Isolated bone lesions incline the diagnosis more towards malignancy than systemic disease; however, several previous reports have shown isolated Takayasu arteritis-associated periostitis. Local inflammation of the periosteum might create a malignancy-like mass and periosteal osteosarcoma is suspected when the mass affects the femoral diaphysis in young adults. As patient presentation and imaging findings of Takayasu arteritis-associated periostitis might mimic periosteal osteosarcoma, it is imperative to rule out malignancy and maintain a broad differential diagnosis.

This abnormality is not seen in red blood cells from healthy individuals (figure). We suggest that the presence of the H63D haemochromatosis-associated allele is partly the cause of the exceptionally high serum ferritin concentrations, which brings about the abnormal red blood cell morphology.

A 20-year-old daycare teacher presented to our hospital reporting a generalised erythematous maculopapular rash. The patient also had a fever, myalgia, nausea, reduced urine output, peripheral oedema, and dyspnoea on exertion. She reported that the rash had rapidly increased in size over the past 72 h—coinciding with a doubling of the dose of her lamotrigine which she was prescribed for bipolar affective disorder.Apart from her mental health condition, she had no other significant medical history.
On examination, we found the patient to be feverish with a temperature of 40·3°C and bradycardic with a heart rate of 42 beats per min. She had a morbilliform rash—prominently seen over her trunk and extremities; there was no mucosal or genital involvement (figure). Hepatosplenomegaly and mild oedema of both the patient's legs were also noted.
An electrocardiogram showed sinus bradycardia (figure). Laboratory investigations showed a leukocytosis of 14·03 × 109 per L (normal 4·5–11) with an eosinophilia of 1·08 × 109 per L (normal 0–0·5). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated at 24 mm/h (normal 0–29).
The patient's aspartate aminotransferase was 42 units per L (normal 8–33) and alanine aminotransferase was 79 units per L (normal 7–55): indicating a transaminitis. The blood urea nitrogen concentration was 50 mg/dL (normal 6–21) and creatine concentration was 5·6 mg/dL (normal 0·5–1·2).
Screening for hepatitis A, B, and C viruses was reactive only for hepatitis A virus IgG. An autoimmune panel was negative for antinuclear and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies. However, a Monospot test was positive; a cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgG test was also positive.
Considering the findings in the round—the transaminitis and acute renal failure showed multiorgan involvement, the positive Monospot test indicated active Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection, and the positive IgG test suggested previous CMV infection—we made a diagnosis of drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome induced by lamotrigine with a concomitant infection. We considered that the EBV was either a new infection or a reactivation of a previous infection with the virus.
We stopped the lamotrigine and gave the patient a course of pulse steroids which gradually led to an improvement in her symptoms and renal function.
DRESS syndrome is an idiosyncratic drug-induced delayed type IV hypersensitivity severe multisystemic reaction that typically develops within 2–8 weeks of exposure. The proposed pathogenesis is a reactivation of latent herpesviruses which can be triggered by certain medications—including lamotrigine; a cross-reaction is thought to occur between the virus-specific T lymphocytes and the medications. In our case, the underlying cause of DRESS syndrome could be explained two ways: firstly, the concurrent lamotrigine use and a primary EBV infection or, secondly, lamotrigine-induced reactivation of EBV which then caused DRESS syndrome. Whatever the sequence of events, the treatment remains the same: immediate cessation of the drug causing the problem, systemic corticosteroids, or other immunosuppressants—including intravenous immuno-globulin in steroid-resistant cases (video).
output: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome induced by lamotrigine
target: No association has been found between viral infection or reactivation and DRESS syndrome

A 52-year-old man visited our hospital to have a general checkup. Routine gastrointestinal endoscopy showed a twisted lumen with a corkscrew appearance in the distal oesophagus. No other abnormality was identified (figure A). Our patient did not have any symptoms of dysphagia or retrosternal pain. A single-contrast barium examination of his oesophagus confirmed a spiral staircase peristalsis and an absence of peristalsis in the oesophageal body. CT of the mediastinum was done, and virtual endoscopy of the oesophagus showed the typical features of corkscrew oesophagus (figure B). Although manometry might be necessary to diagnose corkscrew oesophagus, we did not recommend this to our patient because his corkscrew oesophagus had been diagnosed, without any previous symptoms. In the future, our patient will need to be treated with drugs such as muscle relaxants and anxiolytic agents, in conjunction with either antireflux therapy or surgical myotomy. Currently, we only advise him not to consume cold fluids to prevent the development of symptoms.

A 35-year-old man presented to our department with palpitations and mild shortness of breath. He was of Haitian origin and had emigrated to the USA when he was 24 years old. A physical examination, an electrocardiogram (ECG), a full blood count, and a comprehensive metabolic profile showed no abnormalities. However, a transthoracic echocardiogram showed a 3 cm × 2 cm echolucent lesion in the apex of the left ventricle (figure; video 1). The patient did not report having a fever or any other systemic problems, but he had been to Haiti 5 months earlier. A cardiac MRI showed a solitary, avascular lesion located in the anterior wall of the left ventricle (figure; video 2); this lesion had no communication with the left ventricular cavity and was non-fatty and cystic. No pericardial or valvular abnormalities were seen. A CT scan of the heart confirmed the lesion was cystic and without any calcification; the coronary arteries were normal and, importantly, were not compressed by the mass. CT scans and MRIs of the head, chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no further cysts in any other organs. Serum serology by western blot testing for antibodies against specific IgG glycoproteins was negative for Echinococcus granulosus and Trypanosoma cruzi but positive for Taenia solium. The patient was then treated for 2 weeks with oral albendazole 400 mg twice a day. He reported no further symptoms and the lesion was no longer visible on a further transthoracic echocardiogram (figure; video 3) repeated 1 week after completing the treatment; a repeat cardiac MRI showed that the lesion had decreased considerably in size. Cysticercosis is endemic in Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa and Asia. The disease can develop after consuming foods contaminated with faeces that contain T solium eggs shed from a human carrier. The brain, skeletal muscle, and subcutaneous tissue are involved most frequently; isolated cardiac cysticercosis is rare. The need for concomitant treatment with steroids—particularly in neurocysticercosis—has been much debated because of concerns about seizures and worsening neurological symptoms on the initiation of anthelmintic therapy. In cases of isolated cardiac cysticercosis, there is no consensus for the routine use of steroids. In our patient, given that there was only mild oedema around the solitary lesion, the ECG was normal, and because he was on a cardiac monitor in hospital when albendazole was started, we were able to keep him under observation. Furthermore, it is of note that in other inflammatory cardiac conditions—such as pericarditis—steroids have been linked to increased relapse and recurrence. The rapid response to anthelmintic therapy in this case—reassuringly confirmed on repeat imaging—shows that in select cases, such as this one, albendazole may be used without steroids, with close clinical and cardiac monitoring and serial imaging.

A 46-year-old man presented to our hospital with abdominal pain and fever. In his medical history he reported three previous episodes of varicella zoster. On examination, he had a temperature of 38·3°C, small cervical lymph nodes, and some right upper quadrant tenderness.A CT of the patient's abdomen showed bilateral adrenalitis (figure). Laboratory investigations showed marked cholestatic hepatitis—including a raised alkaline phosphatase (1 995 U/mL; normal 30–135).
12 days later he developed thrombocytopenia (29 × 109 per L; normal 150–400), markedly elevated acute phase reactants—C-reactive protein concentration 266 mg/L (<3·1), D-dimer 12 696 μg/L (<500), ferritin 8 626 μg/L (<300), and soluble interleukin-2 receptor 2 481 U/mL (<846). We found him to have anasarca with pleural effusions, ascites, and subcutaneous oedema (figure).
Serum creatinine was 44 μmol/L, and urine microalbumin: creatinine ratio 387 (normal <2·0). Serum protein electrophoresis showed albumin 14 g/L, normal gamma globulins, and no monoclonal proteins. Interleukin-6 concentration was 39·6 pg/mL (<1·8) and vascular endothelial growth factor 212 pg/mL (31–86). SARS-CoV-2 nasal swabs, HIV, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) serology were negative.
18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT showed diffuse enlarged lymphadenopathy up to 3 cm, mild hepatosplenomegaly, and ascites, pleural effusions, and subcutaneous oedema. Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy were normal; biopsy specimens taken from along the gastrointestinal tract were normal. Bone marrow biopsy showed moderate haemophagocytosis with no fibrosis.
Excisional biopsy of the largest cervical lymph node showed many regressed germinal centres, prominent vascularity, very prominent follicular dendritic cells, and marked plasmacytosis (appendix); immunohistochemical stain for HHV-8 was negative.
Considering the patient in the round—thrombocytopenia, anasarca, reticulin fibrosis of the bone marrow, renal dysfunction, and organomegaly, acronymed to TAFRO—we diagnosed a variant of idiopathic multicentric Castleman's disease.
The patient was treated with numerous agents and ultimately responded to a combination of bortezomib, dexamethasone, baricitinib, siltuximab, and ciclosporin.
TAFRO is an aggressive variant of idiopathic multicentric Castleman's disease. The diagnosis is elusive; patients are often initially thought to have viral illness or haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. The lymphadenopathy and organomegaly are typically mild, and gamma globulins often normal. Patients decline rapidly and may be refractory to initial therapy, so early diagnosis is essential. Adrenalitis can be an important early clue, but because an adrenal biopsy is often unhelpful, clinical recognition is essential (video).

A 46-year-old man presented to our hospital with abdominal pain and fever. In his medical history he reported three previous episodes of varicella zoster. On examination, he had a temperature of 38·3°C, small cervical lymph nodes, and some right upper quadrant tenderness.A CT of the patient's abdomen showed bilateral adrenalitis (figure). Laboratory investigations showed marked cholestatic hepatitis—including a raised alkaline phosphatase (1 995 U/mL; normal 30–135).
12 days later he developed thrombocytopenia (29 × 109 per L; normal 150–400), markedly elevated acute phase reactants—C-reactive protein concentration 266 mg/L (<3·1), D-dimer 12 696 μg/L (<500), ferritin 8 626 μg/L (<300), and soluble interleukin-2 receptor 2 481 U/mL (<846). We found him to have anasarca with pleural effusions, ascites, and subcutaneous oedema (figure).
Serum creatinine was 44 μmol/L, and urine microalbumin: creatinine ratio 387 (normal <2·0). Serum protein electrophoresis showed albumin 14 g/L, normal gamma globulins, and no monoclonal proteins. Interleukin-6 concentration was 39·6 pg/mL (<1·8) and vascular endothelial growth factor 212 pg/mL (31–86). SARS-CoV-2 nasal swabs, HIV, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) serology were negative.
18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT showed diffuse enlarged lymphadenopathy up to 3 cm, mild hepatosplenomegaly, and ascites, pleural effusions, and subcutaneous oedema. Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy were normal; biopsy specimens taken from along the gastrointestinal tract were normal. Bone marrow biopsy showed moderate haemophagocytosis with no fibrosis.
Excisional biopsy of the largest cervical lymph node showed many regressed germinal centres, prominent vascularity, very prominent follicular dendritic cells, and marked plasmacytosis (appendix); immunohistochemical stain for HHV-8 was negative.
Considering the patient in the round—thrombocytopenia, anasarca, reticulin fibrosis of the bone marrow, renal dysfunction, and organomegaly, acronymed to TAFRO—we diagnosed a variant of idiopathic multicentric Castleman's disease.
The patient was treated with numerous agents and ultimately responded to a combination of bortezomib, dexamethasone, baricitinib, siltuximab, and ciclosporin.
TAFRO is an aggressive variant of idiopathic multicentric Castleman's disease. The diagnosis is elusive; patients are often initially thought to have viral illness or haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. The lymphadenopathy and organomegaly are typically mild, and gamma globulins often normal. Patients decline rapidly and may be refractory to initial therapy, so early diagnosis is essential. Adrenalitis can be an important early clue, but because an adrenal biopsy is often unhelpful, clinical recognition is essential (video).

output:
Based on the clinical presentation and MRI findings, the diagnosis is:

**Uveal melanoma with metastatic disease**

The key features supporting this diagnosis include:
- Longstanding blindness in the affected eye (suggesting a pre-existing intraocular mass)
- Orbital mass on MRI
- Widespread metastatic disease (hepatic masses, lymphadenopathy, osseous lesions) characteristic of metastatic uveal melanoma
- The pattern of metastases (particularly hepatic) is classic for uveal melanoma

The right eye was enucleated for palliative relief and to obtain tissue for diagnosis. What is the diagnosis?
output:
Metastatic uveal melanoma

The MRI shows an intraocular mass in the right eye (note the abnormal appearance of the right globe compared to the normal left eye). Given the clinical presentation of:
- Blind eye with new inflammation and pain
- Intraocular mass on MRI
- Metastatic disease pattern (hepatic masses, lymphadenopathy, osseous lesions)

This constellation of findings is classic for uveal melanoma with metastatic disease. Uveal melanoma has a characteristic metastatic pattern with a strong predilection for the liver. The patient likely had an undiagnosed primary uveal melanoma that caused her blindness years earlier and subsequently metastasized.

A 31-year-old woman reporting a headache and epigastric pain for the past 12 h attended our unit. She had a history of gestational hypertension and 5 days earlier had a caesarean section at term; there had been no post-partum haemorrhage and she had been allowed home. The patient's haemoglobin concentration had been 11·7 g/dL (normal >10 post partum), and the serum creatinine concentration 48 μmol/L (normal <90); she was normotensive and on no medication.On examination, we found the patient to be lethargic: her blood pressure was 193/102 mm Hg, and she had hyper-reflexia and bilateral clonus. A spot urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio was 57 mg/mol (normal <30), her haemoglobin concentration was 9·5 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 764 mIU/L (normal <600), alanine transaminase 127 IU/L (normal <70), and the serum creatinine concentration 115·0 μmol/L were raised: indicating possible post-partum pre-eclampsia with partial HELLP—Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets—syndrome and acute kidney injury.
We started the patient on fluids, and intravenous labetalol and magnesium sulphate. Over the next 24 h, she passed 10·9 L of clear urine despite a total fluid intake of 3·7 L. Laboratory investigations for polyuria (appendix) excluded osmotic diuresis and post-partum hypopituitarism; however, her urine osmolality was 228 mOsmol/kg (normal >600), suggestive of diabetes insipidus causing pure-water loss.
A water deprivation test showed an inability to concentrate urine fully: the plasma osmolality reached 301 mOsmol/kg—maximum endogenous antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release occurs above the threshold of 295 mOsmol/kg—and her urine osmolality failed to rise sufficiently (figure). A desmopressin test with a vasopressinase-resistant ADH analogue found urine osmolality increased by 13% to 426 mOsmol/kg (figure). We did not assess plasma ADH or copeptin levels because the polyuria resolved when liver function recovered. She was allowed home 4 days later; her blood pressure and urine were normal.
Taken together, the findings suggested a partial central diabetes insipidus (DI) due to a transient deficiency in ADH caused by an excess of vasopressinase resulting from impaired liver function because of the HELLP syndrome. The polyuria abated when the transaminitis resolved. Further, we believe the increase in urine concentration after desmopressin was small because of wash-out of the renal medullary concentrating gradient from water diuresis.
DI is characterised by a failure of the kidneys to conserve water due either to ADH deficiency (central DI) or resistance (nephrogenic DI) resulting in hypotonic polyuria. In pregnancy, DI occurs when the breakdown of ADH by placental vasopressinase is enhanced because of either increased production in multiple pregnancy or—as in our patient—decreased hepatic catabolism. Gestational DI commonly occurs in the third trimester, coinciding with peak placental vasopressinase synthesis, and rarely in the early post-partum period.
Given pre-eclampsia—the most frequent cause of acute kidney injury in pregnancy—typically results in oliguria, a good urine output in such patients may be falsely reassuring: if the urine output is above 3L per day and urine osmolality is less than 300 mOsmol/kg, gestational DI should be considered.
Finally, if gestational DI is missed, patients are at high risk of severe hypernatraemia resulting from the standard pre-eclampsia management of fluid restriction, and seizures, as the magnesium sulphate will be rapidly excreted. Therefore, in the context of polyuria, it might be necessary to increase fluids; the magnesium sulphate infusion rate might also need to be increased and levels monitored for toxicity (video).

CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a very large stone in the neobladder. What is the predominant composition of this patient’s stone?
output:
Based on the clinical presentation of a patient with an orthotopic neobladder constructed from intestinal segments presenting with a large neobladder stone, the diagnosis is:

**Calcium phosphate (struvite/infection) stone** or more specifically **Struvite stone (magnesium ammonium phosphate)**

However, given the intestinal neobladder context, the most likely predominant composition is:

**Calcium phosphate stone**

Patients with neobladders constructed from intestinal segments are prone to metabolite stones, particularly calcium phosphate stones, due to chronic bacteriuria, mucus production, urinary stasis, and the altered urinary environment (more alkaline urine) created by the bowel mucosa.

4. Alkaline urinary pH from the intestinal segments
5. Metabolic abnormalities including hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis

The large, dense stone visible in the neobladder on CT is characteristic of this complication in patients with urinary diversions using intestinal segments.

A 25-year-old woman came to the accident and emergency department with a 12-h history of sudden onset regurgitation and complete dysphagia. She had had gastric banding in 2008, for morbid obesity. A plain chest radiograph showed an abnormal appearance of the gastric band (figure). Normally, a gastric band appears as a single radio-opaque bar lying diagonally, at 40–50 degrees to the vertebral column. When a gastric band slips, part of the gastric fundus herniates through the band, initially causing the left side of the band to move caudally and subsequently forcing the anterior part of the band further caudally; an annular appearance of the band results (figure). On the basis of the history and this radiographic finding, the band was deflated in the emergency department, and the patient was given urgent laparoscopic band removal. With the increase in obesity surgery it is important to highlight such complications, as emergency deflation and band removal is necessary to prevent necrosis of the herniated stomach.

A 34-year-old woman who collapsed during a mountain trek in northern Spain was initially assessed at an emergency rescue centre. She was unresponsive, asystolic, and pulseless, had unreactive dilated pupils, and had a tympanic temperature of 18°C. Advanced life support was started, and the woman was transferred to our hospital. She arrived 2 h and 25 min after the first evaluation—she was still in asystole, had unreactive dilated pupils, and had a core temperature of 20·2°C. An arterial blood sample showed a pH of 6·81, a lactate concentration of 10·3 mmol/L (normal 0·5–1), and a potassium concentration of 4·4 mmol/L (normal 3·5–5). Peripheral venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) support was started and a fine ventricular fibrillation rhythm was immediately seen on an electrocardiogram (ECG). The patient also started gasping, ventilator asynchronies appeared, and a burst suppression pattern was seen on a bispectral index monitor; these difficulties disappeared after she was given sedatives.During the first few hours of extracorporeal support, the patient had coagulopathy, bleeding, lung oedema (figure), and a highly variable ECMO flow. However, once the woman was stable, her body temperature was progressively increased at a rate of 3°C per h. The patient regained pupillary reactivity after 3 h of extracorporeal support. When her temperature reached 30°C, coarse ventricular fibrillation was observed. She was then defibrillated, which resulted in a posterior effective rhythm—meaning that 6 h and 10 min after the initial assessment there was return of spontaneous circulation. When her temperature was 32°C, an ECG showed sinus rhythm with classic Osborn—or J–waves, seen clearly in lead V3 (figure). The patient's neuron-specific enolase was found to be 93·4 ng/mL (normal range 1·5–13·5) on day 1 in the intensive care unit (ICU); by day 2 it had fallen to 55·1 ng/mL; other laboratory investigations normalised during the patient's recovery (appendix).
The heating process was continued until the patient's temperature was 35°C. ECMO was stopped after 45 h and 40 min. The patient was successfully extubated on day 2 of her stay in the ICU.
A neurological evaluation at the end of day 2 found no abnormalities, and the patient was moved from the ICU on day 6. She was allowed home on day 11. A month after the episode, she had resumed her normal activities of daily living.
Neurological sequelae are common after prolonged periods of cardiac arrest. The maintenance of extracorporeal support and neuroprotection along with regimented temperature management until adequate biventricular function is recovered—as in our case—may be key in preventing brain damage. We kept the patient on extracorporeal support for a total of 45 h and 40 min, which is substantially longer than previuously reported times (appendix). In cases of hypothermia and asystole, resuscitation using ECMO as a means of oxygen redistribution and temperature management should be considered.

In 2012, an 84-year-old Chinese man presented with progressive, chronic left atraumatic knee pain and swelling. His medical history was notable for pulmonary tuberculosis treated in China in 1951 and rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed in 2006. His joint pain progressed despite use of disease modifying drugs and steroid injections. Antitumor necrosis factor inhibitors were not used because of concerns of tuberculosis reactivation. Clinical examination showed he had antalgic gait, knee effusion, stiffness, and joint-line tenderness. Laboratory results included erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 88 mm/h and C-reactive protein of 205 mg/L. Radiographs showed severe tri-compartmental degenerative arthritis (figure A).The patient underwent total knee arthroplasty in August, 2012 (figure B). Extensive synovitis was noted and pathological examination showed granulomatous inflammation (figure C). Staining of synovial tissue for acid-fast bacilli and tuberculosis PCR were negative. The patient's knee symptoms initially improved, but 5 months after total knee arthroplasty he developed a draining sinus from the knee incision. He underwent irrigation and debridement of the knee with exchange of the polyethylene tibial insert. Initial synovial tissue fluid cultures were negative, but subsequent acid-fast bacilli cultures from synovial tissue and joint fluid grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Sputum cultures were negative for pulmonary tuberculosis. He started a course of antituberculosis therapy including rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for treatment of tuberculosis prosthetic joint infection in February, 2013. He was advised to undergo a two-stage resection-revision arthroplasty but declined further surgery and thus an implant retention strategy was pursued. The patient completed 12 months of antituberculosis therapy in February, 2014. He has since continued rifampicin and isoniazid treatment with a plan for long-term suppressive therapy in the setting of retained prosthesis. At his latest follow-up, 2 years after initial diagnosis of tuberculous prosthetic joint infection, the incision had healed without clinical sign of infection and his knee has a pain-free range of motion from 0–95°.
Tuberculous arthritis accounts for 1–5% of people with tuberculosis. Scarce data are available for optimum management of tuberculous prosthetic joint infection. This case illustrates an unusual reactivation of tuberculosis in an isolated extra-pulmonary site after joint replacement surgery. Prompt initiation of antituberculosis therapy might enable implant retention, although continuation of suppressive therapy might be needed. In the setting of globalisation and the increasing use of immunomodulatory therapies and joint replacement surgeries, this case illustrates the need for tuberculosis to be thought about early in the differential diagnosis for culture-negative prosthetic joint infection in patients with previous exposures or epidemiological risk factors.

A 68-year-old Polish man was admitted to our hospital because of continued, painless, and worsening jaundice, and malaise. 2 months earlier he had a Whipple's pancreaticoduodenectomy for suspected carcinoma of the pancreas. He initially presented with mild weight loss and pain in the epigastric area. He did not use alcohol above recommended limits and had not travelled abroad recently. On examination his skin and sclera were jaundiced, and he had excoriations on all four limbs and his torso. There was no ascites, oedema, lymphadenopathy, or orbitopathy. Serum tumour markers were within normal limits, and tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. A CT scan showed a mass in the head of the pancreas, normal liver parenchyma, and dilated extrahepatic and intrahepatic bile ducts and pancreatic duct proximally to the pancreatic head, and stricture of the pancreatic part of the common bile duct. Lymph nodes and abdominal vessels were normal.When we saw the patient, his total bilirubin (8·36 mg/dL), AST (89 IU/L), ALT (51 IU/L), GGT (443 IU/L), and ALP (712 IU/L) were increased. Antinuclear antibodies were detected at a titre of 1:1 280, with grainy fluorescence, but other antibodies—namely, antimitochondrial antibodies, smooth muscle antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, or liver–kidney microsome antibodies—were not found. An abdominal ultrasound scan showed dilatation of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, and stricture of the common bile duct. Magnetic resonance cholangio-pancreatography (MRCP) showed multiple strictures of the patient's bile ducts (figure). A percutaneous liver biopsy specimen showed mixed inflammatory infiltration surrounding neocholangioles, with IgG4 in plasmocytes—approximately 60 per large field view, an IgG4:IgG ratio of more than 40%, mild fibrosis (grade 2 on the Batts-Ludwig scale), and cholestasis. The patient's serum IgG4 concentration was elevated at 380 mg/dL (normal 10–140). Looking at the presentation and the results in the round, we made a diagnosis of IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis and pancreatitis.
We therefore started treatment with prednisone 40 mg once daily for 2 months, followed by azathioprine 2·0 mg/kg once a day. After 2 months, a repeat MRCP showed that the stenosis of the bile ducts had reduced (figure). Also, the patient's total bilirubin concentration and liver enzyme levels normalised, and his malaise improved.
A post-factum analysis of the head of the pancreas removed at the initial operation stained positively for IgG4, and a mixed inflammatory infiltration with IgG4 plasmocytes was seen.

Patients with IgG4-related disease are often misdiagnosed as having a malignancy because of the non-specific signs and pseudotumour-like lesions; they may—as in our case—have unnecessary surgical procedures and investigations. A full clinical assessment of any patient presenting with jaundice and a pancreatic mass must include measurement of IgG4 concentrations and a biopsy before surgeons put knife to skin.

A 37-year-old hairdresser presented to our hospital with pain and swelling in her left leg and pain in her lower back. The pain in her back, which she thought was muscular, began as an ache, at the same time as the pain started in her leg, 5 days before. On the day of admission, over a period of 3 h, the back pain had become much worse and her leg had rapidly become swollen and more painful. As a hairdresser, she said she was on her feet for several hours every working day. She had no medical history of note: she did not smoke and was otherwise fit and well. The woman took no medication except for a combined oral contraceptive pill containing drospirenone and estradiol. On examination, the left leg—from the hip to the calf—was markedly swollen, painful, and cyanotic, consistent with a diagnosis of phlegmasia cerulea dolens. All pulses were palpable, and a sensory examination was normal; the lower part of her leg had a mottled, dusky appearance and a prolonged capillary refill time, and was cold to the touch.A full blood count showed a haemoglobin concentration of 12·9 g/dL, a white blood cell count of 10·8 × 109 per L, and a thrombocyte count of 235 × 109 per L. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 32 mm/h (normal 0–27). The patient's C-reactive protein concentration was 29 mg/L (normal 0–1) and D-dimer concentration was 4·13 μg/mL (normal <0·5). Her international normalised ratio (INR) was 1·0, activated partial thromboplastin time was 25 s (normal 23–36), and fibrinogen concentration was 4·54 g/L (normal 2·0–4·3). Her serum electrolyte, urea, creatinine, and creatine kinase concentrations were all within the normal range.
An ultrasound scan of the patient's pelvis and upper leg showed deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in the left common iliac vein that extended into the left common femoral vein. Other investigations including anti-thrombin, anti-cardiolipin antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, prothrombin variant, and factor V Leiden were negative.
Using catheter-directed thrombolysis with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator the DVT was dissolved. However, conventional angiography to confirm that the clot had dissolved showed a persistent narrowing of the left common iliac vein at the level of the right common iliac artery (figure). We decided against stenting the stenotic iliac vein because her signs and symptoms had resolved and there was angiographic evidence of good collateral venous circulation (figure). The patient was started on warfarin with a target INR of 2·0–3·0.
Some degree of compression of the left common iliac vein between the fifth lumbar vertebra and the right common iliac artery is found in 22% of cadavers. Despite this, less than 5% of all left leg venous congestive disorders are attributable to severe compression of the left common iliac vein. May–Thurner syndrome—also known as iliac vein compression syndrome, a condition which gives patients discomfort and swelling of the left leg due to venous congestion—typically manifests in women in their thirties and forties with signs and symptoms of acute or chronic (or both) left leg venous congestion and DVT. input: A 21-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with an 8-month history of swelling and pain in the right thigh. MRI of the right leg revealed a large periosteal femoral mass and thrombus in the right femoral vein, for which she received anticoagulation therapy. The patient subsequently experienced dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, and a chest x-ray was done. What is the likely diagnosis?
output:
Based on the clinical history of a young patient with a large periosteal femoral mass (highly suggestive of a primary bone sarcoma, specifically osteosarcoma) and the chest X-ray findings showing multiple dense, calcified/ossified nodules ("cannonball" lesions) characteristic of bone-forming metastases, the diagnosis is metastatic osteosarcoma. The dense nature of the lung nodules corresponds to ossification of the metastatic tumor deposits.

A 27-year-old woman came to our hospital with increasing diffuse pain around the joints of her shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, and ankles. She was well known to us because of her long history of problems due to autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1—with a mutation in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene.We first met her when she was 18 years old, after she was referred by her paediatrician for severe hypoparathyroidism, which was treated with alfacalcidol and calcium carbonate. The treatment resulted in the development of nephrocalcinosis at the age of 15 years. When she was 22 years old, she returned with a 3-month history of worsening dysphagia and vomiting because of achalasia and oesophageal candidiasis: she was unable to take her medication orally. She had also lost a substantial amount of weight—at its nadir her body mass index was 15 kg/m2. She was admitted as an emergency with a total serum calcium concentration of 1·44 mmol/L (normal range 2·20–2·55) and prolonged QTc on her electrocardiogram. We started her on replacement therapy with subcutaneous recombinant human parathyroid hormone (rhPTH; 1–34) and colecalciferol. The dose of rhPTH (1–34) varied from 20 μg once to twice a day and hypocalcaemia was adequately controlled over 5·5 years—mean albumin-adjusted serum calcium was 2·11 mmol/L.
The pain, she came to see us with, had developed after 3 years of treatment with the rhPTH (1–34) and had increased progressively. We first ruled out any inflammatory and autoimmune causes of the arthritis. Additional investigations showed that she had a low bone density of the distal radius (Z score SD −3·0, normal score SD −2) and increased markers of bone formation: alkaline phosphatase was 271 IU/L (normal range 42–98), osteocalcin was 87 ng/mL (normal range 2–12). A bone scan with whole-body early images showed precocious, intense bone uptake in the peripheral joints and in the axial skeleton, with no activity in the heart, kidneys, or bladder (figure). A 37-year-old hairdresser presented to our hospital with pain and swelling in her left leg and pain in her lower back. The pain in her back, which she thought was muscular, began as an ache, at the same time as the pain started in her leg, 5 days before. On the day of admission, over a period of 3 h, the back pain had become much worse and her leg had rapidly become swollen and more painful. As a hairdresser, she said she was on her feet for several hours every working day. She had no medical history of note: she did not smoke and was otherwise fit and well. The woman took no medication except for a combined oral contraceptive pill containing drospirenone and estradiol. On examination, the left leg—from the hip to the calf—was markedly swollen, painful, and cyanotic, consistent with a diagnosis of phlegmasia cerulea dolens. All pulses were palpable, and a sensory examination was normal; the lower part of her leg had a mottled, dusky appearance and a prolonged capillary refill time, and was cold to the touch.A full blood count showed a haemoglobin concentration of 12·9 g/dL, a white blood cell count of 10·8 × 109 per L, and a thrombocyte count of 235 × 109 per L. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 32 mm/h (normal 0–27). The patient's C-reactive protein concentration was 29 mg/L (normal 0–1) and D-dimer concentration was 4·13 μg/mL (normal <0·5). Her international normalised ratio (INR) was 1·0, activated partial thromboplastin time was 25 s (normal 23–36), and fibrinogen concentration was 4·54 g/L (normal 2·0–4·3). Her serum electrolyte, urea, creatinine, and creatine kinase concentrations were all within the normal range.
An ultrasound scan of the patient's pelvis and upper leg showed deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in the left common iliac vein that extended into the left common femoral vein. Other investigations including anti-thrombin, anti-cardiolipin antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, prothrombin variant, and factor V Leiden were negative.
Using catheter-directed thrombolysis with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator the DVT was dissolved. However, conventional angiography to confirm that the clot had dissolved showed a persistent narrowing of the left common iliac vein at the level of the right common iliac artery (figure). We decided against stenting the stenotic iliac vein because her signs and symptoms had resolved and there was angiographic evidence of good collateral venous circulation (figure). The patient was started on warfarin with a target INR of 2·0–3·0.
Some degree of compression of the left common iliac vein between the fifth lumbar vertebra and the right common iliac artery is found in 22% of cadavers. Despite this, less than 5% of all left leg venous congestive disorders are attributable to severe compression of the left common iliac vein. May–Thurner syndrome—also known as iliac vein compression syndrome, a condition which gives patients discomfort and swelling of the left leg due to venous congestion—typically manifests in women in their thirties and forties with signs and symptoms of acute or chronic (or both) left leg venous congestion and DVT. Rarely—as may have happened in our patient—engorged epidural veins, acting as collaterals, can cause low lumbar nerve root compression and back pain. Interestingly, the compressed left common iliac vein forms a barrier against clot passage, thereby affording the patient some protection against pulmonary embolism. Risk of a DVT is further increased by conditions that raise intra-abdominal or thoracic pressures, pregnancy, pelvic obstruction, right heart failure, prolonged periods of bed rest, standing or sitting, hypercoagulable states, injection of irritating drugs via a left leg cannula, and the presence of a foreign body (eg, a left femoral vein catheter).
With regards to use of a stent to prevent narrowing of the iliac vein in patients with May–Thurner syndrome, the jury is still out; long-term anticoagulation is necessary even with stenting.
