A 61-year-old woman came to our neurosurgery clinic complaining of spasms and episodic pain on the left side of her face; the spasms had been present for 20 years and the pain for 5 years. She said that initially the facial spasms affected only the corner of her left eye but over the years progressed to involve most of the muscles of the lower left side of her face. For the past 7 years, she had been given botulinum toxin injections twice per year, which had provided some relief. The pain, which developed alongside the spasms, was characterised by frequent episodes of excruciating, lancinating pain—rated by the patient as very severe using a visual analogue pain scale—along the ophthalmic and maxillary branches of the trigeminal nerve. The woman described several things—including chewing, touching her face, and brushing her gums—that clearly triggered the pain. Taking carbamazepine lessened the pain, but she stopped the drug because she could not tolerate the associated drowsiness. She never had any problems affecting the right side of her face. A neurological examination was normal, including intact corneal reflexes. She had no medical history of a stroke, transient ischaemic attack, or demyelinating disease.MRI of her brain showed a dolichoectatic left vertebral artery that indented and displaced both the facial and trigeminal nerves (figure). Considering the patient's symptoms and their development in the round, we made diagnoses of both hemifacial spasm and trigeminal neuralgia—a combination known as painful tic convulsif. We carried out decompression of both nerves with a keyhole craniotomy, using a retrosigmoid approach (figure; appendix). Pleasingly, for both the patient and us, on waking up after the operation, she reported immediate and complete resolution of all her symptoms; at follow-up, 1 month later, she was still free of both the pain and the spasms.
Hemifacial spasm is a movement disorder affecting the muscles supplied by the facial nerve; in most cases it is caused by compression of the nerve root at the exit of the brainstem. In over 85% of patients, local injection with botulinum toxin results in easing of the symptoms. Trigeminal neuralgia is a rare, episodic facial pain that is unilateral. It may be mistaken for a dental problem because it usually affects the two lower branches of the trigeminal nerve: the maxillary and the mandibular. Microvascular decompression of the trigeminal nerve root is the most effective and long-lasting treatment.
Harvey Cushing first coined the phrase painful tic convulsif, in 1920, to describe the combination of the symptoms of hemifacial spasm and trigeminal neuralgia. The common source of our patient's two diagnoses shows that surgical microvascular decompression can be an effective and long-lasting treatment for either conditions—presenting alone or together—where medical treatments have failed.
output: Painful tic convulsif (combined hemifacial spasm and trigeminal neuralgia)

A 27-year-old woman came to our hospital with increasing diffuse pain around the joints of her shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, and ankles. She was well known to us because of her long history of problems due to autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1—with a mutation in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene.We first met her when she was 18 years old, after she was referred by her paediatrician for severe hypoparathyroidism, which was treated with alfacalcidol and calcium carbonate. The treatment resulted in the development of nephrocalcinosis at the age of 15 years. When she was 22 years old, she returned with a 3-month history of worsening dysphagia and vomiting because of achalasia and oesophageal candidiasis: she was unable to take her medication orally. She had also lost a substantial amount of weight—at its nadir her body mass index was 15 kg/m2. She was admitted as an emergency with a total serum calcium concentration of 1·44 mmol/L (normal range 2·20–2·55) and prolonged QTc on her electrocardiogram. We started her on replacement therapy with subcutaneous recombinant human parathyroid hormone (rhPTH; 1–34) and colecalciferol. The dose of rhPTH (1–34) varied from 20 μg once to twice a day and hypocalcaemia was adequately controlled over 5·5 years—mean albumin-adjusted serum calcium was 2·11 mmol/L.
The pain, she came to see us with, had developed after 3 years of treatment with the rhPTH (1–34) and had increased progressively. We first ruled out any inflammatory and autoimmune causes of the arthritis. Additional investigations showed that she had a low bone density of the distal radius (Z score SD −3·0, normal score SD −2) and increased markers of bone formation: alkaline phosphatase was 271 IU/L (normal range 42–98), osteocalcin was 87 ng/mL (normal range 2–12). A bone scan with whole-body early images showed precocious, intense bone uptake in the peripheral joints and in the axial skeleton, with no activity in the heart, kidneys, or bladder (figure). The images suggested that bone cells were being overstimulated by the rhPTH (1–34)—appearing like so-called super bone scans seen in patients with hyperparathyroidism. The rhPTH (1–34) was discontinued and within 48 h the patient's joint pain stopped. However, she then developed a transient hypocalcaemia requiring high doses of intravenous and oral calcium with alfacalcidol; she had concomitantly low urinary calcium excretion, indicative of hungry bone syndrome. The bone scintigraphy returned to normal 1 year after the rhPTH (1–34) was stopped (figure).
In patients with hypoparathyroidism refractory to conventional treatment, rhPTH (1–34) therapy can effectively control hypocalcaemia, but whether it is safe in the long term is unclear. Further, abnormally increased metabolic activity of the bone may occur despite adequate calcaemic control, possibly due to the pharmacokinetics of the treatment. Bone scintigraphy—including an early scan—can be useful in detecting iatrogenic hyperparathyroidism in patients receiving either rhPTH (1–34) or rhPTH (1–84) treatment (video).

An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm, with recurrence of ventricular pre-excitation, a PR interval of 90 ms (typical 120–200) and a delta wave. Laboratory investigations—including high-sensitivity troponin T and N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide—were within typical range.
A cardiac MRI showed patches of intramyocardial fat which co-localised to areas with late gadolinium enhancement (figure 1). Furthermore, although more prominent in the left ventricle, fat was also detected in right ventricular para-septal structures and moderator band. Ventricular sizes, wall thickness, and systolic function were preserved, with no regional wall motion abnormalities even in the segments with abnormal tissue.
We reviewed the patient's paediatric records—including previous cardiac MRIs. The first scan, aged 5 years, showed several ventricular masses suggestive of rhabdomyomas; scans over the next 15 years showed a progressive reduction in the size of the ventricular masses which co-localised to the regions detected by the late gadolinium enhancement, suggesting fibrofatty replacement (figure 2).

Testing of the patient's DNA using an extensive genetic panel for both hypertrophic and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy was negative.
Considering the pattern and location of the fibrofatty replacement, and possible tuberous sclerosis complex, we concluded that the cardiac MRI findings were likely related to involuting rhabdomyomas. We explained the findings to the patient and advised treatment with β blockers and continued follow-up with regular cardiac imaging.

Rhabdomyomas are the most common cardiac tumours in childhood, usually occurring in association with tuberous sclerosis complex; they may regress or even disappear or—as we believe has occurred and is illustrated by the images in our patient—present with intramyocardial fat foci in adults.

input: A baby boy born at 39 weeks of gestation had bilious emesis, failure to pass meconium, and abdominal distention within 24 hours after birth. A water-soluble contrast enema showed a uniformly distended and shortened colon. What is the most likely diagnosis?
output:
Based on the clinical presentation of a newborn with bilious emesis, failure to pass meconium, and abdominal distention, combined with the radiographic findings from the contrast enema, the diagnosis is identified. The contrast enema reveals a colon that is **shortened** and lacks the normal redundancy of the sigmoid colon and the splenic and hepatic flexures, resulting in a characteristic **"question mark"** appearance. The description of the colon as "uniformly distended" (or more typically, uniformly narrowed/microcolon in standard descriptions, though variable caliber can exist) and specifically **shortened** without a transition zone is pathognomonic for **total colonic aganglionosis** (a form of Hirschsprung's disease where the entire colon is affected).

input: A 79-year-old man presented with symptoms and signs of upper respiratory tract infection; he had a history of permanent pacemaker implantation. An upright postero-anterior chest radiograph showed a raised right hemidiaphragm delineated by subdiaphragmatic air. Unlike free air, which forms an uninterrupted crescent-shaped subdiaphragmatic radiolucency, this radiograph showed a haustral pattern of subdiaphragmatic lucency (figure), overlapping the upper border of the liver shadow. On examination, clinical findings suggesting acute abdomen from rupture of a hollow viscus were absent and there was no recent history of abdominal surgery to account for the presence of subdiaphragmatic air. The visualisation of a gas filled transverse colon lumen interpositioned between the right hemidiaphragm and the liver on a chest film is called Chilaiditi's sign. A CT scan may confirm these anatomical relations. In our patient's radiograph, the haustral pattern of air was indicative of colonic origin, and the continuity of the subdiaphragmatic air was broken up by the shadow of the vertical plicae semilunares of the colon. Chilaiditi's sign was first described in 1910 by Demetrious Chilaiditi and it is an incidental radiographic finding. This sign can be mistaken for pneumoperitoneum and can lead to needless surgical intervention. Our patient was treated only for his upper respiratory tract infection.

A 51-year-old man attended our outpatient clinic complaining of repeated bouts of pain in his left groin. He said he had a lump that appeared intermittently in the area, and because of this, he regularly wore firm underwear. In his medical history, it was noted that 9 years earlier he had undergone an open flat mesh repair of a left inguinal hernia. 14 months later, however, the problem had recurred; at this stage, he was managed by a different surgeon—who had not been involved in the original operation—who did a further open mesh repair. The second repair was also unsuccessful and the hernia recurred. 9 months later, the patient had another operation to repair the problem: this time, another surgeon did a laparoscopic total extraperitoneal (TEP) repair. Unfortunately, this too was unsuccessful, and the patient's problem recurred 3 months later. At this stage, the patient said he had lost hope in the possibility of his problem being resolved and he decided not to seek further help for some time.On clinical examination, two oblique scars were visible in the left groin area and there was also a palpable ridge above them—suggestive of the mesh used in the previous laparoscopic inguinal repair. We found no evidence of a further hernia despite the patient repeatedly pointing out that the area of the medial groin below the scars was the source of his symptoms.
Given the rather complex history, we decided we needed to do an MRI of the groin while the patient was repeatedly putting the area under strain by increasing his intra-abdominal pressure—in a similar way that coughing, bending over, or lifting a heavy object does. This showed a femoral hernia that contained omentum (figure). We decided to repair the hernia by using a prosthetic mesh plug through an infrainguinal approach to avoid the previously scarred areas. At follow-up 6 months later, the patient was free of symptoms and the problem had not recurred.
A femoral hernia is a protrusion of a peritoneal sac through the femoral ring or canal below the inguinal ligament. It is relatively uncommon in men but more frequent in women. About 5000 femoral hernia repairs are done in the UK each year; 30–40% of cases present acutely with an associated ten-fold increase in risk of mortality. By contrast with a femoral hernia, an inguinal hernia is essentially a defect due to weak connective tissue. As traditional sutured repairs are associated with high recurrence rates, the repair of both femoral and inguinal hernias is often augmented with synthetic prosthetic mesh by using either an open or laparoscopic (colloquially called a keyhole) technique. Laparoscopic approaches include a TEP—as with our patient—or a transabdominal preperitoneal repair. The ideal approach to a successful outcome is dependent on the patient's fitness, informed consent, and the surgeon's skill.
The key message here is that patients presenting with a history suggestive of an earlier recurrence of an inguinal hernia might actually have another problem altogether—in our patient's case, a primary femoral hernia. We believe that ultrasound scans are unreliable in the assessment of such cases, especially when the groin area is disfigured. And we would suggest that an MRI, done with provocation or straining to increase pressure in the affected area during scanning, can be very useful. Furthermore, additional pathology—including indurated lymph nodes, lobulated lipomas, and saphena varix—in the absence of classic diagnostic clinical signs, may be detected.

In March, 2010, a 53-year-old woman developed a black discolouration of her tongue. 4 weeks before developing the discolouration, she had had elective gynaecological surgery, from which she was recovering as an inpatient under our care. She did not smoke, but had a high intake of caffeinated drinks, including six cups of tea and two cups of coffee each day. During the course of her hospital stay she completed a 3-week course of amoxicillin clavulanate and metronidazole for a suspected postoperative pelvic infection. Tongue scrapings confirmed Candida infection, and we diagnosed our patient with lingua villosa nigra (black hairy tongue) caused by a Candida infection secondary to antibiotic use. Lingua villosa nigra is a condition that is often attributed to poor oral hygiene. It is characterised by hypertrophy and elongation of filiform papillae and lack of normal desquamation. The discolouration is thought to be due to secondary infection with porphyrin-producing chromogenic bacteria or yeast. It is more common in people chew tobacco, have caffeinated drinks, or have HIV infection. It is characteristically confined to the posterior two-thirds of the tongue, and generally causes no symptoms. Our patient was treated with a short course of fluconazole and her tongue returned to normal within 7 days.

A 37-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 4-month history of recurrent episodes of flushing of the right side of her face after exercise and hot baths (figure). She explained that the flushing resolved after each episode following 1 h of rest. She reported no medical history.On examination, we found no abnormalities: specifically, the patient's nervous system—including her cranial nerves—was intact. Routine laboratory investigations were unremarkable—including full blood count, liver and kidney function tests, electrolyte concentrations, thyroid function tests, tumour markers, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein concentration. A high-resolution CT scan of the patient's chest, a carotid artery ultrasound, and enhanced MRIs of her head, neck, and cervical and thoracic spine, and cervicobrachial plexus were normal.
Considering the patient's symptoms and the absence of any pathology that might explain her presentation, we made a diagnosis of harlequin syndrome.
After an explanation of the diagnosis and reassurance of the patient, we decided not to offer her any treatment since she was not particularly troubled by the symptoms. At follow-up she reported that the flushing continued and that she was otherwise well.
Harlequin syndrome is characterised by unilateral facial flushing and sweating induced by exercise, heat, and emotion; most cases are idiopathic. However, a thorough examination and an extensive investigation are mandatory in order to rule out all known causes—including a brainstem infarction, multiple sclerosis, syringomyelia, thyroid diseases, a superior mediastinum neurinoma, schwannoma at the lung apex, Pancoast tumour, and dissection of the internal carotid artery.
Unilateral disturbance of the sympathetic innervation of the face leading to an inability of the facial vasculature to dilate in response to normal stimuli is thought to be the cause of harlequin syndrome: a unilateral lack of flushing and sweating.
It should not be confused with Horner's syndrome—a unilateral ptosis, reactive ipsilateral miosis, and hemifacial anhidrosis—although they share similar lesion sites and some clinical manifestations. Most patients with harlequin syndrome—as in our case—do not require medical or surgical treatment unless, of course, there is an underlying disease (video).

A 27-year-old woman presented to our department for evaluation and treatment of dysphagia with recently diagnosed oesophageal stenosis. The patient had progressive difficulty in swallowing during the previous 2 years, first with solids then with liquids. The medical history showed that the patient was admitted to our clinic 5 months earlier for fatigue and she was diagnosed with severe iron deficiency anaemia. 2 months before presenting to our department, the patient underwent an oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), which revealed a 3-mm marked narrowing due to an eccentric oesophageal web 14 cm from the incisors preventing passage of either an adult or a paediatric endoscope (figure A). Biopsies taken from the oesophageal web showed that the mucosa had no substantial alterations. Physical examination showed that the patient was emaciated (BMI 16·9 kg/m2) and had bilateral angular cheilitis and koilonychia (ie, spoon-shaped nails). We completed the evaluation with a barium swallow (figure B) and a CT of the neck to assess the extent of the stenosis and to exclude extraluminal process. The examinations showed a focal stenosis in the upper oesophagus at the C6 level, without signs of malignancy. The EGD and the barium swallow findings with the history of severe iron deficiency anaemia led to a final diagnosis of an oesophageal web associated with Plummer-Vinson syndrome. The oesophageal web was managed by oesophageal dilation, which was done gradually multiple times over 6 weeks with a through-the-scope balloon to 18 mm in diameter (figure C). The patient reported complete resolution of dysphagia symptoms and is planned for regular surveillance of malignant transformation of the hypopharynx or the upper oesophagus with upper endoscopy.Plummer-Vinson syndrome, also known as Paterson-Brown Kelly syndrome, is a rare condition characterised by the triad of dysphagia, iron deficiency anaemia, and proximal oesophageal webs. The majority of reported cases (90%) are middle-aged female individuals. Although the exact pathogenesis of this condition is not fully understood, iron deficiency anaemia represents the most accepted hypothesis. Iron deficiency is postulated to especially affect the epithelial cells of the gastrointestinal tract due to their rapid turnover. Low iron concentrations lead to reduction in the activity of iron-dependent oxidative enzymes, which is speculated to cause mucosal atrophy and degeneration, eventually leading to the development of oesophageal webs after repeated injury. Although mucosal changes probably occur throughout the oesophagus, the postcricoid region incurs the most damage during the swallowing of solid food due to its restrictive skeletal surroundings, and is thus more susceptible to web formation. Barium swallow and EGD have high sensitivity to detect oesophageal webs. Many patients with mild dysphagia might have improved swallowing function through iron therapy alone, which restores impaired oesophageal contraction and the integrity of the oesophageal mucosa. However, long-standing dysphagia is unlikely to respond to iron therapy, necessitating the use of endoscopic oesophageal dilation. The recognition of this syndrome is crucial as it signifies a precancerous condition, with an estimated 4–16% increased risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma of the postcricoid pharynx and the upper oesophageal region. Annual EGD is recommended for the early detection of prematurely malignant transformation.

A 61-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with a 5-day history of sudden-onset, persistent myocloni in his left leg and the left side of his abdomen. Previously, the patient had been fit and well. He reported no recent fever, headache, or trauma.
14 months before admission, the patient had an allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for acute myeloid leukaemia with mutated nucleophosmin 1 which resulted in full remission.
On examination, we found the patient generally well; he had painless, rhythmic myocloni, with a frequency of 0·5–1·0 per s, of the proximal left leg and abdomen. The movements were continuous and would not be triggered or suppressed by any specific movements. The patient had no other atypical findings and cognitively was fully alert and conscious.
Laboratory investigations—apart from a previously described macrocytosis—were within typical range.
On day 1 after admission, an MRI of the patient's brain showed multiple cortico-subcortical fluid-attenuated-inversion-recovery hyperintense lesions without diffusion restrictions or contrast-enhancement (figure).On day 2 after admission, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analyses showed normal cell and protein count; microbial multiplex PCR testing and cytology tests for malignancies were negative.
On day 3, a scalp electroencephalogram (EEG) showed no epileptiform discharges that correlated with the myocloni. Further investigations found no neoplasms.
On day 5, the myocloni extended to the proximal part of the left arm despite the patient being given multiple antiseizure medications.
On day 8 after admission, a biopsy of the brain was done and histopathological analysis of a sample of the biopsy showed T-cell-dominated perivascular lymphocyte infiltrates and endothelial proliferations without evidence of viral infection, demyelination, graft-versus-host disease, or neoplasia.
From day 9 after admission, the patient's condition deteriorated; he became disorientated and confused, then drowsy and stuporous; the myocloni continued.
Repeated MRIs, from days 5 to 12 after admission, showed progression of the multiple cortico-subcortical lesions (figure); the EEG showed right-hemispheric temporo-parietal focal slowing independent of the worsening of the patient's condition.
On day 15 after admission, he developed electroclinical super-refractory status epilepticus, which was finally terminated by continuous intravenous thiopental. At this stage autoimmune encephalitis was suspected and immunosuppressive treatment with prednisolone, plasmapheresis, intravenous immunoglobulins, and rituximab started; serum and CSF—collected prior to initiation of the treatments—was subsequently found to be positive for GABAA receptor antibodies (serum titre 1:320; normal <1:20; CSF titre 1:1), confirming the diagnosis of anti-GABAA receptor encephalitis.
On day 33 and day 185, MRIs showed improvement (figure) with concomitant decreases in serum antibody titres (day 79, 1:20; day 186, <1:20) and serum neurofilament light chain concentrations—day 34, 511·5 pg/mL (99·995 percentile); day 233, 25·4 pg/mL (97·20 percentile).
During the period of hospitalisation, the patient experienced multiple complications, including asystole, which required resuscitation, and critical-illness poly-neuromyopathy. After a prolonged stay in the intensive care unit, the patient was transferred to a neurorehabilitation unit.
At outpatient follow-up, the patient was ambulatory and had mild, residual paresis of his left leg (video); his neurological deficits continued to improve.
Autoantibodies against GABAA receptor cause an encephalitis characterised by seizures, cognitive impairment, psychiatric symptoms, and movement disorders. Underlying pathogenic mechanisms are, in most cases, unclear; associations between haematological malignancies and allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplants—as in our case—causing immune dysregulation may indicate possible aetiologies. Studies have reported a range of 9 to 43 months from completion of allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant to the development of GABAA receptor encephalitis.
Typical MRI changes, in conjunction with the patient's history and symptoms, should prompt consideration of anti-GABAA receptor encephalitis; confirmatory autoantibody results—often available only after a significant length of time—should not delay treatment initiation.

A 65-year-old man attended our hospital with a 15-day history of fever, fatigue, and anorexia. He had been seen at his local hospital before coming to us and had been given a variety of different anti-infective agents and antipyretic drugs to no avail. The patient was previously fit and well. He lived in the rural Henan province, China, and gave no history of recent travel.On examination, apart from an enlarged spleen—measuring on ultrasound 70 mm thick and 175 mm long—and a temperature of 39·6°C, we found no abnormalities.
Laboratory investigations showed decreased white blood cell count of 2·15 × 109 per L (normal 3·5–9·5), red blood cell count of 3·75 × 1012 per L (normal 4·3–5·8), haemoglobin concentration of 9·95 g/dL, platelet count of 78 × 109 per L (normal 125–350), absolute neutrophil count of 1·57 × 109 per L (normal 1·8–6·3), albumin concentration of 31·6 g/L (normal 35–55), and HDL concentration 0·55 mmol/L (normal >0·91). The patient's triglyceride (1·83 mmol/L; normal 1·7), D-dimer (37·58 mg/L; normal 0–0·55), procalcitonin (0·455 ng/mL; normal 0–0·046), ferritin (2508·5 ng/mL; normal 30–400), and 1,3-β-D-glucan (166·50 pg/mL; normal 0–100) levels were raised.
The patient's globulin (27·0 g/L; normal 20–35), fibrinogen (2·75 g/L; normal 2–4), and aspergillus-antigen test for serum galactomannan (0·27 μg/L; normal 0–0·85) were in the normal ranges. The T-SPOT.TB (Oxford Immunotec, Oxford, UK) test was negative. Tests for HIV and tumour markers were negative; blood and bone marrow cultures were also both negative.
On day 2 of the admission, we did a bone marrow aspiration; marrow cytology showed an extremely low myelodysplasia and several haemophagocytic cells.

A 33-year-old homeless woman presented to the emergency room in September, 2012, with 2 days of dry cough, dyspnoea, and fever, and 1 week of pruritic rash. On examination she had a temperature of 41·0°C, blood pressure of 98/65 mm Hg, heart rate of 85 bpm, respiratory rate of 16 bpm, and O2 saturation of 47% on room air. She had a diffuse papular rash with vesicles of different ages with haemorrhagic crust affecting the trunk, extremities, face, and scalp, but sparing the palms and soles (figure). She had normal mental status, cranial nerves, motor, and sensory examination. Chest radiograph showed diffuse bilateral airspace opacities.
Within a few hours of presentation she suddenly became confused, with flaccid paralysis necessitating intubation and admission to the medical intensive care unit. Electroencephalogram showed non-convulsive status epilepticus. MRI brain showed multiple foci of punctate microhaemorrhages throughout the corpus callosum, both temporal lobes, and left posterior cingulate gyrus, consistent with infectious haemorrhagic encephalitis (figure). HIV testing was positive, with CD4 count 4 cells/μL (normal 348–1456 cells/μL), and viral load was 66 000 copies/mL (normal < 50 copies/mL). A skin biopsy sample stained positive for varicella zoster virus (VZV), but negative for herpes simplex virus (HSV).
Zoster-associated encephalitis from disseminated VZV can develop within days of the disseminated rash, and should be strongly suspected in immunosuppressed patients. Characteristic signs of zoster-associated encephalitis include acute delirium, typical signs of stroke such as headache with acute hemiplegia, aphasia, ataxia, hemisensory loss, or visual changes, dependent on the predominant location of the VZV vasculitis. Intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 h for 7–10 days should be started early if there is clinical suspicion of encephalitis.
Our patient was given intravenous aciclovir and multiple antiepileptic drugs to control her seizures. We treated her for VZV pneumonia, aspergillus pneumonia, propofol-induced pancreatitis, Escherichia coli urinary tract infection, and critical illness myopathy. After stabilisation in hospital she was started on antiretrovirals and pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis. After 2 months of rehabilitation she could walk independently and communicate without difficulty. At last follow-up in March, 2014, she had made a near full recovery in terms of her cognitive and motor function.
output: Disseminated varicella zoster virus infection with hemorrhagic encephalitis

A 51-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital for investigation of blackouts occurring in the context of worsening breathlessness (New York Heart Association [NYHA] class IV) and swelling of her legs. 14 months earlier she had a gastric banding operation.The patient had a history of systemic lupus erythematosus for which she had been taking oral azathioprine 50 mg twice a day, prednisolone 5 mg daily, and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice a day for 5 days a week for the past 19 years; she had no significant family history.
On examination, the patient's body-mass index had fallen from 46 kg/m2 pre-gastric bypass to 25 kg/m2; her jugular venous pressure was elevated, heart sounds were normal, and her chest was clear. She had bilateral peripheral oedema to her ankles and abdominal distension. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed right bundle branch block with evidence of right ventricular hypertrophy.
Laboratory investigations showed renal impairment with creatinine 99 μmol/L and estimated glomerular filtration rate 51 mL/min per 1·73 m2. High-sensitivity troponin I was 251 ng/L (normal <32) and plasma concentration of N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) was raised at 32 208 ng/L (normal <400).
Transthoracic echocardiography showed left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) with small cavity, normal ejection fraction, and impaired longitudinal function; and right ventricular dysfunction and bi-atrial dilatation. A cardiac MRI (figure) confirmed LVH with 16 mm maximal wall thickness and non-coronary late gadolinium enhancement. Myocardial T1 relaxation time was normal; a high-resolution CT showed fibrotic changes in the lungs.
Considering the findings in the round, we suspected hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy and stopped this medication. Right heart catheterisation confirmed pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease. Right ventricular biopsy demonstrated marked vacuolation—shown on electron microscopy to be an excess of lysosomes (figure) containing electron-dense, phospholipid-rich lamellar bodies: features that are common to Fabry's disease and hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy. A normal α-galactosidase A level, a normal T1 relaxation time on MRI, and negative genetic tests for abnormalities of the GLA gene excluded the former.
We decided that the patient was not eligible for cardiac transplantation due to her frailty and comorbidities. However, within 12 months after stopping the hydroxychloroquine, her condition was much better: the breathlessness had improved—NYHA class III—and the concentration of NT-proBNP had reduced to 5337 ng/L. In retrospect, we found evidence of LVH and ECG changes before gastric surgery, but we believe that the rapid weight loss may have accelerated the damage to the heart by altering the absorption of the hydroxychloroquine.
Hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy is rare—although the true prevalence is unknown—and related to perturbed lysosomal autophagy. Risk factors—relevant to our case—include older age, female sex, and a high cumulative dose of hydroxychloroquine; we calculated the dose to have been greater than or equal to 2774 g over 19 years. Hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy should be considered in patients with LVH and restrictive cardiomyopathy, as it may be partially reversible after medication withdrawal (video).

In March, 2020, a 59-year-old man presented to Hospital Universitario 12 de Octubre, Madrid, Spain, with a 15-day history of fever, headache, leg myalgia, and weight loss (4 kg). Physical examination showed no pathological findings. Initial diagnostic workup showed an increased concentration of C-reactive protein (16 mg/dL) and lymphopenia (700 lymphocytes per μL). White blood cell count and concentrations of creatine kinase were normal (52 units per L; reference range: 34–171 units per L). Nasopharyngeal exudate was negative for influenza A and B, respiratory syncytial virus, and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). A chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. Symptomatic treatment with oral analgesics and antipyretics (paracetamol 650 mg every 8 h, alternating every 4 h with dipyrone 575 mg every 8 h) was initiated, and the patient showed clinical improvement 4 days after admission. The patient was discharged and scheduled for a follow-up 3 weeks later. At 7 days after discharge, the fever and headache recurred. The patient did not seek medical attention and was not evaluated by a physician until the 3-week follow-up. During this follow-up, the patient reported the fever and headache recurrence, and analysis indicated increased concentrations of inflammatory markers (14 mg/dL of C-reactive protein and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 46 mm per h). The patient was readmitted to the hospital and a PET scan was done, which showed an increase in metabolic activity on the vascular walls of small and medium vessels. A subsequent visceral arteriography showed multiple microaneurysms in the small arteries of the digestive visceral territory and both renal arteries, which suggested polyarteritis nodosa vasculitis (figure). Tests for antinuclear antibodies and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. Hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and HIV serological tests were negative. There was no evidence to suggest the involvement of other organs (five factor score=0). The patient received treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone bolus for 2 days (120 mg daily). The patient was discharged and received oral azathioprine (100 mg daily for 1 week, followed by 150 mg daily indefinitely) and a tapering regimen of oral prednisone (30 mg daily for 1 week, followed by 20 mg daily for 1 week, 1 week off, 10 mg daily for 2 weeks, alternate daily doses of 10 mg and 7·5 mg for 2 weeks, and 7·5 mg daily indefinitely). At the 3-week follow-up, fever, headache, and myalgia had resolved.Polyarteritis nodosa is a rare necrotising vasculitis of medium and small arteries, with substantial associated morbidity and mortality. Clinical features are highly variable; symptoms at onset are usually unspecific, and the differential diagnosis is often broad. Because the patient was admitted during the COVID-19 pandemic, the possibility of an infection with SARS-CoV-2 was initially considered; however, the poor clinical and analytical improvement prompted us to look for other causes of the symptoms and laboratory abnormalities. Accurate diagnosis of polyarteritis nodosa allowed for early initiation of immunosuppressive treatment.

A 38-year-old primigravid woman presented to our hospital at 31 weeks of gestation with severe abdominal pain. She had no uterine contractions, vaginal bleeding, or trauma. She was hypotensive, her abdomen was peritonitic and a fetal heart rate tracing showed fetal distress with bradycardia (60 beats per min [normal range 110–160 beats per min]). We performed a laparotomy within minutes of admission, which revealed that the uterus had split open along its entire length, as well as 1·5 L of haemoperitoneum. We delivered the baby, repaired the rupture, and transfused blood products to prevent consumptive coagulopathy in the mother. Unfortunately, the neonate's Apgar scores were 2 points at 1 min and 4 points at 5 mins, and blood gases within the umbilical cord showed severe metabolic acidosis (pH 6·84, bicarbonate 10·5 mmol/L, partial CO2 pressure 61·6 mm Hg, base excess −23 mmol/L). He died despite resuscitation.As obstetricians, we were perturbed; a spontaneous uterine rupture before the onset of labour in women without a caesarean scar or myomectomy scar is extremely uncommon. However, when we examined our patient following the surgery, we noticed a unilateral Z thumb deformity of her left hand, which we confirmed on x-ray, and thin skin with multiple haemosiderin scars on her left foot (figure). We learned that she had a history of easy bruising in childhood and had sustained an open ankle fracture 6 years earlier while skipping, with rupture of the anterior talofibular ligament, peroneous tertius, and extensor digitorum brevis muscle tendons. Following orthopaedic surgery, she consulted three specialists, all of whom felt that the probability of a connective tissue disorder was low and that she did not require further investigation, given that she had no skin elasticity and her Beighton score was only 2 points.
However, considering the history of unprovoked uterine rupture, the low energy mechanism of the ankle injury, and our clinical findings, we reasoned that her a priori risk of connective tissue disorder was high. Therefore, with the patient's consent, we proceeded with genetic tests using next-generation sequencing of whole blood. The results confirmed a pathogenic, heterozygous variant (c.951+5G→A [p.Gly300_Ala317del]) in the COL3A1 gene, consistent with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. This variant disrupts a splice donor site shown to cause exon skipping and in-frame deletion within the collagen helical domain. Subsequent echocardiography and whole-body magnetic resonance angiography of the patient excluded valvular disease, aortic root dilation, and vascular aneurysms (figure).
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder arising from deleterious missense, splicing, and haploinsufficiency variations in the COL3A1 gene, affects the synthesis of type III collagen, the foundation of the connective tissue in hollow viscera (eg, uterus), vessels, and skin. The physical features are subtle and the Beighton score (which includes the large joints in its calculation) can be misleadingly normal, given that large joint hypermobility and hyperextensibility of the skin—characteristic of the more common forms of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome—are unusual in the vascular form of the disease.
A history of recurrent, atraumatic bruising with haemosiderin pigmentation of the skin (as seen in our patient) suggests pathological soft-tissue fragility and should prompt genetic testing to avoid missing the diagnosis. Pregnant women are especially vulnerable, given that catastrophic complications from peripartum arterial and uterine rupture occur in 5% of women with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Adverse obstetric outcomes are potentially preventable through pre-pregnancy genetic counselling and targeted antenatal surveillance, but only if the syndrome is suspected sooner.

A 4-month-old girl presented to our emergency department with a low-grade fever and a persistent cough—her parents reported a daily productive cough and said the child's stools had become greenish and greasy in recent weeks. The infant was the second child of non-consanguineous parents, born full-term after an unremarkable pregnancy; birthweight was 3·8 kg and meconium was passed on the first day of life.Examination showed insufficient weight gain: the child's weight (4·5 kg) was less than the third percentile on the normal growth curve. On chest auscultation, we heard bilateral crackles. The infant's social interactions and axial tone were good. However, she had a continuous large amplitude action tremor involving all limbs and head (video); the tremor increased at the beginning of the movement and was enhanced by sudden acoustic stimuli. Spontaneous movements were reduced—especially in the lower limbs. Antigravity limb movements were reduced: she could move her arms towards an object in front of her but was unable to reach it.
Laboratory investigations showed normal electrolytes, glucose concentration, and liver enzymes. A depletion of the fat-soluble vitamins was identified—notably vitamin E was 3 μmol/L (normal range 10–20). An x-ray showed bronchovascular markings.
We conducted a sweat test and diagnosed cystic fibrosis, confirmed by genetic analysis—cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene homozygous F508del mutation. We started the patient on pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy and polyvitamin supplementation. 1 week later, the patient's motor function had improved: spontaneous movements had increased, and the tremor had almost disappeared (figure). She could play with her hands and feet and grasp objects. 1 month later, her vitamin E blood concentration was in normal range and neurological examination was normal (video).
Vitamin E deficiency is associated with movement disorders—including ataxia and tremor; neurological symptoms develop after severe and prolonged deficiency. Monitoring and supplementation of vitamin E in patients with cystic fibrosis means that neurological symptoms are rare. In Italy—where our patient was born—screening has been mandatory since 1992. The patient did have expanded newborn screening, but results were negative for all screened diseases: blood concentration of immunoreactive trypsinogen was 49 ng/mL (cutoff value 62). False negatives, while rare, can occur in patients with the more severe class III mutations.
Finally, infants with a history of persistent coughing, unwellness, and a tremor should raise suspicions of having cystic fibrosis—even if all newborn screening tests are negative.

In January, 2019, a 37-year-old, White man presented to Saint-Etienne University Hospital (France) with relapsed Hodgkin lymphoma. A PET-CT scan showed hypermetabolic adenomegaly above and below the diaphragm, without visceral or bone involvement. Two cycles of intravenous chemotherapy (gemcitabine 800 mg/m2, vinorelbine 15 mg/m2, and pegylated liposomal doxorubicin 10 mg/m2 on days 1 and 8 every 21 days) resulted in a complete metabolic response in March, 2019. Consolidation consisted of double umbilical cord blood transplantation (dUCBT; total nucleated cells 15·4 × 107 cells per kg and 19·1 × 107 cells per kg for each cord, CD34+ cells 6·5 × 105 cells per kg and 7·9 × 105 cells per kg) after an intravenous conditioning regimen (thiotepa 5·0 mg/kg, busulfan 3·2 mg/kg, fludarabine 40 mg/m2, thymoglobulin 5·0 mg/kg). Prevention of graft-versus-host disease involved intravenous ciclosporin (3 mg/kg per day) and myclophenolate mofetil (3 mg/kg per day) 3 days before dUCBT and 1 month after.2 weeks after dUCBT, he had sudden central scotoma (count fingers) in his left eye, mild neck pain, and headaches. Retinal fundus imaging showed an acute central retinopathy with macular haemorrhage (figure A), explained by severe thrombocytopenia (3 × 109 cells per L, nadir of platelet count). There was no coagulation abnormality except hyperfibrinogenaemia (5 g/L). Macular optical coherence tomography confirmed presumed sub-inner limiting membrane haemorrhage, which is less common than sub-hyaloid haemorrhage. The patient was closely monitored during first-line therapy, which consisted of platelet transfusions repeated twice daily over 6 weeks (total number 84) to reach a minimum of 150 × 109 cells per L. For the initial 2 weeks, his thrombocytopenia was transfusion-refractory and anti-HLA antibodies were not present.
At 3 weeks of follow-up platelets increased to 20 × 109 cells per L, and fibrin aggregates replaced fresh blood (figure B), preventing good visual recovery. At 6 weeks of follow-up platelets reached 180 × 109 cells per L, and the patient recovered perfect vision (20/20) with almost no fibrin clots and a normal macular appearance (figure C).
The prevalence of retinopathy in patients with severe thrombocytopenia is about 30%. Macular haemorrhage can be sub-hyaloid, sub-inner limiting membrane, or a combination of both; optical coherence tomography can help show the precise location (appendix). Whatever the level of the macular haemorrhage associated with severe thrombocytopenia, first-line therapy does not require invasive ophthalmological treatment (eg, intravitreal injection of recombinant tissue plasminogen activator, anti-VEGF, and gas, laser, or surgery with vitrectomy) conventionally used for other aetiologies with similar clinical presentations (particularly Valsalva retinopathy, Terson retinopathy, and retinal vascular diseases); treatment of the underlying cause (platelet transfusion) initially has the best benefit–risk ratio, considering the fragile background of these patients. Invasive local options should be discussed as second-line therapy, when macular haemorrhage persists despite resolution of severe thrombocytopenia.

A 57-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease from type 2 diabetes was assessed at our specialist unit for a kidney transplant to be donated by his brother. The patient was unsensitised and blood group O; his 59-year-old brother was the same blood type and two-haplotype HLA-matched. Both the patient and his brother were enrolled into our immunological tolerance protocol, which combines a haematopoietic stem-cell transplant with a kidney transplant with the goal of inducing sustained mixed chimerism—a state where the recipient's haematopoietic system has a mixture of both host and donor cells.Notably, the requirements for tacrolimus withdrawal include a stable mixed chimerism of greater than 5% of donor cells, no evidence of rejection on a series of renal biopsies, and no evidence of graft-versus-host disease.
Initially, the donor's haematopoietic stem cells were mobilised using granulocyte colony-stimulating factor. Peripheral blood apheresis was then done, and CD34+ and CD3+ cell products were isolated and cryopreserved.
On day 0, we did a left-sided donor nephrectomy and kidney transplant; the recipient was immediately started on tacrolimus and prednisone.
On day 1, the donor was allowed home and the recipient underwent conditioning with total lymphoid irradiation and an intravenous infusion of rabbit anti-thymocyte globulins.
On day 5, the recipient was allowed home; his urine output at that stage was 3·4 L per 24 h (normal >30–50 cc/kg per day) and his serum creatinine concentration was 0·89 mg/dL (normal 0·74–1·35).
On day 11, the prednisone tapering off was complete.
On day 12, donor CD34+ and CD3+ cell products and haematopoietic stem cells were infused, and mycophenolate mofetil was started and continued for one month.
At 3 months, repeated tests for levels of donor chimerism were sent to guide the tapering and withdrawal of the immunosuppression.
The tacrolimus tapering schedule continued until it was finally stopped at one year, at which point the recipient had a sustained mixed chimerism of 7% donor cells and stable renal function with a serum creatinine concentration of 0·87 mg/dL: we were able to pronounce the patient immunosuppression-free (figure; appendix).
2 months after stopping all immunosuppressive therapy, the patient was well and his kidney function remained stable.
Immune tolerance induction for patients undergoing kidney transplant offers the potential to mitigate the deleterious effects of long-term immunosuppression—including cardiovascular diseases, hypertension, diabetes, and nephrotoxicity—for well selected patients. Ongoing trials are investigating the induction of immune tolerance in both living HLA-mismatched and deceased donor kidney transplants (video).

In January, 2019, a 37-year-old, White man presented to Saint-Etienne University Hospital (France) with relapsed Hodgkin lymphoma. A PET-CT scan showed hypermetabolic adenomegaly above and below the diaphragm, without visceral or bone involvement. Two cycles of intravenous chemotherapy (gemcitabine 800 mg/m2, vinorelbine 15 mg/m2, and pegylated liposomal doxorubicin 10 mg/m2 on days 1 and 8 every 21 days) resulted in a complete metabolic response in March, 2019. Consolidation consisted of double umbilical cord blood transplantation (dUCBT; total nucleated cells 15·4 × 107 cells per kg and 19·1 × 107 cells per kg for each cord, CD34+ cells 6·5 × 105 cells per kg and 7·9 × 105 cells per kg) after an intravenous conditioning regimen (thiotepa 5·0 mg/kg, busulfan 3·2 mg/kg, fludarabine 40 mg/m2, thymoglobulin 5·0 mg/kg). Prevention of graft-versus-host disease involved intravenous ciclosporin (3 mg/kg per day) and myclophenolate mofetil (3 mg/kg per day) 3 days before dUCBT and 1 month after.2 weeks after dUCBT, he had sudden central scotoma (count fingers) in his left eye, mild neck pain, and headaches. Retinal fundus imaging showed an acute central retinopathy with macular haemorrhage (figure A), explained by severe thrombocytopenia (3 × 109 cells per L, nadir of platelet count). There was no coagulation abnormality except hyperfibrinogenaemia (5 g/L). Macular optical coherence tomography confirmed presumed sub-inner limiting membrane haemorrhage, which is less common than sub-hyaloid haemorrhage. The patient was closely monitored during first-line therapy, which consisted of platelet transfusions repeated twice daily over 6 weeks (total number 84) to reach a minimum of 150 × 109 cells per L. For the initial 2 weeks, his thrombocytopenia was transfusion-refractory and anti-HLA antibodies were not present.
At 3 weeks of follow-up platelets increased to 20 × 109 cells per L, and fibrin aggregates replaced fresh blood (figure B), preventing good visual recovery. At 6 weeks of follow-up platelets reached 180 × 109 cells per L, and the patient recovered perfect vision (20/20) with almost no fibrin clots and a normal macular appearance (figure C).
The prevalence of retinopathy in patients with severe thrombocytopenia is about 30%. Macular haemorrhage can be sub-hyaloid, sub-inner limiting membrane, or a combination of both; optical coherence tomography can help show the precise location (appendix). Whatever the level of the macular haemorrhage associated with severe thrombocytopenia, first-line therapy does not require invasive ophthalmological treatment (eg, intravitreal injection of recombinant tissue plasminogen activator, anti-VEGF, and gas, laser, or surgery with vitrectomy) conventionally used for other aetiologies with similar clinical presentations (particularly Valsalva retinopathy, Terson retinopathy, and retinal vascular diseases); treatment of the underlying cause (platelet transfusion) initially has the best benefit–risk ratio, considering the fragile background of these patients. Invasive local options should be discussed as second-line therapy, when macular haemorrhage persists despite resolution of severe thrombocytopenia.

A 75-year-old man with suspected scleral thinning was referred to our ophthalmology clinic. The patient had visited his ophthalmologist in private practice reporting a 10-month history of bilateral, pigmented changes in his sclera.
The patient had a history of severe arthrosis involving several of his joints—including both his shoulders, spine, and both knees and hips—starting in his 60s; he had bilateral total knee endoprostheses of his left knee, aged 70 years, and aged 73 years of the right. He also had physiotherapy treatment. A report when the patient, aged 70 years, had the total knee replacement of his left knee described a deep black discolouration of the cartilage, menisci, and quadriceps tendon.
Additionally, he reported a previous Achilles tendon rupture, dilatative and obliterative arteriopathies—including an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm, which was diagnosed incidentally, resulting in an infrarenal aortic prosthesis at aged 73 years. Also, aged 73 years, the patient was diagnosed with coronary artery sclerosis which did not require treatment; he was found to have peripheral arterial disease. Finally, the patient had prostate stones aged 73 years which were diagnosed after he reported difficulties with micturition; he had a transurethral resection of his prostate.
On examination, the patient was generally well; ophthalmology examination found nasal and temporal dark scleral discoloration on both eyes (figure), with full visual acuity, unremarkable anterior and posterior segments, and normal scleral thicknesses on ultrasound biomicroscopy anterior to the horizontal recti muscles (0·53 mm; typical range 0·4–0·6 equatorial). Coincidentally, we found that both the patient's ear cartilages appeared dark (figure).
Considering the patient's medical history and our findings in the clinic, we suspected a diagnosis of alkaptonuria and referred him to the hospital's clinic for metabolic diseases.
A 24-h urine sample was collected and analysed at the clinic for metabolic diseases; homogentisic acid urine concentration was 9350 mmol/mol creatinine (normal range <30 mmol/mol creatinine). The patient was informed about the diagnosis; his three sons and grandchildren, who have also reported difficulties with their joints, were recommended to have diagnostic testing for alkaptonuria.
The patient was advised to adhere to a low protein diet and was referred to nutritional specialists; he was also referred to the angiology department for reassessment of his peripheral arterial disease. Finally, cost approval for treatment with nitisinone was requested, approved, and started 5 months later.
Alkaptonuria is a rare, autosomal recessive protein metabolism disorder with deficient homogentisate 1,2 dioxygenase, an enzyme that breaks down tyrosine coded for by the HGD gene. Ochronosis describes the accumulation process of homogentisic acid as pigmented deposits in connective tissues; large joints, the cardiovascular system—including heart valves and the intima of vessels; the urogenital system, the skin, and the eyes may be affected, leading to tissue or organ dysfunction and significantly impacting the quality of life. Treatment requires multidisciplinary collaboration, which comprises pain management, physiotherapy, and treating secondary complications such as osteoporosis or osteoarthrosis. Nitisinone, a triketone herbicide—approved for the treatment of inborn errors of tyrosine metabolism, such as hereditary tyrosinaemia type 1—has been shown to decrease urinary and serum homogentisic acid levels and thus may offer a biochemical cure for alkaptonuria; adverse effects of nitisinone include keratopathy or more severe systemic effects such as porphyria, leukocytopenia, or thrombocytopenia.

The patient had a history of severe arthrosis involving several of his joints—including both his shoulders, spine, and both knees and hips—starting in his 60s; he had bilateral total knee endoprostheses of his left knee, aged 70 years, and aged 73 years of the right. He also had physiotherapy treatment. A report when the patient, aged 70 years, had the total knee replacement of his left knee described a deep black discolouration of the cartilage, menisci, and quadriceps tendon.
Additionally, he reported a previous Achilles tendon rupture, dilatative and obliterative arteriopathies—including an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm, which was diagnosed incidentally, resulting in an infrarenal aortic prosthesis at aged 73 years. Also, aged 73 years, the patient was diagnosed with coronary artery sclerosis which did not require treatment; he was found to have peripheral arterial disease. Finally, the patient had prostate stones aged 73 years which were diagnosed after he reported difficulties with micturition; he had a transurethral resection of his prostate.
On examination, the patient was generally well; ophthalmology examination found nasal and temporal dark scleral discoloration on both eyes (figure), with full visual acuity, unremarkable anterior and posterior segments, and normal scleral thicknesses on ultrasound biomicroscopy anterior to the horizontal recti muscles (0·53 mm; typical range 0·4–0·6 equatorial). Coincidentally, we found that both the patient's ear cartilages appeared dark (figure).
Considering the patient's medical history and our findings in the clinic, we suspected a diagnosis of alkaptonuria and referred him to the hospital's clinic for metabolic diseases.
A 24-h urine sample was collected and analysed at the clinic for metabolic diseases; homogentisic acid urine concentration was 9350 mmol/mol creatinine (normal range <30 mmol/mol creatinine). The patient was informed about the diagnosis; his three sons and grandchildren, who have also reported difficulties with their joints, were recommended to have diagnostic testing for alkaptonuria.
The patient was advised to adhere to a low protein diet and was referred to nutritional specialists; he was also referred to the angiology department for reassessment of his peripheral arterial disease. Finally, cost approval for treatment with nitisinone was requested, approved, and started 5 months later.
Alkaptonuria is a rare, autosomal recessive protein metabolism disorder with deficient homogentisate 1,2 dioxygenase, an enzyme that breaks down tyrosine coded for by the HGD gene. Ochronosis describes the accumulation process of homogentisic acid as pigmented deposits in connective tissues; large joints, the cardiovascular system—including heart valves and the intima of vessels; the urogenital system, the skin, and the eyes may be affected, leading to tissue or organ dysfunction and significantly impacting the quality of life. Treatment requires multidisciplinary collaboration, which comprises pain management, physiotherapy, and treating secondary complications such as osteoporosis or osteoarthrosis. Nitisinone, a triketone herbicide—approved for the treatment of inborn errors of tyrosine metabolism, such as hereditary tyrosinaemia type 1—has been shown to decrease urinary and serum homogentisic acid levels and thus may offer a biochemical cure for alkaptonuria; adverse effects of nitisinone include keratopathy or more severe systemic effects such as porphyria, leukocytopenia, or thrombocytopenia.

input: A 15-year-old girl presented with short stature; her height was 1·42 m (3 cm below third percentile) and her bodyweight was 41·8 kg (around 50th percentile). She had a round face and several subcutaneous nodules over her forehead, hands, and knees. She had hypoplasia of her fourth and fifth metacarpals bilaterally (figure). Serum calcium and parathormone concentrations were normal. Genetic testing showed that she was heterozygous for a non-sense mutation affecting GNAS, confirming the diagnosis of pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism. GNAS encodes the α-chain of the heterotrimeric G-protein Gs, which couples receptors for many hormones and neurotransmitters to activation of adenylyl cyclase. Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism is indicative of genomic imprinting. Patients who inherit the mutation from the paternal allele develop pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism, whereas inheritance from the maternal allele leads to pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism and renal resistance to parathormone and hypocalcaemia. Brachydactyly is due to premature closure of the epiphyses in the metacarpals.

A 26-year-old man who had emigrated from Nepal 7 years earlier was referred to the pulmonology clinic with several months of ankle swelling, a 2-month history of cough and unintentional weight loss, and a 3-day history of leg rash. A chest radiograph showed hilar lymphadenopathy (left). Physical examination was notable for erythematous, tender nodules and plaques on the anterior shins (middle). There was also swelling and tenderness of the ankles. Computed tomography of the chest showed enlarged mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes (right) and normal lung parenchyma. Transbronchial biopsy of the right paratracheal and hilar lymph nodes was performed. Histopathological analysis showed noncaseating granulomas. Microbiological studies for fungal and mycobacterial infections were negative, including a nucleic acid amplification test for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?

input: A 15-year-old girl presented with short stature; her height was 1·42 m (3 cm below third percentile) and her bodyweight was 41·8 kg (around 50th percentile). She had a round face and several subcutaneous nodules over her forehead, hands, and knees. She had hypoplasia of her fourth and fifth metacarpals bilaterally (figure). Serum calcium and parathormone concentrations were normal. Genetic testing showed that she was heterozygous for a non-sense mutation affecting GNAS, confirming the diagnosis of pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism. GNAS encodes the α-chain of the heterotrimeric G-protein Gs, which couples receptors for many hormones and neurotransmitters to activation of adenylyl cyclase. Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism is indicative of genomic imprinting. Patients who inherit the mutation from the paternal allele develop pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism, whereas inheritance from the maternal allele leads to pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism and renal resistance to parathormone and hypocalcaemia. Brachydactyly is due to premature closure of the epiphyses in the metacarpals.

A 46-year-old woman, with no contributory history, presented with a 7 month growth in her right hallux. Initially, she had noticed a dark discolouration of the distal aspect of the toe, followed by a gradual non-tender swelling and subsequent effacement of the nail (figure). Results of an initial biopsy suggested that it could be a brown tumour, which prompted further biochemical tests, the results of which revealed a parathyroid hormone (PTH) concentration of 154 ng/L and a serum calcium concentration of 2·67 mmol/L in the setting of normal renal function and vitamin D sufficiency. Her 24 h urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio did not fit the criteria for familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia. Results of parathyroid scintigraphy showed a right inferior parathyroid adenoma. A dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan of the distal radius revealed a bone mineral density of 0·471 g/cm2 (T score −3·7; Z score −3·1). After a right inferior parathyroidectomy and a disarticulation of the distal hallux, PTH fell to 23 ng/L and serum calcium to 2·0 mmol/L. Pathology confirmed the presence of a parathyroid adenoma and a brown tumour of the hallux.
output: Brown tumor of the hallux secondary to primary hyperparathyroidism

A 21-year-old man presented for evaluation of Cushing's syndrome. His medical history was notable for an incidental diagnosis of acrogigantism at the age of 18 years, when he presented for an unrelated illness. At that time, investigations showed hypersecretion of growth hormone (somatotropin), normal serum cortisol, and a 1·6 × 1·8 × 2·0 cm sellar-suprasellar mass without parasellar extension (appendix p 1). He underwent transnasal transsphenoidal resection of the pituitary lesion, after which biochemical remission was reached at the cost of panhypopituitarism, including central diabetes insipidus. Histopathological examination showed a densely granulated somatomammotrophic adenoma with positive immunostaining for growth hormone and prolactin and negative staining for adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). The patient was prescribed replacement therapy with levothyroxine, prednisolone, injectable testosterone ester, and oral desmopressin. Repeat imaging 3 months after surgery showed a partial empty sella and a thin rim of pituitary tissue, suggesting complete resection of the pituitary lesion (appendix p 1). 6 months after surgery, features of hypercortisolism were evident, including prominent weight gain (about 40 kg), extensive broad purple and dehiscent striae, severe proximal myopathy, tinea corporis, and repeated episodes of hypokalaemic periodic paresis. Glucocorticoid replacement was therefore discontinued (6 months before the patient presented to us).Our clinical examination of this man, height 2·12 m, weight 163 kg, and BMI 36·3 kg/m2, showed several catabolic features of Cushing's syndrome and residual features of previous growth hormone excess (figure). Biochemical evaluation showed ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome (post-low-dose dexamethasone suppression test: serum cortisol 604·1 nmol/L [reference: <50 nmol/L]; plasma ACTH 29·5 pmol/L [reference: 1·5–13·9 pmol/L]). Biochemical remission of acromegaly was confirmed by low serum IGF1 and random growth hormone concentrations. Functional imaging with 68Ga-DOTANOC PET-CT scan showed a large pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour (NET) and multiple liver metastases (appendix p 2) and bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (appendix p 3). Biopsy of liver nodules was suggestive of a grade I NET, with negative immunostaining for ACTH. Growth hormone-releasing hormone plasma concentration was normal (9 pg/mL [reference: 5–18 pg/mL]). A diagnosis of pituitary acrogigantism and ectopic ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome (secondary to metastatic pancreatic NET) was considered. Exome sequencing showed no mutations in MEN1, CDKN1B, PRKAR1A, AIP, SDH, or MAX. Considering the metastatic nature of his disease, the patient was prescribed depot, long-acting release intramuscular injections of somatostatin analogue (octreotide 30 mg per month). He developed clinical and biochemical hypocortisolism (0800 h serum cortisol: <13·7 nmol/L; plasma ACTH: <1·0 pmol/L) and started physiological glucocorticoid replacement. Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia was resolved on the follow-up 68Ga-DOTANOC PET-CT scan (appendix p 3).
This case highlights a rare presentation of multiple endocrine tumours in a young man. The patient had two of the three classic multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1-associated tumours (ie, pituitary and pancreatic), satisfying the clinical definition of the disease, even with a wild-type MEN1. About 10–30% of patients with clinical multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 have no mutations on gene sequencing, although they might have large coding-region deletions or duplications in MEN1.
A possibility of inherited multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes should be considered in young patients who develop two or more NETs simultaneously or sequentially. Because an excess of growth hormone and IGF1 is known to accelerate cortisol metabolism, the presentation of Cushing's syndrome can be delayed, as was evident in this case.
output: Cushing's syndrome secondary to ectopic ACTH-secreting metastatic pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor in a patient with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) phenotype and prior pituitary acrogigantism

A 4-year-old boy in a collision with a speeding motorcycle as he crossed the road was referred to our hospital from a peripheral clinic. The child had injuries to his left leg, left arm, chest, and head; there was no history of loss of consciousness.
On examination, the patient was distressed and fractious; his blood pressure was 90/65 mm Hg, pulse was 142 beats per min, and oxygen saturation was 89%; his injured leg and arm had been splinted. He was in pain and had difficulty breathing; his respiratory rate was 43 breaths per min; an intercostal drain, which did not appear to be working, had been inserted for a suspected haemothorax at the clinic. High-pitched bowel sounds were audible all over the left side of the patient's chest and an inward concavity of the anterior abdominal wall—known as a scaphoid abdomen—was seen; no tenderness was found on palpation of the abdomen.
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 9·9 g/dL (normal range 9·5–14); serum sodium concentration was 138·5 mmol/L (normal range 136·0–145·0) and potassium concentration was 3·7 mmol/L (normal range 3·5–5·2).
Chest x-rays showed an opacity of the left hemithorax, loss of normal contour of the left hemidiaphragm, a large intrathoracic air fluid level, and contralateral tracheal deviation indicating the presence of abdominal viscera in the chest (figure). We made a diagnosis of a traumatic diaphragmatic hernia. And because the patient showed both respiratory and haemodynamic compromise, he was supported by 2 L per min oxygen therapy delivered by face mask. He was given fentanyl and paracetamol, both intravenously, because of pain before being intubated in the operating theatre. An emergency thoracotomy was done through a posterolateral approach, during which we found a herniated stomach, spleen, and small bowel, and a central diaphragmatic rupture close to the pericardium and extending anteriorly. Additionally, owing to viability of the visceral contents, reduction and primary repair of the diaphragmatic rupture was done using a non-absorbable suture; he was transfused 150 mL of packed red blood cells intraoperatively.
The patient made a good recovery after the operation and stayed on the ward for a further 6 weeks for management of the femoral shaft fractures. The fractures of the left femur and left humerus were managed using skin traction and sling and swathe, respectively.
At 6 weeks, the child's respiratory and cardiovascular symptoms had abated and skin traction was discontinued and a cast applied for management of the femoral shaft fracture; the patient was then allowed home.
Traumatic diaphragmatic hernia is a rare complication of thoracoabdominal injury that is commonly incorrectly diagnosed yet it carries high mortality. Blunt traumatic diaphragmatic hernia occurs because of a sudden rise in intrabdominal pressure that causes a tear in the diaphragm, leading to the migration of intrabdominal viscera into the thoracic cavity; patients have varying degrees of respiratory and cardiovascular compromise.
The Carter's scheme categorises traumatic diaphragmatic hernia into acute, latent, and obstructive phases. In the acute phase the diagnosis is usually missed in up to 66% of cases due to associated abdominal and musculoskeletal injuries—as happened in our patient; the latent phase comprises non-specific respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms due to herniation of contents in the chest; and finally, the obstructive phase, which is associated with bowel obstruction that may proceed to ischaemia and strangulation.
A CT scan is the gold standard method for diagnosing traumatic diaphragmatic hernia but is not commonly available in many trauma centres in low-resource settings; a chest x-ray is more routinely done. While laparoscopic repair remains the recommended method of treating patients with traumatic diaphragmatic hernia, open surgical repair with or without a mesh is an option in haemodynamically unstable patients and in a low-resource setting where expertise and laparoscopic services are often unavailable. Clinicians assessing patients after traumatic injury should have a high index of suspicion for diaphragmatic hernia with attention paid to radiographic and chest auscultation findings to avoid complications of delayed diagnosis.
Road traffic crashes are the leading cause of death of children and young adults aged 5–29 years with an estimated 1·19 million deaths each year, according to a recent WHO report. About 92% of these road-related fatalities occur in low-income and middle-income countries, for which African countries take the greatest burden due to the young population. Resulting morbidities and disabilities lead to an average 4–5% loss of gross domestic product due to loss of productivity of those killed or disabled.
Uganda—according to WHO—ranks among those countries with the highest traffic death rates at 29 deaths per 100 000 people compared to 24·1 deaths per 100 000 in the African region and globally to 18·1 deaths per 100 000 people.
According to the Uganda police annual traffic report, mortality from road crashes was as high as 19·4% (4806 deaths of 24 728 casualties of road traffic accidents) in 2023. Collisions with pedestrians—as in our patient—constitute 20% of all traffic crashes and 37% of all those pedestrians die.

A 4-year-old boy in a collision with a speeding motorcycle as he crossed the road was referred to our hospital from a peripheral clinic. The child had injuries to his left leg, left arm, chest, and head; there was no history of loss of consciousness.
On examination, the patient was distressed and fractious; his blood pressure was 90/65 mm Hg, pulse was 142 beats per min, and oxygen saturation was 89%; his injured leg and arm had been splinted. He was in pain and had difficulty breathing; his respiratory rate was 43 breaths per min; an intercostal drain, which did not appear to be working, had been inserted for a suspected haemothorax at the clinic. High-pitched bowel sounds were audible all over the left side of the patient's chest and an inward concavity of the anterior abdominal wall—known as a scaphoid abdomen—was seen; no tenderness was found on palpation of the abdomen.
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 9·9 g/dL (normal range 9·5–14); serum sodium concentration was 138·5 mmol/L (normal range 136·0–145·0) and potassium concentration was 3·7 mmol/L (normal range 3·5–5·2).
Chest x-rays showed an opacity of the left hemithorax, loss of normal contour of the left hemidiaphragm, a large intrathoracic air fluid level, and contralateral tracheal deviation indicating the presence of abdominal viscera in the chest (figure). We made a diagnosis of a traumatic diaphragmatic hernia. And because the patient showed both respiratory and haemodynamic compromise, he was supported by 2 L per min oxygen therapy delivered by face mask. He was given fentanyl and paracetamol, both intravenously, because of pain before being intubated in the operating theatre. An emergency thoracotomy was done through a posterolateral approach, during which we found a herniated stomach, spleen, and small bowel, and a central diaphragmatic rupture close to the pericardium and extending anteriorly. Additionally, owing to viability of the visceral contents, reduction and primary repair of the diaphragmatic rupture was done using a non-absorbable suture; he was transfused 150 mL of packed red blood cells intraoperatively.
The patient made a good recovery after the operation and stayed on the ward for a further 6 weeks for management of the femoral shaft fractures. The fractures of the left femur and left humerus were managed using skin traction and sling and swathe, respectively.
At 6 weeks, the child's respiratory and cardiovascular symptoms had abated and skin traction was discontinued and a cast applied for management of the femoral shaft fracture; the patient was then allowed home.
Traumatic diaphragmatic hernia is a rare complication of thoracoabdominal injury that is commonly incorrectly diagnosed yet it carries high mortality. Blunt traumatic diaphragmatic hernia occurs because of a sudden rise in intrabdominal pressure that causes a tear in the diaphragm, leading to the migration of intrabdominal viscera into the thoracic cavity; patients have varying degrees of respiratory and cardiovascular compromise.
The Carter's scheme categorises traumatic diaphragmatic hernia into acute, latent, and obstructive phases. In the acute phase the diagnosis is usually missed in up to 66% of cases due to associated abdominal and musculoskeletal injuries—as happened in our patient; the latent phase comprises non-specific respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms due to herniation of contents in the chest; and finally, the obstructive phase, which is associated with bowel obstruction that may proceed to ischaemia and strangulation.
A CT scan is the gold standard method for diagnosing traumatic diaphragmatic hernia but is not commonly available in many trauma centres in low-resource settings; a chest x-ray is more routinely done. While laparoscopic repair remains the recommended method of treating patients with traumatic diaphragmatic hernia, open surgical repair with or without a mesh is an option in haemodynamically unstable patients and in a low-resource setting where expertise and laparoscopic services are often unavailable. Clinicians assessing patients after traumatic injury should have a high index of suspicion for diaphragmatic hernia with attention paid to radiographic and chest auscultation findings to avoid complications of delayed diagnosis.
Road traffic crashes are the leading cause of death of children and young adults aged 5–29 years with an estimated 1·19 million deaths each year, according to a recent WHO report. About 92% of these road-related fatalities occur in low-income and middle-income countries, for which African countries take the greatest burden due to the young population. Resulting morbidities and disabilities lead to an average 4–5% loss of gross domestic product due to loss of productivity of those killed or disabled.
Uganda—according to WHO—ranks among those countries with the highest traffic death rates at 29 deaths per 100 000 people compared to 24·1 deaths per 100 000 in the African region and globally to 18·1 deaths per 100 000 people.
According to the Uganda police annual traffic report, mortality from road crashes was as high as 19·4% (4806 deaths of 24 728 casualties of road traffic accidents) in 2023. Collisions with pedestrians—as in our patient—constitute 20% of all traffic crashes and 37% of all those pedestrians die.

An otherwise healthy 45-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of gradual visual loss in both eyes. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 in both eyes. Slit-lamp examination showed bilateral—predominantly peripheral—corneal deposits of numerous minute, crystalline materials (figure A and B). The remainder of the ocular examination was unremarkable. A clinical diagnosis of monoclonal gammopathy was made on the basis of shimmering and polychromatic corneal deposits. Serum IgG concentration was 30·3 g/L (normal 8·1–16·9 g/L) and serum electrophoresis showed a monoclonal gammopathy involving IgG-kappa light chain. Our patient was referred to a haematologist and IgG-kappa multiple myeloma was diagnosed by bone marrow biopsy. Treatment was initiated with thalidomide, and no ocular-specific drugs were prescribed. During the 7-year follow-up, while maintained on a low-dose thalidomide, our patient was regularly followed up and her vision remained stable. Although still present, the amount of these corneal crystalline deposits appeared to be decreasing and migrate away from the peripheral corneas (figure C and D).
output: Corneal crystalline deposits secondary to IgG-kappa multiple myeloma (monoclonal gammopathy-associated crystalline keratopathy)
