A 58-year-old man was hospitalised in our intensive care unit for severe, acute respiratory distress syndrome caused by an influenza virus infection. After 31 days, he was gradually weaned off mechanical ventilation. However, on the day after extubation, he had to be reintubated because of further respiratory distress. Emergency intubation was performed after rapid sequence induction using the short-acting anaesthetic agent etomidate, intravenously, at a dose of 0·3 mg/kg, and the muscle relaxant succinylcholine, intravenously, at a dose of 1 mg/kg. Orotracheal intubation was done without any difficulty. However, immediately after intubation, a change was noted on the electrocardiogram (ECG) (figure) and the patient became pulseless. The ECG showed ventricular tachycardia, which developed into ventricular fibrillation. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was initiated along with medical treatments to reduce his serum potassium concentration, which was 9·6 mmol/L; 1 h after the cardiac arrest, the serum potassium returned to within the normal range at 3·3 mmol/L. Of note, our patient had no contraindications to the use of succinylcholine before the reintubation—specifically, his serum potassium concentration was 3·5 mmol/L and he had no neurological signs or muscle weakness.Closer examination of the ECG clearly showed the effects of hyperkalaemia on the heart during the incident: initially, the PR interval was prolonged and the T waves were tented (figure), next the P waves were lost, ST segment changes were seen, and the QRS complexes were prolonged (figure), and finally the QRS complex widened in a sine-wave configuration (figure). Succinylcholine is the first line neuromuscular blocking agent for rapid sequence induction because it is fast-acting. It causes depolarisation of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) located in the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) leading to the efflux of intracellular potassium into the plasma. In cases of muscle denervation, including patients who have been in intensive care for a prolonged period, AChRs are upregulated in both the NMJ and throughout the muscle membrane; immature forms of AChRs are also released. These immature receptors are more sensitive to agonists with depolarisation occurring at lower concentrations and lasting for a longer time with no desensitisation. Succinylcholine in such situations can lead to a massive efflux of potassium from muscles to the plasma, with life-threatening consequences.
In cases of severe hyperkalaemia, treatment should include intravenous calcium salt—chloride or gluconate—to raise the threshold potential and to stabilise the myocardium, and drugs that promote cellular potassium reuptake—eg, insulin, sodium bicarbonate, and β2 agonists. This case serves as a reminder that succinylcholine should be used with caution in patients who have been in the intensive care unit for a prolonged period even without so-called intensive care unit acquired weakness.

A 66-year-old man collapsed at home with chest pain. He was found by paramedics to be in ventricular fibrillation leading to a cardiac arrest. A post-resuscitation electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm and inferolateral ST-segment elevation. On arrival at our department he had an emergency invasive coronary angiogram which showed an occluded left circumflex artery, confirming myocardial infarction (MI). We opened the artery using a balloon, and following recanalisation, we identified a substantial filling defect indicative of a large thrombus (figure). Following stent implantation, normal coronary artery flow was restored and the patient made an uneventful recovery—although brief paroxysms of atrial fibrillation were noted on cardiac monitoring in the ensuing 24 h.The patient enrolled in a research study (NCT03943966) of PET/CT angiography using a novel radiotracer, 18F-GP1, which binds to activated platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors and provides an assessment of thrombus formation. CT angiography confirmed a patent stent that co-localised with intense 18F-GP1 uptake on the PET/CT images, consistent with acute thrombus trapped behind the stent (figure).
Incomplete contrast opacification in the left atrial appendage made assessment on CT challenging. However, the presence of a separate and discrete filling defect raised the possibility of an in-situ appendage thrombus, which was confirmed on the 18F-GP1 PET/CT scan (figure). The clinical diagnosis was therefore changed from type 1 MI—caused by an atherosclerotic plaque rupture—to a type 2 MI—caused by a coronary embolism arising from a left atrial appendage thrombus in the context of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.
The patient was commenced on apixaban 5 mg twice a day, aspirin 75 mg daily, and clopidogrel 75 mg daily. The patient was allowed home after 2 days and made a full recovery.
Differentiation between type 1 and type 2 MIs is important because different therapeutic interventions are required to prevent recurrence. Most MIs—type 1—are due to acute coronary occlusion from a thrombus forming on a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque. In type 2, MIs are caused by a mismatch between the supply and demand of myocardial oxygen in the context of another disease—including coronary embolism—as seen in our patient. Adjunctive invasive or non-invasive imaging can often help clarify the clinical diagnosis and guide management (appendix; video).
output: Coronary embolism from left atrial appendage thrombus causing type 2 myocardial infarction in the context of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation

A 51-year-old man was referred to our department because of reduced exercise tolerance and breathlessness on exertion. He had a medical history of obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome (OSAS), which was being treated with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). He had complained of snoring and a loss of concentration when he was first diagnosed with OSAS, in 2012.The referring pulmonologist said that the patient's Apnoea–Hypopnea Index had improved from 36 events per h to 0·3 events per h after the positive pressure was increased from 4 to 8 cm water (H2O), and for a short period there had been an improvement in the patient's problems, but then the CPAP seemed to make the situation worse—his exercise tolerance decreased further, and he reported insomnia and pronounced morning fatigue.
When we examined the patient, his oxygen saturation was 94%. On auscultation of his chest, we heard a systolic murmur at the left, second intercostal space. An echocardiogram showed a large ostium secundum atrial septal defect (ASD) and an enlarged right ventricle with preserved systolic function (figure). The patient's mean pulmonary artery pressure was 18 mm Hg (normal <25) with no CPAP, indicating no pulmonary hypertension. However, there was evidence of shunting: the pulmonary to systemic output ratio was 2·8:1 (normal 1:1; greater than 1 indicates left-to-right shunting). We therefore concluded that the augmented CPAP had led to the development of his symptoms.
As proof of concept, we took arterial blood samples both at rest and at a positive pressure of 8 cm H2O: these showed that his arterial partial pressure of oxygen reduced from 15 to 11 kPa. We also did an echocardiogram with agitated saline while gradually increasing the positive pressure (0 cm H2O, 8 cm H2O, and 12 cm H2O; appendix). The echocardiogram with the agitated saline clearly showed that the right-to-left shunting increased concomitantly with the CPAP increases: causing a reduction in arterial oxygen saturation. The patient had surgery to close the ASD and his difficulties resolved. The size of his right ventricle reduced and he was able to use his CPAP without any problems. Interestingly, at the time of the initial diagnosis of OSAS, the patient was found to have some dilatation of the right ventricle and pulmonary trunk. An echocardiogram at that time might have resulted in earlier diagnosis of the ASD and earlier surgery.
Around 10% of congenital heart defects are ASDs. Clinically, a fixed, split second heart sound and an ejection systolic murmur over the pulmonary valve can be heard; there may also be signs of right-sided heart failure. An electrocardiogram might show arrhythmias including atrial fibrillation and incomplete right bundle branch block with right—in the ostium secundum—or left—in the ostium primum—axis deviation. Late diagnosis of an ASD might lead to the development of Eisenmenger syndrome when surgery would be contraindicated (video).

The lesions had caused pain while eating, with resultant unintentional weight loss. She also reported a 6-month history of skin blisters on her arms and legs. Biopsy of the gingiva revealed intraepithelial separation and retention of basal cells along the basement membrane. Direct immunofluorescence of the biopsy specimen showed IgG deposition along epithelial-cell membranes, resulting in a “chicken wire” pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Interestingly, at the time of the initial diagnosis of OSAS, the patient was found to have some dilatation of the right ventricle and pulmonary trunk. An echocardiogram at that time might have resulted in earlier diagnosis of the ASD and earlier surgery.
Around 10% of congenital heart defects are ASDs. Clinically, a fixed, split second heart sound and an ejection systolic murmur over the pulmonary valve can be heard; there may also be signs of right-sided heart failure. An electrocardiogram might show arrhythmias including atrial fibrillation and incomplete right bundle branch block with right—in the ostium secundum—or left—in the ostium primum—axis deviation. Late diagnosis of an ASD might lead to the development of Eisenmenger syndrome when surgery would be contraindicated (video).

A 59-year-old man with end-stage renal disease and haemodialysis since 2008 was admitted with painful, non-healing ulcerations on his legs. The lesions developed without known trauma 2 months before admission (figure). Pedal pulses were palpable on both sides and there were no signs of chronic venous insufficiency. Radiography of the soft tissue revealed diffuse calcified arterioles in a mesh-like pattern (figure). Histological examination of skin biopsy showed sclerosis and thrombosis of blood vessels (figure) and von Kossa stains were positive for calcium deposits (figure), confirming the diagnosis of calciphylaxis.Calciphylaxis is a syndrome of systemic medial calcification of the arteries leading to tissue necrosis. Skin biopsy and radiographic features are helpful in the diagnosis; but negative results do not necessarily exclude the diagnosis. Although the pathogenesis remains unclear, several comorbid conditions are known to increase its development. Associated risk factors in our patient were: end-stage renal disease, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and oral anticoagulation with phenprocoumon. Recent reports indicate that low parathyroid hormone levels in association with adynamic bone diseases can also be associated with calciphylaxis. Unfortunately, there is still no standardised treatment for calciphylaxis. Based on previous reports, phenprocoumon was withdrawn in our patient and he was treated with cinacalcet, daily haemodialysis, sodium thiosulfate, and bisphosphonate. After 4 weeks, skin condition improved and the patient was discharged home.

input: A 26-year-old heathy woman developed an axillary mass with white discharge after a spontaneous vaginal delivery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
output:
Accessory breast tissue (ectopic/supernumerary breast tissue) with lactation

This image shows accessory breast tissue in the axilla (also known as polymastia or supernumerary breast tissue along the embryonic milk line) that has become active and is producing milk following childbirth. The white discharge visible is breast milk being secreted from this ectopic breast tissue.

Accessory breast tissue most commonly occurs along the embryonic mammary ridge (milk line), which extends from the axilla to the groin. This tissue may remain dormant until pregnancy and lactation, when hormonal changes cause it to enlarge and potentially produce milk, as demonstrated in this case.

A 46-year-old woman presented to our outpatient clinic in June, 2013, with frequent collapse, ischaemic scalp ulcerations, and hair loss (figure). She had undergone carotid endarterectomy in 2005, after a small right hemispheric stroke, and had no other medical history apart from hypercholesterolaemia. She had no previous dermatological or scalp problems. She took clopidogrel 75 mg, aspirin 80 mg, and simvastatin 40 mg daily.
Magnetic resonance angiography showed occlusion of both common carotid arteries, the innominate artery, and the right vertebral artery, and 80% stenosis of the orifice of the left subclavian artery. The circle of Willis was perfused by the left vertebral artery, and the right vertebral artery was filled retrograde from the left side. Blood supply to the head was maintained by the stenosed left subclavian artery (figure).
We inserted an 8 × 24 mm balloon-expandable Express stent (Boston Scientific, Natick, MA, USA) to the stenosed left subclavian artery via the left groin (appendix). There were no complications. Postintervention transcranial Doppler showed an increase of 120% in the mean velocity of the left medial cerebral artery, from 40 cm/s to 88 cm/s after stenting.
At follow-up in December, 2013, the patient's dizziness and collapse had resolved. Her scalp lesions were almost healed, and hair growth had normalised (appendix).
Ischaemic scalp lesions due to insufficient tissue perfusion are rare. Most cases of scalp ischaemia are caused by giant cell arthritis, malignancy (angiosarcoma or melanoma), radiotherapy, or inflammation. In our case the cause was treatable with revascularisation of the extracranial arteries.

input: A 14-year-old girl presented with progressively growing bilateral painful axillary tumours (figure A). Histopathology showed slightly hyperplastic glandular tissue without cytological atypia within the reticular dermis and fatty tissue (figure B). The glandular epithelium stained positive for oestrogen and progesterone receptors (figure C), which led to the diagnosis of ectopic breast tissue. An MRI scan showed extensive axillary breast tissue without connection to the eutopic breasts (figure D). Ectopic breast tissue occurs in 2–6% of the general population, mainly after incomplete regression along the milk-line. Complete excision was done in our patient because she complained of pain and cosmetic disturbance, and because of the increased risk of primary ectopic breast carcinoma. Ectopic breast tissue should be considered in clinical differential diagnosis of tumours along the milk-line. Histological examination is required to rule out malignancy and in case of a wait-and-see approach, regular breast cancer screening is mandatory.

An 81-year-old man was referred to our clinic with a 1-year history of shortness of breath on exertion. The patient also had a history of cryptogenic liver cirrhosis and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.On examination we found him to have a pan-systolic murmur, fine bilateral basal crackles on chest auscultation, heart rate 73 beats per min, and respiratory rate 17 breaths per min. Oxygen saturation was 96% on room air.
Laboratory investigations showed normal white blood cell count and C-reactive protein concentration. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with first-degree heart block. An echocardiogram showed normal left ventricular size and function with possible bi-leaflet mitral valve prolapse resulting in severe mitral regurgitation (appendix). Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) showed a central jet of mitral regurgitation caused by annular dilatation and non-coaptation of the mitral valve leaflets (figure); using both the standard method—defined as the left ventricular stroke volume minus the aortic net flow—and four-dimensional (4D) flow advanced techniques, the mitral regurgitation was found to be 5 mL (<30 mL is mild; appendix). Additionally, the mitral regurgitation jet was seen swirling around the left atrium, thus leading to an overestimation of the regurgitation using a speckle-doppler trace (figure; video). Furthermore, moderate left ventricular systolic impairment, with a non-ischaemic fibrosis pattern in the lateral and anterior walls, was seen; on T1 mapping, there was globally increased T1 signal and raised extracellular volume (figure). Taken together, the findings suggested non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy secondary to cardiac sarcoidosis—and on discussion with the respiratory team, it became apparent that the patient had, 20 years earlier, indeed been treated abroad for sarcoidosis of the lung.
We consequently decided to defer the planned mitral valve surgery, as it was evident—with the information gleaned from the CMR—that the patient had a primary cardiomyopathy and that his symptoms were unrelated to the mild mitral regurgitation. A respiratory review concluded the problem was chronic and recommended close monitoring of the disease.
Multiparametric CMR imaging is invaluable not only for the accurate assessment of function and sub-phenotyping the aetiology of cardiomyopathy, but also, using 4D flow methods, for more precise quantification of mitral regurgitation that might—as shown in our case—completely change the course of clinical management.

output: Cardiac sarcoidosis with non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy and mild mitral regurgitation

The patient also had a history of cryptogenic liver cirrhosis and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.On examination we found him to have a pan-systolic murmur, fine bilateral basal crackles on chest auscultation, heart rate 73 beats per min, and respiratory rate 17 breaths per min. Oxygen saturation was 96% on room air.
Laboratory investigations showed normal white blood cell count and C-reactive protein concentration. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with first-degree heart block. An echocardiogram showed normal left ventricular size and function with possible bi-leaflet mitral valve prolapse resulting in severe mitral regurgitation (appendix). Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) showed a central jet of mitral regurgitation caused by annular dilatation and non-coaptation of the mitral valve leaflets (figure); using both the standard method—defined as the left ventricular stroke volume minus the aortic net flow—and four-dimensional (4D) flow advanced techniques, the mitral regurgitation was found to be 5 mL (<30 mL is mild; appendix). Additionally, the mitral regurgitation jet was seen swirling around the left atrium, thus leading to an overestimation of the regurgitation using a speckle-doppler trace (figure; video). Furthermore, moderate left ventricular systolic impairment, with a non-ischaemic fibrosis pattern in the lateral and anterior walls, was seen; on T1 mapping, there was globally increased T1 signal and raised extracellular volume (figure). Taken together, the findings suggested non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy secondary to cardiac sarcoidosis—and on discussion with the respiratory team, it became apparent that the patient had, 20 years earlier, indeed been treated abroad for sarcoidosis of the lung.
We consequently decided to defer the planned mitral valve surgery, as it was evident—with the information gleaned from the CMR—that the patient had a primary cardiomyopathy and that his symptoms were unrelated to the mild mitral regurgitation. A respiratory review concluded the problem was chronic and recommended close monitoring of the disease.
Multiparametric CMR imaging is invaluable not only for the accurate assessment of function and sub-phenotyping the aetiology of cardiomyopathy, but also, using 4D flow methods, for more precise quantification of mitral regurgitation that might—as shown in our case—completely change the course of clinical management.

A 75-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital with fatigue and vomiting. She also reported that for the previous 6 months she had muscle weakness, central obesity, and skin fragility. She had a history of dyslipidaemia and hypertension.On examination, we found the patient to be febrile with a temperature of 38°C, her blood pressure was 140/60 mm Hg, and her heart rate between 90 and 100 beats per min. She was cognitively impaired and lethargic.
Laboratory investigations showed an elevated white blood cell count of 11·17 × 109 per L (normal range 4·5–11·5), a raised C-reactive protein concentration of 391·63 mg/L (normal <6), and profound hypokalaemia: serum potassium concentration 1·76 mmol/L (normal 3·5–5).
We started empirical antibiotic treatment with cefoxitin and metronidazole and began an intravenous infusion of potassium chloride. She continued to vomit; her serum potassium concentration remained low and her temperature remained around 38°C, and daily blood glucose levels showed a gradual increase requiring sliding scale insulin.
A CT scan of the patient's thorax and abdomen showed a large mass near the omental bursa (figure) and filling defects in the distal branches of the pulmonary artery, indicating a pancreatic neoplasm with a concurrent pulmonary embolism. Compression ultrasonography with doppler showed a deep venous thrombosis in the patient's left calf; we started her on enoxaparin.
A percutaneous, transgastric, ultrasound-guided biopsy was done and histopathological examination of a biopsy specimen showed a pancreatic adenocarcinoma of low differentiation and pleomorphic giant cells. Immunohistochemistry testing was positive for CK7, MUC1, AE1/AE3, and E-cadherin.
Despite continuous potassium repletion, daily laboratory examinations persistently showed severe hypokalaemia—with average serum potassium concentrations of around 2 mmol/L.
Further exploration of the patient's hypokalaemia found a spot urine potassium concentration of 40·4 mmol/L and a spot urine sodium concentration of 90·9 mmol/L, indicating renal wasting.
Additional investigations found raised plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH; 121·6 pg/mL; normal 4·7–48·8), high cortisol level (51 μg/dL; normal 6·24–18·0), and low levels of thyroid stimulating hormone (0·02 mIU/L; normal 0·5–8·9) in the context of a metabolic alkalosis.
Taken together, the findings indicated a diagnosis of ectopic Cushing's syndrome consistent with an ACTH-secreting pancreatic tumour.
We started treatment with the steroid synthesis inhibitor ketoconazole orally at a dose of 200 mg twice a day. The patient's potassium level returned to normal after 1 month, she was then treated palliatively, and died 3 months later.
Neuroendocrine tumours of the bronchus, lung, thymus, and pancreas, medullary carcinoma of the thyroid, and pheochromocytoma are the most frequent sites of ectopic ACTH-secreting lesions, but they can occur in almost every type of neoplasm. The resulting Cushing's syndrome—also known as paraneoplastic Cushing's syndrome—usually develops rapidly and has features that are more pronounced: some patients present with purple striae, profound hypokalaemia—as seen in our case—and severe hypertension. The more typical features of Cushing's syndrome—the rounding of the face, and weight gain in the recognised distribution—are unusual in cases caused by ectopic ACTH-secreting lesions. Cushing's syndrome may cause a prothrombotic state and as such is a recognised risk factor for thromboembolic disease. Persistent electrolyte disturbances in combination with such tumours should always raise suspicion of ectopic Cushing's syndrome (video).
output: Ectopic Cushing's syndrome secondary to ACTH-secreting pancreatic adenocarcinoma

output:
Zinc deficiency dermatitis (Acrodermatitis enteropathica-like eruption)

The clinical presentation of extensive erosive, erythematous plaques with scaling in a periorificial and acral distribution in a breastfed infant is characteristic of zinc deficiency. In breastfed infants, this can occur due to low zinc content in breast milk or impaired zinc absorption. The condition is also known as acquired zinc deficiency or acrodermatitis enteropathica-like eruption when it occurs in breastfed infants (as opposed to the inherited form of acrodermatitis enteropathica).

A 58-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with a 2-week history of persistent fever and pancytopenia. Physical examination showed no other abnormal findings. However, a septic screen isolated Mycobacterium abscessus from his blood and bone marrow. An 18fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT scan showed an area of increased uptake in the patient's prostate (figure). Prostate specific antigen was 8·06 ng/mL—previously, it had been measured and reported to be 0·8 ng/mL. A transrectal biopsy of his prostate showed granulomatous inflammation. Tissue cultures grew M abscessus. He said he had never had prostatic manipulation before. However, he had been previously diagnosed with benign prostatic enlargement and, 1 year before start of current symptoms, he had surgical resection of a neuroendocrine intestinal tumour.Recently, despite no evidence of residual disease, he had become worried about the possibility of recurrence. He decided to respond to an advertisement he had heard on the radio extolling the benefits of stem cell treatments—including cancer prevention or recurrence. He said the clinic told him that the treatment was a type of “immunotherapy” that would allow his own stem cells to recognise any cancer cells as abnormal and destroy them. Further, he said they explained that the procedure entailed extracting his blood which would then be “stimulated to produce abundant stem cells” and these would then be injected into him intravenously.
A few hours after the infusion, the patient developed profuse vomiting and high-grade fever. He was given intravenous hydration and antibiotics, without resolution. He then attended our hospital.
Initially, we ruled out immunodeficiency—a hallmark of disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacteria—and only after repeat questioning of other possible risk factors did he disclose details of the “stem cell treatment”. We believe the “stem cells” had been contaminated with mycobacteria prior to being transfused into the patient. The infusion—into the blood stream—enabled dissemination and seeding of the mycobacteria in the previously diseased prostate.
The field of stem cell therapy has grown substantially. However, unregulated, unscientifically proven, and irresponsible use has also increased worldwide leading to rising numbers of cases of patients being infected from products contaminated with a variety of different bacteria including Escherichia coli, Enterococcus faecalis, Proteus mirabilis, Enterobacter cloacae, and Citrobacter freundii.
output: Disseminated Mycobacterium abscessus infection with prostatic involvement secondary to contaminated stem cell therapy

input: A 59-year-old man came to our hospital saying that he had been accidentally shot by a fellow hunter during an expedition to the local moorland. He was alone when he walked into the department. During physical examination he was found to be asymptomatic and all his vital signs were stable. His blood pressure was 125/75 mm Hg, and he did not complain of any dizziness or shortness of breath. Furthermore, no active bleeding was noted. An emergency whole-body CT (figure) was done and showed that shotgun pellets were evenly distributed in his body—from his knees to his neck—and that some had penetrated internally to affect several organs. A CT scan of his chest also showed that two of the pellets had reached the mediastinum: one had stopped a few millimetres from the floor of the aortic arch (figure), and the other one penetrated the pericardium, stopping between the pericardium and the lateral wall of the left ventricle (figure). A CT angiogram showed that no contrast agent was leaking from around the aorta or pericardium. We also did an echocardiogram, which, except for a small pericardial effusion, indicated that the patient was haemodynamically stable. The CT angiogram was repeated 24 h later, and, fortunately for the patient, nothing significantly had changed. At this stage, there were no indications for cardiac surgery to remove the pellets so—with the patient's agreement—we decided to take no further action after having weighed up the pros and cons of undertaking high-risk cardiac surgery or leaving the pellets where they were. After a few days of observation and antibiotic prophylaxis ceftriaxone (1 g a day for a week), the patient was discharged. He remained symptom free when seen again several months later.Hunting rifles and shotguns use cartridges that contain variable numbers of small pellets. Once the rifle or shotgun is discharged, these tiny projectiles spread out evenly and circumferentially from the barrel to increase the possibility of hitting a target. Judging by the distribution of the pellets on our patient's torso, we surmised that his fellow hunter had shot him from approximately 20 m. In the assessment of such patients, a key consideration is whether any pellets have penetrated vital organs. Furthermore, it is necessary to decide whether to surgically remove the pellets or simply leave them inside the body, where they will eventually be encapsulated in fibrous tissue.
output: Shotgun injury with multiple pellet wounds and mediastinal penetration (pellets adjacent to aortic arch and pericardium with small pericardial effusion)

A 78-year-old woman presented with marked loss of facial fat. She had a history of juvenile-onset dermatomyositis, which developed at age 10 years and required oral prednisone for 5 years. By age 15 years, her proximal muscle weakness had resolved. However, she developed hirsutism and extensive calcinosis cutis, with firm subcutaneous nodules primarily on her arms and thighs (figure A–C), as well as her back and chest. These calcifications progressed slowly over the past 65 years.
She was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at age 28 years and underwent triple-vessel coronary artery bypass grafting at age 49 years for severe atherosclerotic coronary artery disease.
Hollowing of the cheeks was first noticed about 4 years after the onset of juvenile-onset dermatomyositis, at around age 14 years, which progressed over time (figure D–F), followed by gradual loss of subcutaneous fat from her neck, upper extremities, thorax, and abdomen, sparing the lower extremities. These findings are characteristic of partial lipodystrophy, an uncommon but recognised long-term complication of juvenile-onset dermatomyositis, seen in up to 25% of patients.
Lipodystrophy typically develops 4–5 years after the onset of juvenile-onset dermatomyositis and is thought to result from immune-mediated injury to adipocytes and the surrounding connective tissue, exacerbated by chronic inflammation. Metabolic disturbances such as insulin resistance, overt diabetes, and hypertriglyceridemia frequently accompany subcutaneous fat loss, as shown in this patient's clinical course, and substantially contribute to morbidity. Other features include calcinosis, hirsutism, muscle atrophy, and joint contractures.
Screening for these metabolic abnormalities is recommended as part of the routine follow-up in patients with juvenile-onset dermatomyositis due to their impact on long-term prognosis. Management of lipodystrophy might include cosmetic interventions, such as subcutaneous lipoinjections or silicone (dimethylpolysiloxane) injections to restore facial contour and improve quality of life, along with optimising metabolic control to mitigate cardiovascular risk.
This Clinical Picture underscores the enduring, multisystem impact of juvenile-onset dermatomyositis and the crucial need for lifelong surveillance and supportive care.
output: Partial lipodystrophy secondary to juvenile-onset dermatomyositis

input: A 59-year-old man came to our hospital saying that he had been accidentally shot by a fellow hunter during an expedition to the local moorland. He was alone when he walked into the department. During physical examination he was found to be asymptomatic and all his vital signs were stable. His blood pressure was 125/75 mm Hg, and he did not complain of any dizziness or shortness of breath. Furthermore, no active bleeding was noted. An emergency whole-body CT (figure) was done and showed that shotgun pellets were evenly distributed in his body—from his knees to his neck—and that some had penetrated internally to affect several organs. A CT scan of his chest also showed that two of the pellets had reached the mediastinum: one had stopped a few millimetres from the floor of the aortic arch (figure), and the other one penetrated the pericardium, stopping between the pericardium and the lateral wall of the left ventricle (figure). A CT angiogram showed that no contrast agent was leaking from around the aorta or pericardium. We also did an echocardiogram, which, except for a small pericardial effusion, indicated that the patient was haemodynamically stable. The CT angiogram was repeated 24 h later, and, fortunately for the patient, nothing significantly had changed. At this stage, there were no indications for cardiac surgery to remove the pellets so—with the patient's agreement—we decided to take no further action after having weighed up the pros and cons of undertaking high-risk cardiac surgery or leaving the pellets where they were. After a few days of observation and antibiotic prophylaxis ceftriaxone (1 g a day for a week), the patient was discharged. He remained symptom free when seen again several months later.Hunting rifles and shotguns use cartridges that contain variable numbers of small pellets. Once the rifle or shotgun is discharged, these tiny projectiles spread out evenly and circumferentially from the barrel to increase the possibility of hitting a target. Judging by the distribution of the pellets on our patient's torso, we surmised that his fellow hunter had shot him from approximately 20 m. In the assessment of such patients, a key consideration is whether any pellets have penetrated vital organs. Furthermore, it is necessary to decide whether to surgically remove the pellets or simply leave them inside the body, where they will eventually be encapsulated in fibrous tissue.

**Shotgun pellets in the mediastinum**

A 62-year-old man came to our outpatient clinic with purpura on his eyelids. 7 months before, periocular purpura appeared after a minimal trauma. These lesions did not resolve for months. He also reported fatigue over the previous 6 months. On examination pinch purpura between smooth waxy papules were found (figure).
Histological examination showed accumulation of amorphous eosinophilic masses below the epidermis in the papillary and upper reticular dermis, around sweat glands and hair follicles. Staining for thioflavine T showed yellow-green immunofluorescence (figure). Congo red staining showed apple-green birefringence on polarised light microscopy, indicating amyloid deposits. Serum protein electrophoresis showed the presence of a monoclonal (M) protein. Immunofixation of both serum and urine determined its type: IgA-λ-type Bence-Jones protein. Bone-marrow examination was diagnostic for myeloma. Radiography showed small osteolysis of the head and cervical spine. Further investigations showed bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome and cardiac involvement. The diagnosis of systemic AL-amyloidosis was made from the combination of clinical findings, the presence of amyloid deposits in skin biopsy sample, and the plasma cell dyscrasia. Treatment with bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone was given. Autologous haemopoietic cell transplantation is planned.
Systemic AL-amyloidosis is a rare and severe disease. Bruising purpura around the eyelids combined with yellow waxy papules are typical clinical signs suspicious for systemic AL-amyloidosis. This disease occurs in patients with plasma cell dyscrasia, in particular multiple myeloma. Amyloid is composed of a fibrillar component (immunoglobulin light chain material derived from the abnormal paraprotein) and a nonfibrillar protein termed amyloid P component. It deposits in extracellular tissue of several organs (skin, kidney, heart, liver, and peripheral nerve system). The prognosis depends on the number and severity of internal organ involvement and haematological response to treatment.

Five children—whose ages ranged from 3 to 11 years—attended our temporary medical camp complaining of variously sized protrusions in their abdomens pushing the umbilicus forward. The lesions had been present in all the patients since birth. All the children were spontaneous, normal vaginal deliveries, but none had been assessed by a doctor within the past 12 months. Interestingly, the remote village of Pataase, where we located our camp to provide basic medical care, in a rural area 25 km north of Cape Coast, the capital city of the Central Region of Ghana, was home to a total of 75 children—including the five (figure) with the umbilical protrusions.The three older boys were aged 11 years, 8 years, and 5 years. The two younger boys, whose mother is pictured with them, were identical twins and 3 years old. On physical examination, the umbilical protrusions were all reducible and painless. The aetiological abdominal wall defect under the protruding umbilicus was easily felt, so we made a diagnosis of an umbilical hernia in all the children. We referred all five patients to the nearest hospital for further assessment.
Umbilical hernia is a common condition found in children. The incidence ranges from 10 to 25% of newborn babies, and it appears to be more common among African populations for reasons that are not well understood. The condition is also associated with babies that are either premature or of low birthweight. In utero, the umbilical cord passes through the umbilical ring—a defect in the linea alba—to reach the fetal circulation. After birth, the umbilical ring usually closes spontaneously, with closure occurring within the first 5 years of life, but it may take up until the child reaches teenage years. Without closure, the small intestine can herniate through the umbilical ring; the extent of the fascial opening of the umbilical ring—not the size of the herniation—determines the likelihood of spontaneous closure. Often, the umbilical hernia is reducible—as in our cases. The situation is most serious when the hernia is incarcerated and becomes irreducible: such patients will complain of tenderness and firmness, and erythema will be seen around the hernia. At this stage the umbilical hernia may become strangulated and even rupture.
Management of umbilical hernia begins with observation. If it is reducible and slowly decreasing in size, the recommendation is to watch and wait. Children with large umbilical hernias that do not appear to decrease within the first 2 years of life are candidates for surgical correction. Surgical intervention is certainly indicated in incarcerated umbilical hernia.

A 95-year-old woman attended our oral medicine department reporting a painful white plaque on the left margin of her tongue. The patient had been seen by her dentist 8 months earlier, who concluded that the small, nodular, white patch (figure), opposite a broken tooth, had been caused by trauma; he polished the broken tooth and arranged no follow-up appointments. However, 8 months later, the patient went back to her dentist because of persistent pain; the white patch had progressed, and the dentist referred her to us.The patient had a history of hypertension treated with candesartan; she reported no tobacco use or alcohol consumption.
On examination, she was generally well; in her mouth the original white plaque had developed an ulcerated lichenoid appearance, and three new plaques were present on her tongue (figure). Regional lymph nodes in the neck were not palpable. Two biopsies were taken and each examined at three levels: the first showed squamous cell carcinomatous proliferation—essentially in situ, locally ulcerated, with focal budding of the basal layer and micro-infiltrative subepithelial small clumps or squamous epithelial cells (figure); the second biopsy found an acanthotic leukokeratotic mucosa with sparse subepithelial lymphocytic inflammation, and a few apoptotic bodies (figure). Well differentiated micro-invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue was diagnosed. The second biopsy also showed lichenoid inflammation.
The patient had a partial glossectomy and a sentinel lymph node biopsy which showed no signs of metastasis; no adjuvant treatment was indicated. At her last follow-up 1 year after surgery, the patient was in clinical remission.
Late diagnosis of oral cancers—as with many malignancies—results in poorer prognosis. Notably, oral traumatic lesions typically resolve within 4 weeks once the causative agent is removed.
All new oral white and red patches, whether they appear malignant or not, should be monitored and investigated. Importantly, any plaque, patch, ulcer, lump, or anything that appears atypical needs to be explored and the aetiology found; many head and neck cancers present initially with lesions in the oral cavity. The persistence of pain and any persistent or progressive lesion should be biopsied to avoid missing an oral squamous cell carcinoma or misdiagnosing a lesion that appears to be benign. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), in the UK, guidelines recommend that any non-healing oral ulcer or a lump on the tongue should be referred to a specialist so that patients with a suspected cancer are seen within 2 weeks.

We were all involved with the patient's care. EV, DM, and SW devised the article. EV and DM gathered the data. EV, DM, and BHB did the investigations. EV and DM wrote the original draft. SW reviewed and edited the paper. Written consent for publication was obtained from the patient.
output: Well differentiated micro-invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue

A51-year-old man presented with acute visual floaters and blurry vision in his left eye for 1 week. The patient had been diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis with positive HLA-B27 in his early 20s and had been treated with 40 mg adalimumab every 2 weeks for 1 year. A tuberculin skin test, interferon gamma release assay (QuantiFERON), and chest radiograph were checked before the initiation of adalimumab therapy, none of which revealed signs of tuberculosis. A hepatitis panel was also negative. His visual symptoms developed 5 days after the latest subcutaneous injection of adalimumab. At presentation, his best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. There were no keratic precipitates or anterior chamber cells; however, 11–20 inflammatory vitreous cells were observed within 1 mm × 3 mm slit beam in the anterior vitreous, snowballs in vitreous, and multiple whitish retinal chorioretinitis lesions were seen in the left eye (figure A). Fluorescein angiography showed dye leakage from a local chorioretinitis lesion with segmental vascular leakage peripherally (figure B). The patient did not have any symptoms of chronic cough, fever, headache, or bodyweight loss. The cause of uveitis was then re-evaluated. CT of the chest revealed multiple tree-in-bud infiltrations in both right and left upper lobes (figure C). Positive T-spot test, acid-fast bacilli sputum smears, PCR (9·50 × 104 colony forming units per mL), and sputum culture confirmed pulmonary Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Adalimumab therapy was stopped, and the patient was treated with a full-dose anti-tuberculosis regimen. The patient achieved complete remission with no sign of recurrence after 1 year of follow-up.Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic inflammatory rheumatic disease with systemic involvement, and given that ankylosing spondylitis is commonly associated with anterior uveitis, an underlying infection could easily be missed and eventually lead to irreversible vision loss. In this unique case with posterior uveitis, the absence of respiratory symptoms posed a diagnostic challenge. Our case suggested that ocular manifestations with posterior uveitis could be the first sign of undiscovered newly developed pulmonary tuberculosis in patients with ankylosing spondylitis receiving anti-TNF therapy. The treatment strategy for typical acute anterior uveitis associated with ankylosing spondylitis usually involves intensive topical or systemic corticosteroid and immunosuppressive medications, which is divergent to that of tuberculous uveitis, and thus, an accurate diagnosis is imperative.

A tuberculin skin test, interferon gamma release assay (QuantiFERON), and chest radiograph were checked before the initiation of adalimumab therapy, none of which revealed signs of tuberculosis. A hepatitis panel was also negative. His visual symptoms developed 5 days after the latest subcutaneous injection of adalimumab. At presentation, his best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. There were no keratic precipitates or anterior chamber cells; however, 11–20 inflammatory vitreous cells were observed within 1 mm × 3 mm slit beam in the anterior vitreous, snowballs in vitreous, and multiple whitish retinal chorioretinitis lesions were seen in the left eye (figure A). Fluorescein angiography showed dye leakage from a local chorioretinitis lesion with segmental vascular leakage peripherally (figure B). The patient did not have any symptoms of chronic cough, fever, headache, or bodyweight loss. The cause of uveitis was then re-evaluated. CT of the chest revealed multiple tree-in-bud infiltrations in both right and left upper lobes (figure C). Positive T-spot test, acid-fast bacilli sputum smears, PCR (9·50 × 104 colony forming units per mL), and sputum culture confirmed pulmonary Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Adalimumab therapy was stopped, and the patient was treated with a full-dose anti-tuberculosis regimen. The patient achieved complete remission with no sign of recurrence after 1 year of follow-up.Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic inflammatory rheumatic disease with systemic involvement, and given that ankylosing spondylitis is commonly associated with anterior uveitis, an underlying infection could easily be missed and eventually lead to irreversible vision loss. In this unique case with posterior uveitis, the absence of respiratory symptoms posed a diagnostic challenge. Our case suggested that ocular manifestations with posterior uveitis could be the first sign of undiscovered newly developed pulmonary tuberculosis in patients with ankylosing spondylitis receiving anti-TNF therapy. The treatment strategy for typical acute anterior uveitis associated with ankylosing spondylitis usually involves intensive topical or systemic corticosteroid and immunosuppressive medications, which is divergent to that of tuberculous uveitis, and thus, an accurate diagnosis is imperative.

input: A 44-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of vision loss and pain in the left eye. The symptoms had started after he had passed out for 3 hours in a position that put pressure on his left eye; before losing consciousness, he had taken insomnia medications and consumed alcohol. An anterior segment examination showed hemorrhagic chemosis and a fixed, mid-dilated pupil (left). The intraocular pressure in the left eye was normal. Funduscopy showed diffuse retinal whitening, a finding consistent with infarction, and optical coherence tomography revealed full-thickness retinal edema. Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbit showed engorgement of the extraocular muscles and orbital tissue (right). A diagnosis of ischemic retinopathy and choroidopathy owing to prolonged orbital compression was made. Which of the following is LEAST likely to be found on physical examination in this patient?

A 75-year-old female patient with stage IV adenocarcinoma of the lungs with EGFR exon 21 Leu858Arg mutation presented to the Ophthalmology Department at the Prince of Wales Hospital in Hong Kong in March, 2017, with initial symptoms of bilateral severe dry eyes, followed by sequential ulcerations of the cornea and anterior uveitis causing reduced vision and pain. Blood tests were done and found a substantially raised anti-nuclear antibody titre, positive rheumatoid factor, and syphilis serology (TPPA++ EIA– TP++). Corneal scrapings did not yield any organism growth. The patient denied previous history of syphilis infection but reported a positive drug history of erlotinib use (100 mg daily) for more than 1 year for her lung cancer. Syphilitic uveitis was an unlikely differential diagnosis because examination of her fundi did not reveal any inflammation of the vitreous humour, choroid, or retina, and pupil examination was normal.Slit-lamp photographs with diffuse and assisted illumination revealed an active roundish ulceration on the right inferonasal cornea with an overlying epithelial defect (figure, A). Her left eye showed a healed ulcer (figure, B). Bilateral curly and elongated lashes, upper lid purplish rashes, and nail dystrophy were observed. A clinical diagnosis of erlotinib-related ophthalmopathy was made.
Her ocular inflammation recurred despite the use of artificial tears, bandage contact lenses, treatment for syphilis (three weekly injections of intramuscular benzylpenicillin [2·4 million units]), and topical and systemic prednisolone. After discussion with her oncologists, her oncologists agreed to discontinue erlotinib and her right corneal ulcer healed within 2 weeks. Later, her oncologists suggested that she switch to gefitinib treatment in view of rising carcinoembryonic antigen levels; however, her corneal ulcer recurred within 1 week after starting gefitinib. Gefitinib was then stopped by the oncologists and the ulcer again healed within 2 weeks. The patient's eyes were stable while on artificial tears, but her carcinoembryonic antigen levels were rising, and the patient refused further chemotherapy as advised by her oncologists.
Ocular side-effects of tyrosine kinase inhibitors are not uncommon, but they usually happen within weeks of initiating treatment. Discontinuing the medication is the most definitive treatment. Severe corneal ulcerations would ultimately lead to perforation and loss of sight. A balance between ocular complications and oncological control should therefore be discussed carefully with the patient. Inter-disciplinary care for such patients is essential.

The cornea was normal and a fundoscopic examination found no abnormalities.

A 65-year-old man attended our outpatient clinic for diagnostic evaluation of abnormal blood tests detected during a routine check requested by his cardiologist. The investigations showed a raised serum gamma-glutamyl transferase (406 U/L; normal <60) and a raised serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration of 99·20 μIU/mL (normal 0·27–4·20). The patient's free thyroxine and free tri-iodothyronine were low at 0·67 ng/dL (normal 0·93–1·70) and 1·5 pg/mL (normal 2·0–4·4) respectively. Anti-thyroid antibodies—including thyroid peroxidase antibodies and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies—were not detected.The patient did not report any symptoms indicative of hypothyroidism—specifically fatigue, constipation, or an increased sensitivity to cold. He had no history of thyroid disease.
On general physical examination, the patient did not have a goitre, and his cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes were not enlarged or tender.
Thyroid sonography showed a destructive thyroiditis with a heterogeneous, hypoechoic sonographic pattern and slightly increased vascularisation in both thyroid lobes—without circumscribed nodules (figure; appendix).
In the absence of specific anti-thyroid antibodies, our considered differential diagnoses were: a subacute or infectious thyroiditis, a seronegative autoimmune thyroiditis, or a drug-induced thyroiditis.
Infectious thyroiditis is commonly associated with thyroid pain and elevated inflammatory markers; both of which were not present in our patient. Regarding autoimmune thyroiditis, approximately 5% of cases are seronegative—without detectable autoantibodies—and display a hypoechoic sonographic pattern akin to a destructive thyroiditis; biochemical abnormalities are mild with slight TSH elevation and minimally reduced concentrations of the peripheral hormones. We considered a diagnosis of seronegative autoimmune thyroiditis unlikely in our patient. That left us with the possibility of a drug-induced thyroiditis.
The patient reported that he had been started on amiodarone, because of symptomatic episodes of ventricular tachycardia, 5 months ago. We therefore immediately started oral levothyroxine at a dose of 1·5 μg/kg bodyweight per day, which led to the rapid normalisation of the patient's thyroid hormone levels.
The prevalence of amiodarone-induced overt hypothyroidism is reported to be approximately 5% of amiodarone-treated patients, with subclinical manifestations five times as frequent. In the absence of autoimmunity, the withdrawal of amiodarone can be considered in subclinical cases.
Even though thyrotoxicosis is the most feared endocrinological side-effect of amiodarone—posing diagnostic and therapeutic challenges—the importance of hypothyroidism caused by the drug should not be underestimated, despite its relatively easy clinical management (video).

A 91-year-old man was referred to our cancer centre for assessment and treatment of pulmonary metastases from a previously diagnosed colorectal cancer. The patient had a 2-week history of occasional haemoptysis and mild dyspnoea.The diagnosis of colorectal cancer had been made 2 years earlier after the patient presented with a large persistent peri-anal abscess and obstructive symptoms. The patient had a Hartmann's resection with end colostomy, and the diagnosis was confirmed as Grade 2 adenocarcinoma of the rectum, stage pT3N1; he did not have an adjuvant treatment due to his advanced age and preference. 2 months later, the patient was found to have biopsy-proven recurrence of the malignancy after a colonoscopy. Restaging CT scans found new bilateral pulmonary nodules, considered to be metastases.
When we saw the patient, he was stable. He was breathing comfortably with a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per min, blood pressure was 114/75 mm Hg, heart rate 89 beats per min, oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. He was not cyanotic, and his BMI was 23·5 kg/m2.
On chest auscultation, bowel sounds were audible in the mid and lower posterior thorax bilaterally, but not audible when auscultated from the anterior thorax. Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 15·0 g/dL (normal 12·9–16·5), mean corpuscular volume 104 fL (normal 80–98), leukocyte count 9·0 × 109 per L (normal 3·2–9·4), platelet count 301 × 109 per L (normal 155–371). A CT scan of the patient's chest showed two metastatic pulmonary deposits in the right and left lobes and a large hiatal hernia—reaching the level of the aortic arch—containing the stomach, and small and large intestines; importantly, a segment of bowel was adjacent to one of the metastatic deposits (figure).
Upon reviewing previous imaging, we found that the hiatal hernia had been present 17 years ago and that it had increased in size since that time. Additionally, the patient, on further questioning, did recall occasionally having regurgitation and dysphagia without—until recently—any bleeding, abdominal discomfort, or dyspnoea. Due to the radiation tolerance limit of the bowel adjacent to the metastatic lesions, we decided that it was unsafe for the patient to have ablative-dose stereotactic radiotherapy. Instead, we treated him with lower-dose palliative radiotherapy to control his haemoptysis. At follow-up 2 and ½ weeks after the radiation, the patient reported resolution of the haemoptysis, and stability in terms of his dyspnoea and cough.

They are often surgically corrected on an elective basis due to perceived risks of unpredictable complications such as gastric volvulus, oesophageal and gastric obstruction, incarceration, strangulation, and infarction of the herniated organs. However, they can also be asymptomatic—as was the case with our patient.
Stereotactic ablative radiotherapy delivers precise, high doses of radiation, and is often used in metastasis-directed treatment of oligometastatic colorectal cancer. The small bowel is one of the most radiosensitive organs, and the presence of a loop of bowel adjacent to a target lesion—as was the case in our patient—risks stereotactic ablative radiotherapy causing enteritis, perforation, stricture, and fistula. Lower-dose palliative radiation is effective for controlling haemoptysis from metastatic lesions and has a lower risk of toxicity to nearby organs, but it is inferior to stereotactic radiation in terms of tumour control and in producing a sustained response.

A 76-year-old female patient was admitted to the neurological department of our institution in October, 2016, because of acute dysarthria. Her symptoms started 2 weeks ago at the same time as a severe cold that had developed immediately after she received an influenza vaccine.
The patient was on anticoagulation therapy with dabigatran because of atrial fibrillation and had a history of a deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism 7 years ago. Additionally, the patient was also receiving treatment for hypertension (bisoprolol, amlodipine, and ramipril). As a consequence, a thromboembolic accident or a cerebral haemorrhage was initially discussed. Furthermore, a potential adverse event of the recent influenza vaccination was considered as a differential diagnosis.
Physical examination revealed hypoglossal paresis on the left side (figure, A). No other neurological abnormalities could be found. Blood pressure was 174/103 mmHg at admission. No abnormalities were recorded in routine cellular blood cell count and blood chemistry; in particular, no signs of infection or inflammation were noted. No specific cerebrovascular risk factors were apparent. An initial cranial CT scan ruled out any bleeding or infarction. Doppler sonography of the cranial vessels was unremarkable.However, a left-sided, stage I primary breast tumour was documented in the patient's medical history. This tumour had been diagnosed 9 years ago. At that time, the patient was treated with breast-conserving surgery, radiotherapy of the left breast, and adjuvant endocrine treatment with tamoxifen for 1 year. Tamoxifen therapy was stopped after 1 year as a consequence of deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
During further examination of the acute hypoglossal paresis, cerebral MRI detected a solitary tumoral lesion at the basal skull (figure, B), affecting the left hypoglossal nerve. Except for this solitary lesion, none of the other staging procedures used, including CT scan of the chest and abdomen and bone scan, found any additional metastatic lesions. Therefore, a secondary, solitary metastatic breast tumour at the basal skull was assumed. The patient was treated with locoregional radiotherapy, antiresorptive treatment with zoledronate, and first-line endocrine therapy with an aromatase inhibitor. Furthermore, the patient subsequently received speech therapy. As a result of all these therapeutic measures, the hypoglossal paresis soon regressed completely and the patient is currently without any symptoms 8 months after primary treatment.
Solitary breast cancer metastases are rare, but affected patients often have a good chance of achieving long-term remission. In our case, the work-up to investigate an acute, uncommon clinical finding led to the diagnosis.
output: Solitary breast cancer metastasis to the skull base affecting the hypoglossal nerve

A 6-year-old boy with Ewing's sarcoma presented with generalised skin rash, low grade fever (38°C), and red eyes. Itchiness in the hands and feet preceded the rash. The child received chemotherapy (vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide) and blood transfusion 1 week before the onset of symptoms. Examination revealed purplish discoloration of both palms and soles in a glove and socks pattern (figure, A–C). Lesions resembled petechiae over the trunk, hands and feet, and face. Oral mucosa was erythematous with the rash including both pinnae (figure, D). The boy was neutropenic (haemoglobin 11·5 g/dL, total leucocyte count 0·5 × 106/L, and platelet count 20 × 109/L).
The striking glove and socks distribution of the rash prompted the diagnosis of papular purpuric gloves and socks syndrome (PPGSS) related to parvoviral infection. Parvovirus serology showed immunoglobulin M positivity. Skin biopsy revealed lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate with red-blood-cell extravasation. The boy was initiated on antibiotics (cefoperazone–sulbactam and amikacin, as per unit guidelines for febrile neutropenia), which were stopped 2 days later because he was afebrile and the blood cultures were sterile. Rash resolved with desquamation over the next 2 weeks. Blood counts also normalised after 1 week.
In children, parvovirus B19 infection usually presents as erythema infectiosum. Although uncommon, infection can manifest itself as PPGSS, which is an acute self-limited dermatosis characterised by fever, acral pruritus, oedema, petechiae, and oral lesions. The distinguishing feature is the symmetric erythema of hands and feet, with sharp margins at wrists and ankles. Other causes of PPGSS include cytomegalovirus, Coxsackie virus, and measles virus. The disease is mostly self-limited with a benign prognosis.
Febrile neutropenia is an oncological emergency that needs prompt initiation of antibacterial treatment. Recognition of such a classic manifestation, especially in an immunocompromised host, is essential to avoid aggressive treatment. Unlike patients with erythema infectiosum, individuals with PPGSS are regarded as infectious and should be isolated. Further, immunocompromised children need to be monitored for red-cell aplasia as a manifestation of persistent parvovirus infection. The index child has been well since illness, and completed his chemotherapy in June 2013.
output: Papular purpuric gloves and socks syndrome (PPGSS) related to parvovirus B19 infection

output:
Based on the clinical presentation and imaging findings, this patient has developed an **aspergilloma (fungal ball/mycetoma)** within a pre-existing tuberculous cavity.

The CT images show:
- A pre-existing right upper lobe cavity (sequela of treated pulmonary tuberculosis)
- New intracavitary mass with thickened cavity wall, consistent with a fungal ball

The appropriate management agents for aspergilloma include:

**Itraconazole** or **Voriconazole** (antifungal azoles) - for medical management in patients who are not surgical candidates or have mild symptoms

For definitive treatment, **surgical resection** is often considered for patients with significant hemoptysis who are surgical candidates.

In cases of life-threatening hemoptysis, **bronchial artery embolization** may be used as a temporizing measure.

**Diagnosis: Pulmonary aspergilloma (fungal ball) in a pre-existing tuberculous cavity**

A man aged 42 years with alcohol use disorder and of no fixed abode was admitted to hospital for acute abdominal pain that started 12 h previously. Blood tests showed a high lipase concentration (745 IU/L), and an abdominal CT scan confirmed the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis with one acute necrotic collection, characterised as moderately severe acute pancreatitis according to the Atlanta classification.2 days later, the man presented with acute pain in both legs and local examination showed multiple purpuric erythematous macular lesions. On day 4, these lesions were characterised as subcutaneous erythematous nodules associated with inflammatory oedema of the left ankle although both legs were affected (figure, A).
A punch biopsy was performed and histology showed cytosteatonecrosis in the superficial part of the hypoderm (figure, B), characterised by lobular panniculitis with dense inflammation, and necrosis together with foaming macrophages and so-called ghost adipocytes (without nuclei). No lesions that would suggest vasculitis or T-cell lymphoma were reported. Blood tests ruled out autoimmune disease or vasculitis and the concentration of α1-antitrypsin was normal. Bacteriological and mycobacteriological cultures were negative. Skin lesions, oedema, and pain in the lower limbs resolved spontaneously after 7 days, confirming the diagnosis of pancreatic panniculitis.
Systemic panniculitis is caused by the release of pancreatic enzymes, leading to necrosis of hypodermic fat tissue and sometimes bone tissue. Systemic panniculitis mainly affects men aged 40–70 years who have a history of chronic alcohol use disorder. Lesions are typically dermo-hypodermic inflammatory nodules or plaques, predominantly on the lower limbs and fingers. In case of chronic pancreatitis or pancreatic carcinoma, dermatological lesions might precede the usual manifestations of underlying pancreatic disease by several weeks to several months. Systemic symptoms can occur, such as fever, arthralgia, or bone pain due to intraosseous fat necrosis. Histologically, a predominantly lobular pattern with fat necrosis and ghost adipocytes is pathognomonic. Treatment with glucocorticoids and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs is usually ineffective. Apart from the usual spontaneous resolution of skin lesions with the treatment of pancreatitis, octreotide has been proposed as an option due to an inhibitory effect on lipase activity, and tetracycline has also been proposed in the treatment of panniculitis.

A 39-year-old man was admitted to our department with a 1-day history of pain in his left flank and dizziness. His medical history included poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and a stone in the left upper ureter. On admission to the hospital, he appeared to be in septic shock. His temperature was 38·1°C and his blood pressure was 66/35 mm Hg. Laboratory investigations showed a leucocytosis of 16·58 × 109 per L with 93·6% neutrophils. His renal function was abnormal: blood concentrations of creatinine and urea nitrogen were 0·499 mg/dL and 15·4 mmol/L, respectively. He was hyperglycaemic with a blood glucose concentration of 24·7 mmol/L.Escherichia coli were isolated in a blood culture but not in a urine culture. A CT scan of his abdomen was done immediately and showed a diffusely swollen left kidney (figure). Board-spectrum antibiotics were started empirically and 10 h later an enhanced CT scan showed that the left kidney had expanded because of gas in the parenchyma and para-renal space—especially in the renal veins. Based on these findings, we made a diagnosis of an emphysematous pyelonephritis. Because of the risk of an air embolism, an open, exploratory operation was undertaken. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit after the surgery for further resuscitation and control of his electrolytes. Repeat CT scans done 4 days and 23 days after the operation showed reducing amounts of gas in the left kidney (figure). When we repeated laboratory investigations just before he was discharged, his routine blood tests and renal function had returned to within the normal ranges: his blood creatinine concentration was 0·198 mg/dL, his blood urea nitrogen concentration was 8·6 mmol/L, and his blood glucose concentration was 4·8 mmol/L.
E coli infections in patients with diabetes and urinary tract obstruction, either occurring alone or together, are the cornerstones in the development of emphysematous pyelonephritis. In patients with poorly controlled blood glucose concentrations, the situation is complicated further by possible impairment of tissue circulation. Additionally, the high levels of blood glucose provide microorganisms with a more favourable environment in which to form gas. Mixed acid fermentation of glucose by Enterobacteriaceae is the major pathway of gas formation—carbon dioxide and hydrogen are the main components of the gas.

A 16-year-old girl attended our outpatient clinic complaining about a hard lump on the second toe of her left foot. She said it had been present for 6 years, but that in the past 3 months it had become moderately painful and that the pain was aggravated by walking. She said that the lump had not increased in size. She reported no history of trauma and no relevant medical history.On examination, the patient was fit and well, and all vital signs were within normal limits. The lump was firm and round and located on the proximal phalanx of her second toe of her left foot; there were no overlying skin changes. The lesion was hard, fixed to the bone, and non-tender on palpation; there were no signs of local inflammation. Neuromuscular examination of the lower limbs was unremarkable: we found no other palpable masses.
x-ray showed a 1–1·8 cm well circumscribed, lucent, central medullary lesion within the diaphysis of the proximal phalanx. Cortical expansion and thinning were also present (figure). We saw no fractures on the x-ray.
Laboratory investigations—including inflammatory markers, a full blood count, and calcium and phosphate concentrations—were all within normal limits.
We decided to surgically excise the lesion with intramedullary curettage and subsequent bone grafting because the lesion was painful, and no fracture was seen on the x-rays.
Histological examination of the lesion undertaken postoperatively showed lobules of hyaline cartilage encased by normal bone and fibrous tissue, consistent with a diagnosis of an enchondroma. Cellularity was within normal limits and without atypical cells or mitotic figures (figure).
At follow-up 3 weeks later, the surgical incision had healed well and the patient said the pain had gone.
Enchondromas are benign cartilage-forming tumours that usually develop in the medulla—marrow cavity—of long bones. They typically present during the second decade of life, but they can present at any age. Enchondromas are often an incidental finding because they are usually asymptomatic. However, when pain is the presenting symptom, a chondrosarcoma should be at the top of the differential diagnosis list—especially if the lesion is on the hands or feet. Additionally, fractures should be excluded first. Treatment depends upon the presence of symptoms and size of the lesion: localised asymptomatic enchondromas which are small enough not to provoke pathological fractures and show no signs of increasing in size can be kept under regular observation with repeated radiographical check-ups—usually annually. Symptomatic, large, or rapidly growing enchondromas can be managed surgically (video).

A 16-year-old girl attended our outpatient clinic complaining about a hard lump on the second toe of her left foot. She said it had been present for 6 years, but that in the past 3 months it had become moderately painful and that the pain was aggravated by walking. She said that the lump had not increased in size. She reported no history of trauma and no relevant medical history.On examination, the patient was fit and well, and all vital signs were within normal limits. The lump was firm and round and located on the proximal phalanx of her second toe of her left foot; there were no overlying skin changes. The lesion was hard, fixed to the bone, and non-tender on palpation; there were no signs of local inflammation. Neuromuscular examination of the lower limbs was unremarkable: we found no other palpable masses.
x-ray showed a 1–1·8 cm well circumscribed, lucent, central medullary lesion within the diaphysis of the proximal phalanx. Cortical expansion and thinning were also present (figure). We saw no fractures on the x-ray.
Laboratory investigations—including inflammatory markers, a full blood count, and calcium and phosphate concentrations—were all within normal limits.
We decided to surgically excise the lesion with intramedullary curettage and subsequent bone grafting because the lesion was painful, and no fracture was seen on the x-rays.
Histological examination of the lesion undertaken postoperatively showed lobules of hyaline cartilage encased by normal bone and fibrous tissue, consistent with a diagnosis of an enchondroma. Cellularity was within normal limits and without atypical cells or mitotic figures (figure).
At follow-up 3 weeks later, the surgical incision had healed well and the patient said the pain had gone.
Enchondromas are benign cartilage-forming tumours that usually develop in the medulla—marrow cavity—of long bones. They typically present during the second decade of life, but they can present at any age. Enchondromas are often an incidental finding because they are usually asymptomatic. However, when pain is the presenting symptom, a chondrosarcoma should be at the top of the differential diagnosis list—especially if the lesion is on the hands or feet. Additionally, fractures should be excluded first. Treatment depends upon the presence of symptoms and size of the lesion: localised asymptomatic enchondromas which are small enough not to provoke pathological fractures and show no signs of increasing in size can be kept under regular observation with repeated radiographical check-ups—usually annually. Symptomatic, large, or rapidly growing enchondromas can be managed surgically (video).

A 68-year-old woman presented to our hospital with pain in her left hip. She said it had started 2 weeks previously and had gradually worsened. She gave no history of trauma; however, she did have a history of rheumatoid arthritis, which was well controlled with weekly injections of methotrexate. There was no history of corticosteroid use. She also had a history of squamous cell carcinoma of the anus, which had been treated with chemotherapy. The woman had finished a course of adjuvant external beam pelvic radiotherapy 6 months before seeing us. She did not smoke cigarettes and did not drink alcohol excessively. On examination, she was unable to weight bear due to pain, and had significant groin pain on passive hip flexion and internal and external rotation. An initial plain x-ray and MRI of the patient's pelvis was normal (figure) and provided no clues as to the cause of her symptoms. She was allowed home with simple analgesia; at an outpatient review 6 weeks later, her symptoms had improved.She re-attended 6 months later, reporting a sudden worsening of the pain over the previous 3 weeks. Her mobility was also significantly reduced. We repeated the x-ray of her pelvis, which showed striking avascular necrosis of her left hip, with resorption and proximal migration of the femoral head and erosion of the superior acetabulum (figure). We carried out cemented total hip arthroplasty with acetabular bone grafting because of the patient's severe pain, significantly reduced mobility, and progressive radiographic changes consistent with Association Research Circulation Osseous stage IV avascular necrosis (AVN). 1 year later, the patient required a revision total hip arthroplasty with acetabular reconstruction because of early failure of the acetabular component secondary to ongoing acetabular AVN (figure). We allowed her home 2 days after the operation and at her last follow-up appointment she had made good progress with her rehabilitation.
Hip AVN is a recognised complication of pelvic radiotherapy. Other important causes include trauma, excessive alcohol consumption, infiltrative diseases (such as Gaucher's disease), endogenous or exogenous steroid exposure, sickle cell disease, and viral infections. Symptoms can be vague and early findings of both x-ray and MRI can be subtle—as in our patient. The final pathophysiological event is reduced blood supply to the femoral head, which leads to necrosis and collapse of the bone and articular cartilage, which is why MRI is now recognised as the most sensitive and specific method of diagnosing AVN.
Clinicians should maintain a low index of suspicion for this condition—especially in patients with non-specific hip pain who have previously been treated with radiotherapy.

A 68-year-old woman presented to our hospital with pain in her left hip. She said it had started 2 weeks previously and had gradually worsened. She gave no history of trauma; however, she did have a history of rheumatoid arthritis, which was well controlled with weekly injections of methotrexate. There was no history of corticosteroid use. She also had a history of squamous cell carcinoma of the anus, which had been treated with chemotherapy. The woman had finished a course of adjuvant external beam pelvic radiotherapy 6 months before seeing us. She did not smoke cigarettes and did not drink alcohol excessively. On examination, she was unable to weight bear due to pain, and had significant groin pain on passive hip flexion and internal and external rotation. An initial plain x-ray and MRI of the patient's pelvis was normal (figure) and provided no clues as to the cause of her symptoms. She was allowed home with simple analgesia; at an outpatient review 6 weeks later, her symptoms had improved.She re-attended 6 months later, reporting a sudden worsening of the pain over the previous 3 weeks. Her mobility was also significantly reduced. We repeated the x-ray of her pelvis, which showed striking avascular necrosis of her left hip, with resorption and proximal migration of the femoral head and erosion of the superior acetabulum (figure). We carried out cemented total hip arthroplasty with acetabular bone grafting because of the patient's severe pain, significantly reduced mobility, and progressive radiographic changes consistent with Association Research Circulation Osseous stage IV avascular necrosis (AVN). 1 year later, the patient required a revision total hip arthroplasty with acetabular reconstruction because of early failure of the acetabular component secondary to ongoing acetabular AVN (figure). We allowed her home 2 days after the operation and at her last follow-up appointment she had made good progress with her rehabilitation.
Hip AVN is a recognised complication of pelvic radiotherapy. Other important causes include trauma, excessive alcohol consumption, infiltrative diseases (such as Gaucher's disease), endogenous or exogenous steroid exposure, sickle cell disease, and viral infections. Symptoms can be vague and early findings of both x-ray and MRI can be subtle—as in our patient. The final pathophysiological event is reduced blood supply to the femoral head, which leads to necrosis and collapse of the bone and articular cartilage, which is why MRI is now recognised as the most sensitive and specific method of diagnosing AVN.
Clinicians should maintain a low index of suspicion for this condition—especially in patients with non-specific hip pain who have previously been treated with radiotherapy.

An 11-year-old girl presented to the hospital with 3-week history of an an ulcerated lesion on her cheek, unresponsive to a course of antibiotics. PCR testing of a swab specimen from the lesion was positive for orthopoxvirus DNA and cowpox virus-specific oligonucleotides. Exposure to what animal is the likely route of transmission?
output:
Rodent (specifically, pet rat or wild rodent)

Cowpox virus infection in humans is typically transmitted through contact with infected rodents, which are the natural reservoir hosts for the virus. In Europe, domestic cats that hunt infected rodents can also serve as an intermediate source of transmission to humans. However, the primary reservoir and most likely route of transmission is contact with rodents.
