The skeleton of a human being buried over 1000 years ago, in the medieval archaeological site of Torre Velha, in north-eastern Portugal, was referred to us for analysis and investigation (appendix).On examination, we found the outstandingly well preserved skeleton of an adult who was likely to have been more than 25 years old at the time of death. The person was approximately 1·80 m tall. Notably, out of the six skeletons examined, where height could be ascertained, this individual was the tallest (appendix). Based on pelvic morphology and metric analysis of the skeleton, we concluded that the individual was a man. However, the bi-iliac width of our person was 289 mm, considerably larger than the average width previously reported for ancient Portuguese men (mean 261·8 mm; SD=13·4; Student's t test: t=22·6944; df=124; p<0·001). Additionally, the individual's teeth were worn asymmetrically, indicating probable malocclusion of the jaw and maxillary prognathism (figure; appendix). Bone densitometry analysis showed normal bone mineral density values (0·792–0·999 g/cm2).
Genetic analysis was undertaken using a variety of different methodologies—including the calculation of X chromosome to Y chromosome autosome ratios (0·902 and 0·298, respectively), X chromosome and Y chromosome dosages (approximately 2 and 1, respectively), and X chromosome heterozygosity (approximately 0·2). We also determined the Y chromosome haplogroup to be R1b-P310 (R1b1a1b1a1), a frequent western-European and pan-European lineage, in accordance with the individual's Iberian genetic ancestry (appendix).
Furthermore, using a novel Bayesian method, allowing us to probabilistically assign individuals to karyotypes based on the number of sequencing reads—or DNA fragments sequenced—mapping to the X, Y, or autosomal chromosomes, we concluded our individual's karyotype to be 47,XXY, and rejected models of contamination of XXY and XX or XY (figure; appendix). The closeness of the observed position of the studied individual and theoretical position for an XXY karyotype (figure) strongly agrees with our posterior probability of approximately 1 for this individual having a Klinefelter's syndrome karyotype. Considering the morphological findings—specifically the height, the bi-iliac width, the possible jaw malocclusion, and the maxillary prognathism—the genetic findings—indicating a karyotype of 47,XXY—we concluded that the studied individual had Klinefelter's syndrome.
The prevalence of Klinefelter's syndrome in the general population has previously been reported to be 0·1–0·2%, but many patients remain undiagnosed.
Typically, people with Klinefelter's syndrome are tall, have broad hips, sparse body hair, small testes, and gynaecomastia; they may have mandibular prognathism. Obesity, low glucose tolerance, and diabetes are observed, as well as osteoporosis because of androgen deficiency. Notably, the absence of osteoporosis in our case does not preclude a diagnosis of Klinefelter's syndrome; osteoporosis is only present in approximately 10–40% of cases. Genetically, about 80% of cases are 47,XXY.
DNA from osteological remains is often scarce, degraded, fragmented, and unsuitable for analysis using commonly available techniques for clinical diagnosis of chromosomal aneuploidies. To overcome these limitations, we have devised a novel Bayesian method, which, we believe, is a potentially efficient statistical way of analysing fragmented DNA from a variety of sources (eg, ancient DNA, cell-free DNA, and DNA from forensic cases).

Based on the clinical presentation showing a green-colored hairy appearance of the tongue dorsum in a patient with recent antibiotic use (clindamycin) and tobacco use, this is consistent with:

The appropriate next step in management would be:

This condition is caused by elongation of filiform papillae with accumulation of debris and chromogenic bacteria/fungi. Treatment involves:
- Gentle brushing of the tongue twice daily
- Smoking cessation
- Good oral hygiene
- Discontinuation of any unnecessary medications that may contribute

The condition is benign and typically resolves with conservative measures.

An 80-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of acute-onset severe polyarthralgia of the hands, feet, elbows, and shoulders with associated swelling of the dorsum of the hands and feet. The patient had a preceding history of anorexia and weight loss for 2 months associated with fatigue and prolonged morning stiffness. On examination she had marked stiffness of the neck and shoulders and required high back support (figure A). The patient's hands and feet were swollen with pitting oedema giving a boxing glove appearance of the hands (figure B–D). There was tenderness in the wrists and hands over the metacarpophalangeal joints and proximal interphalangeal joints with reduced range of motion. X-ray of the hands revealed soft tissue swelling with no joint erosions and x-ray of the spine revealed age related degenerative changes with no evidence of an axial spondyloarthopathy. Ultrasound of the shoulders and hands showed subdeltoid and subacromial bursitis with minimal fluid and extensor synovitis in both hands.The patient's blood results showed anaemia, markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (100 mm/hr) and C-reactive protein (50 mg/L); tests for rheumatoid factor, anticitrullinated protein antibody, antinuclear antibody, HLA B27, and multiple myeloma screen were all negative. Joint aspirate of the left wrist did not reveal any evidence of a crystal-related arthropathy. A diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica with remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis and pitting oedema (RS3PE) was made. The patient was started on 20 mg of prednisone per day; however, there was no appreciable response to treatment, and the patient's joint pains, stiffness, and swelling persisted.
The patient's 2-month history of anorexia and weight loss and, particularly, unresponsiveness to moderate dose steroids raised the possibility of a malignancy. On further evaluation and after doing an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, colonoscopy, and ultrasound of the abdomen, the patient was diagnosed with a metastatic, poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the colon, indicating that her steroid resistant polymyalgia rheumatica with RS3PE was paraneoplastic in origin. Paraneoplastic RS3PE often does not respond to steroids alone and should be targeted by treating the underlying malignancy.
RS3PE is an uncommon condition that is characterised as an acute polysynovitis associated with pitting oedema that tends to affect individuals who are older than 50 years. This condition can occur in isolation or be associated with other connective tissue diseases, malignancies, or, more rarely, infections or drugs. Polymyalgia rheumatica RS3PE is very sensitive to low-to-moderate doses of steroids, with a starting dose of prednisone of 15 to 20 mg/day typically showing a substantial response within 24–48 hours of treatment initiation. Methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine, medications that can be useful in patients with steroid resistance, have been studied in these patients; however, the response to steroids has been more pronounced and robust.
The absence of a response to moderate dose of steroids should call into question the diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica RS3PE or suggest a secondary cause of the disease. Before labelling a case as steroid resistant, a search for a secondary cause of the disease—especially a malignancy—should be made, because paraneoplastic RS3PE is not uncommon. In 20–50% of cases, RS3PE has been associated with a malignancy. 75% of cases of paraneoplastic RS3PE are due to solid tumours.

A 6-week-old infant was seen in our emergency department with his family, who reported him to be lethargic and unwell; his abdomen was distended and he had not passed faeces for 4 days.
The patient had been born at full term weighing 3·3 kg (typical range 2·5–4·0) after an uncomplicated pregnancy. He had passed faeces 48 h after birth with a glycerine suppository; from that point on he had passed daily, watery stools, developed repeated vomiting, and had failed to gain weight.
On examination, the infant was emaciated—weighing 3·5 kg (typical range at 6 weeks 2·3–4·9)—with a significantly distended abdomen; he was febrile with a temperature of 38·5°C and tachycardic (heart rate 180 beats per min). The patient had no features of chromosomal abnormalities or suspicion of a neurodevelopmental disorder; he had no family history of gastrointestinal difficulties.
Laboratory investigations showed a leucocytosis of 28·0 × 109 per L (typical range 6·0–17·5), and lactic acidosis with a venous lactate concentration of 3·3 mmol/L (typical range 0·5–2·2). An abdominal x-ray showed significant colonic distension; faeces were seen in the rectum but no air (figure).The patient was resuscitated in the neonatal intensive care unit and was given twice daily rectal irrigations with saline; he was also given intravenous antibiotics (ceftriaxone and metronidazole).
Further investigations included a suction rectal biopsy which found aganglionosis—an absence of ganglion cells—on three sections (section 1 at 1 cm, section 2 at 2 cm, and section 3 at 3 cm). Two transitions from dilated to narrowed colon were seen on contrast enema: one segment in the mid-sigmoid colon and the second in the descending colon (figure).
After a month of inpatient nutritional optimisation—initially the patient had total parenteral nutrition, followed by a combination of oral and nasogastric lavage feeds with breastmilk and formula—the patient had laparoscopic colonic biopsies taken and an end ileostomy. Histopathological examination of samples of the biopsies obtained during this operation confirmed Hirschsprung disease to the level of the distal splenic flexure. The patient was allowed home 7 weeks after the day of his initial admission.
At 11 months old, the patient had a planned laparotomy with Swenson pull-through of his distal transverse colon; this involved taking additional colonic biopsies to assess the location of the ganglion cells, resection of the aganglionic rectum, sigmoid, and descending colon, mobilisation of the splenic and hepatic flexures with takedown of the ligament for Treitz, and pull-through of the normal distal transverse colon to his anal canal with anastomosis 1 cm proximal to the dentate line.
At the age of 1 year and 1 month, the patient had an ileostomy reversal during a planned re-admission.
At his most recent follow-up, at 3 years of age, the patient had been doing well: he had been passing faeces regularly with no evidence of constipation; he was well-nourished and developing normally.
Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (HAEC) is a potentially life-threatening condition that occurs in Hirschsprung disease. HAEC is characterised by abdominal distention, fever, vomiting, and diarrhoea. Other associated symptoms include colicky abdominal pain, lethargy, and passing blood-stained stools. The condition is caused by a large stool burden in an aganglionic segment of bowel leading to bacterial overgrowth and infection. Initial management requires prompt recognition, antibiotics, and rectal irrigations. Delayed diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease can result in life-threatening enterocolitis and severe malnutrition.

input:
A 41-year-old professional hockey referee was referred to our clinic with an 8-month history of walking difficulties; previously he had consulted several orthopaedic surgeons and had undergone physical therapy—with limited benefit—for a presumed knee injury. The patient had no notable medical history, but reported two maternal aunts with Parkinson's disease which had presented at over the age of 65 years; his parents and sister were healthy. On examination he appeared generally fit and well; however, a neurological examination found that he had hypomimia, mild rigidity, and bradykinesia on motor tasks in both legs, but predominantely in the right (video). The patient's gait showed dystonic posturing of the right foot with involuntary plantar flexion and inversion, and asymmetrically reduced arm swing; his walking difficulties improved by running and walking backwards (figure; video). Additionally, despite having difficulties walking, he reported no problems while riding his bicycle (video).Laboratory investigations showed no atypical findings, imaging likewise. Molecular genetic analysis showed compound heterozygous mutations of the parkin (PRKN) gene, confirming a diagnosis of early-onset Parkinson's disease. A levodopa and carbidopa combination, which was titrated up to 100 mg three times a day, provided sustained clinical benefit. At follow-up 6 months later, the patient reported feeling better, without fluctuations of motor function; the bradykinesia had improved and there was less dystonic posturing when walking. He had resumed his professional activities.
PRKN mutations are the commonest type of autosomal recessive Parkinson's disease, accounting for between 14 and 25% of early-onset cases. A delay between symptom onset and diagnosis is often observed because dystonia and parkinsonism may be unrecognised—especially in younger patients. Important clinical clues may be overlooked; for example, people with Parkinson's disease may find running or riding a bicycle easier than walking—as in our case—despite clear motor impairment, which is suggestive of dystonia.
The combination of parkinsonism with lower-limb dystonia in a young patient should alert clinicians to the possibility of Parkinson's disease with a genetic aetiology. Early-onset Parkinson's disease, caused by PRKN mutations, is a possibility, especially if hyper-reflexia, diurnal fluctuations, and levodopa-induced lower-limb dyskinesia are present.
output: Early-onset Parkinson's disease caused by PRKN mutations

A 56-year-old woman presented with a 1 year history of horns growing on the proximal interphalangeal joints of the right index and middle fingers. 3 years previously, the patient had undergone traumatic amputation of these fingers. The patient was not in an immunocompromised state. Physical examination showed opaque, yellowish, scabrous horny outgrowths on the amputated stumps of the proximal interphalangeal joints (figure A). The hyperkeratotic horns showed fungal hyphae on microscopy and grew Trichophyton rubrum in microbiological cultures. A diagnosis of ringworm of the finger was made. The lesions improved after treatment with oral itraconazole at 400 mg per day for 1 week and topical salicylic acid, without relapse (figure B).Ringworm species invade the stratum corneum of the skin, and damage keratinised tissues. T rubrum often induces the clinical feature of hyperkeratosis in tinea pedis. It is the main cause of onychomycosis and leads to thickened nail plates. Moreover, T rubrum can form cutaneous horns, as occurred in the present case.
output: Tinea manuum (ringworm of the finger) caused by Trichophyton rubrum

A 54-year-old man presented to our emergency department reporting several weeks of diffuse abdominal pain. He had no medical history of note.On physical examination we found his abdomen was soft with some slight tenderness and there were diffuse petechiae on his hands and feet. The patient was afebrile and his vital signs were stable.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised serum C-reactive protein concentration of 12·2 mg/dL (normal <0·6).
An abdominal CT scan showed signs of occult ileocecal perforation and segmented small bowel wall thickening. During an explorative laparotomy, we found multiple 5–10 cm haemorrhagic small bowel skip lesions (figure) without any perforations; we did not resect any of the affected segments because they showed active peristalsis.
Further laboratory testing showed the presence of antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies against proteinase 3 of 241 IU/mL (normal <10), haematuria, proteinuria, urinary casts, and normal serum creatinine concentration. Urine output was unremarkable.
We made a diagnosis of granulomatosis with polyangiitis presenting with intestinal manifestations; treatment with prednisolone significantly relieved the patient's abdominal pain and he was allowed home.
1 month later, the patient attended again with acute abdominal pain and peritonitis. A CT scan showed free intra-abdominal air. We undertook a further explorative laparotomy and found several ileal perforations; we carried out a small bowel resection and constructed an ileostomy.
Histopathological work-up of the excised bowel showed necrotic tissue with severe peritonitis and some small vessels with microthrombi and partially enhanced infiltrating granulocytes in the vessel walls; a renal biopsy sample confirmed granulomatosis with polyangiitis. At regular follow-up visits on treatment with prednisolone and cyclophosphamide, no new manifestations of systemic vasculitis were detected.
Skip lesions of the bowel are usually seen in inflammatory bowel disease, distal thromboembolic mesenteric ischaemia, and lupus enteritis.
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small to medium vessel necrotising vasculitis whose exact aetiology is unclear; it mostly affects the respiratory tract and kidneys and there is a potential for multiorgan involvement. First intestinal manifestations leading to surgical complications are extremely rare and depending on the extent of involvement, granulomatosis with polyangiitis may be treated with immunosuppressive agents—including glucocorticoids, cyclophosphamide, or rituximab—the caveat being that such therapies might increase the risk of intestinal perforation (video).
output: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis with intestinal manifestations

A 69-year-old woman with axial and peripheral spondyloarthritis (diagnosed in 2016) was in remission on anti-tumour necrosis factor therapy (adalimumab 40 mg every other week). She presented to our rheumatology unit with a 3-month history of inflammatory back pain and polyarthralgia associated with morning stiffness lasting more than 1 h.These symptoms were associated with asthenia, cough, and a weight loss of 10 kg in the past 3 months. On examination, restricted movement of the lumbar and dorsal spine and tenosynovitis of the first extensor compartment of the left wrist were noted. Both the Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score (ASDAS) and the Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI) reflected active disease (ASDAS=4·7 and BASDAI=7). Her serum C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration was unusually high (24 mg/L). Because the patient was immunocompromised, we performed chest and abdominal CT scans to rule out neoplasm or infection. The chest CT revealed an intracardiac, heterogeneous, obstructive mass in the left atrium, measuring 70 mm by 49 mm suggesting a myxoma, and this was confirmed on cardiac MRI (figure, A). The mass was not present on a CT scan performed in 2017. Considering the overproduction of interleukin (IL)-6 by cardiac myxomas, we measured serum IL-6 concentration, which was 23 pg/mL (normal range <7 pg/mL).
The patient underwent surgical excision (figure, B), and the histopathological assessment confirmed the diagnosis of myxoma, which was positive for calretinin. Adalimumab was discontinued because of the infection risk during surgery. Postoperative follow-up found normalisation of CRP concentration (<3 mg/L) and a decrease in arthralgia intensity. 1 month after surgery, the patient was in remission (ASDAS <1·3, BASDAI=2·4), with a normal serum IL-6 concentration (<7 pg/mL), without reintroduction of adalimumab. Adalimumab was reintroduced 4 months after the surgery to avoid the relapse of the spondyloarthritis. 1 year after the surgery, the patient is still in remission with normal CRP concentration. Cardiac myxoma is rare with an incidence rate of 0·5 per million people, but it is the most common primary benign neoplasm of the heart. Most myxomas are asymptomatic and found incidentally; however, some can mimic systemic diseases. Because of the embolic risk and the risk of cardiac arrest, standard treatment is surgical excision.
output: It is a frequent malignant neoplasm

A chylothorax was suspected. Which of the following pleural fluid tests is most commonly used to diagnose a chylothorax?
output:
Triglyceride level

The most commonly used pleural fluid test to diagnose a chylothorax is the **triglyceride level**. A pleural fluid triglyceride concentration >110 mg/dL (>1.24 mmol/L) is highly suggestive of chylothorax, while a level <50 mg/dL essentially rules it out.

In this case, the milky, yellow appearance of the fluid combined with the patient's history of follicular lymphoma (which can cause chylothorax through lymphatic obstruction or disruption) strongly supports this diagnosis.

She presented to our rheumatology unit with a 3-month history of inflammatory back pain and polyarthralgia associated with morning stiffness lasting more than 1 h.These symptoms were associated with asthenia, cough, and a weight loss of 10 kg in the past 3 months. On examination, restricted movement of the lumbar and dorsal spine and tenosynovitis of the first extensor compartment of the left wrist were noted. Both the Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score (ASDAS) and the Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI) reflected active disease (ASDAS=4·7 and BASDAI=7). Her serum C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration was unusually high (24 mg/L). Because the patient was immunocompromised, we performed chest and abdominal CT scans to rule out neoplasm or infection. The chest CT revealed an intracardiac, heterogeneous, obstructive mass in the left atrium, measuring 70 mm by 49 mm suggesting a myxoma, and this was confirmed on cardiac MRI (figure, A). The mass was not present on a CT scan performed in 2017. Considering the overproduction of interleukin (IL)-6 by cardiac myxomas, we measured serum IL-6 concentration, which was 23 pg/mL (normal range <7 pg/mL).
The patient underwent surgical excision (figure, B), and the histopathological assessment confirmed the diagnosis of myxoma, which was positive for calretinin. Adalimumab was discontinued because of the infection risk during surgery. Postoperative follow-up found normalisation of CRP concentration (<3 mg/L) and a decrease in arthralgia intensity. 1 month after surgery, the patient was in remission (ASDAS <1·3, BASDAI=2·4), with a normal serum IL-6 concentration (<7 pg/mL), without reintroduction of adalimumab. Adalimumab was reintroduced 4 months after the surgery to avoid the relapse of the spondyloarthritis. 1 year after the surgery, the patient is still in remission with normal CRP concentration. Cardiac myxoma is rare with an incidence rate of 0·5 per million people, but it is the most common primary benign neoplasm of the heart. Most myxomas are asymptomatic and found incidentally; however, some can mimic systemic diseases. Because of the embolic risk and the risk of cardiac arrest, standard treatment is surgical excision.
output: It is a frequent malignant neoplasm

An 85-year-old man was admitted to hospital with a 5-day history of fever and neck pain. He had a 12-year history of chronic kidney disease and gouty arthritis; however, the patient did not take urate lowering drugs. On admission to hospital, physical examination revealed neck pain and stiffness. He had a blood pressure of 140/102 mm Hg, pulse rate of 95 per min, respiration rate of 18 breaths per min, and body temperature of 38°C. Laboratory results revealed a white blood cell count of 11 200 cells per mm3 (reference 4 000–10 000) and C-reactive protein level of 12·26 mg/dL (reference 0·0–0·3). MRI findings suggested cervical osteomyelitis and meningitis (figure A). Cervical spine CT revealed curvilinear calcifications of the transverse ligament of the atlas (figure B). After assessing blood cultures, ceftriaxone (2 g every 12 h) and vancomycin (1750 mg loading, followed by 750 mg every 48 h) were administered intravenously as empirical antibiotic treatments. On the second day of admission, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis did not reveal meningitis (white blood cell count 8 cells per μL, glucose concentration 79 mg/dL, and protein concentration 168 mg/dL), and CSF culture and molecular tests were negative for bacteria and mycobacteria. The patient was diagnosed with crowned dens syndrome and administered 20 mg prednisolone, and his symptoms dramatically improved. However, CSF examination under polarising microscopy revealed monosodium urate crystals (figure C). Dual-energy CT confirmed the calcifications to be monosodium urate crystals (figure D). The patient's uric acid concentration was 10·4 mg/dL (reference 0–7·0) and subcutaneous tophi were not apparent on physical examination 9 days after hospital admission. Crowned dens syndrome is a rare finding in calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease and could be clinically similar to meningitis, so it should be suspected when the evidence for infection is unclear. Our patient had a history of gout, and monosodium urate crystals were confirmed by CSF analysis and dual-energy CT, suggesting that the symptoms were caused by gout flare in the cervical spine. Thus, physicians should consider that intrathecal monosodium urate crystal formation can cause meningitis-like symptoms in patients with gout history.
output: Crowned dens syndrome caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition

A 41-year-old woman presented to our clinic because of the sudden appearance of erosions on and swelling of her lips. No other lesions were seen on the rest of her body. She had been taking paracetamol and amoxicillin for 3 days for a sore throat and fever. A 69-year-old woman with a history of myocardial infarction came to hospital after more than 24 h of intermittent chest pain, shortness of breath, and diaphoresis. On admission, a 12-lead ECG showed sinus tachycardia without evidence of ischaemia. Biomarkers of myocardial necrosis were negative. A portable chest radiograph and a bedside transthoracic echocardiogram showed pathognomonic findings of acute type A aortic dissection (figure; videos). The patient underwent urgent repair of the aortic root. The patient survived the immediate postoperative course despite complications of haemodynamic instability, hypotension, and acute renal failure, but later succumbed to multiorgan failure.
Delayed presentation of acute aortic syndrome is plagued by high mortality and morbidity. The location of the intimal tear in acute type A aortic dissection is in the immediate vicinity of the sinuses of Valsalva 65% of the time. The sensitivity and specificity of chest radiography is 81% and 89%, respectively. The sensitivity of transthoracic echocardiography is between 78% and 100%; its specificity ranges from 87% to 96%. Transthoracic echocardiography is a valuable diagnostic tool in cases when more sensitive techniques (transoesophageal echocardiography, CT, magnetic resonance angiography) are not readily available or are impractical.

An 87-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 3-day history of dyspnoea on exertion. She had a history of chronic kidney disease, pulmonary embolism, and recent right-sided ischaemic stroke causing aphasia and hemiparesis. She was taking aspirin, clopidogrel, and atorvastatin.On examination we found the patient to be well and afebrile. Her blood pressure was 134/86 mm Hg, oxygen saturation was 95% on room air, and she had bilateral rhonchi prominent in her lung bases.
Laboratory investigations found a normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 11·4 g/dL; normal 12–16), serum creatinine concentration was 1·34 mg/dL (normal 0·6–1·5), and the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was 36 mL/min per 1·73 m2. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with no signs of ischaemia and chest x-ray showed patchy multifocal airspace opacities in both lungs—indicating possible pneumonia. A chest CT with intravenous contrast showed no abnormalities—ruling out the possibility of a pulmonary embolus—and the upper parts of the patient's kidneys, seen on the same image, also showed no obvious lesions, and notably no intraparenchymal contrast medium (figure). The lung windows of the CT showed ground glass changes.
Over the next 48 h, the patient became oliguric and her serum creatinine concentration increased to 2·4 mg/dL. A non-contrast CT of the patient's abdomen and pelvis (figure) showed renal parenchymal enhancement from retained intravenous contrast medium 53 h after administration. The patient's urine sodium concentration was 36 mEq/L and the fractional excretion of sodium was 0·7%. Considering the findings, we made a diagnosis of contrast-associated acute kidney injury (AKI) in the context of a viral lower respiratory tract infection.
The patient was started on supportive AKI care—including adjustment of medication doses, avoidance of nephrotoxins, and judicious administration of fluids—and antitussives and paracetamol for the chest infection. Her dyspnoea improved and her serum creatinine concentration peaked at 3·7 mg/dL, with an eGFR of 10 mL/min per 1·73 m2, 4 days after the administration of the contrast. 7 days after the initial contrast CT, the serum creatinine concentration returned to the preadmission baseline of 1·3 mg/dL. The patient was then transferred to a nursing facility and seen again 3 weeks later; at that time her kidney function was stable.
Retained intravenous contrast can be seen on a plain radiograph or a non-contrasted CT study of the abdomen more than 24 h after the administration in situations of significant renal impairment—including end stage renal disease or AKI—when the glomerular filtration rate is 45 mL/min per 1·73 m2 or less. Retained contrast accompanied by an acute rise in the serum creatinine concentration—in the absence of other causes of AKI—is highly suggestive of contrast-associated nephropathy. Oliguria and a low fractional excretion of sodium are also typical features. Contrast may be retained in the kidneys for several days—although is it usually cleared within 24–72 h after the injury.
In patients with residual renal function, management is conservative, and outcomes are usually favourable. In patients receiving renal replacement therapy, contrast is cleared through dialysis.
Intravenous contrast used in any clinical setting can result in contrast-associated AKI and debate continues over the level of toxicity of currently used materials. In patients with severe chronic kidney disease or receiving renal replacement therapy risks are greater: here the benefits of imaging should be weighed against the potential harm of the contrast (video).

A 53-year-old man presented to the emergency department of our hospital in January, 2014, after a syncopal episode. He was a regular smoker and recreational drug user, and had taken heroin, cannabis, and benzodiazepine during that week. He had a history of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. On examination he had grey pallor and was dyspnoeic at rest (respiratory rate 23 breaths per minute). His oxygen saturation was 70% on 100% inspired oxygen and his blood sample, which showed anaemia (haemoglobin 54 g/L; normal 130–180 g/L), was chocolate brown (figure). Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7·40 (7·35–7·45) and methaemoglobin 26% (<2%).
Oxidant agents like benzocaine or novocaine, which are sometimes added to street heroin and cocaine, oxidise haemoglobin from its ferrous (Fe2+) to ferric state (Fe3+), and can cause methaemoglobinaemia. This altered form of haemoglobin loses its ability to transport oxygen, and can cause hypoxaemia. Chocolate-coloured blood is typical of methaemoglobinaemia. Unlike deoxyhaemoglobin, methaemoglobin does not brighten on exposure to atmospheric oxygen. In our patient, haemolysis associated with G6PD deficiency caused release of the methaemoglobin from within the red blood cells into the serum.

A 53-year-old man presented to the emergency department of our hospital in January, 2014, after a syncopal episode. He was a regular smoker and recreational drug user, and had taken heroin, cannabis, and benzodiazepine during that week. He had a history of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. On examination he had grey pallor and was dyspnoeic at rest (respiratory rate 23 breaths per minute). His oxygen saturation was 70% on 100% inspired oxygen and his blood sample, which showed anaemia (haemoglobin 54 g/L; normal 130–180 g/L), was chocolate brown (figure). Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7·40 (7·35–7·45) and methaemoglobin 26% (<2%).
Oxidant agents like benzocaine or novocaine, which are sometimes added to street heroin and cocaine, oxidise haemoglobin from its ferrous (Fe2+) to ferric state (Fe3+), and can cause methaemoglobinaemia. This altered form of haemoglobin loses its ability to transport oxygen, and can cause hypoxaemia. Chocolate-coloured blood is typical of methaemoglobinaemia. Unlike deoxyhaemoglobin, methaemoglobin does not brighten on exposure to atmospheric oxygen. In our patient, haemolysis associated with G6PD deficiency caused release of the methaemoglobin from within the red blood cells into the serum.

A 17-year-old man reporting a 3-year history of an acneiform eruption and a 4-month history of worsening swelling of his face, was referred to our specialist joint haematology-dermatology clinic. The patient had been found to have a monocytopenia of 0·2 × 109 per L (normal 0·2–1·0); he had no other past medical problems.On examination he was generally well and vital signs were within normal limits. He had inflammatory papules and pustules without comedones on both cheeks, forehead, and chin. He also had severe facial lymphoedema extending from the jawline to the anterior hairline with debilitating periorbital swelling that limited eye opening (figure). Additionally, numerous cutaneous viral warts were noted on his hands and knees.
Laboratory investigations showed mild macrocytosis and the monocytopenia: haemoglobin concentration was 150 g/L (normal 130–165), mean corpuscular volume 99·7 fL (normal 77–95), neutrophils 3·08 × 109 per L (normal 2·2–6·3), platelets 180 × 109 per L (normal 150–450). Thyroid function, anti-nuclear antibodies, immunoglobulins, and inflammatory markers were unremarkable.
Histopathological analysis of samples of skin biopsies from the chin and lower eyelid showed superficial and deep perifollicular and periadenexal lymphocytic inflammation as well as ectatic blood vessels in the superficial dermis: indicative of the clinical diagnosis of rosacea. No organisms were seen on periodic-acid-Schiff with diastase, Grocott, and Ziehl-Neelsen stains. Prolonged tissue culture did not isolate bacteria, mycobacterium, or fungi.
Notably, the patient had a family history of both myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and acute myeloid leukaemia (AML): his mother was diagnosed with MDS aged 27 years, AML aged 36 years, and she died aged 37 years; a maternal aunt was diagnosed with MDS aged 26 years and had an allogeneic transplant; his maternal grandmother was diagnosed with AML aged 24 and died one year later; and a maternal great aunt, who was diagnosed at an unknown age, with AML.
Putting the findings together—monocytopenia, human papilloma viral infection, lymphoedema, and family history of myelodysplastic syndromes—we suspected the patient had GATA2 deficiency.
Bone marrow studies confirmed MDS: refractory cytopenia of multilineage dysplasia and normal cytogenetics. Genetic testing showed a heterozygous pathogenic GATA2 variant (c.1061 C>T; p.Thr354Met).
The patient was started on low dose oral isotretinoin, vigilant monitoring of his full blood count, and regular manual lymphatic drainage of his face which after one year had significantly improved the rosacea and lymphoedema (figure). The response was sustained 2 years after completion of the therapy.
GATA2 is a zinc finger transcription factor required for haematopoiesis and lymphatic angiogenesis; several pathogenic mutations leading to GATA2 deficiency have been described. The syndrome segregates as an autosomal dominant trait with incomplete penetrance. Clinical manifestations are heterogeneous, and patients usually present in adolescence or early adulthood. Cutaneous infections, panniculitis, and lymphoedema in the setting of cytopenia, especially monocytopenia, should trigger suspicion of GATA2 deficiency. Lymphoedema associated with GATA2 deficiency is usually confined to the lower limbs and genitalia—known as Emberger syndrome—and marked facial lymphoedema, as seen in our patient, has not previously been reported. Most patients with GATA2 haploinsufficiency develop myeloid neoplasms before the age of 50 years and may require haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation which can be curative.

A 4-year old girl was admitted to our hospital after she collapsed at home while having dinner. She had a history of recurrent upper airway infections and wheezing, which were being treated with inhaled β2-adrenoceptor agonist, as an outpatient.On examination in our emergency department, the patient was tachycardic and tachypnoeic with subcostal recession and fine bilateral crackles; oxygen saturation on pulse oximetry was 85% at an oxygen flow rate of 2 L/min. output:
Pseudothrombocytosis due to cryoglobulinemia or red blood cell fragments (schistocytes/burn cells)

The discrepancy between the automated high platelet count (930,000/mm³) and the manual count (115,000/mm³) is caused by **red blood cell fragments (schistocytes/microspherocytes)** being misidentified as platelets by the automated analyzer.

In severe burn patients, thermal injury causes direct damage to red blood cells, resulting in fragmented RBCs (burn cells/schistocytes) circulating in the blood. These small RBC fragments are similar in size to platelets and are erroneously counted as platelets by automated hematology analyzers, leading to **spurious thrombocytosis (pseudothrombocytosis)**.

A 74-year-old female patient presented in November, 2017, with a 3-month history of pain in the upper left thigh. X-ray revealed three osteolytic lesions of the left femur, one of which was breaking the cortical bone. No organomegaly was noted on physical examination. Blood counts and biochemical tests were normal except for mild hypergammaglobulinemia (16·9%) with positive immunofixation for monoclonal immunoglobulin A (0·2 g/dL in the serum, but urine negative).Multiple myeloma was suspected, and whole-body PET scan documented increased fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in several bone sites (SUVmax 4·9–10·9): at the head of humeri, sacrum, iliac wings, right acetabulum, and proximal femurs (figure, A), with extension into the soft tissues surrounding the broken cortex of the left femur.
A routine marrow biopsy from the iliac crest was unexpectedly normal on immunohistology for the plasma cell marker CD138 and the B-cell marker CD20. However, a core biopsy of the left femural neck documented a massive infiltration by mature lymphoid cells with ample cytoplasm and hairy projections positive for CD20, annexin-1 (figure, B), and BRAFV600E, thereby establishing a diagnosis of hairy cell leukaemia.
Morphological and flow-cytometric analyses of peripheral blood did not show any hairy cells, and a sensitive allele-specific PCR assay for BRAFV600E was also negative in both the blood and iliac marrow aspirate.
The patient received chemotherapy with cladribine (0·14 mg/kg per day for 5 consecutive days subcutaneously) and her pain gradually subsided. A PET scan 8 weeks later showed substantially decreased uptake of fluorodeoxyglucose at multiple bone lesions.
Although skeletal involvement can occur in hairy cell leukaemia (in around 3% of cases), patients with hairy cell leukaemia, who are mostly males, usually also present with cytopenias, splenomegaly, circulating hairy cells, and diffuse leukaemic infiltration of the bone marrow. Focal bone lesions accompanied by none of these characteristic features, but rather by a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance as occurred in this woman, represent a challenging differential diagnosis with more frequent neoplasms, especially multiple myeloma.

A 60-year-old woman presented to our emergency department with a 4-day history of mild, diffuse abdominal pain and discomfort in her abdomen. The patient's medical history was unremarkable apart from a cholelithiasis-related cholecystectomy which had been done 12 years earlier.On examination, we found the patient to be generally well; her pulse was 75 beats per min and blood pressure 145/80 mm Hg. She was febrile with a temperature of 38·0°C; she had diffuse left-sided abdominal tenderness.
Laboratory investigations found a mildly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 16 mg/dL (normal <6) and a raised white blood cell (WBC) count of 12·6 × 109 per L (normal range 4–11); carcinoembryonic antigen concentration was within normal range (1·2 ng/mL; typical value for non-smoker or ex-smoker <3·8 and for smokers <5·5).
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed a 3·3 cm × 2·8 cm × 8·0 cm intramural peripherally enhancing hypodense lesion together with pericolic fat stranding and haziness which had caused mild upstream large bowel distention—we presumed it was an abscess in the large bowel wall; features—colonic wall outpouchings—consistent with a diagnosis of acute diverticulitis were also seen (figure). Importantly, no extraluminal air was seen. Considering the patient's clinical condition, particularly the absence of signs of peritonitis, we decided to manage her conservatively; she was started on intravenous fluids and treated empirically with piperacillin and tazobactam. Over the next few days, the patient's symptoms improved; her temperature, WBC count, and CRP concentration reduced. A repeat CT scan 7 days after admission showed almost complete resolution of original findings—indicating spontaneous resolution of the abscess and further confirming the initial diagnosis (figure). The patient was allowed home 8 days after admission and prescribed oral antimicrobial treatment (ciprofloxacin and metronidazole).
6 weeks later, an outpatient colonoscopy showed mild residual stenosis at the site of the previous intramural abscess with no other abnormalities; the patient reported no symptoms or difficulty passing faeces.
Abscesses complicate 15–30% of acute diverticulitis cases; intramural lesions are infrequently reported. Secondary partial intestinal obstruction may occur, but severe obstruction is rare. In most cases, abscesses spontaneously resolve. Conservative treatment is favoured in smaller-sized abscesses (<3–4 cm); further intervention may be needed for larger ones.
The treatment approach depends upon abscess location and the overall medical condition of the patient; conservative management is preferable. The differential diagnosis of such a lesion should include various types of colitis-related abscesses, inflammatory bowel disease, contained perforations, infected enteric duplication cysts, and, most significantly, colon cancer. Importantly, in patients with radiologically confirmed acute diverticulitis, colonic cancer has been found to have a 1-year incidence rate ranging from 1·6% to 2·7%. To exclude an underlying colonic malignancy, patients with acute diverticulitis are advised to undergo colonoscopy approximately 6–8 weeks following their episode.
output: Intramural colonic abscess secondary to acute diverticulitis

A 74-year-old female patient presented in November, 2017, with a 3-month history of pain in the upper left thigh. X-ray revealed three osteolytic lesions of the left femur, one of which was breaking the cortical bone. No organomegaly was noted on physical examination. Blood counts and biochemical tests were normal except for mild hypergammaglobulinemia (16·9%) with positive immunofixation for monoclonal immunoglobulin A (0·2 g/dL in the serum, but urine negative).Multiple myeloma was suspected, and whole-body PET scan documented increased fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in several bone sites (SUVmax 4·9–10·9): at the head of humeri, sacrum, iliac wings, right acetabulum, and proximal femurs (figure, A), with extension into the soft tissues surrounding the broken cortex of the left femur.
A routine marrow biopsy from the iliac crest was unexpectedly normal on immunohistology for the plasma cell marker CD138 and the B-cell marker CD20. However, a core biopsy of the left femural neck documented a massive infiltration by mature lymphoid cells with ample cytoplasm and hairy projections positive for CD20, annexin-1 (figure, B), and BRAFV600E, thereby establishing a diagnosis of hairy cell leukaemia.
Morphological and flow-cytometric analyses of peripheral blood did not show any hairy cells, and a sensitive allele-specific PCR assay for BRAFV600E was also negative in both the blood and iliac marrow aspirate.
The patient received chemotherapy with cladribine (0·14 mg/kg per day for 5 consecutive days subcutaneously) and her pain gradually subsided. A PET scan 8 weeks later showed substantially decreased uptake of fluorodeoxyglucose at multiple bone lesions.
Although skeletal involvement can occur in hairy cell leukaemia (in around 3% of cases), patients with hairy cell leukaemia, who are mostly males, usually also present with cytopenias, splenomegaly, circulating hairy cells, and diffuse leukaemic infiltration of the bone marrow. Focal bone lesions accompanied by none of these characteristic features, but rather by a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance as occurred in this woman, represent a challenging differential diagnosis with more frequent neoplasms, especially multiple myeloma.

The case presents an atypical manifestation (focal bone lesions without cytopenias/splenomegaly), often titled or referred to in literature as "Hairy cell leukaemia presenting as focal bone lesions", but the fundamental diagnostic result is the disease itself.

A 30-year-old white man with no ocular history presented to eye casualty in Sidcup in October, 2012, with bilateral central visual loss, following inhalation of poppers. On examination his visual acuity was 6/12 on the right and 6/18 in the left eye. Slit lamp biomicroscopy showed subtle macular changes in the form of yellow foveal spots (figure). Spectral domain optical coherence tomography showed clear disruption of the foveal cone inner segment–outer segment layer (figure). At follow-up 6 months later, the patient's visual acuity and examination findings remained unchanged, despite cessation of poppers use.
Poppers (slang for various alkyl nitrite compounds) are commonly used in the gay community, for their ability to relax the anal sphincter and known psychoactive effects. Following changes to legislation in 2006, poppers' main ingredient, isobutyl nitrite, was substituted for isopropyl nitrite. Since then, there have been several reports of a new form of visual loss termed poppers maculopathy. The exact mechanism by which poppers cause damage to central photoreceptors is unknown, but there is a clear cause–effect relationship. Despite online warnings outlining the risks of poppers, the number of individuals presenting with associated visual loss is increasing. Fundoscopy findings can be very subtle, with more striking changes seen on optical coherence tomography. The relatively easy availability and widespread use of poppers is underestimated and concerning, given the propensity for permanent damage to the eyes. We would encourage both end-users and healthcare professionals to be aware of the potentially serious and irreversible damage poppers can have on vision.

A 51-year-old woman presented to our emergency room with a 4-day history of fever, chills, abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhoea.1 week before these problems began, the patient had a nevus removed from her right arm. The dermatologists were concerned it may have been a melanoma; she had a history of primary biliary cholangitis treated with ursodeoxycholic acid.
On examination, we found the patient to be unwell but responsive; her blood pressure was 85/59 mm Hg, her pulse was 107 beats per min, temperature was 39·0°C, respiratory rate 27 breaths per min, and oxygen saturation was 94%.
A CT scan of the patient's chest showed air space opacities with air bronchogram indicating a pneumonia in the left and right lower lobes (figure); a CT of the abdomen showed circumferential wall thickening of the right colon and surrounding fat stranding, indicating colitis. Blood cultures grew Streptococcus pyogenes.
10 h after admission, the patient's condition deteriorated and she developed septic shock; she was given intravenous antibiotics, crystalloid fluid, and norepinephrine, and transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU). 24 h after admission, she went into cardiogenic shock with a decreased left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 25% with hypokinesis of the basal and midventricular segments—typical of an inverted takotsubo cardiomyopathy (appendix); on admission her LVEF had been 50%.
Troponin blood concentration was 104 819 ng/L (normal <74). Coronary angiography showed no abnormalities. We made a diagnosis of septic cardiomyopathy, and the patient was treated with dobutamine. After some initial improvement her condition worsened and she was readmitted to the ICU because of pulmonary oedema and a persistent fever (temperature was 38·8°C): LVEF was still decreased at 25%. A whole-body CT scan showed diffuse myocardial calcifications of the left ventricle (figure) but no focus of secondary pulmonary or abdominal infection.
Histopathological examination of a sample obtained at endomyocardial biopsy confirmed myocardial calcifications (figure). Considering the findings in the round, we made a diagnosis of diffuse myocardial calcifications following severe streptococcal sepsis, and high-dose—2 mg/kg—corticosteroids were started. The fever abated and the patient's clinical status improved; she was allowed home 3 months after admission. Corticosteroids were decreased and stopped at 3 months and the patient was treated with dapagliflozin, ramipril, and a cardioverter-defibrillator was implanted. 10 months after initial presentation, she was asymptomatic and her LVEF was 40%; the microcalcifications were still present (appendix).
Diffuse myocardial calcifications following severe sepsis are uncommon and associated with a poor prognosis. High-dose pulses of corticosteroids are recommended but evidence for effectiveness remains weak in the absence of prospective clinical trials (video).

A whole-body CT scan showed diffuse myocardial calcifications of the left ventricle (figure) but no focus of secondary pulmonary or abdominal infection.
Histopathological examination of a sample obtained at endomyocardial biopsy confirmed myocardial calcifications (figure). Considering the findings in the round, we made a diagnosis of diffuse myocardial calcifications following severe streptococcal sepsis, and high-dose—2 mg/kg—corticosteroids were started. The fever abated and the patient's clinical status improved; she was allowed home 3 months after admission. Corticosteroids were decreased and stopped at 3 months and the patient was treated with dapagliflozin, ramipril, and a cardioverter-defibrillator was implanted. 10 months after initial presentation, she was asymptomatic and her LVEF was 40%; the microcalcifications were still present (appendix).

A 26-year-old man came to our emergency department accompanied by coworkers, who said their colleague was having difficulties with his speech. They explained that the factory employee had first complained to them about visual problems on his right side before he stopped talking altogether. They said the whole episode had started 1 h before.On examination, the patient was globally aphasic—he was unable to speak and could not follow verbal requests. He repeatedly held his left hand up against the left side of his forehead indicating to us that he had pain there. On examination he was afebrile and he had no signs of meningism, no cranial nerve abnormalities, no sensorimotor deficits, and no pyramidal signs. Routine laboratory tests were all normal—including blood glucose concentration, full blood count, liver and renal functions, coagulations tests, electrolytes, and C-reactive protein concentration.
MRI of the brain 1 h after admission showed no parenchymal abnormalities on diffusion-weighted imaging or T2-fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences, but there was conspicuous cortical venous dilatation in the left hemisphere on susceptibility-weighted MRI (figure). Contrast-enhanced perfusion-weighted MRI showed hypoperfusion in large areas of the left hemisphere, which did not correspond to any specific arterial territory (figure). Magnetic resonance angiography excluded any intracranial or extracranial large vessel occlusions or constrictions (figure).
The patient's aphasia gradually resolved 2 h after he came to the emergency department, but he then reported a severe pulsating left-sided hemicrania. When he was able to speak again, the patient explained that he had first noticed impaired vision of the right side of both his eyes. He then felt tingling in the fingers of his right hand which spread up his arm and then to his face; a few minutes later he began having difficulty speaking.
Notably the patient had no medical history. Although there was a family history of migraine. 10 h later a repeat MRI showed no parenchymal abnormalities—but at this stage temporal lobe hyperperfusion was apparent, further supporting our original presumed diagnosis of a migraine with a prolonged aura. A 30-year-old man presented to our department in Leiden, Netherlands, with a 6-year history of recurrent solitary swellings. On average, he had 15 episodes per year. The swellings had started on his abdomen and had gradually moved to his chest, neck, and, more recently, his face. The swellings varied in size, were painless, appeared spontaneously, and resolved after 5–7 days. Treatment with high-dose antihistamine had had no effect. There were no other symptoms. The patient was otherwise healthy and did not take any medication.Physical examination revealed a swelling of the right cheek and upper lip. Photos of previous episodes revealed similar swellings of the left cheek (figure, A). The differential diagnoses included angio-oedema, granulomatous cheilitis, sialadenitis, sialolithiasis, and Kimura's disease, but these could not be confirmed by laboratory examination, histopathology, or clinical examination by a dental surgeon. Laboratory examinations, including eosinophil count and C1 esterase inhibitor concentrations, were completely normal except for IgE concentrations, which were elevated (3736 IU/mL, normal range is 0–99). A biopsy of the buccal mucosa showed a dense eosinophilic infiltrate. Ultrasound examination and MRI scan revealed a non-specific infiltration and enhancement of the subcutis.
The elevated IgE concentration and eosinophil in-filtration in the biopsy suggested a parasitic infection. A further inquiry revealed that the patient had consumed raw fish in Taiwan before the first swelling episode. Western blot analysis of serum for reactivity against crude antigens of Gnathostoma spinigerum third-stage larvae (L3) showed the presence of a specific 24 kDa band that was diagnostic for gnathostomiasis. Gnathostomiasis is a helminthic zoonosis, endemic in southeast Asia, which is transmitted through ingestion of larvae of G spinigerum in raw or undercooked fresh water fish, eels, frogs, reptiles, or birds. After ingestion, larvae penetrate the gastrointestinal wall and migrate through the subcutaneous tissue, causing typical migratory swellings and eosinophilia that can recur for years.
A revision of the MRI scan identified a larva of approximately 4·0×0·2 cm (figure, B). The patient was treated with ivermectin 0·2 mg/kg once per day on 2 consecutive days. This treatment was successful because it stimulated the outward migration of the larva (an impression of the head of the larva became visible in the lower lip; appendix), which caused a temporary increase of the swelling. Eosinophilia was now present (1·03×109 cells per L, normal value is <0·50 × 109 cells per L). Further treatment, aiming to preclude potential migration towards the eye socket, consisted of albendazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days. The symptoms resolved within a few days and the patient remains symptom free.

A 32-year-old man presented to our dermatology clinic with a 5-year history of increasing skin folds on his scalp, excessive sweating, joint pain, and development of a deep voice. The patient's medical history was significant for acne keloidalis nuchae which had been treated with antibiotics, isotretinoin, and surgical excision with primary closure of the residual lesions, one year before we saw him.On examination, we found the patient to be generally well; he had thickening of the skin on his scalp with prominent ridges and furrows (figure). He had coarse facial features (figure), acanthosis nigricans of the skin in his neck, axillae, and knuckles. Notably, his feet, hands, and tongue were enlarged. We found no other abnormal signs, and on further questioning, he reported no headaches, seizures, or visual disturbances.
We made a working diagnosis of cutis verticis gyrate (CVG) due to acromegaly.
Laboratory investigations found a raised insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) concentration of 634 μg/L (normal 64–243), a raised growth hormone (GH) concentration of 9·4 μg/L (normal <3), unsuppressed post-glucose GH of 8·92 ng/mL (normal <1), free thyroxine of 1·44 ng/dL (normal 0·93–1·7), thyroid-stimulating-hormone 1·44 μUI/mL (normal 0·27–4·2), HbA1c 5·8% (normal <5·6), and glucose of 110 mg/dL (normal <100).
MRI of the patient's head showed a pituitary macroadenoma measuring 14 mm × 13 mm × 13 mm (figure)—establishing the diagnosis of acromegaly.
The patient was referred to our surgical department and had a transsphenoidal resection of the tumour. After surgery, a repeat MRI showed no residual tumour. A 51-year-old man who had been receiving haemodialysis for 15 years was referred to the Toranomon Hospital (Tokyo, Japan) with progressive calcified nodules on his fingers. He had been undergoing haemodialysis three times per week, for a total of 12 h per week. The patient had been deemed to have end-stage renal disease of unknown cause. He had undergone a parathyroidectomy 2 years before the referral because he was believed to have progressive extraskeletal calcification caused by hyperparathyroidism with constant hypercalcaemia that was refractory to medical treatment; laboratory findings were compatible with secondary hyperparathyroidism. Since the parathyroidectomy, laboratory findings had returned to normal, but the nodules had progressed and made him unable to grip. A family history could not be obtained because the patient was an orphan, but through a careful interview we identified a past medical history of recurrent urolithiasis, which was judged to be the leading cause of the end-stage renal disease. Physical examination showed clubbed fingers with exposed calcified masses (figure A). Radiography showed prominent bilateral calcified deposits (figure B) and nephrocalcinosis. A 67-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 2-month history of a low-grade fever and progressive weakness in the muscles of his face. He also reported drooling and slurred speech.He had a 10-year history of hypertension that was treated with antihypertensives.
On examination we found that he could not close his eyes, wrinkle his forehead, or raise his eyebrows and that the nasolabial folds of his face were flattened—indicating a bilateral lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy (figure). We found no other abnormalities on physical examination.
Laboratory investigations showed a mild anaemia, with a haemoglobin concentration of 11·6 g/dL, a leucocytosis of 17·2 × 109 per L, and a monocytosis of 2·14 × 109 per L. The patient's erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 22 mm/h and C-reactive protein concentration was 10 mg/L. Infectious diseases—including Lyme disease, HIV, syphilis, and herpes zoster—were excluded. Neoplasms—particularly head and neck tumours—were ruled out, and granulomatous diseases, like sarcoidosis, and metabolic and autoimmune diseases—including Guillain–Barré syndrome, systemic autoimmune diseases, and vasculitis were excluded.
A peripheral blood smear showed excessive monocytosis with left shift, dysplastic granulocytes, promonocytes, and blasts (figure). A bone marrow aspiration confirmed the diagnosis of chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia (CMML).
Cytogenetic analysis found trisomy of chromosome 8; DNA sequencing showed mutations in the RUNX1, SF3B1, and CBL genes. Nerve conduction studies found an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy—affecting the facial nerves and the peripheral nerves in the patient's arms and legs. We decided to treat the patient using corticosteroids and intravenous immunoglobulin. He remained afebrile with no improvement of his facial nerve palsy. We decided against using hypomethylating agents because in Europe azacitidine has been approved only for CMML patients with white blood cell counts of less than 13 × 109 per L.
2 months later, while still on steroid therapy, the patient was admitted with a fever, aphthous stomatitis, and arthralgias. Physical examination found an aphthous ulceration on the right side of the tongue, synovitis of the wrists and right knee, and bilateral facial nerve palsy. Soon after admission, the patient complained of an acute onset abdominal pain; he was hypotensive and tachycardic, and had tenderness and rigidity of the right upper quadrant. Multiphase CT scan of the abdomen showed a large haematoma of the right kidney with active bleeding; he also had multiple disseminated microaneurysms—up to 1 cm in diameter—of both interlobar arteries, indicative of a medium-vessel vasculitis (figure). He underwent urgent right radical nephrectomy.
Histology showed a focal necrotising arteritis with mixed inflammatory infiltration and fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls and intramural thrombosis of medium-size vessels—resembling polyarteritis nodosa. We decided to start him on cyclophosphamide and continue with the steroids: this led to a significant decline of acute phase reactants. 10 days later, an aneurysm in the remaining kidney ruptured and we had to do a further radical nephrectomy, resulting in the patient requiring haemodialysis. However, 3 weeks after the cyclophosphamide was started, we noted a significant improvement in his facial nerve palsies.
CMML is a myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative neoplasm, sometimes associated with extrahaematological manifestations: autoimmune inflammatory phenomena can cause a systemic vasculitis, connective tissue diseases, relapsing polychondritis, and a seronegative arthritis. High clinical suspicion for such atypical manifestations should be considered in all patients with CMML (video).
output: Chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia (CMML) with associated polyarteritis nodosa-like vasculitis and bilateral facial nerve palsy

input: A 70-year-old man presented at the Department of Dermatology (HELIOS St. Elisabeth Hospital Oberhausen, Germany) in November, 2016, with a 6-week history of an itchy rash located on the right chest and upper arm (figure, A). His clinical admission diagnosis was herpes zoster virus infection, and he had been previously treated with both acyclovir and brivudine 2 months ago for a total of 10 days each, without clinical improvement. Medical history revealed a lymph node metastasis of a squamous cell carcinoma of unknown primary in the right axilla that had been removed 2 years earlier followed by local radiotherapy of the axilla. Further clinical examination showed an ulcerative lesion on the distal phalanx on the right middle-finger and lymphoedema of the entire right arm. The digital tumour had been present for more than 4 years but had never previously been paid attention to. Histopathological, immunohistochemical, and virological analyses confirmed the suspected diagnosis of human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated periungual squamous cell carcinoma with widespread cutaneous metastases (figure, B). HPV typing was performed with group-specific PCR and reverse line blot hybridisation (Inno-LiPA genotyping extra II assay) and revealed HPV6 and HPV16 in the periungual squamous cell carcinoma and in the cutaneous chest metastases.

A 70-year-old man presented at the Department of Dermatology (HELIOS St. Elisabeth Hospital Oberhausen, Germany) in November, 2016, with a 6-week history of an itchy rash located on the right chest and upper arm (figure, A). His clinical admission diagnosis was herpes zoster virus infection, and he had been previously treated with both acyclovir and brivudine 2 months ago for a total of 10 days each, without clinical improvement. Medical history revealed a lymph node metastasis of a squamous cell carcinoma of unknown primary in the right axilla that had been removed 2 years earlier followed by local radiotherapy of the axilla. Further clinical examination showed an ulcerative lesion on the distal phalanx on the right middle-finger and lymphoedema of the entire right arm. The digital tumour had been present for more than 4 years but had never previously been paid attention to. Histopathological, immunohistochemical, and virological analyses confirmed the suspected diagnosis of human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated periungual squamous cell carcinoma with widespread cutaneous metastases (figure, B). HPV typing was performed with group-specific PCR and reverse line blot hybridisation (Inno-LiPA genotyping extra II assay) and revealed HPV6 and HPV16 in the periungual squamous cell carcinoma and in the cutaneous chest metastases.

A 26-year-old woman, 10 weeks pregnant, attended our hospital with a 1-week history of gradually progressive abdominal discomfort, lethargy, and nausea.On examination, she was pale; blood pressure was 124/74 mm Hg and pulse was 106 beats per min. The patient's spleen was enlarged and extended down to the pelvic brim. She had no abdominal tenderness, vaginal bleeding, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or signs of chronic liver disease including jaundice, clubbing, or ascites.
Abdominal ultrasound with colour Doppler showed a viable intrauterine pregnancy and splenomegaly—measuring 23 cm in oblique craniocaudal length—with peri splenic varices (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed iron-deficiency anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 7·4 g/dL; normal 11·4–14·7), a leukocyte count of 4·2 × 109 per L (3·84–10·0), platelet count of 206 × 109 per L (164–387), and a lactate dehydrogenase concentration of 547 U/L (250–580).
Liver function tests and investigations for thalassaemia, chronic viral and autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, and Wilson's disease were negative.
Peripheral blood film showed teardrop-shaped red cells without blasts. Bone marrow biopsy showed a hypercellular marrow with relative myeloid hyperplasia, megakaryocytic proliferation with atypia, and minimal fibrosis (WHO grade 1/3). DNA sequencing showed a JAK2-V617F mutation with a 31% median allele burden; no BCR-ABL1 fusion gene was found. Cytogenetic analyses showed a 46,XX karyotype. No features of malignancy, lymphoproliferative, or other chronic myeloid disorders were seen.
Taken together with the splenomegaly, we diagnosed pre-fibrotic primary myelofibrosis, using the revised WHO 2016, criteria and scored the patient 0 (indicating a good prognosis) on the Dynamic International Prognostic Scoring System plus.
We started her on aspirin 150 mg once daily, as prophylaxis against myelofibrosis-associated pre-eclampsia, but stopped it when she developed haematemesis at 16 weeks’ gestation. An emergency endoscopy showed large oesophageal and gastric varices due to noncirrhotic portal hypertension.
Following endoscopic variceal ligation, we started propranolol 20 mg twice daily to prevent further bleeding; the patient was then monitored for fetal growth restriction.
From 26 weeks’ gestation, we prescribed 45 μg weekly of pegylated interferon alfa-2a, increasing to 90 μg a week from 29 weeks’ gestation, to reduce the size of the spleen.
At 34 weeks’ gestation, ultrasound scans showed fetal growth restriction. The spleen was 17 cm and had regressed away from the pelvic brim, allowing us to deliver a baby girl, weighing 2080 g with normal Apgar scores, by a lower-segment caesarean section using a Pfannenstiel incision (figure). We did not see the spleen when entering the peritoneal cavity. Mother and baby were allowed home 4 days after the delivery.
We prescribed the patient 40 mg once a day of enoxaparin for 6 weeks—to prevent post-partum thrombosis after an endoscopy, on the day after the caesarean section, showed small varices.
Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) are rare in pregnancy; they are associated with thrombosis, pre-eclampsia, fetal growth restriction, and stillbirth. Interferon alfa-2a is recommended for cytoreduction in pregnancy if high cell counts, multiple symptoms, or a history of thrombosis or poor obstetric outcomes is found. Unlike Janus kinase 2 inhibitors and hydroxyurea, interferon alfa-2a does not cross the placenta and has a proven fetal safety profile; it can reduce spleen size by at least 50% in about half of non-pregnant patients with MPN. Splenomegaly—a cause of obstetric haemorrhage currently unaddressed in existing guidelines—may rupture in labour or obstruct surgical incisions during caesarean section. Interferon alfa-2a might be considered for newly detected or persisting splenomegaly in pregnant patients with MPN, even in the absence of indications for cytoreduction. Ideally, patients should be monitored, in a multidisciplinary setting, for dose-limiting haematologic toxicities and other complications (appendix). Finally, the possibility of portal hypertension in MPN should be considered if splenic varices are detected on ultrasound; elective gastroscopy might avoid unforeseen episodes of acute variceal bleeding as the pregnancy advances.

In December, 2015, an 18-month-old boy with an unremarkable medical history was admitted to the paediatric emergency room for left leg trauma following a fall. A clinical examination showed a leg deformity and total functional impairment of the limb. A radiograph of the leg (figure) revealed a diaphyseal tibial and fibular fracture, with condensed cortical bone and anterolateral bowing (Crawford type I). Café au lait spots were noticed on the child's trunk (figure). After 3 months of immobilisation in an above-knee cast, there were still no signs of bone healing. A clinical examination of the boy's mother revealed multiple café au lait spots and cutaneous neurofibromas, and confirmed the presence of a hitherto undiagnosed case of familial neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). The course of the boy's disease confirmed that he was suffering from NF1-associated congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia (CPT). No cutaneous or visceral neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, or optic gliomas were observed. No other skeletal manifestations were noted. Surgical treatment (resection of the pseudarthrosis area and an induced membrane technique) was initiated 5 months after the fracture. 1 year after surgery, persistent non-union at the distal end of the tibia prompted surgical revision with a second induced membrane technique.Although up to 55% of cases of CPT are associated with NF1, only 3% of patients with NF1 have CPT. Young children often develop CPT long before the appearance of other signs. Most cases are unilateral. Cystic forms (as in the present case) show condensed cortical and thickened bone in the concavity of the deformity, together with a narrow medullary canal. Progression of the deformity can result in a transverse fracture. Crawford's classification is most frequently applied. Surgical treatment of CPT remains a challenge because of refracture, delayed union, non-union, and persistent lower limb disorders. Several surgical options have been described, such as resection and nailing, fibular vascularised grafting, and the induced membrane technique.
This case report demonstrates the importance of diagnosis of pathological fractures in children, since they can reveal NF1.
output: NF1-associated congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia

A 45-year-old man came to our emergency department in August because he experienced an abnormal, unpleasant sensation when his fingers and thumbs were touched; he also said that they were blue and felt weak. 4 h before, he had been paragliding and had flown into a tower of cumulonimbus clouds—entering a summer thunderstorm—where winds carried him rapidly upwards to more than 6000 m above sea level. At this height, the man encountered hail, rain, an air temperature of −25°C, and wind speeds of up to 100 km/h for about 45 min. Because of the worsening dysaesthesia and the paresis of his fingers, the man had been unable to properly control and steer the paraglider and had landed on a rooftop after a further 15 min descent. Notably, the patient had worn thin gloves on his hands in contrast to thick clothing on his lower legs and face. When we first examined the man's fingers, they were cyanotic, swollen, numb, and paretic (figure). We decided to initially warm his hands and then started him on intravenous iloprost 20 μg once daily, oral aspirin 100 mg once daily, subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg once daily, and topical betamethasone once daily. These treatments were continued for 10 days. 2 days after the paraglider's ordeal, blisters appeared on his fingers (figure) that were compatible with a diagnosis of grade 2 frostbite; these lesions were drained, and the dysaesthesia and paresis ameliorated. On the fifth day, erythema and desquamation of the lesions occurred (figure). The swelling reduced after 7 days—although splinter haemorrhages were seen on the tenth day (figure). After 30 days, the fingers and thumbs had fully recovered without any residual tissue damage or sensorimotor deficits.Frostbite develops as a result of thermal injury to the skin and other tissues exposed to cold temperature; it is a recognised problem seen commonly in military personnel, homeless individuals, and winter sports enthusiasts. Grade 1 lesions are characterised by numbness and erythema of the affected skin, without blister formation; when blisters filled with clear fluid are seen, the lesions should be classified as grade 2. Grade 3 lesions are characterised by a blue-grey discolouration of the skin and haemorrhagic blisters resulting in black eschars. Grade 4 lesions involve muscles, joints, and bones and result in tissue necrosis and tissue loss. For grade 4 lesions, the recommendation is that the treating physician should adopt the principle of autoamputation—whereby the damaged tissue spontaneously detaches from the body—rather than carrying out early surgical amputation. Besides rewarming, which is primarily employed to stop vasoconstriction, endothelial injury, and thrombosis caused by the cold, several adjuvant treatments should be considered; aspirin, prostaglandins, and thrombolytic agents can be given because of their antiplatelet and vasodilatory effects. Additionally, damaged tissue should be protected against further insult to avoid it becoming infected. Fortunately, frostbite among paragliders is rare.

A previously well 79-year-old woman presented with the acute onset of coffee-ground emesis. She had no previous history of alcohol intake, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug use, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or ingestion of corrosive agents. Urgent oesophagogastroduodenoscopy was done. She was kept nil-orally and commenced on an intravenous proton-pump inhibitor, fluconazole, and broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a diffuse black appearance of the mucosa from the mid-oesophagus to the gastro-oesophageal junction (figure A), where there was a clearly demarcated boundary with normal mucosa (figure B)—a finding consistent with a diagnosis of acute oesophageal necrosis. This condition is also known as Gurvits' syndrome or black oesophagus. Acute oesophageal necrosis is a rare clinical entity that usually presents with either frank haematemesis or coffee-ground emesis. It has a characteristic endoscopic appearance of circumferential, friable, black-coloured mucosa in the distal oesophagus that ends clearly and abruptly at the gastro-oesophageal junction. It is thought to be caused by oesophageal ischaemia. Multiple factors might be involved, including haemodynamic compromise, malnutrition, drug ingestion, and underlying cardiovascular or renal disease. Although the oesophagus is largely protected from ischaemia by its complex and intricate anastomotic vascular network, there is a watershed area in the distal oesophagus that is more susceptible to ischaemic injury. Management of acute oesophageal necrosis generally involves resuscitation, supportive measures, and treatment of any coexisting illness. Antimicrobial therapy is usually unnecessary, except in the setting of oesophageal perforation, positive cultures, or suspected sepsis. Although complications of perforation and stricture formation are uncommon, acute oesophageal necrosis carries a high overall mortality risk due to its association with other comorbidities and critical illness. However, acute oesophageal necrosis in an otherwise healthy patient often resolves spontaneously and is associated with a more favourable outcome.Repeat oesophagogastroduodenoscopy of our patient 72 h later revealed complete resolution of the initial endoscopic findings (figure C). Our patient was subsequently discharged home following resolution of the injury and remains well at 6-month follow-up.
