A 62-year-old man was referred to our clinic with a dark, atypical-looking lesion on his upper arm because the medical oncologists were concerned that it was possibly an early melanoma (appendix).The patient was otherwise fit and well; he had a malignant melanoma surgically removed from the middle of his back 18 months previously. He reported a history of renal cell carcinoma treated by a partial nephrectomy.
The lesion was examined using reflectance confocal microscopy (RCM) and showed a large, nucleated, solitary cell consistent with a Langerhans cell in the upper epidermis with a round or oval cell body, measuring approximately 20 μm, and highly refractile dendritic branches (figure).
Histology of the lesion confirmed a lentiginous junctional nevus with inflammation: a benign diagnosis.
RCM is an in vivo optical imaging technique used to visualise skin cells, appendages, and processes in real time; the technology allows for subcellular resolution in the horizonal or en face orientation of skin layers down to the papillary dermis showing superficial collagen. RCM uses a low-power, near-infrared, diode laser, emitting light of wavelength 820 nm.
Crucially, RCM cannot distinguish between activated Langerhans cells and dendritic melanocytes. Both have similar refractive indices and morphological features. However, their distribution is different and—as in our patient—a Langerhans cell might be suspected due to its location.
Since RCM is a newer diagnostic imaging approach being used more commonly now than ever before, it is useful to have some awareness of potential pitfalls when interpreting confocal images and identifying cells of interest.
Finally, Langerhans cells may become activated in the context of inflammatory immune response or trauma. While the transformation rate of a melanocytic nevus into cutaneous melanoma is thought to be extremely low—about 1 in 33 000 for men older than 60 years—it remains important to examine and remove suspicious lesions as rates of cutaneous melanoma continue to rise (video).

A 41-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 20-h history of progressively worsening sudden-onset, severe, left-sided neck pain. Additionally, he complained of a headache in the occipital region, odynophagia, and trismus. He reported no medical history of trauma or infection. A physical examination showed he had severely limited neck motion in all directions because of stiffness. Blood tests showed a leucocytosis (13·0 × 109 per L), an elevated serum C-reactive protein concentration (124 mg/L), and a faster erythrocyte sedimentation rate (24 mm/h). A cervical spine x-ray showed swelling in both the retropharyngeal and prevertebral spaces and ill-defined calcifications anterior to the C2 (figure). A CT scan of the cervical spine showed calcifications in the longus colli muscle inferior to the anterior arch of the C1 and marked swelling and effusion in the retropharyngeal and prevertebral spaces (figure). Acute calcific tendinitis of the longus colli muscle was diagnosed, and an oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, loxoprofen, was prescribed for 5 days at a dose of 180 mg per day. The symptoms began to resolve within a few hours, and the range of the patient's neck movements recovered significantly within 2 days. And within 1 week, the patient was completely symptom-free.Acute calcific tendinitis of the longus colli muscle—also known as retropharyngeal calcific tendinitis—is a rare and benign condition caused by basic calcium phosphate deposition in the tendons of the longus colli muscle that is accompanied by an aseptic inflammatory process. The characteristic triad of symptoms is acute-onset neck pain, neck stiffness, and odynophagia. Other symptoms include occipital headaches, a limitation in the range of neck movements, trismus, sore throat, pharyngeal oedema, and a low-grade fever with elevated inflammatory markers. The key point in describing this case is to stress the importance of differentiating this benign condition from other serious or life-threatening conditions presenting in a similar way. The list of differential diagnoses is long but crucially includes retropharyngeal abscess, meningitis, infectious spondylitis, lymphadenitis, epiglottis, and oropharyngeal and spinal neoplasms. In this context, getting the diagnosis right will restrict the number of invasive investigations and possibly the prescription of unnecessary antibiotics or other treatments. The correct diagnosis is clinched by modern imaging methods—a cervical CT being preferable to an x-ray. Antipyretic analgesics, with corticosteroids in severe cases, are effective treatments.

A 31-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 1-week history of fever, myalgia, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. She had no significant medical history, history of recent travel, or alcohol use. She reported no genitourinary symptoms, rashes, oral ulcerations, or pharyngitis. She did say that she had been recently sexually active with a new male partner.On examination, we found the patient to be febrile (temperature 38·2°C). She was tachycardic (heart rate 120 beats per min), tachypnoeic (respiratory rate 44 breaths per min), and she was tender in her right upper quadrant. She was not jaundiced and there were no mucocutaneous lesions seen anywhere.
Laboratory investigations showed a hepatitic picture: alanine aminotransferase was 629 units per L (normal <35), aspartate aminotransferase 634 units per L (normal <30), gamma-glutamyl transferase 182 units per L (normal <38), alkaline phosphatase 143 units per mL (normal <110), and a total bilirubin concentration within normal limits. The patient's C-reactive protein concentration was 192 mg/L (normal <3).
An abdominal ultrasound showed pericholecystic fluid and biliary sludge in a thin-walled gallbladder.
We admitted her with presumed diagnosis of cholecystitis. However, during abdominal laparoscopy, we found numerous vesicles across the surface of the liver—with no evidence of cholecystitis (figure).
Histological analysis of a liver biopsy sample showed a lobular parenchymal lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate; herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) was detected by PCR (AusDiagnostics, Sydney, NSW, Australia).
She was treated with intravenous acyclovir followed by oral valacyclovir for 6 weeks after which she made complete recovery; laboratory investigations returned to normal levels. Notably, having been seronegative at presentation, the patient was found to have seroconverted after 4 weeks showing convalescent type-specific serology—HSV-2 IgG. Subsequent testing of her asymptomatic partner found that he was also HSV-2 IgG positive.

Primary HSV-2 should be considered as a cause of acute hepatitis—even in the absence of jaundice or mucocutaneous lesions and if the patient is immunocompetent. A viral prodrome with a headache and fever is common. Transmission may occur via asymptomatic viral shedding in sexually active individuals. In the acute stages of the illness, PCR is the diagnostic method of choice as patients have usually not seroconverted. The high mortality of patients with untreated HSV-2 hepatitis is greatly reduced with early intravenous acyclovir treatment.

A 62-year-old man was referred to our clinic with a dark, atypical-looking lesion on his upper arm because the medical oncologists were concerned that it was possibly an early melanoma (appendix).The patient was otherwise fit and well; he had a malignant melanoma surgically removed from the middle of his back 18 months previously. He reported a history of renal cell carcinoma treated by a partial nephrectomy.
The lesion was examined using reflectance confocal microscopy (RCM) and showed a large, nucleated, solitary cell consistent with a Langerhans cell in the upper epidermis with a round or oval cell body, measuring approximately 20 μm, and highly refractile dendritic branches (figure).
Histology of the lesion confirmed a lentiginous junctional nevus with inflammation: a benign diagnosis.
RCM is an in vivo optical imaging technique used to visualise skin cells, appendages, and processes in real time; the technology allows for subcellular resolution in the horizonal or en face orientation of skin layers down to the papillary dermis showing superficial collagen. RCM uses a low-power, near-infrared, diode laser, emitting light of wavelength 820 nm.
Crucially, RCM cannot distinguish between activated Langerhans cells and dendritic melanocytes. Both have similar refractive indices and morphological features. However, their distribution is different and—as in our patient—a Langerhans cell might be suspected due to its location.
Since RCM is a newer diagnostic imaging approach being used more commonly now than ever before, it is useful to have some awareness of potential pitfalls when interpreting confocal images and identifying cells of interest.
Finally, Langerhans cells may become activated in the context of inflammatory immune response or trauma. While the transformation rate of a melanocytic nevus into cutaneous melanoma is thought to be extremely low—about 1 in 33 000 for men older than 60 years—it remains important to examine and remove suspicious lesions as rates of cutaneous melanoma continue to rise (video).

There was also an outpouching of the left lower abdominal wall without any underlying masses or fascial defects. Computed tomography of the abdomen was notable only for a protrusion of the left lower abdominal wall. What is the diagnosis?
output:
Herpes zoster-associated pseudohernia (abdominal wall paresis)

The clinical presentation shows:
1. Vesicular/scabbed lesions in a dermatomal distribution (T12)
2. Unilateral abdominal wall bulge without fascial defect on CT
3. Recent onset correlating with the herpes zoster outbreak

A 32-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 1-month history of continuous chest pain, which was worse with movement and on application of pressure to the anterior chest wall. Physical examination showed a pustule on the sole of his left foot (figure A) and multiple pustules on his palms (figure B). Blood analysis, chest radiography, and ECG results were normal. Microscopy and culture for bacteria of the pustules was negative, as was serology for Treponema pallidum and HIV. Immunological tests were done, but no abnormalities were found. A radioisotope scan showed intense activity at the sternoclavicular and first sternocostal joints (figure C). A diagnosis of synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome was made. Treatment with non-steroidal anti-inflammatories and methotrexate was started, resulting in clinical improvement. SAPHO syndrome is characterised by the variable association of osteoarticular manifestations, mainly on the anterior chest wall, and various dermatological conditions—in particular palmoplantar pustulosis and severe acne.
output: SAPHO syndrome (Synovitis, Acne, Pustulosis, Hyperostosis, and Osteitis syndrome)

A 76-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis–myositis overlap being treated with mycophenolic acid and hydroxychloroquine was admitted for weight loss of 19 kg over 1 year, myositis relapse, new constellation of pancytopenia (haemoglobin 6·7 g/dL, white blood cell count 1·82 × 109 per L, and platelet count 88 × 109 per L), proteinuria (0·3 g per day), and low complement C3 concentrations (53 mg/dL [normal C3 range 83–193 mg/dL]). She was afebrile with stable blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation on room air. Extensive malignancy evaluation and infection screen were negative. She was treated for evolving systemic lupus erythematosus with oral prednisolone (0·5 mg/kg per day), intravenous immunoglobulin, and rituximab.
Baseline chest radiograph showed possible pneumatosis and dilated small bowels (figure A), which was confirmed on abdominal radiograph (figure B). The pneumatosis was initially managed conservatively, ie, the patient was allowed a normal diet and did not undergo further abdominal imaging or surgical procedures, as she was asymptomatic and moving her bowels. She then developed acute epigastric pain and tenderness without peritonism. She remained leukopenic with normal lactate concentrations and no acidosis. Abdominal CT showed extensive pneumatosis intestinalis (figure C, D), small bowel dilatation with no transition point, small bowel hypoenhancement, which was concerning for ischaemia, and free gas, suggestive of perforation (figure D). An urgent laparoscopy, however, showed a healthy bowel with segments of small bowel pneumatosis without perforation or dilatation. Pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis was diagnosed. Postoperatively, her abdominal pain resolved with esomeprazole. She cleared bowels and tolerated a soft diet 2 days later. Repeat CT 6 months later showed resolution of pneumatosis and pneumoperitoneum. She was continued on hydroxychloroquine, monthly intravenous immunoglobulin, and tapered prednisolone for her overlapping connective tissue disease. Her weight, cytopenias, and complement concentrations improved.
With a reported prevalence of 0·03% in autopsy studies, pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis is a rare gastrointestinal manifestation of connective tissue disease characterised by submucosal, subserosal free gas-filled cysts, or both. Possible causes include increased luminal pressure, bacterial fermentation, and glucocorticoid-induced intestinal mucosa atrophy. Cyst rupture might cause pneumoperitoneum. Patients with pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis are often asymptomatic and respond well to conservative treatment. Surgery is indicated if there are concerns of bowel ischemia, perforation or peritonitis. Clinicians should have a heightened awareness of pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis in patients with connective tissue disease.

Monozygotic twins, aged 2 years, were referred to our outpatient clinic because of a hairless area 2 cm ×  2 cm in a similar point on their occipital vertices (figure). The twin boys were born prematurely after 33 weeks and 3 days of gestation and it was initially thought that the hairless regions, which also had no skin cover, were caused by a fetal scalp electrode. The twins had otherwise developed normally, with no associated anomalies or syndromes, and the defects on their scalps had healed over with scar tissue. A detailed history was taken from the children's mother, who said that the pregnancy had been uncomplicated and that there was no history of skin conditions in the family. Notably, an ultrasound scan done at gestational week 8 showed an empty yolk sac which suggested that a third fetus had been present and was reabsorbed in utero.After considering the history and examining the lesions, we made a diagnosis of aplasia cutis congenita (ACC)—simply a condition with a congenital absence of skin. Vanishing twin syndrome, which perhaps in our case ought to be described as vanishing triplet syndrome—where usually twin fetuses convert to a singleton—is a rare but well recognised phenomenon that is associated with widespread and predominantly truncal ACC. Non-syndromic ACC of the scalp has been associated with a mutation in the ribosome biogenesis factor (BMS1) gene. The suspected mechanism by which this mutation produces ACC is through an increase in the p21 level, which has been linked to an inhibition of cell proliferation and the formation of scar tissue. Scalp ACC in twins is very rare and we found only two other reported cases after a literature search.
At first glance, the scalp defect is easily confused with other conditions causing areas of hair loss, such as alopecia areata or naevoid conditions. The absence of skin poses a slight risk of CNS infection or of sagittal sinus haemorrhage before the healing occurs. Otherwise, ACC is considered benign once the scalp defect has healed and as such does not require further treatment. Therapeutic options include conservative management or surgery for aesthetic purposes, larger defects, or underlying bone defects. Since this condition is very rare, physicians outside of the dermatological arena should not be chastised for missing this spot diagnosis.

A 63-year-old man presented to our emergency department with a 1-year history of severe nocturia and straining to pass urine. Additionally, he reported having tenesmus and abdominal pain in the 2 weeks prior to attending. The patient had no significant medical history.On examination we found his abdomen to be moderately distended; it was soft and normal bowels sounds could be heard. A rectal examination showed a large pelvic mass with an irregular surface occupying the whole rectal ampulla.
Laboratory investigations found a haemoglobin concentration of 11·8 g/dL (normal 14·0–18·0) and a white blood cell count of 5·41 × 109 per L (normal 4·0–10·0). The patient had a serum creatinine concentration of 1·37 mg/dL (normal 0·80–1·30), a blood sodium concentration of 139 mEq/L (normal 135–145) and a negative urinalysis; the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) serum concentration was 144 ng/mL (normal <4·0).
Multiparametric prostatic MRI showed an 18 cm × 13 cm lesion in the pelvis—made up of numerous, pluri-lobulated cystic areas with a heterogeneous signal; with T2 hyperintensity in some loci—indicating fluid, and T2 hypointensity in other parts—suggestive of intracystic bleeding. The cystic lesions were in the basal and middle portions of the prostate gland, which were completely unstructured and recognisable, only in part, in the mid-apical and anterior portions. No significant lymphadenopathy was seen (figure). A bone scan showed no evidence of metastatic spread. Initially, we considered the mass to be a giant prostatic cystadenoma and a three-dimensional reconstruction model was obtained to choose the most appropriate surgical strategy (figure).
We carried out an open, radical prostatectomy using combined retrograde and anterograde approaches with limited pelvic lymph node dissection. The bladder was completely dislocated anteriorly and ended up in the right portion of the pelvis; it showed no signs of infiltration. Fluid obtained from aspiration of the cysts, sent for extemporaneous cytological analysis, had no neoplastic cells. The final histopathological examination showed a giant multilocular cystadenocarcinoma: ductal and acinar adenocarcinoma (Gleason score 4 + 4=8) mixed with the cystic tumour. Two 1 mm positive surgical margins—one apical and one posterolateral on the right side—were recorded on the prostate.
The tumour stage was pT3bN0 with nine lymph nodes, which when removed showed no tumour involvement. High-power microscopy showed nuclear stratifications, papillary structures, and Roman arch formations in the cystically dilated glands. The first postoperative PSA serum concentration was 0·12 ng/mL.
Because of the aggressive characteristics of the tumour and the adverse risk factors for early biochemical failure—the tumour stage, histology, and high PSA level—we decided to treat the prostate bed with adjuvant radiotherapy together with long-term androgen deprivation therapy.
At 6 month follow-up, the PSA serum concentration was undetectable and the patient had reached a satisfactory continence status using one pad per day.
Prostate cystadenocarcinoma is a very rare malignancy sometimes presenting as a large tumour that may be difficult to diagnose; its cystic nature means that it is not always possible to obtain a preoperative cytological or histopathological confirmation of the diagnosis that might then guide surgical management. Differentiating it from other pelvic cystic masses—including its benign counterpart, prostatic cystadenoma—is key. A particularly high PSA serum concentration—as seen in our patient—remains, we believe, the most valuable indicator of malignancy, even if preoperative imaging shows no metastatic spread and intraoperative cytological analysis does not indicate a tumour (video).

A 29-year-old woman was referred to our renal clinic because of pain in her right flank and severe hypertension; her blood pressure was more than 180/110 mm Hg. She was diagnosed as having treatment-resistant-hypertension because her blood pressure remained high at 157/105 mm Hg despite being treated with three antihypertensive drugs, including a diuretic, at maximum doses. 24-h ambulatory monitoring showed increased daytime and nocturnal (non-dipper pattern) blood pressures. She had no history of previous medical difficulties. She was of normal weight and did not report having headaches or palpitations. On physical examination, she was not found to have oedema or any other relevant clinical findings.Considering the patient's young age, the absence of a family history or other risk factors for hypertension, and the high level and acute increase in her blood pressure, we commenced investigations for secondary causes of hypertension. The laboratory investigations we did included a full blood count, plasma-renin activity, blood concentrations of creatinine, cystatin C, potassium, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), and aldosterone. We also requested a urinalysis and a 24-h urine test with levels of albuminuria, cortisol, catecholamines, and metanephrines. Finally, we completed the screening with a duplex ultrasound of the kidneys and echocardiography.
Renal parenchymal disease was ruled out because there was no albuminuria on urinalysis and serum creatinine and cystatin C concentrations were within normal range. Other causes—such as obstructive sleep apnoea—were discounted because of a low index of suspicion. A normal echocardiogram enabled us to rule out the possibility of coarctation of the aorta. A normal aldosterone-to-renin ratio allowed us to exclude primary aldosteronism; a normal TSH enabled us to eliminate thyroid disease; Cushing's syndrome was precluded because of a normal 24-h urinary cortisol and so was the possibility of a phaeochromocytoma because of normal concentrations of 24-h urinary catecholamines.
Interestingly, the only abnormal laboratory investigation was a low serum potassium concentration (3·3 mmol/L). However, the ultrasound of the right kidney showed a vascular malformation, raising the possibility of renal artery stenosis. A CT angiogram of the right kidney showed stenosis of the right renal artery, seven variously sized aneurysms—coalescing into a mass of approximately 34 × 27 mm in the right kidney—and an arteriovenous fistula from one of the aneurysms near the right renal artery to the ipsilateral right ovarian vein (figure). The patient was diagnosed with fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD). FMD is a non-atherosclerotic and non-inflammatory vascular disease that can result in arterial stenosis, aneurysm formation, and dissection or occlusion, or both, of medium-sized arteries. It is usually diagnosed radiographically because histology is not typically available. There are two subtypes: multifocal FMD, the more common, has the appearance of a so-called string of beads, whereas focal FMD looks like a circumferential or tubular stenosis. Classic appearances can evolve with complicated aneurysm and fistula formation. Kidney-related diseases—including diseases of the renal parenchyma and stenosis of the renal arteries—are among the most common causes of secondary hypertension in non-obese patients with low indices of suspicion for obstructive sleep apnoea.

A 27-year-old woman attended our accident and emergency unit reporting fatigue and recurrent pain in the right side of her chest; the tiredness, which had been present for several years, had recently worsened.The patient had been diagnosed with anorexia nervosa (AN) at the age of 17 years; she severely restricted her diet, resulting in significant weight loss. She was prescribed antidepressants and hormone replacement therapy for previously disturbed periods.
On examination she was very unwell and markedly cachectic; her pulse was 98 beats per min, her blood pressure was 68/45 mm Hg, and her oxygen saturation was 90% and BMI was 10 kg/m2. Laboratory investigations showed a pancytopenia with a white blood cell count of 2·07 × 109 per L (normal 3·5–11·0), haemoglobin concentration of 10 g/dL (normal 12–16), and a platelet count of 78·0 × 109 per L (normal 150–440). The patient's serum glucose concentration was 51 mg/dL (normal 70–100); liver function tests were as follows: alanine aminotransferase 347 units per L (normal <33), aspartate transaminase 173 units per L (normal <32), and lactate dehydrogenase 293 units per L (normal 135–214).
An initial CT scan of the patient's chest showed an apical condensation; on subsequent scans the lesion appeared with some excavation (figure). No signs of a pulmonary embolism were seen. Investigations for common viral, fungal, and bacterial causes of lung infections—including tuberculosis—were negative. A sample obtained from a lung biopsy, which we decided to do because the patient's chest pain was worsening, showed inflammatory changes surrounding an unknown material, indicating inhalation of a foreign body. No signs of malignancy were seen.
We prescribed amoxicillin and clavulanate and commenced enteral feeding. After 4 weeks in hospital the pancytopenia was still present, so we did a bone marrow aspirate which showed some hypocellular spicules with an increase in adipocytes surrounded by abundant extracellular pinkish material—indicating gelatinous transformation (figure).
The patient was commenced on enteral nutrition with a progressive energetic regimen and concomitant correction of fluid and electrolyte imbalances; her weight increased from 32·5 kg to 39·5 kg and her BMI from 10 kg/m2 to 12 kg/m2. After 2 months of treatment the white cell count and platelet count had returned to normal levels. The patient then went to a specialised centre to continue with psychiatric and nutritional care.
The severity of AN is determined by the BMI: less than or equal to 17 kg/m2 is considered mild, 16 kg/m2 to 16·99 kg/m2 is moderate, 15 kg/m2 to 15·99 kg/m2 is severe, and less than 15 kg/m2 is extreme. Patients with a very low BMI—as in our case—are at high risk of developing the refeeding syndrome which occurs when rapid and inappropriate feeding is initiated after a long period of starvation. AN is also associated with an increased risk of gelatinous bone marrow transformation, which is reversible with treatment (video).

A 3-year-old girl was referred to the dermatology department with blonde, straw-like, and unruly hair. The child's parents reported that since birth her hair had been sparse and slow growing. And from about one year of age, her parents had difficulty combing her hair.5 months earlier, the patient had a fever, dyspnoea, and chest pain; he had been seen in the community and a chest CT had shown bilateral dense sub-pleural infiltrates in both lower lobes of the lungs—more on the left. Investigations had found a raised C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 18·8 mg/dL (normal 0–0·5). The patient was initially diagnosed and treated for a community acquired pneumonia with oral cefuroxime and roxithromycin with limited clinical response; he was swapped on to oral levofloxacin for a further 14 days. The patient recovered and a CT scan, 1 months later showed almost complete disappearance of the infiltrates.
His medical history was unremarkable, he had no history of travelling abroad, no contact with animals, and he was employed in home renovation.
On examination, we found cyanosis in toes 1 and 5 of his left foot; arterial pulses were detected in the groin but they were absent in the popliteal fossae of both legs. He was afebrile.
CT-angiography showed filling defects the right kidney and spleen suggesting infarcts (appendix) and obstructions of the left femoral artery and right popliteal artery (figure). We started low-molecular-weight heparin.
Thrombi were extracted from the left iliac, common femoral and superficial femoral, and the right deep and superficial femoral arteries resulting in the restoration of blood flow to both legs.
Chest CT with angiography also showed large masses on the cusps of the aortic valve and trans-oesophageal echocardiography found a bicuspid aortic valve with masses attached to the aortic and ventricular surfaces of the valve.
Significant laboratory abnormalities included a raised CRP concentration 15·1mg/dL. Tests for anticardiolipin and anti-β2 glycoprotein 1 antibodies were both strongly positive. Tests for anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-Sm antibodies were negative; blood cultures were also negative.
At operation to replace the aortic valve, large vegetations were found over the left anterior-posterior commissure with destruction of the left aspect of both leaflets (figure). Cultures of samples of the values did not grow organisms but were positive on PCR for Coxiella burnetii; Q fever serology was also positive. We therefore made a diagnosis of antiphospholipid syndrome following Q fever. The patient was treated with doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine; he was allowed home after 8 days. 3 months later, both IgG anticardiolipin antibodies and anti-β2 glycoprotein 1 IgG antibodies remained high. The patient completed an 18-month course of the antibiotics without any further problems.
The diagnosis of antiphospholipid syndrome depends upon the detection of a lupus anticoagulant, or anticardiolipin or anti-β2-glycoprotein 1 antibodies. Acute Q fever can be complicated by antiphospholipid syndrome leading to infective endocarditis with large vegetations and multiple emboli. Thromboembolic events following a pneumonia should prompt investigations for antiphospholipid syndrome; a finding which mandates testing for C burnetii and undertaking echocardiographic studies (video).

A 35-year-old Libyan woman was referred to us from another institution with the diagnosis of massive pericardial effusion and pericardial tamponade. On admission to us, she was hypotensive, tachycardic and tachypnoeic. Electrocardiography showed unspecific low QRS voltage and ST-T segment flattening. Chest x-ray showed cardiomegaly. We did an emergency pericardial aspiration which yielded 1500 ml of yellow coloured fluid. A transthoracic echocardiogrm showed multiple cystic formations approximately 1·5–2 cm within the pericardial cavity (figure A), and confirmed the need for surgery. We did a standard median sternotomy and thoroughly irrigated the pericardium with hypertonic saline; multiple cysts were removed from the pericardium (figures B and C). Our patient was diagnosed with a ruptured intrapericardial hydatid cyst and pericardial tamponade. We established the diagnosis based on the gross appearance of the removed cysts, the echocardiogram results, and a high ESR. Hydatid disease is endemic in Libya, a southern Mediterranean country. Serological tests were not available. After surgery she was treated with oral albendazole for 12 days. She recovered well and was discharged 12 days after surgery. Pericardial tamponade due to hydatid disease is a rare condition that has been seldom reported in the literature.
output: Ruptured intrapericardial hydatid cyst with pericardial tamponade

A 49-year-old man with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus was referred for an internal medicine consultation because of worsening heartburn for the past 3 months. The patient regularly ate pickled anchovies (raw anchovies in vinegar sauce). His overall health was good, and findings from physical examination were unexceptional. Laboratory results showed peripheral eosinophilia (1·7 × 103 cells per μL, normal 0·5 × 103 cells per μL) but were otherwise unremarkable. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed characteristic findings of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and Barrett's oesophagus (confirmed by pathological study); an isolated, thickened gastric fold (which was biopsied; figure); and no macroscopic evidence of erythema, oedema, erosive gastritis, ulcerations, tumour-like nodules, or worms. Nevertheless, histological assessment showed a striking eosinophilic inflammatory infiltrate and a sectioned larva of the nematode Anisakis simplex embedded in the gastric mucosa (figure). Additionally, serum IgE specific for A simplex was increased. We gave the patient omeprazole to treat his gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and specific preventive recommendations to avoid ingestion of potentially contaminated seafood (eg, by freezing or suitably heating fish) and decrease the risk of anaphylaxis due to A simplex. 10 months after the diagnosis of anisakidosis was made, his blood eosinophil count was within normal limits, and both gastroscopy and examination of gastric biopsy samples showed no abnormalities.
Anisakidosis, a disease caused by any member of the family Anisakidae that occurs worldwide, usually results from consumption of raw or undercooked marine fish or squid contaminated with the larvae of A simplex or Pseudoterranova decipiens. Although symptomatic gastro-oesophageal, intestinal, ectopic, and allergic diseases are the most common clinical presentations in human beings, this case shows that symptomless eosinophilic gastritis with secondary eosinophilia can also develop. In view of the popularity of raw seafood consumption, clinicians should keep anisakidosis high on their list of differential diagnoses for a wide range of disorders, especially in patients known to have these dietary habits.
output: Anisakidosis (gastric anisakiasis caused by Anisakis simplex)

Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed characteristic findings of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and Barrett's oesophagus (confirmed by pathological study); an isolated, thickened gastric fold (which was biopsied; figure); and no macroscopic evidence of erythema, oedema, erosive gastritis, ulcerations, tumour-like nodules, or worms. A 52-year-old man presented to the emergency department with fevers and chills in December, 2014, and was admitted with a diagnosis of pneumonia. CT to exclude pulmonary embolus showed diffuse osseous lytic lesions, and he was also found to have anaemia and an IgG kappa monoclonal protein of 55·8 g/L on protein electrophoresis (a single band). After a bone marrow biopsy he was given a diagnosis of plasma cell myeloma and was treated with four cycles of CyBorD chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone) in preparation for an autologous stem cell transplantation.
The aspirate from the bone marrow sampling showed a substantial increase in plasma cells (figure). The bone marrow core biopsy sample showed a hypercellular marrow with increased plasma cells, estimated to occupy 80% of marrow cellularity by CD138 immunohistochemistry. We saw that the neoplastic plasma cells had two distinct immunophenotypes: one population expressed CD138, kappa, and CD56; the other expressed CD138, kappa, CD20, and CD79a. Morphological differences were visible on routine haematoxylin and eosin staining, with prominent nucleoli in the CD56 area (figure). We could not create a more extensive immunophenotype because of tissue limitations, and too few events were captured by flow cytometry to allow characterisation using this technique.
output: Plasma cell myeloma with biclonal plasma cell populations

An 80-year-old man with a 6-month-history of shortness of breath on minimal exertion and fatigue was admitted to our unit for a planned operation to replace his stenotic aortic valve. The surgery was uneventful and a temporary ventricular epicardial pacing lead was placed on the free wall of the right ventricle. The patient remained haemodynamically stable in sinus rhythm post-surgery and was extubated 8 h later. The following day he was transferred from intensive care to our high dependency unit with the temporary epicardial pacemaker in VVI mode: stimulation amplitude 10 V, sensitivity 1 mV, and back-up pacing rate of 44 beats per min. A pacing check at that time showed no problems.2 days after the operation the patient had a cardiac arrest during mobilisation and physiotherapy; chest compressions were started, and the patient was re-intubated. The defibrillator showed ventricular fibrillation and he was shocked into sinus rhythm using 200 joules biphasic.
A telemetry review showed a spike on a T wave as a possible cause of the cardiac arrest: sinus rhythm was present during the first two cardiac cycles—heart rate 76 beats per min—followed by a premature pacing spike which produced a paced cardiac cycle. Another intrinsic cardiac cycle then followed. However, during the repolarisation phase of this cycle, a second pacing spike was seen falling on the T wave; this spike triggered polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that apparently degenerated into ventricular fibrillation (figure).
The patient was stabilised post-resuscitation and extubated 4 h later; he recovered well and was allowed home 12 days later. 1 month later he was well and asymptomatic when reviewed in our outpatient clinic.
Indications for temporary cardiac pacing include the management of bradyarrhythmias—specifically atrioventricular block—and both atrial and ventricular tachyarrhythmias. In cardiac surgery, insertion of temporary epicardial pacing wires is common practice; it both optimises myocardial function in patients, who postoperatively develop haemodynamically significant arrhythmias, and helps maintain a stable cardiac rhythm.
However, placement of epicardial pacing leads is not without risk. In the short term, function deteriorates mainly due to the inflammation around the surfaces of the myocardium and the leads. Daily checking of the pacemaker's pacing (the depolarisation of the atria or ventricles resulting from an impulse delivered from the generator down a lead to the heart) and sensing (the detection by the generator of intrinsic atrial or ventricular depolarisation signals) parameters after cardiac surgery is therefore paramount.
Pacemaker under-sensing occurs when the pacemaker fails to detect spontaneous myocardial depolarisation—as probably happened in our patient—and is a common reason for the appearance of inappropriate ventricular pacing spikes. When the spikes fall on the T wave, then the patient may develop a tachyarrhythmia—including polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Increasing the pacemaker rate above that of the intrinsic heart rate may reduce the possibility of production of inappropriate ventricular pacing spikes.
output: Pacemaker-induced ventricular fibrillation due to undersensing (R-on-T phenomenon)

A 31-year-old HIV-positive man presented to the hospital on June 30, 2022, with a vesicular rash (figure A), perianal lesions, swollen inguinal lymph nodes, and arthralgia of the right knee. Under antiretroviral therapy, the HIV viral load was below the limit of detection, and his CD4+ T-cell count was 802 cells per μL. Given the rising number of monkeypox cases in Europe at that time and the patient's history of unprotected sexual contact with a man 1 week before symptom onset, an infection with monkeypox virus was suspected. Specimens from two different skin lesions yielded a positive PCR result (cycle threshold values of 20 and 21) for monkeypox virus. The patient was discharged and self-isolated.11 days later a follow-up examination was scheduled, the rash and lymphadenopathy had completely resolved, but a marked swelling of the right knee was noted (figure B). Arthrocentesis was performed, resulting in aspiration of 60 mL of cloudy synovial fluid. Analysis of the synovial fluid showed a cell count of 16 127 cells per μL with 88·5% mononuclear cells (lymphocytes) and 11·5% neutrophil granulocytes. The synovial fluid PCR yielded a positive result for monkeypox virus (cycle threshold value of 27). Laboratory test results were unremarkable apart from a slightly elevated C-reactive protein of 18 mg/L.
Bacterial cultures and broad-range PCR of synovial fluid, serological testing for rheumatoid factor, anti-citrullinated protein antibodies and antinuclear antibodies, human leukocyte antigen B27, and PCR for Lyme disease were all negative. A second arthrocentesis was needed 8 days later due to reoccurrence of effusion. PCR of synovial fluid was again positive for monkeypox virus (cycle threshold value of 33), whereas PCR of whole-blood was negative for monkeypox virus. MRI showed synovitis, joint effusion, and a marked oedema of the medial femoral condyle with a subchondral demarcation zone of 1 cm, compatible with the diagnosis of arthritis and osteomyelitis (figure C–E). Treatment with non-steroidal-anti-inflammatory drugs led to improvement of arthralgia and swelling within 3 weeks.
Viruses are common triggers of arthritis, but viral bone infection has only rarely been reported. However, viral osteomyelitis was a typical complication of smallpox. Referred to as osteomyelitis variolosa, it affected 2–5% of children and 0·25–0·50% of all patients infected with smallpox. No cases of monkeypox-related arthritis or osteomyelitis have been described in the literature so far. Considering that variola virus and monkeypox virus are closely related, we believe that monkeypox virus might lead to arthritis and potentially osteomyelitis.

A 10-year-old girl with an antenatal diagnosis of Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome was referred to our institution with a 1-day history of rectal bleeding. She had stools of normal consistency and frequency, had not been on any medication recently, and had no abdominal pain or other accompanying symptoms.Her physical examination revealed extensive red–purple masses on her right lower leg. These masses on the right lower quadrant felt like a paste when palpated. Laboratory tests revealed that her haemoglobin concentration was 10·6 g/dL, white blood cell count was 9000 cells per μL, and platelet count was 221 000 cells per μL; coagulation tests were normal. D-dimer was high and thromboelastogram results were normal.
An intravenous dose of tranexamic acid 10 mg/kg was started, and colonoscopy was done, which showed continuous submucosal involvement of the rectum and sigmoid, with areas of erythema and whitish zones suggestive of lymphatic lesions, without mucosal erosions (figure, A). Large varices were observed with extensive involvement through the descending, transverse colon, hepatic angle, and ascending colon (figure, B). They extended towards the lumen, in the shape of grape clusters, leaving only a small segment towards the caecum free of disease. The ileum could not be visualised. No mucosal lesions were evident. MRI enteroclysis showed concentric mural thickening of the rectum and proximal sigmoid of the right colon, especially at the level of the caecum and the proximal aspect of the ascending colon. Concentric thickening and hyperaemia of the adjacent rectum wall were also observed. Compared with an examination done 3 years previously, there was evidence of increased involvement of the intestinal wall and adjacent tissues. Given the impossibility of surgical resection, the patient has been treated with oral rapamycin 1·5 mg per day for the past 10 months. She has presented with two episodes of self-limiting rectal bleeding since she started rapamycin, and has been undergoing strict follow-up with a paediatric multidisciplinary team (including surgery, haematology, traumatology, and endocrinology).
Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome is a congenital vascular malformation, with a pathogenesis that is not completely understood. Alteration in the fetal mesoderm has been postulated, as a result of intrauterine damage causing dilation of the arteriovenous anastomosis, deep vein obstruction with varices, or hypertrophy of the lymphatic vessels. Gastrointestinal tract involvement is observed in up to 20% of cases, usually in the rectum and sigmoid, which can manifest as gastrointestinal bleeding, usually during the first decade of life. Since most of the time the bleeding is self-limiting and the involvement of the colon is distal, the patient should be followed up and treated for anaemia if necessary. Angiographic intervention such as embolisation of the bleeding vessel can sometimes be successful. Endoscopic therapy is usually preferred for localised lesions or postoperative residual disease. Endorectal resection extending to the transverse colon has been reported in cases of more extensive disease. Involvement of the ascending colon is very unusual, and the extensive involvement of the bowel makes this particular case unique and challenging.

A 55-year-old woman was admitted to our department with gradual onset of pain in her hands, hips, and knees, which had progressively limited her mobility over the past 6 years. She also reported feeling tired and feverish.On examination we found the patient to have skin sclerosis, microstomia, and reduced mobility in most of her joints. She also had white papules with ulcerations on the skin over her trunk, arms, and legs, but predominantly they were grouped around the large joints—hips, knees, and elbows (figure). We noted a palpable tendon friction rub on the joints of the patient's hands; there was no swelling or tenderness.
Laboratory investigations found a raised C-reactive protein concentration of 33 mg/L (normal 0–5), anaemia with a haemoglobin concentration of 8·2 g/dL, and a moderately elevated creatine kinase of 480 U/L (normal <200).
Tests for autoantibodies found increased titres for antinuclear antibodies (1:2560; normal <1:160) and highly elevated antibodies against double-stranded DNA (>200 U/L; normal <100). Anti-Sjögren's syndrome type A (SSA) and anti-Sjögren's syndrome type B (SSB) antibodies were raised and antibodies against PM/Scl-75 and PM/Scl-100 were strongly positive on immunofluorescence. Autoantibodies to rheumatoid factor (30 U/mL; normal <14) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies (19 U/mL; normal <5) were positive.
An x-ray of the patient's pelvis showed generalised massive multilocular calcinosis (figure) and an x-ray of her hands showed calcification around the tips of her fingers and thumbs (figure). MRI of the patient's thighs showed myositis and fasciitis. A CT scan of the patient's chest showed interstitial lung disease. Ultrasound scans of the patient's joints—specifically her hands and fingers—showed polyarthritis.
Taking these findings in the round, we made a diagnosis of systemic sclerosis together with polymyositis and polyarthritis. We started the patient on a combination of methotrexate, baricitinib, and intravenous immunoglobulins to modulate the immune response, and prostaglandins to cause vasodilation. Within 8 months, the ulcerative calcinosis of the patient's skin, her myositis, and her fasciitis had improved substantially; her pain had also substantially reduced.
Although calcinosis cutis is described in many diseases—including metastatic diseases, lymphomas, and metabolic diseases—it may occur secondary to medical treatments and trauma. Massive infiltrations—as in our patient—are rare and we were fortunate that our multimodal, disease-targeted pharmacological therapy combination was effective. Clinicians using such combined therapies for prolonged periods of time should remain mindful of the risk of infection (video).
output: Systemic sclerosis with polymyositis and polyarthritis (overlap syndrome with calcinosis cutis)

The day before his attendance, he had been seen by his general practitioner and started on oral amoxicillin and clavulanic acid. However, his cheek continued to swell, and he developed a temperature of 39·4oC, prompting the referral.The patient had no medical history; he had all his childhood vaccinations. Additionally, he reported no sexual contacts other than with his male partner.

A 64-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation with portal vein and superior mesenteric vein thrombosis was admitted to hospital with haematemesis. He was diagnosed with non-cirrhotic portal hypertension leading to variceal bleeding. He had two endoscopies with variceal banding and gastric variceal glue injection within 1 month that were unsuccessful; hence, he was referred to a tertiary unit for further management. Given his performance status and comorbidities, he was neither a candidate for surgery nor transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt; therefore, after careful counselling, glue embolisation of the culprit vein was performed via an endovascular approach. Post-procedure, the patient developed left homonymous hemianopia, which gradually worsened, leading to cortical blindness. The visual disturbance was further investigated with a CT scan (figure A). The CT images showed a right occipital infarct and multiple, scattered, high-density foci in subarachnoid space. Further MRI and MR angiogram (figures B–E) supported right distal posterior cerebral artery occlusion, probably due to glue embolisation.Unfortunately, our patient did not consent to further investigations to determine the mechanism, although a non-contrast echocardiogram did not show any cardiac sequelae of septal defects. After appropriate specialist consultation, his stroke has been managed with lifelong anticoagulation due to portal vein and superior mesenteric vein thrombosis and he had conservative management for the neurological symptoms, leading to partial improvement of his vision.
Glue embolisation acts as definitive treatment of gastric varices in selected cases, although complications do occur in 0·5–4·3% of patients. In a large retrospective case series (n=753), distant glue embolisation complications were reported in five patients (0·7%, one pulmonary, one brain, and three splenic). Embolisation to the right atrium and beyond has been reported in previous case studies, including systemic arterial embolisation due to septal defects. However, cerebral embolisation is uncommon but can present with cortical blindness, similarly to our case. Therefore, informed procedural consent must include glue embolisation and a high index of suspicion must be shown if a patient develops acute respiratory or neurological complications after the intervention.

A 10-year-old boy was brought to our emergency room with generalized tonic-clonic seizures that had started one hour before. There was a three-year history of seizures treated with phenytoin (5 mg per kg twice daily) and headache associated with fever. The patient went into cardiopulmonary arrest (RR 5 per min, HR 40 per min, SBP 50 mmHg, weak pulse, capillary refill >15 sec). On examination, he was unconscious (GCS: 3/15), with both pupils dilated and unresponsive. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was done, but vital signs did not return; the patient was declared dead. In postmortem analysis, a coronal section of the brain showed bilateral ventricular cavities collapsed, and generalized cerebral oedema with cortical and subcortical distribution of numerous intraparenchymal cysts of various sizes, some with visible larvae (figure). Microscopically, the cysts contained the larvae preserved (figure) or in degrees of decomposition (figure). Interstitial deposits, fibrosis, gliosis, and necrosis were also found.

A 23-year-old woman was referred to our hospital for a recurrent discharge of something resembling a white string from her anus. She explained that the problem had started 4 months ago and that she had no other symptoms. She said she had eaten raw fish as sashimi approximately 6 months earlier and that the discharge had started 2 months later. A physical examination found no abnormalities and the blood test results were all normal. However, based on her history, we suspected she had diphyllobothriasis and did a screening abdominal ultrasound scan, which showed a hyperechoic strand-like structure floating freely and moving autonomously in her intestinal tract (figure; videos 1 and 2). A subsequent capsule endoscopy showed a tapeworm (figure); a coprological examination was positive, confirming the diagnosis of diphyllobothriasis. We treated the patient with diatrizoate (Gastrografin, Bayer, Reading, UK) given through a duodenal tube to ensure that the scolex of the cestode was expelled: the complete, uninjured tapeworm measured 210 cm in length when we examined it outside the patient's body (figure). Mitochondrial DNA analysis of the COX-1 and NAD-3 gene sequences identified the causative cestode as Diphyllobothrium nihonkaiense—based on comparisons with homologous sequences in GenBank.D nihonkaiense is the principal cestode causing diphyllobothriasis in Japan. It can infect anyone—regardless of immune status—who eats raw or undercooked fish harbouring infective larvae: once infected, the patient then becomes the worm's second intermediate host. Presenting symptoms include diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and bloating—although up to 30% of patients report no problems.
Oral praziquantel remains the first-line treatment, with the introduction of the radio-opaque contrast medium Gastrografin into the duodenum via a tube the second choice: using Gastrografin ensures complete deworming—ie, discharge of the whole organism, including the scolex—as in our case. Diphyllobothriasis is typically diagnosed by detecting the cestode's ova or proglottids in the patient's faeces. However, the examination of stool samples for the ova is not routinely done in many clinics or hospitals; the detection is sometimes difficult and not definitive. Moreover, once a large part of the worm's body is excreted, the ova are undetectable for some time afterwards. Capsule endoscopy has been reported as a useful alternative for diagnosing diphyllobothriasis, but it is expensive and carries the risk of capsule retention—occurring in approximately 2% of all patients undergoing small bowel capsule endoscopy. In our patient, the abdominal ultrasound vividly showed the tapeworm moving in the intestinal fluid in the gut. And although intestinal gas may sometimes prevent visualisation of the worm, we believe that an abdominal ultrasound scan offers a practical, real-time, non-invasive way of screening for diphyllobothriasis.

A 10-year-old girl was referred to the Ophthalmology Department at Cantonal Hospital St Gallen, Switzerland, for intermittent divergent strabismus. Ophthalmologic examination revealed prominent bilateral corneal nerve fibres (figure A and B; white arrows) and multiple nodules along the eyelid margins (figure A and C; black arrows). She also had distinct facial features that included a narrow face, prominent chin, bulging lips, and nodules on the tongue and ears (appendix p 1). During planned strabismus surgery, a biopsy of one eyelid nodule was performed due to the unusual appearance of these lesions. Histological analysis revealed a neuroma, which prompted further systemic evaluation and led to the diagnosis of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B (MEN2B), an autosomal dominant tumour predisposition syndrome.
Urgent paediatric evaluation did not find biochemical evidence of phaeochromocytoma, but found elevated tumour markers calcitonin (129 ng/l; normal range <3 ng/l) and carcinoembryonic antigen (3·2 ug/l; normal range <3·2 μg/l) and a suspicious sonographic thyroid nodule (appendix p 2), which indicated a medullary thyroid carcinoma. The diagnosis of MEN2B was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, revealing the de novo, pathological, heterozygous RET proto-oncogene mutation Met918Thr. This is a high risk mutation that has an 100% incidence for aggressive early-onset medullary thyroid carcinoma, and prophylactic thyroidectomy is recommended after diagnosis. The patient did not show signs of dry eyes in infancy or throughout childhood, and did not have any dental, urinary, or skeletal atypicalities. Moreover, her growth variables and cognitive development (intelligent quotient) were within the normal range.
Our patient underwent a complete thyroidectomy with central lymphadenectomy, which would have been performed in the first year of life if the RET mutation had been known about. Histological analysis confirmed medullary thyroid carcinoma with lymphogenic metastasis and focal angioinvasion. After surgery, her carcinoembryonic antigen levels normalised (below 3·2 μg/l), but her calcitonin levels only dropped by 50% (63 ng/l). A cervicolateral lymphadenectomy was performed 3 months later, and incomplete biochemical control was reached with a minimum calcitonin level of 4·6 ng/l. One year later, the patient is healthy and taking daily L-thyroxine 112 ug, with no long-term surgical complications.
An intestinal endoscopy was given due to long-standing flatulence and revealed ganglioneuromatosis, which will be observed clinically. Follow up also includes regular screening for phaeochromocytoma and medullary thyroid carcinoma metastases.
Prominent corneal nerves and the development of multiple mucosal and cutaneous nodules in childhood should raise suspicion of MEN2B, warranting urgent investigation to manage early-onset medullary thyroid carcinoma.

The patient said the pain started 3 days after he had condomless penetrative and receptive anal intercourse with a man; he then developed a fever, chills, and inguinal lymphadenopathy. input: Various cases in professional sports have brought the matter of doping—the use of performance-enhancing drugs—to the attention of the broad public. Here, we present a case of doping in a 21-year-old amateur bodybuilder. The man presented to our clinic feeling generally unwell. He was subfebrile and had massive, deep ulcerations, abscesses, and pustules located on his chest and upper back (figure). Persistent questioning revealed a history of continuous abuse of anabolic-androgenic steroids (testosterone enantate 250 mg plus metandienona 30 mg twice weekly), which was consistent with the diagnosis of a severe acne conglobata that was anabolic-androgenic steroid induced. Additional investigations showed a substantial impairment in sperm concentration and reduced testicular volume. Skin lesions showed rapid improvement after discontinuation of anabolic-androgenic steroid abuse and with antiseptic and antibiotic therapy. However, the extensive scarring is likely to remain with the young man for the rest of his life.

A 62-year-old woman with a medical history of hypertension and well-controlled diabetes mellitus type 2 was found unresponsive on the floor at home by her family. Her family reported that the day before admission she had appeared more tired and weak with altered mental status, but before that had been in normal health. On examination she had Glasgow coma score (GCS) of 3, a temperature of 39·4°C, tachycardia, and systolic blood pressure ranging from 170–200 mm Hg. She had weakness in her legs bilaterally, but review of systems was otherwise negative. In view of her low GCS score she was intubated for airway protection, and required vasopressors because she was hypotensive, febrile, tachycardic, and not responding to fluids. A CT scan of her head and subsequent MRI showed profound hydrocephalus (figure).An external ventricular drain was fitted for possible acute hydrocephalus, but her intracranial pressure was found to be 5 mm Hg (normal 5–15 mm Hg) and remained 5–10 mm Hg so the drain was removed 2 days later. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tests were normal. We made a diagnosis of sepsis secondary to pneumonia, on the basis of chest radiographs showing consolidation and blood culture results, as the cause of her altered mental status, which returned to normal after treatment with antibiotics. She was discharged to a rehabilitation facility and has now returned to her normal baseline. In view of her previously normal medical history the clinical team decided her hydrocephalus had probably been present since birth.
This case shows the brain's ability to maintain normal mental status and function in spite of profound chronic hydrocephalus. In contrast to normal pressure hydrocephalus, compensated hydrocephalus can be asymptomatic until an external insult, such as an infection as in this case, and can lead to syncope or even sudden death. Compensated hydrocephalus, also known as hydrocephalus ex vacuo, is a form of communicating hydrocephalus—ie, one that does not obstruct the flow of CSF. Compensated hydrocephalus is usually seen in elderly people as the result of brain volume loss due to ageing or a disorder that causes the brain to shrink, such as Alzheimer's disease, leukodystrophy, or encephalomalacia resulting from focal damage caused by a stroke or traumatic brain injury. Clinicians should be aware of this condition that might be found incidentally on imaging in asymptomatic patients. Unless dictated by clinical examination, as in this case, additional work-up is not necessary.

A 36-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of sore throat and progressive dysphagia. She had no history of any serious illness, chronic cough, or other chest symptoms. She had been taking various courses of antibiotics, including amoxicillin and a combination of amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid, and paracetamol for sore throat without any relief.
General physical examination revealed normal findings, but oral examination found an enlarged right palatine tonsil with central ulceration (figure). Fiberoptic nasopharyngoscopy did not identify any pharyngeal or laryngeal lesions, but a firm 3 cm right-upper cervical lymphadenopathy was detected during clinical examination. CT scan images showed a tumoural right tonsil infiltrating the base of the tongue and associated with necrotic cervical lymph nodes. A thoracic CT scan did not detect any pulmonary or nodal disease.A biopsy sample was taken from the ulcerated area of the right tonsil. Histopathological examination revealed granulomas and caseous necrosis consistent with tuberculosis. The culture from the tonsil biopsy sample and lymphadenopathy puncture was positive for acid-fast bacilli, suggesting the presence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Serological tests for HIV and syphilis were negative. The tuberculin skin test was positive, with a 3 cm bulla.
The patient was started on a daily oral multidrug therapy consisting of 2 months of isoniazid (5 mg/kg), rifampicin (10 mg/kg), pyrazinamide (25 mg/kg), and ethambutol (15 mg/kg), followed by 4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin at the same doses. Treatment resulted in rapid resolution of the sore throat and progressive regression of the cervical lymph node.
Isolated tuberculosis of the tonsil in the absence of active pulmonary tuberculosis is an exceptional clinical entity and often mistaken for a malignancy. This infection is acquired by inhalation of tubercle bacilli, and commonly presents with sore throat and cervical lymphadenopathy.
Differential diagnosis of pharyngeal tuberculosis includes traumatic ulcers, haematological disorders, actinomycosis, syphilis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and cancer. Diagnosis is based on histopathological findings and on the identification of tubercle bacilli.

A 69-year-old woman was admitted to our ward with fever and respiratory failure. 3 weeks earlier she had been treated with ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection, caused by Escherichia coli; she had a history of diabetes.On examination she was oriented in time, place, and person; her blood pressure was 130/70 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats per min, respiratory rate was 15 breaths per min, temperature 37·1°C, and oxygen saturation 94%. She had harsh vesicular breath sounds that were diffusely reduced with no added noises.
Laboratory investigations showed the patient's white blood cell count was 15·2 × 109 per L (normal 3·84–10·0), neutrophils 83%, C-reactive protein concentration (CRP)was 9·97 mg/dL (normal <0·5), procalcitonin concentration was 0·5 ng/mL (normal 0–0·5), and D-dimer concentration was 3490 ng/mL (normal 0–500).
A CT angiogram showed bronchopneumonia and bilateral pulmonary nodules—raising the suspicion of metastases (figure). A full-body CT, with contrast medium, showed thrombosis of the left renal vein and homolateral thickening of calyces’ walls and renal pelvis. Urine cytology was negative for any urothelial malignancy. Our working diagnosis at this stage was septic emboli from a nephritic focus. However, despite 8 days of ceftazidime and clarithromycin, and enoxaparin, the patient's condition worsened. Given the working diagnosis, we did a transoesophageal echocardiography and broncho-alveolar lavage. The echocardiogram showed some thickening of the free margin of the aortic valve cusps with normal function; the mitral valve flaps showed some thickening with mild insufficiency. A set of blood and urine cultures were done which were negative for any infection and malignancy. At this stage, we suspected the patient had an autoimmune disease and we decided to start methylprednisolone empirically. The patient's condition improved, and she was able to go home 11 days later. At follow-up 1 month later, she reported rusty sputum, a persistent cough, and back pain; investigations showed a raised white blood cell count of 16·76 × 109 per L, neutrophils 90·5%, CRP concentration 15·2 mg/dL. An autoimmune screen showed no atypical results. An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT of the chest showed three excavated lesions with hypermetabolic perimeters; we suspected either an inflammatory or an infectious process and the patient was readmitted.
A CT scan of the chest confirmed the pulmonary lesions and indicated that they were probably septic emboli (figure); arterial blood gas analysis indicated respiratory failure. Cultures of blood, urine, broncho-alveolar lavage fluid, and a sample of a lung biopsy showed non-extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing strain E coli, mucoid phenotype, characterised by a thick polysaccharide wall impervious to antibiotics. We started the patient on voriconazole and—according to culture antibiogram—ceftazidime and ampicillin combined with sulbactam. The methylprednisolone was gradually reduced over the next 8 weeks; the two largest chest lesions were drained. After 38 days of antibiotic treatment, the patient's symptoms had improved; she was no longer in respiratory failure and cultures of blood, urine, broncho-alveolar lavage fluid, and pleural fluid were negative. A chest CT scan showed a decrease in the size of the pulmonary lesions.
Although rare, an E coli urinary tract infection can spread to the lungs, causing a pneumonia. Mucoid phenotypes have been shown to be associated with advanced disease states—specifically in Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii infections. A mucoid phenotype has never been shown to underlie the development of invasive disease after an E coli urinary tract infection, but such a possibility cannot be ruled out.

input: A 27-year-old man was admitted to Shinshu University hospital with overt jaundice and ascites 8 days after long exposure to sunlight. He had been diagnosed with erythropoietic protoporphyria 6 years previously and was prescribed cimetidine (800 mg/day) at that time to downregulate Δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase-2 activity and reduce free protoporphyrin concentrations. Lactulose was also given to promote defaecation and to limit re-absorption of protoporphyrin, although its role in the management of erythropoietic protoporphyria has not been established. The patient was observed to have hallucinations, prolonged prothrombin time (international normalised ratio of 2·1), and elevation of serum total bilirubin (9·5 mg/dL) after admission; as a result, we diagnosed acute liver failure and did two rounds of plasma exchange. Acute viral hepatitis, Wilson's disease, and autoimmune hepatitis were ruled out by blood tests. His plasma looked icteric under regular white light, but turned red under ultraviolet A in the intensive care unit, suggestive of very high concentrations of porphyrins (figure, A). Ascites drained from the patient also turned red under ultraviolet A (figure, B). Erythrocyte protoporphyrin was markedly increased at the time of admission (5727 μg/dL red blood cells; compared with the normal range of 30–86 μg/dL red blood cells), which supported the diagnosis of rapid aggravation of erythropoietic protoporphyria. After two rounds of plasma exchange, the patient's hepatic function slowly recovered.Hepatopathy induced by erythropoietic protoporphyria can show fulminant aggravation. Since plasma protoporphyrin is very sensitive to light and rapidly declines during sample preparation, erythrocyte protoporphyrin measurement is recommended to detect erythropoietic protoporphyria activity. However, this measurement is uncommon and takes time to assess, which can delay accurate diagnosis. Ultraviolet A has increasingly been used in hospitals to check the quality of handwashing. When we encounter patients with acute liver failure of unknown cause, direct examination of body fluids—eg, plasma and ascites—under ultraviolet A could be a simple and useful method to screen for erythropoietic protoporphyria. Samples should therefore be protected from light when a porphyrin measurement is ordered.
output: Acute liver failure induced by erythropoietic protoporphyria

input: A 27-year-old man was admitted to Shinshu University hospital with overt jaundice and ascites 8 days after long exposure to sunlight. He had been diagnosed with erythropoietic protoporphyria 6 years previously and was prescribed cimetidine (800 mg/day) at that time to downregulate Δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase-2 activity and reduce free protoporphyrin concentrations. Lactulose was also given to promote defaecation and to limit re-absorption of protoporphyrin, although its role in the management of erythropoietic protoporphyria has not been established. The patient was observed to have hallucinations, prolonged prothrombin time (international normalised ratio of 2·1), and elevation of serum total bilirubin (9·5 mg/dL) after admission; as a result, we diagnosed acute liver failure and did two rounds of plasma exchange. Acute viral hepatitis, Wilson's disease, and autoimmune hepatitis were ruled out by blood tests. His plasma looked icteric under regular white light, but turned red under ultraviolet A in the intensive care unit, suggestive of very high concentrations of porphyrins (figure, A). Ascites drained from the patient also turned red under ultraviolet A (figure, B). Erythrocyte protoporphyrin was markedly increased at the time of admission (5727 μg/dL red blood cells; compared with the normal range of 30–86 μg/dL red blood cells), which supported the diagnosis of rapid aggravation of erythropoietic protoporphyria. After two rounds of plasma exchange, the patient's hepatic function slowly recovered.Hepatopathy induced by erythropoietic protoporphyria can show fulminant aggravation. Since plasma protoporphyrin is very sensitive to light and rapidly declines during sample preparation, erythrocyte protoporphyrin measurement is recommended to detect erythropoietic protoporphyria activity. However, this measurement is uncommon and takes time to assess, which can delay accurate diagnosis. Ultraviolet A has increasingly been used in hospitals to check the quality of handwashing. Samples should therefore be protected from light when a porphyrin measurement is ordered.

A 47-year-old woman presented to our institution with a 1-month history of swelling and a painless skin plaque on her left breast. 6 years earlier, the patient had been treated for luminal A invasive ductal carcinoma in the superomedial quadrant of the left breast; she had neoadjuvant chemotherapy, breast-conserving surgery, radiation therapy—a whole breast dose of 50 Gy plus a 10 Gy boost to the tumour bed—and oral tamoxifen. The patient had been found to have no recurrence of the tumour at any subsequent follow-up appointments. She had no history of breast trauma or lymphoedema.
On physical examination, we found the patient was generally well; she had a 1 cm purple plaque on the inferolateral quadrant of her left breast, approximately 1·5 cm from the areola (figure).Breast ultrasound examination showed skin thickening, subcutaneous oedema, and a predominantly hypoechoic nonmass finding in the inferomedial quadrant of the left breast with irregular borders, regional distribution, and central hypervascularity on power Doppler (figure). Diagnostic mammogram showed a developing asymmetry in the inferomedial quadrant of the left breast, as well as skin thickening and parenchymal oedema that were more pronounced compared with her previous mammograms (figure). Histological examination of a sample obtained by ultrasound-guided core biopsy showed solid epithelial proliferation with marked cellular atypia—initially deemed suspicious for recurrence of the carcinoma (figure). Immunohistochemistry results were positive for CD31, ERG, and D2-40 on most target cells and for CD34 in subgroups of target cells (appendix), along with very high Ki67 expression (90% of target cells), findings compatible with post radiation angiosarcoma.
On post-biopsy follow-up—54 days after the first ultrasound examination—the previously 1 cm wide skin lesion had progressed to a 4 cm irregular violaceous plaque with subtle areas of yellowish discoloration on adjacent skin (figure). On ultrasound examination, the lesion appeared as an irregular, hypoechoic mass with thick echogenic rind; the high central vascularity on power Doppler remained visible (appendix).
The findings, diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment options were discussed with the patient and together the decision was made to proceed to mastectomy of the affected breast.
On the day of mastectomy—60 days after the first ultrasound examination—additional satellite lesions and morphological changes in the nipple-areola complex were seen adjacent to the irregular violaceous plaque, with progression of the areas of yellowish skin discoloration (figure).
Histopathological analysis of a sample of the surgical specimen, which measured 9·0 cm × 7·0 cm X 6·0 cm and invaded the nipple, dermis, and parenchymal breast tissue, confirmed the diagnosis of post-radiation angiosarcoma. CT scans of the patient's head, chest, and abdomen showed no evidence of metastases.
The patient made an uneventful recovery from the operation and was allowed home 24 h later. At follow-up 3 months after the mastectomy, a new 1 cm violaceous skin lesion surrounded by a yellowish halo appeared in the mastectomy scar (appendix); recurrence of the post-radiation angiosarcoma was confirmed by histopathological analysis of a sample obtained from surgically excised tissue.
Post-radiation angiosarcoma is an uncommon aggressive complication of radiotherapy for breast cancer, with a median latency period of 5–6 years. About one in every 1000 patients treated with radiotherapy for breast cancer may be at risk of developing the condition, and global incidence is expected to rise as the number of patients undergoing breast-preserving surgery plus radiotherapy increases. Typically, the tumour arises within the skin and subcutaneous tissues previously included in the irradiation field—this is unlike primary breast angiosarcomas which usually originate deep within the breast parenchyma. Patients with post-radiation angiosarcomas may develop breast swelling, erythema, skin thickening, and painless erythematous patches or plaques in previously irradiated areas, as well as areas of yellowish discoloration on circumjacent skin which is related to haemoglobin degradation products. Lymph node involvement is uncommon. Imaging findings, when present, are often non-specific and include skin and trabecular thickening, developing asymmetry on mammogram, and solid, irregular masses on breast ultrasound examination.
Surgical excision with negative margins is considered the standard treatment; prognosis is poor even with complete tumour resection, with 5-year survival rates of about 40%.
