The patient had been found to have no recurrence of the tumour at any subsequent follow-up appointments. She had no history of breast trauma or lymphoedema.
On physical examination, we found the patient was generally well; she had a 1 cm purple plaque on the inferolateral quadrant of her left breast, approximately 1·5 cm from the areola (figure).Breast ultrasound examination showed skin thickening, subcutaneous oedema, and a predominantly hypoechoic nonmass finding in the inferomedial quadrant of the left breast with irregular borders, regional distribution, and central hypervascularity on power Doppler (figure). Diagnostic mammogram showed a developing asymmetry in the inferomedial quadrant of the left breast, as well as skin thickening and parenchymal oedema that were more pronounced compared with her previous mammograms (figure). Histological examination of a sample obtained by ultrasound-guided core biopsy showed solid epithelial proliferation with marked cellular atypia—initially deemed suspicious for recurrence of the carcinoma (figure). Immunohistochemistry results were positive for CD31, ERG, and D2-40 on most target cells and for CD34 in subgroups of target cells (appendix), along with very high Ki67 expression (90% of target cells), findings compatible with post radiation angiosarcoma.
On post-biopsy follow-up—54 days after the first ultrasound examination—the previously 1 cm wide skin lesion had progressed to a 4 cm irregular violaceous plaque with subtle areas of yellowish discoloration on adjacent skin (figure). On ultrasound examination, the lesion appeared as an irregular, hypoechoic mass with thick echogenic rind; the high central vascularity on power Doppler remained visible (appendix).
The findings, diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment options were discussed with the patient and together the decision was made to proceed to mastectomy of the affected breast.
On the day of mastectomy—60 days after the first ultrasound examination—additional satellite lesions and morphological changes in the nipple-areola complex were seen adjacent to the irregular violaceous plaque, with progression of the areas of yellowish skin discoloration (figure).
Histopathological analysis of a sample of the surgical specimen, which measured 9·0 cm × 7·0 cm X 6·0 cm and invaded the nipple, dermis, and parenchymal breast tissue, confirmed the diagnosis of post-radiation angiosarcoma. CT scans of the patient's head, chest, and abdomen showed no evidence of metastases.
The patient made an uneventful recovery from the operation and was allowed home 24 h later. At follow-up 3 months after the mastectomy, a new 1 cm violaceous skin lesion surrounded by a yellowish halo appeared in the mastectomy scar (appendix); recurrence of the post-radiation angiosarcoma was confirmed by histopathological analysis of a sample obtained from surgically excised tissue.
Post-radiation angiosarcoma is an uncommon aggressive complication of radiotherapy for breast cancer, with a median latency period of 5–6 years. About one in every 1000 patients treated with radiotherapy for breast cancer may be at risk of developing the condition, and global incidence is expected to rise as the number of patients undergoing breast-preserving surgery plus radiotherapy increases. Typically, the tumour arises within the skin and subcutaneous tissues previously included in the irradiation field—this is unlike primary breast angiosarcomas which usually originate deep within the breast parenchyma. Patients with post-radiation angiosarcomas may develop breast swelling, erythema, skin thickening, and painless erythematous patches or plaques in previously irradiated areas, as well as areas of yellowish discoloration on circumjacent skin which is related to haemoglobin degradation products. Lymph node involvement is uncommon. Imaging findings, when present, are often non-specific and include skin and trabecular thickening, developing asymmetry on mammogram, and solid, irregular masses on breast ultrasound examination.
Surgical excision with negative margins is considered the standard treatment; prognosis is poor even with complete tumour resection, with 5-year survival rates of about 40%.

input: An erythematous, non-scaling indurated plaque appeared on the forehead of a 34-year-old white man. Over a period of approxinately 1 year, it extended onto the scalp, resulting in a linear non-scarring alopecia, seemingly following the lines of Blaschko (figure). Initial therapy with topical glucocorticoids failed, and a skin biopsy was taken. Histopathological examination showed a normal epidermis, accumulation of mucin in the dermis, and lymphocytic panniculitis (figure). Linear cutaneous lupus profundus was diagnosed. Laboratory tests were normal, apart from positive antinuclear antibodies (1:200) and slightly increased C3d complement. Under oral hydroxychloroquine therapy the disorder resolved within 12 weeks, followed by complete regrowth of hair. No relapse occurred during 1 year of maintenance treatment. The face and scalp are predilection sites of cutaneous lupus erythematosus profundus. This can result in an alopecia areata-like clinical picture or non-scarring linear alopecia, which has thus far mainly been reported in east Asians.

A 55-year-old woman with a 29-pack-year history of smoking presented with a 1.5-year history of pain in her fingers, wrists, hips, knees, and ankles. On physical examination, clubbing and slight thickening of the skin of the fingers and toes were noted (left image, right foot). There was mild tenderness on palpation of all her affected joints but no erythema or swelling. A cardiopulmonary examination was normal. Radiographs of the forearms, hands, femurs, tibia, and feet showed symmetric periostitis of the tubular bones (right image, right ulna and radius, arrows). Which of the following is the most appropriate next test in her evaluation?
output:
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest

The clinical presentation of digital clubbing, symmetric periostitis of tubular bones, and arthralgia in a patient with significant smoking history is classic for **Hypertrophic Osteoarthropathy (HOA)**, also known as **Pachydermoperiostosis** when primary, or secondary HOA when associated with underlying disease.

Given her 29-pack-year smoking history, the most important next step is **chest CT** to evaluate for an underlying **lung malignancy**, particularly **non-small cell lung cancer**, which is the most common cause of secondary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy.

A 32-year-old woman presented to our department for an evaluation of possible cardiac manifestations of tuberous sclerosis complex.The patient had been diagnosed with tuberous sclerosis complex in her early childhood when she started having daily focal seizures. Genetic analysis when she was 16 years old confirmed a TSC1 (Q783X) de novo mutation. During adolescence, she had continued anticonvulsant medication—a combination of carbamazepine and valproate—and remained free from further seizures. However, after the initial diagnosis, regular follow-up imaging was not performed.
1 year before the assessment in our department, the patient was diagnosed with a papillary thyroid carcinoma for which she underwent a right hemi-thyroidectomy with lymphadenectomy. Following the operation, she reported an increase of the focal seizures—thought to be provoked by stress. A neurological examination, at the time, was unremarkable and no dermatological signs specific to tuberous sclerosis complex were found—such as hypomelanotic macules, or facial angiofibromas. Further, because of the lack of regular follow-up over the previous 17 years, extensive additional investigations were requested by the neurologist who saw her: brain MRI showed typical cortical tubers (figure) and a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma adjacent to the foramen of Monro—without any signs of obstruction (figure). Compared to an MRI from 17 years earlier, the giant cell astrocytoma showed no significant increase in size. Abdominal MRI showed cyst-like lesions in the patient's left kidney, which was thought to be a fat-poor angiomyolipoma (figure).
For completeness and because screening for the cardiac manifestations of tuberous sclerosis complex had not been done previously, the patient was referred to our department: cardiac MRI showed myocardial fatty foci (figure) with no cardiac rhabdomyomas. A 43-year-old man who developed numbness and impaired fine motor skills in his left arm lasting approximately 10 min while chanting during a football match, attended our emergency room. The patient, who was visiting Germany for the UEFA European Football Championship, explained that the problems started at the end of the first half. He said he had been chanting continuously during the game. Despite complete resolution of the symptoms, he was concerned enough to seek help, and at half-time he came to our hospital by ambulance. We decided to admit him to our stroke unit for further investigations. He had no medical history; he said he had consumed a moderate amount of alcohol. He was a non-smoker.
On examination the patient was generally fit and well; his pulse was 92 beats per min, blood pressure was 140/90 mm Hg, and his oxygen saturation was 94%. Physical examination found no abnormalities.
Laboratory investigations showed a mildly elevated LDL cholesterol (142 mg/dL; normal range <115). A coagulopathy was excluded: clotting factors II and V were within normal range, tests for antiphospholipid syndrome were negative, antithrombin III activity was in normal range, and protein S and C levels were normal. The patient's homocysteine serum concentration was slightly elevated (15 μmol/L; typical range 3·7–13·9), genotyping found the wild-type variant of the MTHFR gene.
MRI showed a small acute embolic ischaemic lesion in the postcentral gyrus of the right hemisphere (figure 1); doppler and duplex sonography of extracranial and intracranial vessels and multimodal imaging—including magnetic resonance angiography—ruled out any atherosclerotic plaques, dissection, or vasculitis (figure 1). Electrocardiogram monitoring during more than 72 h of telemetry found no abnormalities.
Transoesophageal echocardiography showed a patent foramen ovale (PFO) with spontaneous passage of bubbles and accentuation with Valsalva manoeuvre; no septal aneurysm was seen (figure 2). Atrial size and valvular structures were normal, and no intracardiac thrombi were seen. The Risk of Paradoxical Embolism score was 8—indicating an 84% chance that a stroke is PFO-related. Venous ultrasound imaging showed no deep vein thromboses in the legs, pelvis, or vena cava. The patient left the hospital after 3 days with a prescription for an antithrombotic treatment. He took a flight back to his home country a day later.
The role of a PFO in young patients with acute ischaemic stroke has been the subject of much debate: several studies have shown PFO closure may reduce risk of recurrent strokes in young patients with cryptogenic stroke. A possible pathophysiologic mechanism is paradoxical embolism through the PFO facilitated by intrathoracic pressure elevation during pressing or coughing. We hypothesise that a paradoxical embolism in our patient was possibly provoked by continuous chanting—a provoking factor not previously reported—and we therefore advised him to avoid intensive chanting until interventional PFO closure.

A 55-year-old man was admitted to the emergency department with a recurrence of chest pain, dyspnoea, cephalea, and pallor; he reported that he had been having repeated episodes of the symptoms for the past 24 h.
6 months before, the patient had a subacute ischaemic stroke of the left posterior circulation attributed to significant atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease; he had a medical history of type 2 diabetes and degenerative disease of the lumbar spine. He was prescribed low-dose aspirin, atorvastatin, and metformin.
On examination he was unwell and distressed; he had cold and clammy skin, and marked hypertension with a blood pressure of 250/140 mm Hg and pulse rate of 88 beats per min and oxygen saturation of 95%.
Laboratory investigations showed a leukocyte count of 25·3 × 109 per L (reference range 3·9–10·2), haemoglobin concentration of 20·2 g/dL (reference range 13·5–17·2), creatinine concentration 2·4 mg/dL (reference range 0·7–1·2), an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 29 mL/min, blood glucose concentration 214 mg/dL (reference range fasting <100), D-dimer concentration of 3·4 μg/mL (reference range <0·5), lactate concentration 6·5 mmol/L (reference range 0·5–1·6), and pH 7·25 (reference range 7·34–7·45) with a base excess of –7 mmol/L (reference range 2–3).
Invasive monitoring of the patient's blood pressure and heart rhythm—using a peripheral catheter in the radial artery—showed severe cyclic variation with reciprocal changes of the heart rate at intervals of 15 min: with systolic pressure ranging between 45 mm Hg and 310 mm Hg; diastolic pressure ranging between 35 mm Hg and 160 mm Hg; and the heart rate fluctuating between 70 beats per min and 130 beats per min (figure 1; appendix).
CT angiography of the aorta showed no abnormalities—ruling out acute aortic syndromes such as acute aortic dissection, intramural haematoma, and penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer; however, a mass was seen in the centre of the right adrenal gland (figure 2). Iodine-123-labelled metaiodobenzylguanidine SPECT showed isotope uptake in the right adrenal gland, with no metastatic lesions (figure 2; appendix).
Treatment via continuous intravenous administration of urapidil und crystalloids had no significant effect on haemodynamic parameters; however, only low doses of urapidil were used since up-titration was limited by recurring symptomatic hypotension. Thereafter, phenoxybenzamine—an oral non-competitive, non-selective alpha-blocking agent—was initiated, which quickly led to sustained stabilisation of the patient's blood pressure. 4 days after admission, we added propranolol. A 26-year-old man with an 8-year history of breathlessness on exertion was referred to our hospital for assessment. Previously, he had been noted to have clubbing of his toes and a heart murmur.On examination, we found the patient to be peripherally and centrally cyanosed; he had grade 3 clubbing of his toes but not of his fingers (figure); his pulse was 82 beats per min, blood pressure was 110/72 mm Hg, and, notably, oxygen saturations were 98% in his hands and 86% in his toes while breathing room air, and he had grade 2 dyspnoea. He had a parasternal heave with a palpable second heart sound; on auscultation, the pulmonary component of the second heart sound was accentuated and closely split.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised haemoglobin concentration (20·0 g/dL; normal 13·2–16·6 in men) and haematocrit (52%; normal 38–48 for men).
An electrocardiogram showed right ventricular hypertrophy with right axis deviation; a chest x-ray showed a dilated main pulmonary artery with peripheral pruning (appendix). A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a 7 mm patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) with right-to-left shunting (appendix).
Catheterisation showed an elevated pulmonary artery pressure of 120/68 mm Hg (normal 18/8–25/15) and a mean pressure of 108 mm Hg (normal 12–16) and an indexed pulmonary vascular resistance of 20·1 Wood units per m2 (normal 1–3; figure).
Because of the supra-systemic pulmonary artery pressures, we believed surgery was not feasible and therefore started the patient on oral sildenafil and bosentan.

He was treated with phlebotomy on both occasions and his symptoms improved. At his last follow-up, he remains on sildenafil and bosentan and continues to have grade 2 dyspnoea.

A 40-year-old woman with a history of chronic pancreatitis and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease presented with fatigue, malaise, dizziness, difficulty ambulating, diarrhoea, easy bruising, and a diffuse rash involving her extremities and trunk that had been present for several days. She explained that she had limited her diet to consist mostly of bread, rice, dumplings, and the occasional egg white to reduce the symptoms she suffered from her gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. Her diet was also devoid of red meat, fish, chicken, fruits, and vegetables.On physical examination, she had extensive, non-palpable, perifollicular haemorrhages involving her extremities (figure), ecchymosis (figure), and gingival bleeding. Corkscrew hairs, visible with the unaided eye, were seen all over her skin—although they were much more apparent with dermoscopy (figure). Her laboratory results showed haemoglobin 8·3 mg/dL, haematocrit 25·2%, and a plasma vitamin C concentration of <5 μmol/L (normal range 23–50 μmol/L). Endoscopy of the upper gastrointestinal tract and colonoscopy of the lower bowel did not find a source of bleeding.
A biopsy of the skin from her right lower leg showed a corkscrew shaped profile of the hair follicle, and histopathological examination showed follicular hyperkeratosis and plugging (figure). Taken together, the clinical, laboratory, and histopathological findings were consistent with a diagnosis of scurvy. Vitamin C must be obtained from dietary sources and it is essential for hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues for the synthesis of collagen. It is also important for immune system function and iron absorption. Scurvy rarely affects adults but may be seen in some individuals with malnutrition or malabsorption. Signs and symptoms usually occur by the third month of inadequate consumption, and treatment is with vitamin C supplementation. Early diagnosis and treatment of scurvy can be life-saving, so recognition of the physical findings is important. This patient was given intravenous vitamin C followed by daily oral supplementation and her symptoms resolved within a few weeks.

A 71-year-old man with renal cell carcinoma with symptomatic bilateral lung metastases and multiple subpleural lesions started second-line cabozantinib (60 mg orally daily) after disease progression on pazopanib. After 3 months of therapy, in May, 2018, the patient presented at the emergency department and complained of a worsening of his dyspnoea, leading us to suppose that disease progression had occurred. However, a CT scan revealed an impressive volumetric reduction of the lung nodules but the onset of an apical grade 3 left pneumothorax (figure). The patient was admitted to hospital at the University Hospital of Verona (Verona, Italy) and was treated with thorax drainage with complete pneumothorax resolution and no further sequelae. Given this excellent response, cabozantinib treatment was continued. So far, the patient remains on cabozantinib treatment, with a treatment duration of 5 months. A second case of pneumothorax was observed in a 69-year-old woman with metastatic renal cell carcinoma 1 month after beginning second-line cabozantinib at a dose of 60 mg daily. The patient had one subpleural lung lesion 5 cm in size. In May, 2018, the patient presented at the emergency department with a sudden worsening of dyspnoea, which led to a diagnosis of grade 3 pneumothorax, admission to the Oncological Department of the University Hospital of Verona, and treatment with drainage of the pneumothorax, which was ipsilateral to the pulmonary metastasis. Treatment with cabozantinib was continued, with a partial response recorded at subsequent disease evaluations. Cabozantinib therapy is still ongoing in this patient 6 months since the start of treatment.Tumour necrosis—as a result of a rapid, dramatic response to cabozantinib—of subpleural lung metastases might explain the pathogenesis of the pneumothorax in both these cases. Cabozantinib is the only approved tyrosine kinase inhibitor that has been shown to increase overall survival, progression-free survival, and overall responses compared with everolimus in previously treated patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma. Only two grade 3 and one grade 4 pneumothorax were reported with cabozantinib in the pivotal METEOR phase 3 trial. Pneumothorax, potentially related to the outstanding clinical activity of cabozantinib, is therefore an adverse event that must be considered in patients with peripheral lung or pleural metastases and unexpected onset of dyspnoea.

input: A 53-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 1-month history of dizziness and episodes of hypotension during his outpatient haemodialysis sessions. In addition to end-stage renal disease, the patient had a history of a large anterior myocardial infarction and subsequent percutaneous coronary interventions with stent placement; this had resulted in an ischaemic cardiomyopathy, which had required the implantation of a left ventricular assist device 5 years before this admission. On examination, the patient had a distended jugular vein, a pulsatile liver, and prominent, pulsating facial veins (figure, video 1). An echocardiogram showed severe tricuspid regurgitation that was caused by annular dilatation and this, in turn, had resulted in malcoaptation of the valve leaflets (video 2). The patient was also noted to have significant enlargement and dysfunction of the right ventricle, as well as diastolic septal shift, indicating volume overload of the right ventricle (video 2). Ventricularisation of the right atrial pressure tracing—with C-V waves that indicated severe tricuspid regurgitation—was seen during cardiac catheterisation. Despite treatment with intravenous ionotropes, the patient's right ventricular failure worsened and, sadly, he died in a hospice, 6 weeks after he first came to see us.Right ventricular failure after left ventricular assist device implantation is unfortunately common and results in significant morbidity and mortality. It is important to be able to recognise both the common features—such as jugular vein distension and a pulsatile liver—and the rare features, such as pulsation of the facial vein, in the diagnosis of right ventricular failure with concomitant tricuspid regurgitation. Renowned Scottish cardiologist Sir James Mackenzie was one of the first physicians to publish a detailed description of pulsation of the facial vein associated with tricuspid regurgitation, in 1892, and the phenomenon has been the subject of much debate since then. Transmission of atrial pulsations to the facial vein are usually prevented by venous valves present around the lower border of the mandible and in the jugular venous system. However, incompetence—and even complete absence—of these valves has been reported in patients with longstanding tricuspid regurgitation and elevated central venous pressure.

However, a CT scan revealed an impressive volumetric reduction of the lung nodules but the onset of an apical grade 3 left pneumothorax (figure). The patient was admitted to hospital at the University Hospital of Verona (Verona, Italy) and was treated with thorax drainage with complete pneumothorax resolution and no further sequelae. Given this excellent response, cabozantinib treatment was continued. So far, the patient remains on cabozantinib treatment, with a treatment duration of 5 months. A second case of pneumothorax was observed in a 69-year-old woman with metastatic renal cell carcinoma 1 month after beginning second-line cabozantinib at a dose of 60 mg daily. The patient had one subpleural lung lesion 5 cm in size. In May, 2018, the patient presented at the emergency department with a sudden worsening of dyspnoea, which led to a diagnosis of grade 3 pneumothorax, admission to the Oncological Department of the University Hospital of Verona, and treatment with drainage of the pneumothorax, which was ipsilateral to the pulmonary metastasis. Treatment with cabozantinib was continued, with a partial response recorded at subsequent disease evaluations. Cabozantinib therapy is still ongoing in this patient 6 months since the start of treatment.Tumour necrosis—as a result of a rapid, dramatic response to cabozantinib—of subpleural lung metastases might explain the pathogenesis of the pneumothorax in both these cases. Cabozantinib is the only approved tyrosine kinase inhibitor that has been shown to increase overall survival, progression-free survival, and overall responses compared with everolimus in previously treated patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma. Only two grade 3 and one grade 4 pneumothorax were reported with cabozantinib in the pivotal METEOR phase 3 trial. Pneumothorax, potentially related to the outstanding clinical activity of cabozantinib, is therefore an adverse event that must be considered in patients with peripheral lung or pleural metastases and unexpected onset of dyspnoea.

input: A 53-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 1-month history of dizziness and episodes of hypotension during his outpatient haemodialysis sessions. In addition to end-stage renal disease, the patient had a history of a large anterior myocardial infarction and subsequent percutaneous coronary interventions with stent placement; this had resulted in an ischaemic cardiomyopathy, which had required the implantation of a left ventricular assist device 5 years before this admission. On examination, the patient had a distended jugular vein, a pulsatile liver, and prominent, pulsating facial veins (figure, video 1). An echocardiogram showed severe tricuspid regurgitation that was caused by annular dilatation and this, in turn, had resulted in malcoaptation of the valve leaflets (video 2). The patient was also noted to have significant enlargement and dysfunction of the right ventricle, as well as diastolic septal shift, indicating volume overload of the right ventricle (video 2). Ventricularisation of the right atrial pressure tracing—with C-V waves that indicated severe tricuspid regurgitation—was seen during cardiac catheterisation. Despite treatment with intravenous ionotropes, the patient's right ventricular failure worsened and, sadly, he died in a hospice, 6 weeks after he first came to see us.Right ventricular failure after left ventricular assist device implantation is unfortunately common and results in significant morbidity and mortality. It is important to be able to recognise both the common features—such as jugular vein distension and a pulsatile liver—and the rare features, such as pulsation of the facial vein, in the diagnosis of right ventricular failure with concomitant tricuspid regurgitation. Renowned Scottish cardiologist Sir James Mackenzie was one of the first physicians to publish a detailed description of pulsation of the facial vein associated with tricuspid regurgitation, in 1892, and the phenomenon has been the subject of much debate since then. Transmission of atrial pulsations to the facial vein are usually prevented by venous valves present around the lower border of the mandible and in the jugular venous system. However, incompetence—and even complete absence—of these valves has been reported in patients with longstanding tricuspid regurgitation and elevated central venous pressure.
output: Superior vena cava syndrome with severe tricuspid regurgitation

input: A 48-year-old man presented with a 2 day history of fever, headache, chills, neck stiffness, and nausea and vomiting. He had a history of two episodes of viral meningitis, which occurred 30 and 13 years before this presentation. An examination confirmed meningism without focal neurological deficits. Results of CSF tests showed protein concentration of 120 mg/dL (normal 12–60 mg/dL), normal glucose concentration, red blood cells 26 cells/μL, and white blood cells 327 cells/μL (10% neutrophils, 84% lymphocytes, 6% monocytes). CSF Gram stain and cultures were negative. Diff-Quik stain of CSF showed many large activated monocytes with several deep nuclear clefts visible as so-called cloverleaf nucleus (green arrowhead, figure A), footprint-shaped nucleus (white arrowhead, figure B), and bean-shaped nucleus (green arrow, figure C), with a background of normal monocytes (black arrowheads, figure A, B) and lymphocytes (black arrows, figure A, B). The features of these activated monocytes were compatible with those of Mollaret's cells, and CSF herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV2) PCR assay was positive. Large degenerated monocytes were present as ghost cells (asterisks, figure B), observed in the slide background. A diagnosis of Mollaret's meningitis was made. The patient was discharged without antimicrobial therapy and recovered completely.Mollaret's meningitis was first described by the French neurologist Pierre Mollaret in 1944. The disease is characterised by recurrent (at least three episodes), benign (no long-term sequelae) and brief (2–5 day) episodes of aseptic lymphocytic meningitis, alternating with symptom-free interval, mostly caused by HSV2 infection. The disease is usually self-limited, and antiviral therapy is routinely not recommended. It is therefore also known as recurrent benign lymphocytic meningitis. Typically, results of CSF studies show hypercellularity and predominantly lymphocytic pleocytosis with positive HSV2 DNA by PCR assay. Cellular cytomorphological features of CSF characteristically show diagnostic Mollaret's cells, which are multiple activated large monocytes with deep nuclear clefts giving rise to various convoluted, eye-catching shapes of nuclei, such as cloverleaf, bean, and footprint patterns. Usually degenerated monocytes known as ghost cells are present, scattered at the background of the slide. Recognition of these cells in the CSF is crucial for a timely and accurate diagnosis because it could prevent extensive and costly diagnostic studies and antimicrobial therapies.

A 40-year-old-woman presented to our outpatient clinic with a 6-month history of pain in her throat and a feeling that she had a foreign body in the submandibular region. She said the pain was pricking, intermittent, bilateral, non-radiating, aggravated by eating solid food, and moderate to severe in intensity. She reported no history of trauma or previous operations—specifically a tonsillectomy. The patient was previously fit and well and had no medical history.At examination, on bimanual palpation—tolerated by the patient without the use of any anaesthetic spray—we found tender bony prominences in both tonsillar fossa; bilateral grade 1 tonsillar hypertrophy was also present. We found no other physical abnormalities and all laboratory investigations were normal. CT showed bilaterally elongated styloid processes; with three-dimensional reconstruction the abnormalities were clearly seen, and the enlarged styloid processes measured—3·9 cm on the left side and 3·5 cm on the right side (reference range 2·5–3 cm; figure).
Initially, we decided to treat the patient conservatively with analgesics and neuropathic pain medications; this had no effect. We then carried out a bilateral transoral tonsillectomy with styloidectomy; both the elongated styloid processes were visualised during surgery and about 1 cm and 2 cm of the elongated styloid processes were resected from right and left sides respectively, bringing their lengths down to within the reference range.
Notably, the foreign body sensation resolved following surgery. At 3 months' follow-up, the patient was symptom-free.
Eagle syndrome, also known as styloid or stylohyoid syndrome, is a very rare entity which was first described in 1937. Watt Weems Eagle, born in Statesville, North Carolina, was the first chief of the ear, nose and throat division at Duke Medical Center. Classically, the syndrome is characterised by orofacial pain, dysphagia, and the sensation of a foreign body in the throat. The condition is usually seen in women older than 30 years and can be confused with a wide array of head and neck disorders—including trigeminal neuralgia, glossopharyngeal neuralgia, temporal arteritis, migraine, and cervical arthritis—hence its presentation to dentists, neurologists, and otolaryngologists. The exact pathophysiology behind this syndrome is still unknown. However, it is associated with a history of neck trauma, tonsillectomy, and the presence of an arcuate foramen. Most cases can be managed conservatively but surgery may be indicated in unresponsive cases (video).

Given the late gestational age of the fetus, amniocentesis was deferred and, on discussion with the mother, it was decided to deliver the baby; an uncomplicated elective caesarean section delivered, at 38 weeks’ gestational age, a 3410 g neonate (41st percentile for gestational age). Apgar scores were 8 and 9 (typical range: between 7 and 10). Maternal and fetal cord blood samples were collected and sent to a toxoplasmosis reference laboratory. Results confirmed maternal toxoplasmosis: T gondii IgG Sabin-Feldman dye test positive 1:8000 (normal <1:16), low IgG avidity testing, T gondii IgM ELISA positive 10·0 (normal <2·0), AC/HS 400/400, IgA ELISA positive, and IgE ELISA positive, indicating a diagnosis of an acute infection with T gondii acquired during the third trimester of pregnancy.
Examination of the placenta was notable for chronic villous inflammation with multiple cysts identified within the chorionic villi and membranes with positive immunohistochemical stains for T gondii.

Neonatal brain MRIs showed severe dilatation bilaterally of the lateral and third ventricules, cortical thinning, aqueductal stenosis, and bilateral periventricular and basal ganglia calcifications. Ocular involvement was also noted with bilateral peripheral retinal lesions and vitritis. The infant was admitted to our neonatal intensive care unit for 45 days receiving pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine with folinic acid, steroids, supportive measures, and feeding therapy. Due to symptomatic hydrocephalus, a ventriculoperitoneal shunt was put in place after 35 days of life.
At follow-up 6 months later, the infant was recovering well, still on antiparasitic therapy with the ventriculoperitoneal shunt in place; he was meeting his milestones appropriately, although there was a concern for congenital palsy of the right upper arm.

A 77-year-old man presented to our neurology clinic reporting short episodes of unsteadiness followed by loss of consciousness brought on by standing from a sitting position. The problem had been present for 2 weeks and had led to frequent falls. He had a history of hypertension—treated with amlodipine, atenolol, and perindopril—and hypercholesterolaemia—treated with ezetimibe. He was a non-smoker.A neurological examination was unremarkable. A working diagnosis of orthostatic hypotension was made, and the perindopril was stopped.
3 days later, the patient returned, reporting difficulties speaking and more severe gait problems. On examination, he was mildly dysarthric, with a broad-based gait, and impaired tandem walking.
A CT scan showed subacute ischaemia in the left cerebellar hemisphere. We diagnosed a cerebellar infarction and started the patient on aspirin.
Diffusion-weighted MRI showed ischaemic foci in both cerebellar hemispheres (figure) and the right occipital lobe; there was contrast enhancement of the vessels walls of both vertebral arteries, where MR angiography also demonstrated luminal narrowing (figure; appendix). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 23mm/h and the serum C-reactive protein concentration was 8 mg/L; all specific autoantibody tests were negative.
A duplex ultrasound of the vertebral arteries showed luminal narrowing with elevated flow velocities of >300 cm/s (normal <75) and longitudinal, hypoechogenic vessel wall thickening. Axial imaging showed a concentric, hypoechogenic signal—the so-called halo sign—in the vertebral artery (figure). Ultrasonography of the right temporal artery also showed a bilateral halo sign (appendix).
Upon discussion of the results with the patient, he reported that he had previously experienced jaw claudication and tenderness over the temporal artery 2 years earlier; at the time he had been treated with prednisone.
A biopsy of the right temporal artery established a diagnosis of giant-cell arteritis (GCA; appendix). Corticosteroid therapy was started, and 1 week later the patient reported improvement of his symptoms.
GCA can present in a wide variety of ways; the typical symptoms are headache, claudication of the jaw and tongue, loss of vision in one eye, fever, myalgia, weight loss, anorexia, and fatigue. Rarely, GCA presents with symptoms of a posterior circulation stroke because of vertebral artery involvement. Distinguishing GCA from other vessel wall abnormalities on duplex ultrasound is key: atherosclerosis or dissection—which can be similarly hypoechogenic—are usually eccentric rather than concentric. As vertebral artery imaging is routine in the evaluation of large vessel disease after a stroke, recognition of the halo sign—even in the absence of systemic inflammatory markers—should raise the suspicion of GCA (video).

output: Giant cell arteritis with posterior circulation stroke

A 64-year-old man attended our dermatology clinic with a rectangular-shaped pruritic rash on the upper part of his right thigh and oval pink plaques on his right forearm. The patient said that the lesions had developed gradually over the previous few weeks. 3 months earlier, he had developed necrotising fasciitis of his right forearm after a fishing trip; tissue cultures had grown Vibrio vulnificus and an emergency fasciotomy had been done by plastic surgery colleagues. To repair the wound on his arm, a split-thickness rectangular patch of skin had been harvested from the upper part of the patient's right thigh and grafted onto the lesion on his right forearm. Both sites had healed well in the weeks following the operation but then the pruritic rashes began to appear. The patient was initially treated with topical sulfadiazine, which because it had no effect, prompted the referral to our clinic.On examination, we found well defined red plaques on both his forearm and thigh; he was otherwise fit and well.
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a skin biopsy showed acanthosis, elongation of rete ridges, parakeratosis, and dermal immune infiltrates: the features of psoriasis. We therefore made a diagnosis of a psoriatic isomorphic response at both the donor graft site and the recipient site. The patient was treated with betamethasone ointment with complete disease resolution after 2 weeks.
Interestingly, the patient had been diagnosed with psoriasis when he was 55 years old. He had not remembered having a previous episode of psoriasis, but on review of his medical records after the diagnosis, we found that he had developed pink, scaly papules on his chest and back 9 years earlier. A biopsy at the time had confirmed psoriasis and the patient had been treated with topical triamcinolone for 3 weeks with no episodes of recurrence recorded.

The phenomenon can present with a range of different skin disorders—including psoriasis, lichen planus, vitiligo, and vasculitis. It can also occur in patients without prior evidence of the underlying dermatological disease. Injuries precipitating the isomorphic response include physical trauma (eg, scratches, cuts, and injections), foreign substances (eg, tattoo ink), pressure (eg, a tight waistband), and even radiation—producing the so-called radiation recall reaction.
The clinical and histological features of the lesion are usually identical to that of the underlying dermatosis, and it should be treated in the same manner (video).

A 50-year-old man presented to the hospital with perineal pain that had been troubling him for 5 years. He described it as a mild, dull ache that was aggravated by riding his motorcycle. The patient did not report any bothersome lower urinary tract symptoms. He was able to generate a reasonable urinary stream, and preoperative uroflowmetry showed a maximum flow rate of 11·2mL/s, a voided volume of 215 mL, and a post-void residual volume of 20 mL.In 2014, he had mild left loin pain caused by a 1·5 cm left renal calculus; this was treated with extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy. However, after the operation he still had the pain, and repeated ultrasound scans of his abdomen and cultures of his urine since that time showed nothing abnormal. He had sought help from many private practitioners and had been treated for chronic pelvic pain syndrome.
The patient came to see us in 2017 because he was still troubled by the pain. A hard swelling was felt during clinical examination of his perineum; it was palpable 4 cm above the anal verge in the midline. During urethral calibration, resistance was felt 15 cm from the urethral meatus—admitting only an infant's feeding tube of French gauge 6. A plain x-ray of the pelvis showed a radio-opaque shadow inferior to the pubic symphysis (figure), and a retrograde urethrogram showed the obstruction in the bulbar urethra, suggestive of a calculus about 2 cm in diameter (figure).
A full blood count and analysis of the patient's blood chemistry were both normal, and urine analysis showed no abnormalities. The stone was retrieved by ventral urethrotomy with a perineal approach (figure), and at subsequent follow-up appointments the patient reported that he was doing well with complete relief from his perineal pain.
Urethral stones usually present with acute urinary retention or with symptoms indicative of an obstruction of the lower urinary tract; perineal, rectal, and urethral pain, and a palpable urethral mass are uncommon presentations. Importantly, stones in the bulbar urethra—ie, outside the bony pelvis and below the perineal membrane—are likely to be missed on routine transabdominal ultrasonography, as in this case. The bulbar urethra is the widest portion of the urethra and the stone might have been retained there after crossing the sphincter. Urethroscopy performed at the time of surgery showed the stone lying in the dilated bulbar urethra with enough space at the side of the stone to allow uninterrupted urinary flow. The stone had a relatively smooth surface, which probably explained the absence of any lower urinary tract symptoms. Simple palpation of the perineum helped us to arrive at the correct diagnosis. This case highlights urethral stones as one of the causes of chronic pelvic pain syndrome and reinforces the importance of clinical examination of genitalia and perineum in the evaluation of patients.

The patient did not report any bothersome lower urinary tract symptoms. He was able to generate a reasonable urinary stream, and preoperative uroflowmetry showed a maximum flow rate of 11·2mL/s, a voided volume of 215 mL, and a post-void residual volume of 20 mL.In 2014, he had mild left loin pain caused by a 1·5 cm left renal calculus; this was treated with extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy. However, after the operation he still had the pain, and repeated ultrasound scans of his abdomen and cultures of his urine since that time showed nothing abnormal. He had sought help from many private practitioners and had been treated for chronic pelvic pain syndrome.
The patient came to see us in 2017 because he was still troubled by the pain. A hard swelling was felt during clinical examination of his perineum; it was palpable 4 cm above the anal verge in the midline. During urethral calibration, resistance was felt 15 cm from the urethral meatus—admitting only an infant's feeding tube of French gauge 6. A plain x-ray of the pelvis showed a radio-opaque shadow inferior to the pubic symphysis (figure), and a retrograde urethrogram showed the obstruction in the bulbar urethra, suggestive of a calculus about 2 cm in diameter (figure).
A full blood count and analysis of the patient's blood chemistry were both normal, and urine analysis showed no abnormalities. The stone was retrieved by ventral urethrotomy with a perineal approach (figure), and at subsequent follow-up appointments the patient reported that he was doing well with complete relief from his perineal pain.
Urethral stones usually present with acute urinary retention or with symptoms indicative of an obstruction of the lower urinary tract; perineal, rectal, and urethral pain, and a palpable urethral mass are uncommon presentations. Importantly, stones in the bulbar urethra—ie, outside the bony pelvis and below the perineal membrane—are likely to be missed on routine transabdominal ultrasonography, as in this case. The bulbar urethra is the widest portion of the urethra and the stone might have been retained there after crossing the sphincter. Urethroscopy performed at the time of surgery showed the stone lying in the dilated bulbar urethra with enough space at the side of the stone to allow uninterrupted urinary flow. The stone had a relatively smooth surface, which probably explained the absence of any lower urinary tract symptoms. Simple palpation of the perineum helped us to arrive at the correct diagnosis. This case highlights urethral stones as one of the causes of chronic pelvic pain syndrome and reinforces the importance of clinical examination of genitalia and perineum in the evaluation of patients.

**Giant urethral calculus**

A 4-year-old boy was brought to our hospital with an 18-month history of progressive swelling in his neck. His parents said that over the previous few months he had begun to snore. Before he was seen by us he had been treated empirically at another hospital for extra-pulmonary tuberculosis without any improvement of his symptoms.On examination he had widespread lymphadenopathy, most markedly in the neck and axilla (figure); the nodes in the neck were suppurative. He had hepatosplenomegaly but was not malnourished. Our initial differential diagnosis was tuberculosis, filariasis, or lymphoma. Blood tests showed the boy to be anaemic, with a haemoglobin concentration of 7·3 g/dL. He had a raised platelet count (1000 × 109 per L), a significantly raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and raised lactate-dehydrogenase levels. Blood cultures and an HIV test were negative. We did a lymph node biopsy, bone marrow aspiration, and CT scan of his head and neck. The lymph node biopsy result showed granulomatous infiltration with negative infective stains and the bone marrow was normal. A CT scan of the boy's head showed widespread lymphadenopathy, and a lytic lesion in the skull (figure). Considering all the information together, we made a provisional diagnosis of a histiocytic disease such as Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH); the degree of lymphadenopathy was phenotypically consistent with Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes (RDD) disease. Full histological analysis, including immunological staining, was not available in Kenya; however, our local expert's opinion was that the pathology was consistent with the provisional diagnosis. So due to the severity and duration of the patient's symptoms, he was started on treatment with prednisone 40 mg/m2 daily for 4 weeks, tapered over 2 weeks, and vinblastine 6 mg/m2 per week for 6 weeks.
Happily, over the next 6 months, the boy's symptoms dramatically improved on continuation therapy: vinblastine, prednisone, and mercaptopurine (figure). We will continue treatment until he has completed a total of 52 weeks of chemotherapy.
In the process of reviewing the case for publication in The Lancet, the histology was examined by an expert in France, who confirmed that our patient did indeed have a rare form of mixed type histiocytosis—LCH and RDD. All the boy's histocytes strongly expressed S100, with around 30% of these cells also expressing CD1a or CD207.
Histiocytosis encompasses a range of conditions in which there is abnormal proliferation or differentiation and function of the mononuclear phagocyte system. LCH is the most common histiocyte disorder, with clinical presentations ranging from multisystem disease to single indolent lesions. RDD is also called sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy due to its propensity to cause large lymphadenopathy, and has a wide range of clinical presentations. Mixed type histiocytosis—as in our patient—is an unusual but well documented occurrence. Usually, treatment for histiocytosis is tailored to the individual. However, in severe, multifocal disease and in low-income and middle-income settings where sophisticated histopathological analysis may not be available, it might be appropriate to treat patients with chemotherapy empirically.

A 27-year-old man came to our emergency department with shortness of breath, a cough, and a globus sensation, which had all started earlier in the day. He also complained of an itchy rash on his neck, chest, and arms, which had developed 2 weeks earlier. During the previous 6 weeks, he had been repeatedly exposed to tear gas while working as a photojournalist at different protests around Hong Kong; the last exposure was 11 days before he came to see us. He said he had worn a full-face respirator during recent episodes.The patient had attended our department on three previous occasions because of the rash. He had been given oral prednisolone, antihistamines, and topical steroids but his symptoms had not improved. He had a history of allergic rhinitis; he had no history of asthma or bronchitis.
On examination we found the patient to have a blanchable, maculopapular rash over his neck, upper trunk, and arms—consistent with an allergic contact dermatitis (figure). His respiratory rate was 18 breaths per min and his oxygen saturation was 100% on room air; there was no evidence of angio-edema involving the upper airway. His lung fields were clear on auscultation.
Blood investigations showed no abnormalities: the patient's absolute eosinophil count and serum IgE concentration were normal.
A chest x-ray and thoracic CT showed no abnormalities. Bronchoscopy showed mild pharyngitis but severe tracheobronchitis (figure; video). No pathogens were detected with PCR or culture of the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. We decided not to do a bronchial biopsy of the severely inflamed bronchi because we were concerned about the risk of bleeding caused by the procedure. Lung function tests showed normal spirometry but a significant bronchodilator response: an increase of 19%, 640 mL in forced expiratory volume in 1 s, and a slightly reduced oxygen diffusion capacity of 71% (normal range 75–125%).
Considering the patient's presentation in the round we believe the patient had severe tracheobronchitis and an allergic contact dermatitis due to repeated exposure to tear gas. The patient was admitted and given intravenous hydrocortisone, inhaled fluticasone and vilanterol, and 50 mg/day of oral prednisolone. His condition improved and he went home after 4 days.
At follow-up 6 weeks later, the patient's shortness of breath had improved but he still had the cough. We repeated the bronchoscopy, which showed improvement in the tracheobronchitis (figure).
Lung function tests showed a significant bronchodilator response only in small airways: an increase of 18% in forced expiratory flow between 25% and 75% of the forced vital capacity (appendix).
We recommended that he continue with the inhaled fluticasone and vilanterol. Notably, the patient's skin rash recurred following re-exposure to tear gas. He was given three more short courses of oral prednisolone. 4 months later at a follow-up appointment his dermatological and respiratory symptoms had resolved.
o-Chlorobenzylidene malononitrile (CS) has become the most commonly used tear gas agent—often deployed by producing microparticles 3–10 μm in size with pyrotechnic devices like grenades or canisters. CS is a potent agonist of the transient receptor potential cation channel A1, which is expressed in nociceptors in the skin and mucous membranes; it triggers pain and an acute inflammatory reaction. Exposure also causes immediate intense irritation of the eyes, nose, mouth, skin, respiratory tract, and gastrointestinal tract in a dose-dependent manner—these effects lead the individual to be temporarily incapacitated.
Repeated exposure has been associated with chronic bronchitis and allergic contact dermatitis which—as in our patient—may occur despite a normal eosinophil count and serum IgE concentration.
output: Severe tracheobronchitis and allergic contact dermatitis due to repeated tear gas exposure

A 51-year-old woman, who had a history of rheumatic heart disease, was admitted to hospital with a recent onset of reduced level of consciousness and right-sided weakness. Initial neurological examination was consistent with a right-sided hemiplegia. A CT scan of her head confirmed infarction of the left basal ganglia and left paraventricular regions of the brain. Examination of her cardiovascular system found her heart to be in atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 110 beats per min. A diastolic murmur was heard on auscultation at the apex. A non-contrast chest CT scan showed a 6 cm diameter, high attenuation circle in the left atrium (figure). Further investigation using transthoracic echocardiography (figure) revealed a mobile left atrial mass with concentric circles around the periphery, consistent with a free-floating thrombus; it also showed severe mitral stenosis with a dilated left atrium filled with dense spontaneous echo contrast and no left atrial appendage thrombus.The woman, who was first diagnosed with rheumatic heart disease 10 years ago, was taken to surgery, where the free-floating mass was removed and the mitral valve replaced. Subsequent pathological examination confirmed a giant thrombus with a smooth outer shell, and an area below the surface containing multiple haemorrhagic regions. The variable consistency of this subsurface area may have been the cause of the concentric circles seen on CT scan and transthoracic echocardiography.
Left atrial ball thrombi almost always form in the setting of mitral valve disease and are linked to high rates of embolism. Prompt surgical removal is the recommended and appropriate therapeutic intervention.

A 17-year-old transgender man attended our hospital with a 2-month history of intermittent right-sided abdominal pain, nausea, early satiety, profuse night sweats, and 14 kg weight loss.For the past 14 months, he had been undergoing hormonal gender reassignment—female to male—with weekly intramuscular injections of 32 mg of testosterone cypionate.
On examination he showed secondary male sexual characteristics: he had a deep voice and he had facial hair and acne. He was thin with a body-mass index of 18·5 kg/m2. On deep palpation he had increased mild tenderness of the right upper abdominal quadrant, compared to the left side.
MRI of the patient's abdomen showed a 17·5 cm × 7·2 cm × 8·0 cm enhancing mass in the left hemiliver with numerous small surrounding satellite lesions and tumour thrombi in the main, right, and left portal veins (figure). Core needle biopsy of the liver mass showed hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with clear cell change (figure); androgen receptor (AR) nuclear staining was seen in 40% of the cells (figure). Liver tissue outside the tumour was normal—confirmed on staining with trichrome, reticulin, periodic acid-Schiff, and iron.
The patient's serum alpha-fetoprotein concentration was 4320 ng/mL (normal less than 8·3) with a non-reactive hepatitis serology panel—including hepatitis A virus IgM, HBsAg, HBcAg IgM, and hepatitis C virus antibody.
We treated him initially with yttrium-90 (90Y)-loaded glass microspheres (TheraSphere, Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA, USA) at a dose of 160 Gray (Gy), delivered by intra-arterial injection to the involved segments of his liver, 1·48 gigabecquerel (GBq) to segment 4 and 1·87 GBq to segments 2 and 3.
MRI of the patient's abdomen 2 months after the treatment showed new lesions in the right hemiliver (figure) and his alpha-fetoprotein concentration had increased to 10 933 ng/mL. The patient stopped taking the exogenous testosterone after we discussed with him the possible effects it might be having upon the tumour. He was then started on intramuscular injections of leuprolide—a synthetic gonadotropin-releasing hormone—at a dose of 30 mg every 30 days to prevent the development of secondary female sexual characteristics.
He returned for a second treatment of 90Y-loaded glass microspheres to the right hemiliver at a dose of 151 Gy: 4·42 GBq to segments 5–8. He was found to have partial radiographic response in both the right and left hemiliver lesions and subsequently received additional 90Y-loaded glass microsphere treatment. The patient continues to be monitored for progression of the disease. Future treatment—if necessary—may include systemic targeted therapy or immunotherapy in a clinical trial.
HCC is mostly found in men and studies have linked the AR to development of the disease. AR expression and its role in HCC remains unclear. AR is overexpressed in the nuclei of approximately 74% of HCCs in men and 38% in women; it is associated with advanced disease and poor survival. Preclinical work suggests AR may play a role in the early development of HCC, but knocking out AR signalling in the later stages of the disease does not attenuate tumour growth. AR staining is not routinely obtained in patients with HCC and antiandrogen therapy is not indicated.
The relationship between exogenous testosterone and development and progression of HCC in peripubertal transgender patients is unknown. Further, it is unknown whether continuation of testosterone in patients positive for AR nuclear staining affects the outcome of the disease (video).

A 66-year-old man attended our hospital for endoscopic surveillance of a 20 mm gastric antral ulcer. 4 weeks earlier, the patient had presented with haematemesis and melena; a Forrest IB gastric ulcer—active oozing—was found at gastroscopy, and was treated by adrenaline injection, bipolar coagulation, and endoscopic hemoclipping (figure).The patient had a medical history of oesophageal cancer—surgically treated by an Ivor Lewis oesophagectomy 5 years earlier—and common variable immunodeficiency, for which he was receiving monthly intravenous immunoglobulin.
The ulcer had first been discovered 3 months earlier during routine surveillance endoscopy of the oesophagectomy anastomosis. Analysis of samples of biopsies taken during both gastroscopies had shown no evidence of malignancy or Helicobacter pylori; IgG testing for H pylori was also negative. Notably, the patient did not have a history of alcohol misuse or use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatories. He had received all childhood vaccinations—including measles—and he reported no recent contact with cats or other pets. During the period of surveillance, the ulcer had failed to heal and it continued to actively bleed despite confirmed concordance of the patient to a high dose of a proton pump inhibitor twice daily and sucralfate four times a day.
On examination, we found the patient to be alert and well looking. His abdomen was soft, with no tenderness or signs of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 110 g/L (normal 138–172), which did not change during the admission. We took additional biopsies from the ulcer's edge and the patient remained on our ward for further monitoring and treatment with a proton pump inhibitor given intravenously.
Histopathological analysis of samples of the gastric ulcer biopsies showed chronic active inflammatory changes with multiple inclusion bodies in the mucosal epithelial lining, stromal cells, and capillaries (figure). The inclusion bodies were characterised by enlarged nuclei containing bright granular aggregates, surrounded by clear halo and typical owl's-eye morphology. Cytomegalovirus was confirmed as the cause on immunohistochemistry. No helicobacter organisms, dysplasia, or signs of malignancy were seen. Furthermore, the patient had a detectable viral load for cytomegalovirus of 1812 IU/mL; immunoglobulin levels demonstrated an IgG of 4·23 (normal 6·0–16·0 g/L), IgA <0·10 (normal 0·8–3·0 g/L), and IgM <0·20 (normal 0·4–2·5 g/L).
We started treatment with valganciclovir; 1 week later viral load for cytomegalovirus was 332 IU/mL, 270 IU/mL after 2 weeks, and after 4 months, the ulcer had healed completely. The patient had no further episodes of upper gastrointestinal bleeding, with undetectable levels of viral load of cytomegalovirus.
Common variable immunodeficiency is characterised by reduced serum levels of immunoglobulins with reduced or absent specific antibody production.
Cytomegalovirus-related gastric ulcers are not uncommon as a cause of gastrointestinal bleeding; a global deficiency in immunoglobulin—as in our case—and specifically of IgA, will result in a greater susceptibility of patients becoming infected with the virus. Infectious causes—including cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, measles virus, varicella zoster virus, Toxoplasma gondii, and Epstein-Barr virus—should be considered as a possible cause of a gastric ulcer that fails to heal in immunocompromised patients (video).

Analysis of samples of biopsies taken during both gastroscopies had shown no evidence of malignancy or Helicobacter pylori; IgG testing for H pylori was also negative. Notably, the patient did not have a history of alcohol misuse or use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatories. He had received all childhood vaccinations—including measles—and he reported no recent contact with cats or other pets. During the period of surveillance, the ulcer had failed to heal and it continued to actively bleed despite confirmed concordance of the patient to a high dose of a proton pump inhibitor twice daily and sucralfate four times a day.
On examination, we found the patient to be alert and well looking. His abdomen was soft, with no tenderness or signs of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 110 g/L (normal 138–172), which did not change during the admission. We took additional biopsies from the ulcer's edge and the patient remained on our ward for further monitoring and treatment with a proton pump inhibitor given intravenously.

The inclusion bodies were characterised by enlarged nuclei containing bright granular aggregates, surrounded by clear halo and typical owl's-eye morphology. Cytomegalovirus was confirmed as the cause on immunohistochemistry. No helicobacter organisms, dysplasia, or signs of malignancy were seen. The patient had no further episodes of upper gastrointestinal bleeding, with undetectable levels of viral load of cytomegalovirus.

input: A 55-year-old woman presented with a non-healing, painless pigmented macule with a superficial ulceration on the left planta, which she said had been there for 6 months. She could not recall any history of trauma and did not report any family history of cutaneous diseases. On physical examination, an irregular pigmented macule with a superficial ulceration and brown haemorrhagic crusts was observed on the left plantar near the heel (figures). A skin biopsy showed a malignant melanoma and immunohistochemical examination of biopsied tissue sections showed positive staining for melanoma associated antigens using the antibodies HMB-45, Melan-A, and S100. The patient was diagnosed with an acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM). She underwent a wide local excision with a sufficiently large margin from the lesion's border. A sentinel lymph node biopsy of the inguinal nodes was negative. Fortunately, there was no evidence of recurrence during 5 years of follow-up.ALM is the least common (accounting for 4–10% of all melanoma diagnoses) of the four major subtypes of cutaneous malignant melanoma that typically occur on the palms, the soles of the feet, and the nail beds. However, even though they are uncommon, it is the commonest subtype of melanoma among people with darker skin types—including those of Asian or African descent. Patients with ALM tend to have a poor prognosis, mainly because of the delay in diagnosis and the advanced state of the disease at presentation. Previous research has shown that 25–33% of melanomas on the feet are incorrectly diagnosed when they are first seen by a doctor. Melanomas presenting as an ulcer on the foot can be challenging because the list of differential diagnoses for such a lesion is long. Therefore, even though ALM is a rare cause of ulceration on the foot, it must be considered when examining atypical acral lesions or ulcers that fail to heal.

On physical examination, an irregular pigmented macule with a superficial ulceration and brown haemorrhagic crusts was observed on the left plantar near the heel (figures). A skin biopsy showed a malignant melanoma and immunohistochemical examination of biopsied tissue sections showed positive staining for melanoma associated antigens using the antibodies HMB-45, Melan-A, and S100. The patient was diagnosed with an acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM). She underwent a wide local excision with a sufficiently large margin from the lesion's border. A sentinel lymph node biopsy of the inguinal nodes was negative. Fortunately, there was no evidence of recurrence during 5 years of follow-up.ALM is the least common (accounting for 4–10% of all melanoma diagnoses) of the four major subtypes of cutaneous malignant melanoma that typically occur on the palms, the soles of the feet, and the nail beds. However, even though they are uncommon, it is the commonest subtype of melanoma among people with darker skin types—including those of Asian or African descent. Patients with ALM tend to have a poor prognosis, mainly because of the delay in diagnosis and the advanced state of the disease at presentation. Previous research has shown that 25–33% of melanomas on the feet are incorrectly diagnosed when they are first seen by a doctor. Melanomas presenting as an ulcer on the foot can be challenging because the list of differential diagnoses for such a lesion is long. Therefore, even though ALM is a rare cause of ulceration on the foot, it must be considered when examining atypical acral lesions or ulcers that fail to heal.

A 58-year-old man, who after reporting several days of abdominal pain was found to have acute kidney injury, was transferred to our unit from a regional hospital.In the preceding 6 months, the patient had been diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia; he had no personal or family history of nephrolithiasis, bowel disease, or weight loss. Notably, the year before this presentation, his kidney function had been found to be normal with the serum creatinine concentration recorded as 71 μmol/L (normal range 60–115).
On examination, the patient was clinically well with a blood pressure of 122/66 mm Hg, heart rate of 95 beats per min, respiratory rate of 18 breaths per min, and an oxygen saturation of 95% on room air.
Laboratory investigations confirmed acute kidney injury—his serum creatinine concentration was 703 μmol/L with preserved urinary output; his remaining serum biochemistry was unremarkable. The urinary protein/creatinine ratio was 39 mg/mmol (normal range 0–12·5).
The patient was admitted to the nephrology ward for a kidney biopsy which showed acute tubular injury with abundant intratubular calcium oxalate crystals; the background kidney was healthy, with little scarring, and only 1/14 obsolete glomeruli (figure).
A detailed dietary history found that the patient had been eating 500–1000 g of almonds daily over the last four years—corresponding to approximately 2–4 g of oxalate per day. He had no evidence of malabsorption; his faecal elastase concentration was >500 ug/g (typical range 200 to less than 500).
A CT of the kidney, ureter, and bladder showed a non-obstructing 1·4 cm calculus in the lower pole of the right kidney and a non-obstructing 0·6 cm calculus in the distal left ureter (figure). We concluded the patient had a diet-related secondary hyperoxaluria; frontotemporal dementia is associated with unusual, compulsive eating habits.
As he was asymptomatic, we decided to manage him conservatively; the patient was started on a low-oxalate, high-calcium diet with a high fluid intake and reviewed regularly. At his last appointment, the patient's laboratory results showed his serum creatinine concentration was improving (478 μmol/L).
Hyperoxaluria causes calcium oxalate stones by raising urinary saturation of calcium oxalate; hyperoxaluria can result from ingestion of oxalate-rich foods, such as rhubarb, spinach, beetroot, almonds—as in our case—and chocolate. Hyperoxaluria is less common than hypercalciuria as a cause of calcium oxalate stones.
Non-obstructive kidney stones of less than 15 mm can be treated conservatively and monitored closely; an increase in the size of the stone or complications, such as infections, may result in a more proactive approach.

A 63-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of an insidious fever with chills and a non-productive cough. He had lost 5 kg in weight. He also had type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidaemia. He was a farmer involved in rice cultivation and palm oil plantation in the central region of Sarawak, Malaysia.On examination, we found no abnormalities. Initial laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 12·6 g/dL, a platelet count of 399 × 109 per L, and total white blood cell count of 11·4 × 109 per L; neutrophils 66·2%, lymphocytes 22·5%, and eosinophils 1·7%. Renal and liver function tests showed no abnormalities.
Plain chest x-ray showed a left hilar mass with blunted left costophrenic angle. Sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli were negative.
The patient's fever persisted—despite a week of empirical treatment with oral antimicrobial agents—and we carried out a CT of the thorax which showed an enhancing, 2·5 cm × 4·1 cm × 2·5 cm mass at the aorto-pulmonary window abutting the left main bronchus and descending thoracic aorta (figure).
A primary lung malignancy was suspected because of the constitutional symptoms with negative tuberculosis work-up, and the CT finding.
White light flexible bronchoscopy showed a grossly abnormal and stenotic left main bronchus with an endobronchial nodule (appendix); narrow band imaging showed the mucosa to be diffusely thickened (appendix). An endobronchial biopsy was taken, and bronchial brushings were collected. The bronchoscopy findings reinforced our working diagnosis of a lung malignancy.
Despite the development of a low-grade temperature post procedure, the patient's blood investigations remained normal and microbiological analyses remained negative. We therefore let the patient go home with a 2-week course of oral amoxicillin and clavulanic acid, while awaiting the histopathological and microbiological analysis.
2 weeks later, the patient attended our outpatient clinic for review: the endobronchial biopsy showed inflamed granulation tissue with underlying stroma infiltrated by neutrophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells, with proliferation of small blood vessels lined by benign endothelial cells. There were no granuloma or multinucleated giant cells seen. Periodic acid–Schiff and Ziehl–Neelsen stains showed no fungal elements or acid-fast bacilli. Analysis of the bronchial brushings was negative for bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterium.
However, the patient was found to be febrile and unwell: pulse rate 139 beats per min, blood pressure 114/64 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 38°C.
He was immediately admitted to hospital, but he developed septic shock requiring mechanical ventilation and vasopressor support in the intensive care unit. We empirically gave the patient intravenous meropenem (25 mg/kg per day). Blood cultures grew Gram-negative bacilli with a safety pin appearance and confirmed as Burkholderia pseudomallei by conventional biochemical testing and mass spectrometry. The patient gradually improved and was allowed home after a month of intensive care. He completed 6 months of eradication therapy with oral co-trimoxazole; a CT scan after 3 months of treatment showed resolution of the left hilar mass (appendix).
Melioidosis is a common infectious disease in southeast Asia, usually presenting as an acute febrile illness with pneumonia or chronic illness. It may present atypically—as in our case where we found an isolated mediastinal mass—representing a lethal trap for the unwary (video).

A 37-year-old woman with a 1-month history of fatigue, weight loss, palpitations, and dyspnoea, attended our clinic for investigation.
12 months earlier, the patient had embolisation of pelvic varicose veins, using glue and lipiodised oil, for pelvic venous disorder; she had reported a history of pelvic congestion syndrome with chronic pelvic pain beginning after a pregnancy 5 years earlier. The pain worsened just before the onset of menstruation. She also had symptomatic varicose veins in her legs. Venograms had confirmed abdominal-pelvic venous insufficiency with reflux in a dilated left ovarian vein, tortuous pelvic varicosities near the uterus, and bilateral dilated utero-vaginal venous plexuses.
The patient had no history of recent viral infection or neck pain; she was prescribed no medication.
On examination the patient was generally unwell; her blood pressure was 132/70 mm Hg, her pulse was 97 beats per min, and her BMI was 20·7 kg/m2. She had a firm, hard moderate-sized goitre but no signs of Graves’ orbitopathy.
Laboratory investigations showed hyperthyroidism; the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration was biologically undetectable, the free thyroxine (FT4) concentration was above 100·0 pmol/L (typical range 12·0–22·0), and the free triiodothyroxine (FT3) concentration was 36·0 pmol/L (typical range 3·1–6·8). Tests for TSH-receptor antibodies were negative. Thyroglobulin concentration was 1143 ng/mL (typical range 3·5–77·0); C-reactive protein concentration was within typical range (<5 mg/L). Thyroid peroxidase antibodies were also within the normal range. Urinary iodine concentration was raised at 10·01 μmol/L (typical range 0·35–1·60).
123Iodine thyroid scintigraphy showed no significant uptake with a blunted measured value of 0·4% at 120 min (average value 12% at 120 min for a mean TSH of 1·2 mIU/L in France; appendix).
Considering the findings in the round, we ruled out thyrotoxicosis factitia because of the raised thyroglobulin concentration and concluded the most likely diagnosis was an iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis. As stated above, the patient was not prescribed amiodarone—a recognised cause of iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis—or any other drugs associated with thyroiditis and thyrotoxicosis, and she had no history of recent radiographic contrast exposure. However, an unenhanced abdominal CT scan showed lipiodised oil in the ovarian veins (figure 1); additionally, an unenhanced CT scan of the patient's neck, which we requested to give further weight to our conclusion that the patient had thyrotoxicosis secondary to the lipiodised oil, showed a very high density of the thyroid (147 Hounsfield units [HU]; typical range 80–100; figure 2).
The patient was commenced on oral prednisone at a dose of 1 mg/kg per day until laboratory investigations showed she was euthyroid; the corticosteroids were gradually reduced over 5 months.
At follow-up 18 months later, she was well with normal thyroid function.
Excessive intake of iodine can cause hyperthyroidism; mainly this occurs after exposure to iodinated radiographic material or treatment with amiodarone. Interestingly, a study proposed a cutoff level of 117 HU for the density of the thyroid seen on unenhanced CT scan to distinguish patients with amiodarone-induced hyperthyroidism from healthy controls and from euthyroid amiodarone-treated patients (appendix). With this in mind, we suggest that a hyperdense thyroid, seen on an unenhanced CT scan—with a density level above 120 HU—should raise the possibility of iodine overload and subsequent testing of the serum TSH concentration.

A 70-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital reporting puffy eyelids and swelling of both legs. She had a 7-year history of nephrotic syndrome and hypertension.On examination, she had swollen eyelids and oedema in both legs; her blood pressure was 172/81 mm Hg.
Laboratory investigations showed serum albumin concentration of 2·9 g/dL (normal 4·1–5·1), creatinine 0·81 mg/dL (0·46–0·79), and LDL cholesterol 296 mg/dL (65–163). Urinalysis showed severe proteinuria of 9·3 g/gCr (<0·3) with greater than 100 red blood cells per high-power field and greater than 50 white blood cell per high-power field in the urine sediment.
Tests for hepatitis B and C viruses, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and double-stranded DNA antibodies were negative; free light chain κ was 27·4 mg/L (normal 3·3–19·4), free light chain λ was 15·6 mg/L (5·7–26·3), and free light chain κ:λ ratio was 1·76 (0·26–1·65).
Cryoglobulin was negative. Malignancy screenings were all negative. Bone marrow biopsy specimen was normal. Renal biopsy was performed; light microscopy revealed membranoproliferative pattern of the glomeruli (figure). Immunofluorescence microscopy revealed the presence of IgG, C3, and C1q in the mesangium with aggregates in the capillary wall. Electron microscopy revealed microtubules with a diameter of almost 40 nm and a distinct hollow core (figure). Based on these findings, immunotactoid glomerulopathy (ITG) associated with monoclonal gammopathy was diagnosed. Oral prednisolone (40 mg/day) administered initially, normalised the urine sediment; remission of proteinuria was incomplete. Intravenous rituximab facilitated complete remission after 1 month.
ITG is a rare glomerular disease encountered in 0·06% of native kidney biopsies; its management remains poorly defined. ITG is characterised by electron microscopic findings of deposits comprising straight, long microtubules with hollow cores and a diameter of greater than 30 nm. Cryoglobulinaemic glomerulonephritis—which should be distinguished from ITG—has deposits comprising short, curved microtubules or fibrillary substructures of diameters less than 30 nm.
ITG has IgG monoclonal and polyclonal variants: the monoclonal type has a higher incidence of haematological conditions—including lymphoma, multiple myeloma, and monoclonal gammopathy. Monoclonal ITG is more commonly treated with clone-directed therapy and associated with frequent remissions and less end-stage kidney disease; it should therefore be subclassified into monoclonal and polyclonal variants. Recently—as seen in our case—improved prognosis in ITG may be possible due to rituximab-based therapy (video).

input: A 34-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use and hepatitis C infection presented to the ophthalmology clinic with a 1-week history of pain and decreased vision in his right eye.
