A 26-year-old woman presented at week 20 of pregnancy with a 3-month history of fever, cough, and breathlessness. She had hearing loss, epistaxis, nasal crusting, haemoptysis, and a purpuric rash over her legs. No significant weight loss was reported. Chest x-ray (with abdominal shield) showed bilateral cannonball opacities, and contrast-enhanced chest CT (with abdominal shield) revealed multiple nodules, without pleural effusion or lymphadenopathy (figure). Ultrasound of the patient's abdomen and pelvis showed a single live fetus and no abnormalities. Her haemoglobin concentration was 8·3 g/dL, total leucocyte count was 8·6 × 109/L, platelet count was 600 × 109/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 65 mm/h, and C-reactive protein concentration was 186 mg/L. The patient's serum anti-proteinase 3 antibody concentration was 102 U/mL. Sputum acid-fast bacilli and fungal smear, serum β-D-glucan and galactomannan, and Mantoux test results were all negative. A diagnosis of granulomatosis with polyangiitis was made.
The patient commenced remission induction therapy with intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g once daily for 3 days) and rituximab (1000 mg, two doses 2 weeks apart). She showed substantial improvement over the next 2–3 days and delivered a healthy baby girl at term. The patient commenced oral prednisolone immediately after induction therapy, starting at 60 mg/day for 1 month followed by taper every two weeks. She has received remission maintenance therapy with oral prednisolone (5 mg/day) and intravenous rituximab (500 mg every 6 months) for 1 year, and is planned to continue this treatment for at least 2 years total duration. A follow-up chest x-ray 6 months after the initial treatment showed complete resolution of lung nodules.
Cannonball opacities on chest x-ray usually suggest metastatic malignancies such as choriocarcinoma, lung carcinoma, renal cell cancer, or endometrial carcinoma, but, less frequently, can be due to other conditions, such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis, fungal infections, and tuberculosis. The most common chest radiological finding at presentation in patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis is bilateral nodules or masses (reported in up to 90% of patients in case series). In the current case, hearing loss, purpuric rash, and upper respiratory symptoms led us to suspect granulomatosis with polyangiitis. The absence of pleural effusion or lymphadenopathy on chest radiology made a diagnosis of malignancy or infection less likely, the normal pelvic ultrasound helped to rule out choriocarcinoma, and the negative Mantoux test, sputum workup, and fungal serology helped to rule out infection. Elevated concentrations of anti-proteinase 3 antibodies and the patient's rapid response to immunosuppression contributed to confirmation of the diagnosis. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small-vessel vasculitis that can mimic malignancy and infections. This diagnosis should be suspected in patients with lung nodules when there are accompanying upper respiratory tract symptoms, rash, neuropathy, or eye, ear, or renal involvement.

SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR on a nasopharyngeal swab was negative.
CT pulmonary angiography showed a central pulmonary embolism without right ventricular dysfunction (figure). Magnetic resonance venography showed venous thrombus formation in the left internal iliac vein—including the common iliac vein—with extension into the inferior vena cava (figure; appendix).

Plasma coagulation factor activities were normal for all other extrinsic and intrinsic coagulation factors—including von Willebrand factor.
Mixing the patient's plasma in a 1:1 ratio with standard human plasma showed a deficiency of fibrinogen and factor XIII; thrombelastography confirmed the result (for details see appendix).
LMWH was increased to a therapeutic dose leading to an anti-factor Xa activity of 0·5–1·0 IU/mL (therapeutic range 0·5–1·0).
On day 5, the patient developed pain in the left lower back and left gluteal region; CT venography showed an increase in the thrombus in the inferior vena cava. The LMWH dose was increased to obtain supratherapeutic anti-factor Xa activity (1·0–1·5 U/mL). On the following day, the pain had reduced.

Activation of the coagulation system producing thromboses in the context of thrombocytopenia and hypofibrinogenaemia—as occurred in our patient—is similar to heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and to that seen in critically ill COVID-19 patients (video).

A 45-year-old woman attended our dermatology outpatient clinic for her 3-monthly skin cancer surveillance appointment. Numerous actinic keratoses, in addition to two full thickness skin grafts were noted on examination of the dorsal hands (as illustrated by the graft on the right dorsal hand in the figure).Significantly in her medical history, the patient had two cadaveric-donor renal transplants because of renal failure secondary to chronic glomerulonephritis—first aged 17 years, and then aged 41 years. She was prescribed immunosuppressive therapy, which included tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisolone.
Aged 38 years, the patient was diagnosed with an invasive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the right dorsal hand which was treated with surgical resection and full thickness skin graft reconstruction. Histopathology confirmed a well-differentiated SCC; depth of invasion of 8 mm, with evidence of perineural invasion of nerves of <0·1 mm in diameter, but without lympho-vascular space invasion. The SCC was excised with adequate histopathologic margins; no evidence of locoregional nodal or distant metastatic disease was found.
Aged 39 years, the patient developed numerous actinic keratoses on her dorsal hands which were treated with conventional photodynamic therapy and 6-monthly topical 5-fluorouracil (which she continues to receive).
Aged 42 years, the patient developed a second invasive SCC of the left distal phalanx of the fifth finger which was again treated with surgical resection and full thickness skin graft reconstruction; histopathology again confirmed a moderately differentiated SCC, depth of invasion 1·5 mm, without evidence of perineural or lympho-vascular space invasion. The lesion was excised with adequate histopathologic margins; no evidence of locoregional nodal or distant metastatic disease was found.
The repeated development of malignancies and other skin lesions only on her hands caused us to review the case more circumspectly, and the absence of significant photodamage in other sun-exposed areas aroused our suspicion of an alternative aetiology.
The patient, who had skin phototype 1, had reliably informed us that she had adopted effective photoprotective measures, which included avoidance of sun exposure, use of sunscreen, and wearing photoprotective clothing, since the first transplantation.
However, upon closer questioning, she also said that, for more than 20 years, she had regular, monthly manicures which used unregulated ultraviolet radiation A (UVA) emitting lamps to set the nail polish.
Repeated exposure to UVA rays is well described in the setting of cutaneous carcinogenesis, acting via a direct DNA-damaging mechanism, to cause both photo-ageing and the development of keratinocyte malignancies. This effect is greatly amplified in immunosuppressed patients, particularly solid organ transplant recipients.
While it is difficult to conclude that manicure-associated UVA exposure was the sole driver of carcinogenesis in our patient, the absence of precancerous lesions and keratinocyte malignancies at sites other than the dorsal hands suggests it might have been a significant contributor.
A practical approach towards mitigating the risk of cutaneous carcinogenesis in the setting of unregulated UVA-emitting lamps might include advising patients to specifically request the use of a light-emitting diode lamp during manicures to minimise cumulative UVA exposure. We advocate for specific inquiry regarding such practices in patients attending transplant and dermatology clinics to inform at-risk populations about the need for photoprotection and risk of carcinogenesis.

Radiographs of the knees and wrists showed calcification of the cartilage in both knees (figure A), both ulnocarpal joints, and right trapeziometacarpal joint (figure B), suggesting calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease.
Further laboratory investigations revealed hypomagnesemia (serum magnesium 1·15 mg/dL) with renal magnesium wasting (fractional excretion of magnesium 19·3%) and hypocalciuria. Serum calcium, urate, ferritin, alkaline phosphatase, rheumatoid factor, and intact parathyroid hormone concentrations were within normal limits. There were no clinical or historical features suggestive of alternative causes of arthritis, such as psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, palmoplantar lesions, or recent genitourinary or gastrointestinal infections. Genetic testing was performed and a complete deletion of the HNF1B coding sequence was identified. This finding confirmed a diagnosis of HNF1B-related disease, characterised by maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 5, Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome, and secondary CPPD disease due to hypomagnesaemia.
An abdominal CT scan was performed to look for structural atypicalities commonly associated with HNF1B mutations, including renal cysts, pancreatic atrophy, and uterine anomalies. Although none of these findings were present, the CT scan revealed calcification involving the pubic symphysis and bilateral hips (figure C). The diffuse distribution of calcifications in CPPD disease is often linked to genetic or metabolic disturbances. This case highlights the importance of thorough evaluation in patients presenting with extensive CPPD disease and multisystem involvement. The triad of hypomagnesaemia, diabetes, and Müllerian anomalies (associated with Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome) should prompt consideration of HNF1B-related disease. The patient's arthritis was managed with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and magnesium supplementation was initiated. She was given a combination of glipizide and insulin for her diabetes, with the addition of empagliflozin for improved glycaemic control and to mitigate renal magnesium loss—potentially by enhancing transcellular magnesium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule through upregulation of the transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily M member 6, and increasing paracellular reabsorption in the loop of Henle.

Current mining practices—including digging for thinner and harder to reach seams leading to increased cutting of rock and therefore higher exposure to silica—may be a contributing factor. CWP and PMF should be considered in the differential diagnosis in both current and former coal miners presenting with respiratory problems regardless of age or the duration of coal mine employment. A man aged 57 years, who had had herpes zoster 10 years previously, visited our emergency room with a tingling ache in his right lower back. Physical examination revealed neither eruption nor trauma on the body surface. However, an abdominal wall protrusion was observed on his right side, especially while he was standing (figure). Abdominal imaging using contrasted computer tomography did not reveal any abnormalities.Abdominal muscle paralysis was considered as the possible diagnosis and 60 mg loxoprofen, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, was administered for his back pain once daily for 5 days. 5 days after the initial visit, dome-shaped papules with overlying small, dark-coloured vesicles appeared on his trunk and extremities, suggesting disseminated herpes zoster. The patient was treated with 1000 mg oral valacyclovir three times daily for 7 days, along with the same regimen of loxoprofen as already described. The vesicular papules dried up after 5 days and became brown scabs within a week. The protruding abdominal wall flattened within a month, and the patient's lower back pain gradually abated within a couple of months.
Herpes zoster is characterised by the reactivation of the varicella zoster virus, which causes a vesicular rash, typically restricted to a single dermatome. However, some patients develop disseminated herpes zoster; these patients are more likely to be immunosuppressed. It is rare for this condition to occur in an immunocompetent host, as it did in this case.
Post-herpetic abdominal pseudohernia is uncommon, occurring in 2% of patients with herpes zoster. Although pseudohernia should be suspected when a patient develops abdominal paresis coincident with or after a herpetic rash, abdominal paresis can also very rarely precede a rash. Awareness of this clinical condition might help physicians anticipate herpes zoster, allowing prompt treatment.

A 56-year-old man was referred to our specialist unit after presenting to his primary care clinic with a dry cough and breathlessness on exertion that were slowly worsening. He had been a smoker for 7 years but quit over a decade earlier. Also, he had worked for 8 years in underground coal mines, in Kentucky, USA. He left the profession when he was 26 years old following the collapse of a wall in the mine that left him disabled after a head injury and the development of seizures. During his time in the industry, he had worked exclusively at the coal face, primarily drilling and bolting into the ceiling of the mine to prevent collapses—known in the trade as a roof bolter. He said he wore a dust mask inconsistently because it made breathing difficult.The patient's vital signs were within normal limits and a physical examination was unremarkable. Pulmonary function testing showed moderate obstruction without a bronchodilator response: forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) to forced vital capacity (FVC) ratio was low at 0·58 (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey III fifth percentile lower limit of normal [LLN] 0·67), with a low FEV1 of 1·97 L, 59% predicted (LLN 2·58 L), a normal FVC of 3·52 L, 81% predicted (LLN 3·41 L), a normal total lung capacity of 6·58 L, 107% predicted (LLN 5·06 L), and a normal diffusion of 25·3m L/mm Hg per min, 88% predicted (LLN 17·69 m L/mm Hg per min).
CT scan of the patient's chest showed numerous bilateral pulmonary nodules and an irregular right upper lobe mass with mediastinal lymphadenopathy (figure). A PET scan showed the lung mass and mediastinal lymph nodes with heterogeneous hypermetabolic uptake (appendix). Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and endobronchial ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration of his mediastinal lymph nodes showed no infection, granuloma, or cancer. However, it did show anthracotic pigment laden macrophages. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis (CWP) was suspected, but because of his relatively young age and short mining tenure, a transthoracic, CT-guided biopsy of his lung mass was done. Histopathological examination showed areas of focal collagenous fibrosis associated with anthracosis and polarised silicate particles; there was no evidence of cancer, granulomas, vasculitis, or infection (figure). We therefore made a definitive diagnosis of CWP and progressive massive fibrosis (PMF).
PET scans—as our patient's imaging illustrates—may fail to reliably distinguish PMF from malignancy as both are commonly hypermetabolic. Historically, CWP and PMF develop in miners with mining tenures of 25 years or more. However, in recent years, rates of severe disease have been increasing in younger miners with short mining tenures, despite improved health and safety regulations. Current mining practices—including digging for thinner and harder to reach seams leading to increased cutting of rock and therefore higher exposure to silica—may be a contributing factor. CWP and PMF should be considered in the differential diagnosis in both current and former coal miners presenting with respiratory problems regardless of age or the duration of coal mine employment. Early detection is crucial to prevent further dust exposure and delay progression of disease; effective treatments are lacking, and morbidity is irreversible (video).

On March 11, 2017, a 59-year-old woman came to our hospital's emergency department. She had been unwell for 7 days, with recurrent epigastric pain of acute onset that radiated into her right hemithorax, intensified during respiratory movements, and was accompanied by mild dyspnoea. Vomiting and dysphagia were absent. She had presented to our hospital because of the same symptoms 4 days before admission, but she was discharged after examination and investigations had shown no notable abnormalities: chest radiograph and electrocardiogram (ECG) were normal, as were C-reactive protein and troponin concentrations. She smoked 20 cigarettes daily, did not drink alcohol, and took atorvastatin.On admission, a chest radiograph revealed a right pleural effusion (figure, A). Considering her symptoms and her increased concentrations of serum D-dimer, a CT of the chest was done to rule out a pulmonary embolism, within 3 h of her arrival at the hospital. However, the chest CT unexpectedly showed a mediastinal collection (figure, B), arising from the oesophagus through an orifice that was about 1 cm in diameter. She was started on meropenem. A subsequent endoscopic assessment showed a distal oesophageal perforation communicating with a para-oesophageal abscess (figure, C,D), which was drained in the same procedure. The fluoroscopy after the drainage did not show any mediastinal leakage from the abscess; 24 h after the fluoroscopy, a right thoracic tube was placed because dyspnoea was worsening, and the increased pleural effusion fulfilled the criteria for diagnosis of empyema. The existence of an oesophago-pleural fistula was later suspected because there was a high pleural fluid-serum amylase gradient (pleural amylase concentration 5050 IU/L, concomitant blood amylase level 76 IU/L), and methylene blue was present in pleural fluid after its administration into the abscess cavity. In addition to these observations, the patient also had unremittent fever and bilateral lung opacities, consistent with acute respiratory distress syndrome, so she underwent right thoracoscopy for debridement, drainage, and urokinase instillation. Culture from a mediastinal abscess sample grew Streptococcus oralis and Candida glabrata, thus clindamycin and anidulafungin were added to her treatment regimen.
Eventually, her respiratory insufficiency worsened, so an oesophagectomy was done 7 days after the right thoracoscopy. The patient's condition between the two surgical procedures was characterised by malaise, intermitent fever, and slowly worsening dyspnoea. A new chest CT chest had revealed a right multiloculated pleural empyema. The oesophagectomy involved gastric tubulisation, cervical oesophagogastric anastomosis, and splenectomy. Pathological evaluation showed acute and chronic oesophageal inflammatory changes, multinucleated foreign body giant cells on the abscess wall, and no evidence of neoplasia. The patient was discharged 30 days after admission, and was prescribed atorvastatin, omeprazole, and paracetamol at discharge. Six follow-ups have been made as of June, 2018. She was well in her last follow-up in March, 2018; chest and abdominal CT showed no new, clincally significant abnormalities. The patient was able to eat all kinds of food, and presented with no odynophagia, dysphagia, vomiting, chest pain, abdominal pain, or dyspnoea.
Oesophageal perforation is an uncommon but potentially life-threatening condition. More than 50% of cases are iatrogenic and most of them occur during endoscopy. Other causes of oesophageal perforation include spontaneous perforation (typically resulting from vomiting, called Boerhaave's syndrome), ingestion of a foreign body, trauma, and malignancy. Diagnosis and treatment are often delayed because symptoms might mimic other more frequent disorders. A multidisciplinary approach in specialised centres is strongly recommended to minimise the high morbidity and mortality associated with this complex and challenging condition.

input: A 23-year-old man with autism spectrum disorder and chronic constipation presented to the emergency department with a 1-week history of abdominal pain on his left side, nausea, and vomiting. Physical examination was notable for abdominal distention and mild tenderness to palpation on the left side of the abdomen. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
output:
Based on the clinical history of a 23-year-old man with autism spectrum disorder and chronic constipation, combined with the CT findings showing massive dilation of the rectum and sigmoid colon filled with heterogeneous fecal material (fecal impaction), the diagnosis is a giant fecaloma. The dilation of the rectum (megarectum) distinguishes this from classic Hirschsprung's disease (where the rectum is typically narrow/collapsed), and the solid nature of the contents distinguishes it from volvulus.

A 26-year-old woman presented with recurrent superficial thrombophlebitis on all four limbs, deep vein thrombosis involving the lower limbs, fever, a large fungating non-healing ulcer on the left cubital fossa (figure 1A), episodic abdominal pain, and weight loss for the past 4 months. CT showed thickening and segmental dilatation of the ascending aorta, aortic arch, descending thoracic and abdominal aorta, and its major branches (figure 1B). Whole body 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET showed 18F-FDG avid circumferential wall thickening of the whole aorta and its major branches, without any organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, or lung involvement, suggesting active type V Takayasu arteritis. Skin biopsy revealed suppurative necrotising (predominantly neutrophilic) inflammation of the deep dermis (figure 1C), mixed inflammatory infiltrates, secondary vasculitis (lymphocytic), absence of granulomas, and testing for acid-fast bacilli was negative, consistent with a diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum. The patient was started on oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg) with monthly cyclophosphamide pulses (15 mg/kg) for 12 months. A marked improvement in symptoms and complete healing of the skin lesions with some scarring was seen after 6 months of therapy (figure 1D).Pyoderma gangrenosum is an uncommon manifestation of Takayasu arteritis reported in 1–30% of patients in various studies. Superficial thrombophlebitis and venous thrombosis are also rarely described in Takayasu arteritis. The sites involved include the subclavian vein, jugular vein, and cephalic vein.

The angiography images show characteristic findings of PAN:

- Irregular vessel caliber with areas of stenosis and dilatation
- "String of beads" appearance of affected arteries

The clinical features supporting this diagnosis include:

- Negative ANCA (PAN is typically ANCA-negative)

output:
Hepatojugular reflux (abdominojugular test positive)

The mechanism of this physical examination finding is:

**Impaired right ventricular compliance/right heart failure**

When abdominal pressure is applied, venous return to the right heart increases. In a normal heart, the right ventricle can accommodate this increased preload without significant elevation in central venous pressure. However, in patients with right heart failure or elevated right-sided filling pressures (as in this patient with decompensated heart failure), the right ventricle cannot handle the additional volume load, resulting in a sustained elevation of jugular venous pressure.

This positive abdominojugular reflux test indicates elevated right atrial pressure and is a sign of volume overload and right ventricular dysfunction, consistent with this patient's presentation of decompensated heart failure.

A 33-year-old woman, 28 weeks pregnant, reporting 2 months of increasing discomfort and swelling in her upper abdomen, attended a routine antenatal appointment with her midwife. The patient had otherwise been fit and well and had no previous medical problems; she had stopped using combined oral contraceptives several years earlier.On examination, the woman was well; vital signs were within normal limits and her BMI was 27·3 kg/m2. She was not jaundiced and had no features of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, or infection.
Laboratory investigations—including full blood count, C-reactive protein concentration, urea, creatinine, albumin, electrolytes, and liver function tests—showed no abnormalities.
The findings of an abdominal ultrasound were confirmed by an MRI which showed a 13 cm heterogeneous mass in the left lateral liver segments (figure); no features of liver cirrhosis or vascular malformations were seen.
The patient was referred to our hepatobiliary surgical unit for further investigations—at this stage we were unable to conclude if the mass in the liver was either benign or malignant.
Following the recommendation of our multidisciplinary tumour board, the lesion was biopsied. Histopathological examination of a sample of the biopsy showed hepatocytes without atypia, arranged in two-cell thick trabecular and bland hepatocytes surrounded by fibrous septa containing artery branches; inflammatory infiltrate; and features of chronic cholestasis. Immunohistochemistry showed patchy staining of hepatocytes for glutamine synthetase; CD34 showed patchy sinusoidal staining; glypican 3 and heat shock protein 70 were negative; and staining for oestrogen receptors was positive, and negative for progesterone receptors. The morphology and immune profile were indicative of focal nodular hyperplasia, and we concluded no further intervention was needed. The patient delivered, by caesarean section, a healthy baby girl at gestational age 39 weeks and 6 days.
A CT will be done 6 months after the delivery to check on the liver mass, which we anticipate will reduce in size. For the longer term, the patient will require an ultrasound examination if she becomes pregnant again to ascertain if it has grown further. Additionally, if the mass continues to cause symptoms, and does not reduce in size, there is the option of a laparoscopic resection.

Focal nodular hyperplasia is the second most common benign liver lesion—predominantly occurring in women aged 20–40 years; it rarely bleeds and carries no risk of malignant transition. Hepatocellular adenomas are more common in women and may grow under oestrogen stimulation in pregnancy or oral contraceptive use; large or growing hepatocellular adenomas are at risk of malignant transformation and bleeding.
Fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma—which was a possible differential diagnosis in our case considering the patient's age, gender, and clinical presentation—characteristically appears as a lobulated heterogeneous mass with a central scar in an otherwise normal, non-cirrhotic liver; it is a rare, but highly aggressive liver cancer that demands urgent treatment.

CT scans are associated with radiation issues. And abdominal ultrasounds are not diagnostic—although a contrast-enhanced ultrasound may suggest the diagnosis. Therefore, the three principles of assessing liver masses in pregnancy are: multimodal imaging, multidisciplinary evaluation, and morphologic assessment by histology.

Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated progressive mandibular bone resorption extending from the mandibular body to the condylar regions, prompting referral to the departments of rheumatology, haematology, and oral surgery for further evaluation. A 33-year-old woman, 28 weeks pregnant, reporting 2 months of increasing discomfort and swelling in her upper abdomen, attended a routine antenatal appointment with her midwife. The patient had otherwise been fit and well and had no previous medical problems; she had stopped using combined oral contraceptives several years earlier.On examination, the woman was well; vital signs were within normal limits and her BMI was 27·3 kg/m2. She was not jaundiced and had no features of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, or infection.
Laboratory investigations—including full blood count, C-reactive protein concentration, urea, creatinine, albumin, electrolytes, and liver function tests—showed no abnormalities.
The findings of an abdominal ultrasound were confirmed by an MRI which showed a 13 cm heterogeneous mass in the left lateral liver segments (figure); no features of liver cirrhosis or vascular malformations were seen.
The patient was referred to our hepatobiliary surgical unit for further investigations—at this stage we were unable to conclude if the mass in the liver was either benign or malignant.
Following the recommendation of our multidisciplinary tumour board, the lesion was biopsied. Histopathological examination of a sample of the biopsy showed hepatocytes without atypia, arranged in two-cell thick trabecular and bland hepatocytes surrounded by fibrous septa containing artery branches; inflammatory infiltrate; and features of chronic cholestasis. Immunohistochemistry showed patchy staining of hepatocytes for glutamine synthetase; CD34 showed patchy sinusoidal staining; glypican 3 and heat shock protein 70 were negative; and staining for oestrogen receptors was positive, and negative for progesterone receptors. The morphology and immune profile were indicative of focal nodular hyperplasia, and we concluded no further intervention was needed. The patient delivered, by caesarean section, a healthy baby girl at gestational age 39 weeks and 6 days.
A CT will be done 6 months after the delivery to check on the liver mass, which we anticipate will reduce in size. For the longer term, the patient will require an ultrasound examination if she becomes pregnant again to ascertain if it has grown further. Additionally, if the mass continues to cause symptoms, and does not reduce in size, there is the option of a laparoscopic resection.
Regarding benign liver tumours, haemangiomas are the most prevalent. They occur more frequently in woman; and are often diagnosed in young women in the third, fourth, and fifth decades of life. Focal nodular hyperplasia is the second most common benign liver lesion—predominantly occurring in women aged 20–40 years; it rarely bleeds and carries no risk of malignant transition. Hepatocellular adenomas are more common in women and may grow under oestrogen stimulation in pregnancy or oral contraceptive use; large or growing hepatocellular adenomas are at risk of malignant transformation and bleeding.
Fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma—which was a possible differential diagnosis in our case considering the patient's age, gender, and clinical presentation—characteristically appears as a lobulated heterogeneous mass with a central scar in an otherwise normal, non-cirrhotic liver; it is a rare, but highly aggressive liver cancer that demands urgent treatment.
Pregnancy necessitates a different diagnostic evaluation approach of large liver lesions; radiological investigation with gadolinium-enhanced MRI has shown toxicity to the fetus in animal studies. CT scans are associated with radiation issues. And abdominal ultrasounds are not diagnostic—although a contrast-enhanced ultrasound may suggest the diagnosis. Therefore, the three principles of assessing liver masses in pregnancy are: multimodal imaging, multidisciplinary evaluation, and morphologic assessment by histology.

A 36-year-old woman had dyspnoea on exertion with intermittent chest tightness that occurred during and outside of exertion. She did not disclose any systemic diseases and there was no family history of cardiovascular or pulmonary conditions. An electrocardiogram done during a treadmill test showed ST segment depression without atypical serum concentrations of creatinine kinase or troponin I. A coronary CT angiography showed a so-called rosary-bead appearance and luminal irregularity with ectatic changes over the coronary arteries (figure A–C). Cardiac catheterisation revealed diffuse aneurysmal formations, triple vessel disease (figure D–F) with narrowing over the distal end of the left anterior descending artery, and near-total stenosis over the proximal segment of the left circumflex coronary artery. Her serum cholesterol concentration was 167 mg/dL, low-density lipoprotein concentration was 100 mg/dL, and fasting glucose concentration was 91 mg/dL, which were within normal range. Laboratory studies showed typical C-reactive protein concentration and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and negative results for serum antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, HIV, viral hepatitis, and syphilis. Although the patient did not present with weight loss, livedo reticularis, HBsAg positivity, or elevated diastolic blood pressure or creatinine concentration, typical microaneurysm formations of polyarteritis nodosa were found in the coronary vessels, which is usually the result of transmural necrotising inflammation in the arteries.
Polyarteritis nodosa involving the coronary arteries was diagnosed based on the American College of Rheumatology 1990 classification criteria and the 2012 revised International Chapel Hill Consensus for vasculitides. The patient underwent percutaneous coronary intervention, and a stent was deployed at the left main coronary artery. She was placed on dual antiplatelet therapy, with oral clopidogrel 75 mg and aspirin 100 mg prescribed once daily (until week 138) and oral atorvastatin 20 mg once daily for better lipidaemia control. Oral prednisolone 5 mg was given to the patient during hospitalisation but was discontinued after discharge, due to the patient's concerns about the adverse effects of long-term use. 28 months later, the patient suffered from sudden chest tightness at night. This time, invasive coronary angiogram showed diffuse aneurysmal formations over the left anterior descending artery and right coronary artery. However, there was no indication for further stent placement, and she was discharged from hospital after the procedure. The patient last received cardiac catherisation 6 months ago, and no stent was placed. The patient is still on daily atorvastatin and clopidogrel, and continues to be monitored by appointment once every 3 months.
Polyarteritis nodosa is a disease that causes the inflammation and proliferation of the vascular intima, leading to luminal narrowing and possible vessel occlusion. Polyarteritis nodosa usually leads to multiple microaneurysm formations at the site of the weakened and inflamed vessel walls, the rupture of which can cause severe internal bleeding or death. Although coronary aneurysms can also occur in other conditions—such as Kawasaki disease, Takayasu's arteritis, or arterial infections—the patient's initial presentation, laboratory results, and imaging characteristics of the coronary aneurysms are clinically helpful in the differential diagnosis of various causes of coronary aneurysms. In summary, coronary polyarteritis nodosa is very rare but can be lethal, and early diagnosis with adequate treatment is crucial for better prognosis.

A 71-year-old woman with no medical history of note presented to the Department of Internal Medicine of the Vall d'Hebron University Hospital in August, 2013, with 1 month of joint pain. She also had cutaneous oedema with subcutaneous hardening that started in her legs, then spread to the trunk and arms, affecting the distal region of the limbs. On examination she had mild erythema and mild pitting leg oedema, and hardening of the subcutaneous tissue of the limb, lumbar, and breast areas. Both forearms showed a linear depression in the skin parallel to the course of the superficial veins, more obvious on raising the arm, that was consistent with the groove sign (figure). Blood tests showed a remarkable eosinophilia of 5·2 × 109/L (normal range <0·7 × 109/L). Skin and muscle biopsy showed macrophage infiltration of the fascia with scarce eosinophils, perimisial inflammation, and a dense eosinophilic infiltrate of the vessels, suggestive of eosinophilic fasciitis.
We started the patient on oral prednisone 1 mg/kg per day, that was tapered by 10 mg every 2 weeks to 10 mg daily, starting methotrexate after 3 months as a second-line agent, with rapid resolution of the eosinophilia and the cutaneous oedema, but slow and incomplete recovery of the subcutaneous hardening. 10 months after onset of the disease the hardening of the subcutaneous tissue has started to improve, mainly in the upper limbs, the last area to be affected by the disease. The patient is still taking methotrexate and steroids.
Eosinophilic fasciitis is an uncommon scleroderma-like disorder, first described by Shulman in 1974, characterised by induration of the skin, peripheral eosinophilia, hypergammaglobulinaemia, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Groove sign is a characteristic finding of eosinophilic fasciitis, consisting of a depression along the course of the superficial veins, more marked on elevation of the affected limb. Because the upper dermis and epidermis are spared by the fibrotic process, and the connective tissue around the veins is relatively immobile, the superficial layers of skin can bow inward as the peripheral venous pressure falls.

A 71-year-old woman with no medical history of note presented to the Department of Internal Medicine of the Vall d'Hebron University Hospital in August, 2013, with 1 month of joint pain. She also had cutaneous oedema with subcutaneous hardening that started in her legs, then spread to the trunk and arms, affecting the distal region of the limbs. On examination she had mild erythema and mild pitting leg oedema, and hardening of the subcutaneous tissue of the limb, lumbar, and breast areas. Both forearms showed a linear depression in the skin parallel to the course of the superficial veins, more obvious on raising the arm, that was consistent with the groove sign (figure). Blood tests showed a remarkable eosinophilia of 5·2 × 109/L (normal range <0·7 × 109/L). Skin and muscle biopsy showed macrophage infiltration of the fascia with scarce eosinophils, perimisial inflammation, and a dense eosinophilic infiltrate of the vessels, suggestive of eosinophilic fasciitis.

The patient is still taking methotrexate and steroids.

A man aged 65 years presented to the otorhinolaryngology outpatient clinic at All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi (India), in January, 2018, with a 1-year history of progressive dysphagia to solids, cervical borborygmi (see video appendix 1), sensation of lump in throat, occasional regurgitation of undigested food, and halitosis. He denied any history of weight loss, recurrent cough, hoarseness, or pain. On physical examination a gurgling sound was elicited on pressing the neck (see video appendix 1). Video fluoroscopy revealed stasis of barium in the dilated upper oesophagus extending from C6 to T1 vertebrae (figure and video appendix 2). Trans-nasal oesophagoscopy revealed a large Zenker's diverticulum containing food residue (video appendix 3). The patient underwent endoscopic diverticulectomy. On the day after surgery, the dysphagia and gurgling sounds to liquids disappeared; the patient remained asymptomatic at 12-month follow-up visit.Zenker's diverticulum is an acquired pulsion pseudo-diverticulum originating in Killian's dehiscence, an area bounded by the oblique fibres of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor and the transverse fibres of the cricopharyngeus muscle. It occurs because of increased intraluminal pressure in the hypopharynx during swallowing, caused by an inadequately relaxed cricopharyngeal upper oesophageal sphincter. Boyce's sign, a gurgling sound due to noise of splashing fluid accumulated in a large Zenker's diverticulum, can be heard on palpation. Although small diverticula might not cause symptoms, larger diverticula are usually symptomatic and surgery could be warranted.

Video fluoroscopy revealed stasis of barium in the dilated upper oesophagus extending from C6 to T1 vertebrae (figure and video appendix 2). Trans-nasal oesophagoscopy revealed a large Zenker's diverticulum containing food residue (video appendix 3). The patient underwent endoscopic diverticulectomy. On the day after surgery, the dysphagia and gurgling sounds to liquids disappeared; the patient remained asymptomatic at 12-month follow-up visit.Zenker's diverticulum is an acquired pulsion pseudo-diverticulum originating in Killian's dehiscence, an area bounded by the oblique fibres of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor and the transverse fibres of the cricopharyngeus muscle. It occurs because of increased intraluminal pressure in the hypopharynx during swallowing, caused by an inadequately relaxed cricopharyngeal upper oesophageal sphincter. Boyce's sign, a gurgling sound due to noise of splashing fluid accumulated in a large Zenker's diverticulum, can be heard on palpation. Although small diverticula might not cause symptoms, larger diverticula are usually symptomatic and surgery could be warranted.

A 52-year-old man attended our hospital reporting breathlessness on exertion that had been worsening over the past 2 weeks. He had smoked 20 cigarettes a day for the past 40 years. He had no other symptoms—specifically no systemic or gastrointestinal complaints. The patient had tried to quit smoking 4 months earlier and had started vaping: he had been using commercially available e-cigarettes which did not have any Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) added.The symptoms started some days after the patient had added a new flavour—blueberry—to the vaping fluid.
On examination, we found the patient to be apyrexial, with a blood pressure of 120/80 mm Hg, a heart rate of 70 beats per min, and in sinus rhythm. Auscultation of his chest found no heart murmurs, but we heard vesicular breath sounds with discrete bilateral crepitations over the lung bases.
A high-resolution CT scan of the patient's chest (figure) showed lower lobe predominant, bilateral consolidations in a peribronchovascular distribution—the pattern of organising pneumonia. Extensive diagnostic work-up did not provide any evidence for an infectious or rheumatological aetiology: C-reactive protein concentration and leucocyte count were normal. Antibody screening for hypersensitivity pneumonitis and collagen vascular disease was negative. Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for any pathogenic agents; however, it showed a lymphocytic alveolitis with 70% lymphocytes.
Histopathological examination of a transbronchial lung biopsy confirmed an organising pneumonia, with interspersed pigment-containing macrophages indicating foreign body inhalation.
The patient stopped vaping e-cigarettes and was prescribed systemic steroid therapy, starting with 40 mg of oral prednisolone per day for 4 weeks, reducing by 10 mg per day every 4 weeks—he is currently on 10 mg per day. After 4 months there was no improvement in the patient's symptoms and the imaging findings remained unchanged. 6 months after he first presented, we repeated the bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and cryobiopsy: we found no signs of lymphocytic alveolitis, but histopathology reported a diagnosis of non-specific interstitial pneumonia. We concluded the patient had e-cigarette, or vaping, product use-associated lung injury (EVALI) that had taken a chronic course—starting with the organising pneumonia and evolving into a fibrosing non-specific interstitial pneumonia. Most cases of EVALI reported in the literature have involved patients using e-cigarettes with THC or cannabidiol added to the vaping liquid, where vitamin E is thought to be important in causing the lung damage; however, concerns about the effects of the constituents of the flavourings have also been raised. EVALI cases comprise heterogeneous lung pathologies including acute eosinophilic pneumonia, diffuse alveolar damage and acute respiratory distress syndrome, and—as we initially found in our case—an organising pneumonia (video).

A 41-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of progressive vision loss and headaches. MRI revealed a large sellar tumour with suprasellar extension, which was deemed a probable pituitary macroadenoma (figure A, B). The patient underwent transsphenoidal surgery because of visual field defects and headaches. Histological analysis after surgery revealed a giant cell tumour of bone (GCTB) and symptoms improved; however, 2 months later the large sellar–clival remnant compressing the optic chiasm (figure C, D) motivated a second surgery by pterional craniotomy. After surgery, tumour regrowth occurred (figure E, F), causing diplopia and blurred vision. A third decompressing operation aiming for maximal debulking before denosumab commencement was done endoscopically; however, only partial tumour removal was achieved (figure G, H). Denosumab (120 mg subcutaneously every 28 days) was initiated, and a marked response was noted after 6 months of treatment (figure I, J). After 14 months of denosumab, the patient remained symptom-free without needing further operations (figure K, L).GCTB represent 5–10% of bone tumours, classically affect long bones (<1% of all GCTB have a cranial location) and, although benign, can be locally aggressive. GCTB are histologically characterised by large multinucleated giant cells, but the clinical or radiological differential diagnosis can be challenging. Denosumab, an inhibitor of receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL), can be used to treat GCTB, because RANKL is overexpressed by mononuclear neoplastic stromal cells. As shown here, denosumab should also be considered in the early management of sellar–clival GCTB. This case also highlights the sustained reduction in tumour mass achieved by denosumab, sparing the patient from further operations. If feasible, surgical resection is still preferable as the definitive treatment, because the effect of denosumab wears off after stopping treatment and tumour regrowth can occur. Lifelong denosumab treatment will thus be likely required in this case; however, increasing the intervals between denosumab administration can be attempted to prevent or minimise adverse events, such as osteonecrosis of the jaw or atypical femoral fractures. Although GCTB is usually managed by rheumatologists, oncologists, or orthopaedics, sellar or parasellar GCTB might be first seen by endocrinologists, ophthalmologists, or neurosurgeons, who should be aware of this entity and the potential role of denosumab in its management.
output: Giant cell tumour of bone (GCTB) of the sellar-clival region

A 60-year old woman presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of a painful, swollen left knee and a fever. She had a medical history of osteoarthritis, hypertension, and hyperlipidaemia.On examination she looked unwell; she was tachycardic (heart rate 104 beats per min) and febrile (temperature 39·1°C). She had an effusion on her left knee.
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8·1 g/dL, platelet count of 90 × 109 per L and white blood cell count was 5·1 × 109 per L, but with 6% blasts—confirmed on blood smear. 7 months earlier the patient's blood tests had been normal. Analysis of fluid obtained from arthrocentesis was consistent with pseudogout. An infection screen was negative. However, given the fever with functional neutropenia, we decided to commence her on broad spectrum antibiotics.
Bone marrow examination showed 20–25% blasts and morphology consistent with acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) with myelodysplasia-related changes (figure). Flow cytometry dot plots of the marrow aspirate showed approximately 21% CD34+ and CD117+ myeloblasts (figure). The patient's karyotype was complex—among several abnormalities it included monosomy of chromosome 17 (appendix). Additionally, a pathogenic mutation of the TP53 gene with a variable allele frequency of 64% was detected by next generation DNA sequencing using a 49 gene panel.
Given the patient's comorbidities, her unfit physical state, the complex karyotype, and the TP53 mutation, it was decided, after discussion with her, to try a combination of the hypomethylating agent—azacitidine—and the oral BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax. The patient developed multiple life-threatening events over subsequent weeks including atrial fibrillation, confusion, and renal failure without tumour lysis. After discussion of options, the family opted for comfort measures and the patient was transferred for care in a hospice and died 6 days later.
Among older patients—especially those with adverse genetic findings—AML is often resistant to chemotherapy and long-term survival rates remain low at 10%. Traditionally, treatment involves intensive chemotherapy followed by allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for fit patients. However, most older AML patients are unfit for curative-intent therapy and receive palliative lower intensity regimens. Oral inhibitors of mutant IDH1, IDH2, and FLT3 proteins—found in approximately half of AML patients—are now approved treatments in some countries. In addition to azacitidine with venetoclax, various other combinations have shown improved survival in subpopulations of older AML patients; none of these strategies, however, have been particularly successful in patients with TP53 mutations (appendix; video).
output: Patients with TP53 gene mutations achieve higher cure rates with conventional intensive chemotherapy

A 35-year-old woman presented to our emergency room with a 3-day history of dizziness, nausea, and fatigue. The patient said she had been diagnosed with a brain tumour 2 years earlier; at that time, she reported having diplopia as well as dizziness and fatigue. A stereotactic tumour biopsy was considered, but not done because she made a full recovery with high-dose steroid treatment.On examination, we found no neurological abnormalities, but she had a low blood pressure of 83/39 mm Hg.
Laboratory investigations showed severe hyponatraemia: sodium concentration was 109 mmol/L (normal 135–145). Urine osmolality was 336 mmol/kg (normal 200–1200)—suggesting impaired water excretion—and the urine sodium excretion was 44 mmol/L (normal 60–140)—indicating syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) secretion.
Further endocrine testing confirmed impaired production of corticotropin-releasing hormone: the patient's basal cortisol concentration was 52 nmol/L (normal 166–507) and her adrenocorticotropic hormone concentration was inadequately low 8·2 ng/L (normal <46·0).
A brain MRI showed a contrast-enhancing subthalamic tumefactive lesion, several periventricular lesions, and a lesion adjacent to the midbrain tectum (figure; video); the MRI of the spinal cord was normal.
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed eight leukocytes per μL (normal <5) and a CSF:serum albumin ratio of 6·5 (normal <6·3) with no oligoclonal bands. Further testing showed serum anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies (titre 1:32; normal <1:10), indicating neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD). After 3% saline bolus, fluid restriction, and high-dose steroid treatment, the patient recovered and a further brain MRI, 1 month later, showed marked regression of the subthalamic lesion (figure; video). Off-label rituximab treatment was started 2 months after the patient presented initially, and she remained asymptomatic over the following 6 months while having continuous hydrocortisone replacement.
Retrospective chart analyses reported a SIADH secretion prevalence of about 15% in NMOSD; tertiary adrenal insufficiency due to inflammatory and demyelinating processes affecting the hypothalamus is rare and has mostly been described in multiple sclerosis. The brain circumventricular organs have osmoregulatory functions and are enriched with aquaporin-4 water channels; every patient with SIADH secretion and lesions affecting these organs should be tested for NMOSD. Notably, routine CSF analysis in NMOSD can be normal (video).

input: A 57-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of shortness of breath and dizziness. The physical examination was notable for pallor. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin of 4.4 g per deciliter (reference range, 11.6 to 15.5), an elevated reticulocyte count, an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level, and a low haptoglobin level. The results of hemoglobin electrophoresis and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase testing were normal, and methemoglobin and direct antiglobulin tests were negative. A peripheral blood smear (left, Giemsa staining) showed poikilocytosis, nucleated red cells (black arrows), and polychromatic cells (white arrows). The peripheral blood smear also showed bite cells (left, red arrows), blister cells (left, asterisks), and erythrocyte inclusions (middle, Giemsa staining). The erythrocyte inclusions were identified as Heinz bodies on the basis of positive staining with methyl violet (right). Which of the following is the most likely etiology of this patient’s hemolytic anemia?
output:
Based on the clinical presentation and laboratory findings, the most likely diagnosis is:

**Oxidative hemolytic anemia (drug-induced or toxin-induced)**

The key findings supporting this diagnosis include:
- Severe hemolytic anemia with evidence of hemolysis (elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, elevated reticulocytes)
- **Bite cells** (red arrows) - characteristic of oxidative damage where splenic macrophages remove Heinz bodies
- **Blister cells** (asterisks) - another marker of oxidative injury
- **Heinz bodies** - denatured hemoglobin precipitates confirmed by methyl violet staining, pathognomonic of oxidative stress to red blood cells
- Normal G6PD testing and hemoglobin electrophoresis ruling out G6PD deficiency and hemoglobinopathies

This constellation of findings indicates oxidative hemolytic anemia, most commonly caused by exposure to an oxidizing drug or toxin (such as dapsone, sulfasalazine, nitrites, or other oxidant compounds).

A 63-year-old man attended our department reporting a 3-month history of diffuse pain in both hands. During the subsequent hemithyroidectomy, an ectopic parathyroid gland was discovered and removed, which resulted in an improvement in the calcium and parathyroid hormone concentrations, measured during the operation. Histology showed a clear cell parathyroid adenoma. A 40-year-old man, with no medical history of note, came to see us with a dent in his head (figure). He had noticed the asymmetry about 5 years before, and it had increased progressively ever since. On examination, the scalp was normal. CT of the head showed massive destruction of bone, within a well defined area. A technetium-99m methylene diphosphate bone scan showed increased metabolic activity at the edges of the area. These findings were consistent with Gorham's disease—a rare idiopathic disorder in which one or several bones are destroyed and replaced by connective and vascular tissue. Gorham's disease of the ribs or thoracic vertebrae can lead to chylothorax and life-threatening respiratory failure. Radiotherapy and surgery are the main therapeutic options.

A 9-year-old girl was admitted to our hospital with status epilepticus. Earlier in the day, she had complained of a headache and started vomiting. She then lost consciousness and began having a fit; the status epilepticus lasted 30 min and was stopped by phenobarbital. She had a congenital heart defect—truncus arteriosus with interventricular communication—which was surgically corrected a few days after birth. The girl was on long-term treatment with low-dose aspirin as the antiaggregant. She had no features of Marfan's or Ehlers–Danlos syndromes. Laboratory investigations showed leucopenia, low platelet count, and anaemia. Her C-reactive protein (CRP) was 45 mg/L and her erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 50 mm/h. Her liver enzymes were also slightly raised. A CT scan of her brain showed an intraparenchymal haematoma and intraventricular haemorrhage. Three-vessel arteriography showed a right Sylvian artery aneurysm (figure). Successive blood cultures and broad-range 16S recombinant DNA PCR—as well as PCR for herpes simplex viruses 1–5—were all negative. At this stage, our working diagnosis was endocarditis leading to the mycotic cerebral aneurysm, despite no signs of a fever. We drained the haematoma and commenced treatment with antibiotics; 2 days later, we embolised the aneurysm. The patient recovered and had a mild, left-sided hemiparesis when she left hospital after 4 weeks.1 month later, the girl was brought to the hospital again: weary and malnourished. She was admitted to the paediatric rheumatology unit, where she stayed for 6 weeks for investigation of non-infectious vasculitides associated with autoimmune diseases such as Sjögren's syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus, or juvenille idiopathic arthritis. Investigations showed hyperglycaemia, transaminitis, and raised inflammatory markers—CRP concentration was 10 mg/L and ESR was 50 mm/h. All specific autoantibody tests were negative; however, a liver biopsy specimen showed features of a non-specific, subacute hepatitis without fibrosis or granuloma, and the concentration of peripheral naive T cells was low. Diagnoses under consideration at this stage were an autoimmune vasculitis with or without acquired and congenital immunodeficiencies—a thymectomy had been done at the time of her original operation just after her birth.
At 3-month follow-up, a further cerebral aneurysm was detected, this time involving the contralateral left Sylvian artery (figure). The patient remained tired and benefited from enteral tube feeding. Her liver enzymes were raised to three times the upper limit of normal and her CRP was 15 mg/L. The aneurysm was again embolised and the right ventricle to pulmonary artery conduit was changed; culture of the explanted material did not show anything. We repeated an infectious screen—including Q fever serology, which was positive. A PCR test of liver biopsy material, obtained 3 months earlier, for Q fever was also positive. The girl was treated for 12 months with doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine and made a complete recovery.
Strokes in children are very uncommon. Beware of blood culture-negative and broad-range recombinant DNA PCR-negative results: the diagnosis might be Coxiella burnetii or Q fever.

A 42-year-old man with a history of an intermittent disorder of speech fluency beginning around the age of 4 years without any obvious triggers attended our unit for further investigation; he had agreed to participate in our MRI study on speech production.
The patient had no medical history and on clinical examination we found him to be fit and well.
However, he had moments when his speech fluency was lost; these were episodic, brief—rarely lasting longer than 30 secs—and occurring mostly, but not exclusively, at the beginning of words, and usually, but not always, with consonants rather than vowels. The episodes were markedly exacerbated by environmental stressors and were attenuated by cueing and external rhythms. Previously, several attempts had been made to treat and improve speech fluency with no lasting effect; the speech difficulty remained.
Notably, in his personal history, the patient had left school early to take up a technical apprenticeship. He had avoided professions which were more language-related and obtained an academic degree in engineering after 4 years of evening school.
More recently, he had just participated in speech therapy focusing on different kinds of block releasing techniques, combined with anti-anxiety training. An uncle and his daughter—the patient's cousin—had shown similar speech dysfluencies since they were children.
For our study, we used real-time MRI to non-invasively visualise the movements of the tongue and the oropharynx while the patient read a specially selected piece of text from a screen positioned in his field of vision as he was in the scanner.
The video clip, with 55 MRI images per second, showed a midsagittal cross-sectional plane covering the mouth, mandibular nasal cavities, pharynx, and larynx (figure; video). The intermittent repetitions of syllables and sounds, prolongations of sounds, and audible or silent blockings were visible as spasms and repetitive movements in parts of the tongue, lips, and velum. The video also showed fluent sounding segments of speech, thereby ruling out permanent speech disorders. A speech-language pathologist confirmed the diagnosis of stuttering and categorised it as moderate.
The patient was reassured that the visualisation had delineated his condition clearly and it enabled him to gain a greater understanding into its mechanics.
Stuttering affects about 1% of the adult population, mostly males, and has a high heritability. Relapse after therapy—which includes fluency shaping and block modification techniques—is frequent and often results in the condition continuing for many years. Stuttering can impair social development. Attempts to stop or to avoid stuttering may result in verbal, visual, or situational avoidance, and not speaking in circumstances where the patient would be expected to may be misinterpreted as inappropriate behaviour. Anxiety disorders—including social anxiety disorder and generalised anxiety disorder—are present in about half of the affected individuals and addressing them improves therapy outcomes.
The real-time MRI, which demonstrated the mechanical pathogenesis of the primary symptoms, has improved our understanding of and updates our thinking about stuttering; it gives a better understanding of what the inner articulators do wrong during this type of dysfluent speech.
Additionally, in clinical practice the method may be useful in identifying dysfunctional motor behaviour in speech production disorders. Further, it could potentially be used in visual biofeedback settings to aid in the acquisition and reinforcement of new speech patterns. We acknowledge that the use of a single slice MRI is a limitation that may possibly be overcome with future advances in MRI technology.

input: A 51-year-old woman with a diagnosis of scleroderma-polymyositis overlap syndrome presented to our rheumatology department with widespread subcutaneous skin lesions. On examination, widespread subcutaneous calcification was noted, affecting the elbows, shoulders, hips, knees, buttocks, and ankles. She was positive for anti-nuclear antibodies, anti-La, anti-Ro, and anti-PM-SCL-75 antibodies. Tests for parathyroid hormone, renal function, calcium, and vitamin D were normal. Extensive investigation including PET-CT and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, and chest, abdomen, and pelvis CT excluded malignancy. A biopsy sample of the right thigh showed extensive calcification of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue in association with acute inflammation and necrosis. We found no evidence of calcification of the walls of the dermal and subcutaneous small vessels to suggest calciphylaxis. The appearance of the biopsy sample was consistent with dystrophic calcinosis cutis (figure). The x-ray images showed widespread subcutaneous calcification at the elbows, knees, ankle (including the Achilles tendon), and pelvis. Given the severity of the presentation, we obtained a CT scan of her pelvis to further characterise the extent of disease and to monitor the response to treatment (figure). The widespread distribution of the disease, with long bands of symmetrical subcutaneous calcification, was consistent with a diagnosis of calcinosis universalis. This condition is a more diffuse form of dystrophic calcinosis cutis than calcinosis cutis circumscripta, which is localised to a small area or joint. Calcinosis cutis is extremely rare in overlap connective tissue disease syndromes, with only few reported cases in the scientific literature.The patient is being treated with prednisolone, methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, and minocycline. Previous treatments have included rituximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate, intravenous immunoglobulin, and cyclophosphamide. A temporary improvement was seen in her condition with intravenous thiosulphate. She has had recurrent hospital admissions requiring treatment with intravenous antibiotics for skin and soft tissue infections at the site of calcinosis. Despite these interventions, her calcinosis remains severe and progressive and she is being considered for further intravenous sodium thiosulphate therapy.
output: Calcinosis universalis (dystrophic calcinosis cutis associated with scleroderma-polymyositis overlap syndrome)

A 42-year-old woman with a sudden onset of abdominal pain requested to see us urgently. 5 years earlier she had been diagnosed with paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) and had missed multiple follow-up appointments. Despite having a large PNH clone—greater than 50% of PNH granulocytes—the patient had been asymptomatic with only mildly elevated haemolytic parameters and treatment with eculizumab had been deferred.On examination, she was afebrile and she had slight scleral icterus; vital signs were stable. The patient's liver was palpable with soft edges and there was right upper quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs. The spleen was also palpable approximately 3 cm below the left costal margin.
Laboratory investigations showed elevated liver enzymes: aspartate aminotransferase 164 U/L (normal 13–35), alanine aminotransferase 116 U/L (normal 7–38), total bilirubin concentration 2·9 mg/dL (normal 0·2–1·3). D-dimer concentration was raised at 11 420 ng/mL (normal <500), lactate dehydrogenase was 1 111 U/L (normal 135–214), and her haemoglobin concentration was low at 9·2 g/dL (normal 11·5–15·5).
A CT scan and MRI of the patient's abdomen showed splenomegaly with a heterogeneous appearance of the liver with hypointensity along the vascular territory, tapering occlusion of the hepatic veins, and focal narrowing at the level of the confluence (figure): findings consistent with chronic Budd–Chiari syndrome.
After consultation with the hepatology service, no acute interventions were recommended. The patient was started on apixaban 5 mg twice a day and the anti-complement factor 5 inhibitor, ravulizumab—starting with a loading dose of 3000 mg intravenously (weight-based dose), followed 2 weeks later with a maintenance dose of 3600 mg every 8 weeks.
Notably, deep sequencing of the PIGA gene showed five mutations: two frameshift (p.F150fs, p.E120fs), two missense (p.C81Y, p.S155Y), and one splice site (c.981+1G>A) at a mean total variant allele frequency of 16%.
The patient showed significant clinical improvement with resolution of her abdominal pain after 2 weeks of treatment.
PNH is a non-malignant disorder genetically defined by somatic loss-of-function mutations of the PIGA gene in haematopoietic stem cells. The mutations result in impaired biosynthesis of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI), a glycolipid structure that attaches specific proteins to the cell membrane. Impaired GPI-anchoring results in a deficiency of all GPI-linked proteins on the membranes of blood cells derived from the mutant clone. Among the GPI-linked proteins affected, deficiency of CD55 and CD59 on erythrocytes is responsible for increased sensitivity to complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis—the cardinal symptom of PNH.
In addition to haemolysis, PNH causes bone marrow failure and thrombophilia—the commonest cause of death. While thrombosis may occur at any site, unusual locations are typical of PNH-related hypercoagulability—including hepatic vein thrombosis or Budd–Chiari syndrome which is seen in 10–25% of patients. Thrombosis can be either the initial presentation or can occur in the course of the disease; it is likely to be related to haemolysis as shown by the preventive effects of complement blockade treatment on the rate of this complication (video).

A 43-year-old man was referred to our specialist clinic for α1 antitrypsin deficiency; CT scans showed basal predominant bullae, suggestive of the disease. On review in the clinic, he had no respiratory symptoms. He was a lifelong non-smoker, without any environmental or occupational exposures of note. He reported a history of recurrent bilateral pneumothoraces in his twenties that required bilateral pleurectomies. There was no family history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or emphysema. However, his daughter had a spontaneous pneumothorax at the age of 14 years and his younger sister had a spontaneous pneumothorax at the age of 31 years. Spirometry and the diffusion capacity of the patient's lungs for carbon monoxide were normal. His serum concentration of α1 antitrypsin was normal (concentrations of less than 11 μmol/L are considered abnormal and put the patient at high risk for the development of emphysema). A high-resolution CT scan of his chest (figure) showed numerous, thin-walled cysts in both lungs—predominantly in the bases and sub-pleural areas. These cysts were surrounded by normal lung tissue without evidence of emphysema. A high-resolution CT scan of the chest of his sister, undertaken after she had a spontaneous pneumothorax, showed two small, thin-walled cysts in the left lower lobe (appendix). Given the imaging findings and his family history, genetic testing was done. The patient was found to be heterozygous for a deletion at position 469_471 in the Folliculin (FLCN) gene—confirming a diagnosis of Birt-Hogg-Dubé (BHD) syndrome. Family screening was also done (figure) and all affected family members—the patient's father, two elder sisters, and the patient's son—had high-resolution CT scans of the thorax and MRIs of the kidneys.BHD syndrome is a rare autosomal dominant condition, caused by germline mutations in the FLCN gene. It is characterised by skin fibrofolliculomas, multiple lung cysts, spontaneous pneumothorax, and renal cancer. The cysts in BHD syndrome have several characteristics that may help distinguish them from other causes of diffuse cystic lung disease: they are basal predominant, thin-walled cysts, lentiform in shape and with a predilection for the subpleural region. The most serious complication of BHD syndrome is renal cancer, which has a prevalence of 24–37% in these patients. Once the diagnosis is made, all patients with BHD syndrome should undergo renal imaging at yearly intervals. Pneumothorax occurs in up to 25% of patients and the recurrence rate approaches 75%.
Lung cysts are commonly found on CT scans of the chest and have a wide range of aetiologies including smoking and rare genetic causes such as lymphangioleiomyomatosis. Lung cysts often have distinct characteristics that help to narrow down the diagnosis. In all patients presenting with a pneumothorax, it is crucial to ask about family history and consider doing a high-resolution CT scan of the thorax.

A 24-week pregnant 18-year-old woman was seen at her local health-care centre where she was found to have a respiratory rate of 38 breaths per min, a blood pressure of 250/90 mm Hg, and a heart rate of 39 beats per min. She collapsed and required intubation and ventilation. A chest x-ray showed bilateral infiltrates—pulmonary oedema—and she was treated with furosemide and nitroglycerin and transferred to our intensive care unit.She was not taking any medication, but she did have an etonogestrel—a progestagen only—contraceptive implant put in 6 months earlier. Around the time the implant was put in, she also had a lump in her right breast; a biopsy found it to be benign proliferative breast tissue. She had no significant medical or social history and there was no history of breast or ovarian cancer in her family.
On examination, we found the patient's breasts were asymmetrical; both were erythematous, tender, and had focal, palpable, mobile masses (figure). The skin of both breasts had a peau d'orange pattern. We found no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. At this initial assessment, we were concerned for possible inflammatory breast cancer; a diagnostic mammogram and an ultrasound (figure) showed large bilateral masses. Given the skin findings, the rapid growth, and the large, irregular, and heterogeneous nature of the masses, our radiologist assigned a Breast Imaging-Reporting and Data System category of 5—indicating that we considered the lesion highly suspicious of malignancy.
Histopathological examination of samples taken from both breasts, using core-needle biopsies, showed prominent pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia (PASH) and mammary hamartomas.
We then removed the implant, and 1 week later, the patient reported significant reduction in breast size, pain, pressure, and erythema. We advised her against future use of exogenous hormonal therapies with the aim of reducing the likelihood of recurrence. She is planning to have both masses excised and oncoplastic reconstructive surgery carried out.
PASH masses can resemble breast cancer both on examination and at imaging, and tissue sampling is imperative for diagnosis. PASH is a hormone-sensitive process and rapid progression can occur with sudden hormonal changes, which given the timeline we believe was the case with our patient—the contraceptive implant being the source of the excess hormone. PASH should be considered as an important differential diagnosis of breast hypertrophy in a premenopausal patient, particularly in the context of changes to the hormonal milieu.
The risk of developing breast cancer is not increased with PASH, and so follow-up using standard mammographic screening is recommended (video).

A 45-year-old woman presented to our emergency department with a 4-h history of diplopia and vertigo.
The patient had been found to have a bicuspid aortic valve without any significant dysfunction; the bicuspid valve had been diagnosed when she was aged 25 years by transthoracic echocardiography when investigated for a systolic murmur. The patient was a non-smoker; she had previously been fit and well, and she was taking no medications.
On examination after admission, she was well and alert; her temperature was 36·7°C, blood pressure 186/105 mm Hg, and pulse rate 83 beats per min. She had ataxia in her arms.
An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm. Laboratory investigations showed a mildly increased C-reactive protein concentration of 18 mg/L (normal <5); leukocytes and procalcitonin concentration were in normal range.
A brain MRI showed cerebellar bilateral ischaemic lesions; and transoesophageal echocardiography showed findings consistent with a marked thickening of the aortic leaflets with hypoechogenic masses, which was causing mild aortic regurgitation (figure; video).The hospital endocarditis team assessed the patient; empirical treatment with antibiotics—amoxicillin and ceftriaxone—was started after collection of four samples for blood cultures. Additionally, serological testing for bacteria—including Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella spp, Aspergillus spp, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Brucella spp, and Legionellla pneumophilia—causing blood culture-negative endocarditis, was carried out.
Antibiotics were stopped after 3 weeks—given from day 1 of the admission to day 21—after all microbiological results came back negative. Assays for antiphospholipid, rheumatic factor, and antinuclear antibodies were also negative; moreover, a workup for disseminated intravascular coagulation was also negative.
To investigate for possible peripheral emboli, a thoracic CT scan was done which showed a left inferior lung mass with mediastinal and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (figure). An 18fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT showed intense metabolic fixation of all tumour targets (figure). After lymphadenomectomy puncture, histopathological analysis of samples of a transthoracic needle biopsy of the lesion showed a solid architecture invasive adenocarcinoma; mucin-secreting cells were strongly positive for tumour marker thyroid transcription factor-1 and intensely positive (3+ in 100% of cells) for ALK-EML4 on immunohistochemical analysis. Fluorescence in situ hybridisation analysis found an ALK gene rearrangement in 93% of the nuclei, characterised by supernumerary red signals.
A diagnosis of marantic endocarditis was made and tyrosine kinase inhibitor treatment with crizotinib—an ALK inhibitor—was initiated on day 19. The patient described a transient visual disturbance 48 h later. Brain MRI showed additional small ischaemic lesions; owing to the perceived risk of intracranial bleeding due to recent brain infarcts, anticoagulation was not initiated. No subsequent neurological events were noted.
2 months after crizotinib initiation, the heart valve lesions had disappeared with no perforation or deterioration of function (figure; video). An 18F-FDG PET/CT confirmed a complete metabolic response (figure).
At 7-year follow-up, the patient is alive and well without cancer or evidence of marantic endocarditis.
Advanced malignancy is associated with marantic endocarditis, although it may be found with autoimmune diseases including systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis. Treatment of the underlying cause—in our case the malignancy—may lead to resolution of the valvular lesions.

The 4-day history and 1-month treatment duration fit the timeline for dapsone toxicity or acquired methemoglobinemia.

An 80-year-old woman was referred to the Chitose City Hospital (Chitose, Japan) with a 6 month history of a slowly increasing asymptomatic lumbar subcutaneous mass. She had been attending dialysis three-times a week for 10 years for chronic renal failure. A laboratory assessment showed the following abnormalities: serum calcium of 1·95 mmol/L (normal range 2·05–2·55), serum phosphorus of 3·3 mmol/L (0·74–1·52 mmol/L), serum intact parathyroid hormone of 142 ng/L (10–65 ng/L), and serum creatinine of 787 μmol/L (53–106 μmol/L). She was poorly compliant with taking phosphate-binding medications and dietary restrictions. Physical examination showed a firm, irregularly shaped, immobile subcutaneous nodule measuring 9 cm in the major axis on her right lumbar area (figure, A). CT scans showed a lobular calcified mass with fibrous capsules in the subcutis (figure, B, C). 67Ga-scintigram showed an abnormal gallium accumulation corresponding to the right lumbar mass, with no other pathological uptake (figure, D). After a diagnosis of secondary tumoral calcinosis was made, the patient was managed by use of a phosphate-restricted diet, phosphate-binding medication, and an intensifying dialysis programme, which aimed to reduce the serum concentration of calcium–phosphorus products.
output: Tumoral calcinosis (secondary to chronic renal failure/secondary hyperparathyroidism)

A 16-year-old boy was referred to our emergency department after falling off his motorcycle. He had no past medical history. On examination, he had a right sided hemiplegia and grade 4/6 systolic murmur. Brain MRI showed a left middle cerebral artery infarction (figure A). At echocardiography, a vegetation attached to a flail anterior mitral leaflet, and severe mitral regurgitation were seen (figure B), suggestive of ruptured chordae tendineae caused by infective endocarditis. A 1 cm diameter ring-form cystic lesion was also seen on the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve (figure B). Blood cultures grew Streptococcus viridans. We diagnosed our patient with an embolic stroke due to infective endocarditis. Our patient had a mitral valve replacement 4 weeks after presentation. During the operation, the cystic mass and vegetation were removed (figure C and D); histological examination showed a blood cyst and infective endocarditis. Cardiac blood cysts are congenital; they are usually asymptomatic, but can predispose to regurgitation, infective endocarditis, and cerebral emboli. However, they usually regress spontaneously and rarely persist into adolescence or adulthood.
