A 75-year-old woman who attended for a routine x-ray appointment was given the all-clear after the image was reported as having no atypical findings (figure). On examination the patient was generally well; a chest examination found no abnormalities.
Laboratory investigations—including a complete blood count, serum C-reactive protein concentration, and serum cryptococcal antigen—showed no atypical findings; tumour markers—including carcinoembryonic antigen, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, and squamous cell carcinoma antigen—were also normal.
Chest CT showed a nodule measuring 10 mm located dorsally to the heart and descending aorta and obscured by bronchial shadowing, making visibility difficult by chest x-ray (figure).
A provisional diagnosis of lung metastasis from the rectal and anal cancer was made; the patient had a thoracoscopic partial pulmonary resection with no postoperative problems. Histopathological examination of a sample of tissue removed from the 12 mm × 8 mm lesion, during the operation, showed a moderate to well differentiated tubular adenocarcinoma confirming the diagnosis of lung metastasis from the rectal cancer.
At 3-month follow-up, no evidence of recurrence of cancer was seen on a repeat chest x-ray reviewed by a radiologist and the AI package. The patient reported that she was well with no respiratory symptoms.
In recent years, there have been many attempts to provide easy chest x-ray-based automated diagnosis using machine learning and deep learning. Computer-aided diagnosis is beginning to be incorporated in diagnostic processes, reducing physicians’ workloads.
The diagnostic performance of AI-based chest x-ray has reached the same accuracy as that of radiologists, and in some cases may exceed it (video).

A 40-year-old woman was referred to our clinic by her optometrist because she had lesions on her retina suggestive of age-related macular degeneration (AMD). She was otherwise well: with no systemic or visual symptoms.In her medical history, the patient had no previous problems with her eyesight. However, at the age of 10 years, she had developed end-stage renal disease—initially diagnosed as post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis—which eventually resulted in her having a right kidney transplant when she was 22 years old. 6 years later, aged 28 years, she developed signs of rejection and required hospitalisation. At that stage, a kidney biopsy led to a diagnosis of dense deposit disease (DDD). She received a second kidney transplant at age 39 years.
She had been prescribed a combination of immunosuppressive drugs—prednisolone, mycophenolate, and tacrolimus—for the past 2 years, and her blood pressure had remained stable without pharmacotherapy.
On examination, we found her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Fundus examination showed drusen-like deposits in the macula and numerous lesions in the peripheral retina of both eyes (figure). Optical coherence tomography showed subretinal dome-shaped deposits—known as drusen—in the peripheral retina, with some encroaching in the macular region of both eyes (figure). Drusen is the plural form of druse, a German word meaning node or geode.
Considering the situation in the round, including the patient's age and medical history, and the appearance and distribution of the fundus lesions, we concluded that the drusen were a feature of DDD rather than AMD. The patient continues to be followed up by both her nephrologist and ophthalmologist.

Patients with DDD have diffuse, dense deposits in the glomerular basement membrane, and unlike other forms of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, they also typically have drusen deposits in Bruch's membrane of the eye. It is a rare disease that usually presents in children aged 5–15 years old and eventually leads to end-stage renal disease.
Drusen in patients with DDD typically develop after more than 20 years, and although the retinal lesions do not directly cause visual impairment, vision can deteriorate, most commonly due to macular detachment, central serous chorioretinopathy, or choroidal neovascularisation similar to patients with AMD.
Anyone under the age of 50 years found to have retinal drusen should therefore be assessed for renal disease at the time of presentation, and should have regular ophthalmic examinations to monitor for the development of potential vision-threatening changes (video).

A 2-year-old boy presented for severe frostbite after being outside on a cold day (mean temperature –18°C). The child had reportedly spent 20–30 minutes outside and was found without gloves. Eight fingers (1–5 on the right hand, and 1, 2, and 5 on the left hand) first appeared pale, then developed severe blisters. He was admitted for wound care, surgical debridement of necrotic skin, and pain control. At first, radiographs of the hands were typical (appendix). The patient was discharged home after 2 weeks, following a favourable evolution. 1 year later, he presented with widened interphalangeal joints in the eight fingers affected by frostbite. On x-ray, there was substantial damage to the metaphyses and epiphyses (figure A). Conservative treatment (occupational therapy and splinting) was started. During follow up, joint damage progressed to deformity and growth restrictions in the affected fingers (appendix). At the age of 17 years, there is substantial joint and bone damage, finger shortening, and nail dystrophy in the eight fingers affected by frostbite (figure B and C). The patient does not report any joint pain or stiffness and has a near-typical functional status.
Frostbite is cold-induced tissue damage, with lack of supervision and alcohol and drug use as common risk factors in children and adolescents. Short-term complications include severe pain, infections, and tissue necrosis (ranging from skin blisters to extensive gangrene). Long-term sequelae include neuropathic pain, vasospasm, nails dystrophy, and risk for squamous cell-carcinoma. Additionally, frostbite arthropathy can appear months to years after the acute episode. In an immature skeleton, frostbite arthropathy can exceptionally result in physeal, growth plate, and epiphyseal destruction of affected phalanges. The frequency of this complication is unknown, with only a few historical cases published. Physicians should be aware of this rare complication of severe paediatric frostbite, which can occur even after an initially favourable evolution. In the absence of curative treatment, prevention of cold-induced injuries (especially in at-risk familial and environmental contexts) remains crucial.
output: Frostbite arthropathy with physeal and epiphyseal destruction

A 45-year-old man presented to the rheumatology outpatient unit with bilateral swelling of the hands from the proximal segments of the fingers to the wrist that developed gradually over the past 3 years (figure). The oedema was non-pitting and was not affected by raising the hands. Function of the hands and fingers was not impaired. He had no generalised or pretibial oedema. The patient reported drinking 1–1·5 L of wine per day; medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Blood tests and an ultrasound scan confirmed hepatitis (alanine aminotransferase [ALT] 175 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase [AST] 170 IU/L, albumin 4·68 mg/dL) with a positive antibody test for hepatitis C virus; hepatitis B virus and HIV tests were negative. Rheumatoid factor was 29 IU/mL (normal <14 IU/mL); anti-nuclear antibodies, anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies, complement, protein electrophoresis, and total bilirubin were normal. On further questioning he admitted that he had been injecting high-dose sublingual buprenorphine for more than 5 years, preferentially in the wrist either into or around the veins, three to four times a day.Puffy hand syndrome is a complication of intravenous drug misuse. Users themselves are often aware of the risk, particularly from hand injections, but most physicians, including addiction specialists and general practitioners, rarely encounter this presentation and might not be familiar with it. The frequency of puffy hand syndrome is unknown. The pathogenesis of the oedema probably includes venous and lymphatic insufficiency, and the direct toxicity of injected drugs. Biopsy samples of skin and subcutaneous tissue and lymphangiograms can show destruction of the lymphatics that leads to fibrosis of the subcutaneous tissue, probably due to soluble compounds of the drugs that damage lymphatic vessels. Treatment with low-stretch bandaging and the wearing of elastic garments help to decrease the volume in puffy hand syndrome.

A 30-year-old woman was referred to our urology clinic reporting a 2-year history of pain in the right flank. The patient said the pain was worse after physical exercise or after standing up for a long time; after these activities, she said a painful abdominal mass would be present, which subsequently disappeared when she rested for a few minutes in a supine decubitus position. Additionally, she reported that her symptoms, which had started without any identified reason, had been getting worse and had begun to affect her ability to carry out her daily routine. The patient had no medical history and said she was otherwise healthy.
On examination, she was generally well; blood pressure was 95/65 mm Hg, pulse was 70 beats per min, and oxygen saturation was 100%. We found no masses or organomegaly. However, she showed us photographs of the abdominal mass in her right iliac fossa, which appeared after standing up for 30 min or after doing physical exercise.
Laboratory investigations were within typical range—notably renal function was normal. Urinalysis showed proteinuria of >300 mg/dL (typical range <150) and microhaematuria.
A CT and MRI showed bilateral simple renal cysts and a calyceal diverticulum, but these findings were not a satisfactory explanation of the patient's symptoms; there was no dilation of any part of the urinary system.
Intravenous urography (IVU), while the patient was standing over a period of 30 min, initially showed the right kidney in a typical position in the abdomen with no dilation of any part of the urinary tract (figure). However, during the investigation, the right kidney gradually descended towards the pelvis causing increasing ureteral ectasia. And by the end of the 30 min, the right ureter had completed folded over itself producing an acute obstructive uropathy with the patient reporting intense pain (figure).
After discussion with the patient—who reiterated that the severity of the pain impacted upon her daily life—we proceeded to do a laparoscopic right nephropexy to the abdominal wall. The patient recovered and was allowed home 2 days after the operation.
6 months later, a diuretic renogram showed preserved parenchymal function and non-obstructive excretion curves. A multiphase renal CT scan showed no complications or stenosis of the upper urinary tract; the patient was able to return to work and to do physical exercise.
Nephroptosis, also known as floating kidney, is a differential diagnosis of unexplained abdominal pain which would include renal or intestinal infarction, nutcracker syndrome, ovarian vein syndrome or pelvic inflammatory disease in young women, and complications of a pelvic cyst—renal or ovarian.Vertical nephroptosis, defined as a renal drop in the vertical position of ≥5 cm or the height of two vertebral bodies, is usually an accidental finding on IVU. Only 10% of patients—typically young, thin women—develop symptoms. Surgical correction is needed when it causes chronic complaints and worsens the quality of life—as in our patient. The symptoms, when present, are usually diagnostic. Complications include impaired renal function; ureteral obstruction and subsequent calculi and pyelonephritis; and hypertension and renal ischaemia resulting from elongation, twisting, or angulation of renal vessels.
output: Nephroptosis (floating kidney) with acute obstructive uropathy

The patient had also been previously treated successfully with interferon for a hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection when he was 35 years old.
On examination we found moderate, bilateral ankle effusions, pain on both active and passive movement of the joints and marked bone deformity of his feet—he had pes planus and hypertrophic growth of the midfoot region. He also had tenderness at the plantar fascial insertions but no gouty tophi.
x-rays of his feet showed significant heterotrophic ossification of the entheses of all hind and midfoot bones (figure) and fluid analysis from an ankle joint aspirate showed monosodium urate crystals.
We therefore attributed his symptoms to a gout flare precipitated by acute kidney injury and septicaemia. We treated him with colchicine and the pain reduced; we later confirmed that the gout flare had resolved with a dual-energy CT scan that showed no urate crystals. Despite the negative finding on the dual-energy CT scan, the patient continued to experience arthralgia in his ankles. We carried out further investigations to clarify the additional, underlying aetiology—namely, the X-linked hypophosphataemia. The serum phosphate concentration was low (0·63 mmol/L; normal 0·75–1·50) and the calcitriol concentration was also low (19 pmol/L; normal 48–190); additional investigations were normal (appendix). CT scans of the patient's feet, ankles, and pelvis showed extensive enthesopathy (figure).

Hypophosphataemia is caused by poor absorption of phosphate in the intestine and impaired renal tubular reabsorption, with normal serum calcium, parathyroid hormone, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels. The calcitriol is often low or normal in X-linked hypophosphataemia: findings that would be unexpected in cases where there is an increased level of calcitriol.
Patients have a range of medical problems depending on age. In children, problems include delayed and disproportionate growth, craniosynostosis, and rickets. In adults, problems include inappropriate mineralisation of fibrocartilage—tendons insert into bone leading to the development of spurs or enthesophytes, which results in joint stiffness and pain or enthesopathy—as in our patient. Adult patients mainly complain of arthralgia of the knees, hip, and back. Traditional treatment with oral phosphate and calcitriol may improve the rate of growth and mineralisation in childhood but fails to stop the progressive enthesopathy and arthropathy found in adulthood. Arthralgia may develop because of degenerative arthropathy which is a consequence of the progressive enthesopathy altering the architecture and mechanics of the foot.
Enthesopathy can occur in psoriatic arthritis, heavy metal exposure, skeletal fluorosis, hyperparathyroidism, and other heritable forms of hypophosphataemia. HCV-related osteosclerosis—which was included in the differential diagnoses in this case—can cause bone pain; however, it is not associated with enthesopathy and is characterised by accelerated bone turnover (video).

A 52-year-old right-handed woman was referred to our clinic reporting a 4-year history of spontaneous unpredictable episodes of dizziness. The patient was seen remotely due to restrictions imposed because of the COVID-19 pandemic. She described the episodes as a sudden sensation of feeling like the room was spinning for 5–40 s; they were happening approximately three times a day and she could identify no triggers. Occasionally, the episodes were associated with nausea and vomiting; they had also caused her to fall but did not result in any impairment of consciousness. The patient reported no visual symptoms, tinnitus, or headache. She was otherwise in good health and took no regular medication.The referral, from the otorhinolaryngology clinic via the family doctor, reported a negative Dix-Hallpike test and failure to improve the patient's symptoms with the Epley manoeuvre. The referrer diagnosed Ménière's disease—a triad of tinnitus, vertigo, and hearing loss—and prescribed the patient a trial of betahistine, bendroflumethiazide, and prochlorperazine with no benefit.
On remote examination the patient appeared well, although further examination was limited as there was no opportunity to test for nystagmus.
Laboratory investigations, previously arranged by the family doctor, had shown no atypical findings—full blood count, renal profile, and liver function were all within normal range. A brain MRI, which had been done 1 year before our consultation, as part of the initial work-up, showed normal brain parenchyma and ventricular system. We requested a further MRI to include high-resolution axial T2-weighted sequences of the posterior fossa; this showed a prominent left-sided vascular loop extending into the internal auditory meatus and causing compression of the left eighth cranial nerve—consistent with our suspected diagnosis of vestibular paroxysmia (figure). We prescribed the patient carbamazepine and she reported that her symptoms had resolved completely soon after commencing the treatment.
Vestibular paroxysmia is a rare cause of spontaneous, brief, and recurrent attacks of vertigo; episodes can be significantly disabling. The diagnosis—as in our patient—often goes unrecognised for many years. The key features differentiating vestibular paroxysmia from more common causes of vertigo are the spontaneity, the brevity, and the frequency. Regarding spontaneity, attacks are not typically triggered by head movement; syndromes to consider if attacks are triggered by head movement include benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, central positional nystagmus (caused by cerebellar and brainstem lesions), and bow hunter syndrome (vertebrobasilar insufficiency resulting from vertebral artery occlusion during neck rotation, usually from cervical spondylosis). Regarding brevity, attacks are usually < 1min; syndromes to consider if episodes are longer include Ménière's disease (typically attacks last 20 min to 12 h) and vestibular migraine (5 min to 72 h). And finally, regarding frequency, attacks occur up to 30 or more times per day; syndromes where episodes are less frequently include vertebrobasilar transient ischaemic attacks and epileptic vertigo.
Although infrequently encountered, vestibular paroxysmia is a condition to be aware of since it is an eminently treatable cause of dizziness and could very easily be mistaken for more common causes. MRIs typically show neurovascular compression of the eighth cranial nerve—radiologists should be asked to specifically look for this.

A 68-year-old woman undergoing a routine surveillance endoscopy—part of her follow-up for a Barrett's oesophagus—was found to have a solitary, black lesion, approximately 4 mm in diameter, in the gastric body (figure). Biopsy samples were taken and microscopic examination showed gastric body mucosa with heavily pigmented cells in the lamina propria that infiltrated the crypts without destroying them (figure). Immunohistochemical examination of the biopsied tissue section showed positive staining for melanoma associated antigens using antibodies. Her medical history included the enucleation of her left eye 13 years earlier to remove a primary uveal melanoma; she had been discharged from routine follow-up. We then decided to carry out another gastroscopy to take deeper gastric biopsy samples. These showed infiltration of the muscularis mucosae by melanocytes with mild atypia. A full-body CT scan showed multiple lesions in her liver, which on subsequent MRI were confirmed to be melanin-laden metastases (figure). Gene mutation panel testing of the gastric biopsy specimens and of the ocular specimens taken at the time of the eye operation 13 years earlier showed the same oncogenic mutation: Gln209Leu in GNA11. Tests for the common cutaneous melanoma mutations in BRAF, NRAS, and KIT genes were negative. The patient was enrolled in a clinical trial testing a combination of selumetinib and paclitaxel chemotherapy for metastatic uveal melanoma. Uveal melanoma is a rare cancer representing less than 5% of all melanomas; it has a nearly 50-fold lower incidence rate than that of cutaneous melanomas. It is an aggressive disease, predominantly spreading to the liver in up to 50% of patients. Median survival with liver metastases is less than 6 months. Currently, there are no effective non-surgical treatments for metastatic uveal melanoma. Surveillance and monitoring of the liver—after treatment of the primary lesion—are recommended so that patients can receive early locoregional treatments. The length of time patients should be followed up is not established in current clinical guidelines. Uveal melanoma is associated with an almost linear continuation of recurrence over time and beyond 10 years without a plateau in risk of recurrence. Thus, late recurrences are not uncommon: 5 and 10 year cumulative metastasis rates are 25% and 34%, respectively. Cutaneous and uveal melanomas are biologically distinct. Uveal melanomas lack the typical cutaneous melanoma-associated mutations in the BRAF, NRAS, and NF1 genes, but have somatic mutations in the GNA11 and QNAQ genes in around 90% of cases; in cutaneous melanomas mutations in these genes are found in less than 10% of cases. Mutations in these genes activate the mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase oncogenic pathway, providing a rationale for using MEK1/2 inhibitors, selumetinib for example, as agents in clinical trials results—although to date the results have been disappointing. Functionally activating mutations in GNAQ and GNA11, as well as in CYSLTR2 and PLCB4, leads to the subsequent activation of pathways—which include the phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase and Yap/Hippo pathways—downstream beyond the MAP kinase pathway. These may offer potential novel therapeutic targets. Genetic profiling of primary uveal melanomas has some prognostic value. For example, inactivating mutations in the BAP1 gene—found in approximately 50% of cases—are highly likely to metastasise, whereas mutations in the SF3B1 and EIF1AX genes, occurring in approximately 19% and 24% of uveal melanoma cases, respectively, are less likely to metastasise.

input: A 46-year-old man presented with left lower quadrant pain, tenderness, and rebound tenderness on examination. He was afebrile and did not have leucocytosis. The abdominal CT showed a hypodense pericolonic oval mass of 2·5 cm with adjacent fat stranding: a classic picture of epiploic appendagitis (figure). Epiploic appendages are roughly 50–100 pedunculated adipose structures protruding from the serosal surface of the colon from the caecum to the rectosigmoid junction. Torsion of the pedicle or central venous thrombosis could cause epiploic appendagitis, which can simulate diverticulitis, appendicitis, and cholecystitis. Fever, chills, and leucocytosis are usually absent. In addition to the CT indicating this diagnosis, a non-compressible hyperechoic mass connected to the adjacent colon at the point of maximum tenderness on ultrasonography is indicative of epiploic appendages. Epiploic appendagitis needs only conservative management and pain control; however, failure to recognise this diagnosis could lead to unnecessary intervention.

A 28-year-old Egyptian woman was referred to our specialised gestational trophoblastic disease clinic for treatment. She explained that 2 years earlier, her menstrual cycle had changed and become irregular with prolonged heavy bleeding lasting between 15 and 20 days; before this, her periods had been regular, lasting 30 days with 5 days of bleeding. The woman had two children and no history of contraceptive use, hormonal therapy, or any other medications. 3 months after the irregular bleeding started, the patient visited her local gynaecologist, who reported no uterine or cervical disease and prescribed diosmin tablets. At this stage, the patient's haemoglobin concentration was 10 g/dL—importantly, her urine and serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels were not measured. The bleeding did not improve, and she had dilation and curettage of the uterus, during which a biopsy specimen was taken from the endometrium: histology showed a disordered proliferative endometrium. The woman was advised to take combined oral contraceptive pills, which only resulted in a reduction of the bleeding.6 months later, a transvaginal ultrasound showed focal anterior myometrial thickening, with increased blood flow seen on doppler ultrasound, which was reported as being adenomyosis (figure). Hysteroscopic endometrial resection was recommended, but the procedure was not completed because of severe bleeding during surgery. The bleeding continued postoperatively and the patient's general condition deteriorated: her haemoglobin concentration dropped to 6 g/dL. She was given a blood transfusion to stabilise her condition and then returned to theatre for a life-saving, uncomplicated abdominal hysterectomy. Histopathological examination of the uterus showed an invasive mole with no evidence of uterine perforation. The serum hCG concentration was 550 IU/L, and she was treated with two courses of methotrexate, which led to remission.
Our case illustrates that a crucial investigation of the cause of uterine bleeding—which can be attributed to numerous conditions including fibroids, adenomyosis, and an invasive mole—is a pregnancy test. An ultrasound cannot clearly differentiate between some of the causes and an endometrial biopsy might not detect lesions located deep in the myometrium.
To reiterate, hCG levels in the urine should be checked during the initial assessment of abnormal uterine bleeding because trophoblastic tumours are often easily cured with the single agent methotrexate without the need for a hysterectomy.

In adults, EMH typically occurs in the presence of myeloproliferative malignancies. That it is also associated with other conditions—including thalassemia—is well appreciated.
Sites commonly affected are the spleen, liver, and lymph nodes; paravertebral areas, heart, chest, thymus, kidney, adrenal gland, prostate, pleura, nerves in the skin and spinal canal may be involved, but less frequently. On discovering a site of EMH, extensive investigations should be made to find the cause; appropriate treatment can then be started.
EMH in unusual locations—as seen in our patient—needs regular monitoring, and in selected cases where the lesion is causing local symptoms, surgical resection might be considered; not a realistic possibility in this case.

A 28-year-old Egyptian woman was referred to our specialised gestational trophoblastic disease clinic for treatment. She explained that 2 years earlier, her menstrual cycle had changed and become irregular with prolonged heavy bleeding lasting between 15 and 20 days; before this, her periods had been regular, lasting 30 days with 5 days of bleeding. The woman had two children and no history of contraceptive use, hormonal therapy, or any other medications. 3 months after the irregular bleeding started, the patient visited her local gynaecologist, who reported no uterine or cervical disease and prescribed diosmin tablets. At this stage, the patient's haemoglobin concentration was 10 g/dL—importantly, her urine and serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels were not measured. The bleeding did not improve, and she had dilation and curettage of the uterus, during which a biopsy specimen was taken from the endometrium: histology showed a disordered proliferative endometrium. The woman was advised to take combined oral contraceptive pills, which only resulted in a reduction of the bleeding.6 months later, a transvaginal ultrasound showed focal anterior myometrial thickening, with increased blood flow seen on doppler ultrasound, which was reported as being adenomyosis (figure). Hysteroscopic endometrial resection was recommended, but the procedure was not completed because of severe bleeding during surgery. The bleeding continued postoperatively and the patient's general condition deteriorated: her haemoglobin concentration dropped to 6 g/dL. She was given a blood transfusion to stabilise her condition and then returned to theatre for a life-saving, uncomplicated abdominal hysterectomy. Histopathological examination of the uterus showed an invasive mole with no evidence of uterine perforation. The serum hCG concentration was 550 IU/L, and she was treated with two courses of methotrexate, which led to remission.
Our case illustrates that a crucial investigation of the cause of uterine bleeding—which can be attributed to numerous conditions including fibroids, adenomyosis, and an invasive mole—is a pregnancy test. An ultrasound cannot clearly differentiate between some of the causes and an endometrial biopsy might not detect lesions located deep in the myometrium.
To reiterate, hCG levels in the urine should be checked during the initial assessment of abnormal uterine bleeding because trophoblastic tumours are often easily cured with the single agent methotrexate without the need for a hysterectomy.

This is a classic presentation where the mobile cecum twists, causing obstruction and ischemia, indicated by the specific "comma" or "bean" shape on the X-ray.

A 64-year-old woman presented with multiple asymptomatic, erythematosus papulopustular facial lesions (figure, A). The patient had been diagnosed with rosacea, and received oral doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily for 3 weeks as first-line therapy by her family doctor. Because of the poor response to therapy, she had been referred to our dermatology clinic for further evaluation. On clinical examination, the eruptions, which were practically asymptomatic, had a rosacea-like appearance. They had emerged and gradually worsened over a period of 5 weeks. There were no pathological findings on physical examination and routine laboratory test results were normal. Microscopic examination of specimens collected from the patient's skin by epidermal scraping showed many Demodex folliculorum mites (figure, B, magnification ×100). The patient showed substantial improvement after treatment with oral metronidazole (250 mg three times daily for 2 weeks) and subsequent weekly topical permethrin (cream 5%).
Demodex spp are common saprophytic vermiform mites, which asymptomatically parasitise the hair follicles and the pilosebaceous glands of mammals. In human beings, two species of acarid mite have been identified: Demodex folliculorum and Demodex brevis. Sites favoured by Demodex spp mites include the scalp, forehead, and chin, and areas around the orbit, nose, and mouth. Demodex spp have been implicated in the development of various facial conditions, including pityriasis folliculorum, rosacea-like demodicidosis (also known as demodicosis), pustular folliculitis, demodectic blepharitis, and so-called “demodicidosis gravis”. Clinical features of Demodex spp infestation include erythematopapulous and pustulous skin lesions together with erythematodesquamative changes of the face. Furthermore, demodicidosis should also be considered in any patient with rosacea-like dermatitis resistant to conventional rosacea therapies.
Although there is no consensus to how and what degree infestation with Demodex spp mites contributes to skin pathology, there is evidence that demodicidosis is a condition distinct from common rosacea. The prevalence of Demodex spp carriers increases with age. It is possible that large numbers of demodex mites can stimulate inflammatory or allergic reactions by mechanical blockage of follicles, or by acting as vectors for microorganisms, which ultimately results in connective tissue damage and telangiectasia. Another interesting hypothesis is that inflammatory response may be stimulated by antigenic proteins related to a bacterium (Bacillus oleronius) isolated from D folliculorum.

input: A 5-year-old boy presented to our department with a 2-day history of acute febrile illness. During evaluation, his blood samples were found to be so lipaemic (figure) that it caused interference in analyte measurements. The child was born of a non-consanguineous marriage, there was no history of failure to thrive or developmental delay, and there were no reports of any previous episodes of acute pancreatitis. Neither xanthomata nor hepatosplenomegaly was found at clinical examination. Laboratory test results found a normal fasting blood glucose concentration (4·5 mmol/L). However, triglycerides were found to be very high at 21·4 mmol/L (normal level <1·7 mmol/L). Total serum cholesterol was 5·5 mmol/L (normal level <5·2 mmol/L), LDL cholesterol by direct measurement was 0·7 mmol/L (normal level <2·6 mmol/L), and HDL cholesterol was 0·5 mmol/L (normal level >1·0 mmol/L). Investigations for secondary causes of hyperlipidaemia were negative. Dilated fundus examination showed creamy white discolouration of retinal blood vessels (figure) suggestive of lipaemia retinalis; no retinal haemorrhages or exudates were seen. Fasting lipid profiles of other family members were normal. Taking into account the young age of the patient, the lipaemic plasma, the hypertriglyceridaemia, the lipaemia retinalis, and the lack of indications that his difficulties were secondary to any other diseases causing hypertriglyceridaemia, the boy was diagnosed with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome (FCS). As treatment is mainly dietary fat restriction, the child was started on a low-fat diet—less than 10% of total calories—with medium-chain triglyceride supplements.FCS is characterised by impaired or absent activity of lipoprotein lipase (LPL)—the key enzyme in catabolism of triglyceride rich lipoproteins, particularly chylomicrons. LPL is also involved in the accumulation of chylomicrons which give the milky appearance of the plasma. Bi-allelic mutations in the LPL gene account for around 80% of cases of FCS; the remainder are caused by mutations in one of four genes encoding proteins that interact with LPL. Early recognition and treatment of hyperlipidaemia are crucial to prevent systemic complications like acute pancreatitis. Many patients with elevated triglycerides do not have lipaemia retinalis for reasons that are unclear. The lipaemic appearance of the retinal blood vessels may persist after normalisation of the triglycerides on laboratory testing. Most systemic diseases have eye signs. The importance of an ophthalmological examination as a crucial component of a thorough medical examination cannot be overlooked.

A 58-year-old man with a 31-month history of seeing peoples’ faces as distorted and, in his words, appearing “demonic” visited our laboratory for assessment. The patient stated that the distortions—severely stretched features of the face, with deep grooves on the forehead, cheeks, and chin—were present on every person's face he encountered, but he reported no distortions when looking at objects, such as houses or cars. The patient said that even though faces were distorted, he was still able to recognise who they were. Notably, he reported no distortions when viewing facial images on a screen or on paper. The distortions were not accompanied by delusional beliefs about the identities of the people he encountered—such as his family or friends.
The patient had a history of bipolar affective disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. Additionally, he had a significant head injury at the age of 43 years that led to hospitalisation. He also had possible carbon monoxide poisoning at the age of 55 years, which occurred 4 months prior to the onset of his distortion symptoms. He was not prescribed any medications. He reported no use of illicit substances.
On initial assessment, the patient was well and not distressed; he had some mild low back discomfort. The distortions were very distressing to him initially, he said, but he had become habituated to them. Neuropsychological testing indicated no obvious abnormal general cognitive function; Mini-Mental State Examination score was 30/30. He had no deficits of visual acuity (10/10 in both eyes) or colour vision (Ishira plates: 25/25; Farnsworth–Munsell 100-hue test: average discrimination). Computer-based face perception tests indicated mild impairment in recognition of facial identity but normal recognition of facial expression. No laboratory investigations were done at this stage.
Whole-brain T1-weighted and T2-weighted MRI scans showed a round lesion—T1 dark and T2 bright—measuring approximately 1 cm, located on the superior aspect of the head of the left hippocampus, displacing it inferiorly about 3 mm; despite this, the internal anatomy of the left hippocampus was preserved. The impression from the neurologist was that the lesion was probably an arachnoid cyst in the left hippocampal head; other observations included normal ventricle size, unremarkable midline structures, clear paranasal sinuses, and mild cerebral atrophy.
At 1-year follow-up, a repeated MRI showed no change in the size of the cyst.
As the patient reported no distortion when viewing facial images on a screen or on paper, we asked him to compare an in-person face to a photograph of the face taken in the same room under identical lighting conditions. By alternating between observing the in-person face—perceived as distorted—and the photo on a computer screen—perceived as undistorted—he provided real-time feedback on the perceived differences. We then used image-editing software to modify each photo until it matched his in-person perception (figure).Based on the patient's description of his visual perception, the neuropsychological assessment, and the distortion visualisations, we concluded that he had prosopometamorphopsia.
Prosopometamorphopsia is a rare neurological disorder of visual perception in which faces appear distorted in shape, texture, position, or colour. In most cases, the distortions occur all the time, whether the patient sees the face in person, on a screen, or on paper, thus making it difficult for patients to assess the accuracy of illustrations depicting their perceptual abnormalities because the illustration itself will appear distorted.
Prosopometamorphopsia's aetiology is varied and can occur in the context of head trauma, cerebral infarction, epilepsy, migraine, and hallucinogen-persisting perception disorder. The disorder can also manifest without detectable structural brain changes.
Our patient's unusual phenomenology, combined with computer software, enabled us to generate photorealistic visualisations of the distortions he experienced. Such images, we believe, have not been generated before (video).

A 34-year-old man presented to our department with a 4-month history of constant, progressive epigastric abdominal pain. He also reported that he had lost a substantial amount of weight and that his clothes no longer fitted him. The patient had recently been given a course of Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy with no improvement in his symptoms. Additionally, he had sought help from traditional healers who superficially cut the skin over his abdomen with a sharp blade—a process known as scarification—with the aim of relieving the pain.He was a non-smoker and drank alcohol occasionally; he had no medical history and no family history of malignancy, liver disease, or viral hepatitis.
On examination, we found the patient to be cachectic but comfortable at rest; blood pressure was 99/60 mm Hg, heart rate 96 beats per min, temperature 35·0°C, respiratory rate was 18 breaths per min, peripheral oxygen saturation was 96% on room air, and he was not jaundiced. He had a mass in the right upper quadrant of his abdomen which was firm and palpable 8 cm below the subcostal margin; several scarification marks were observed (figure).
Abdominal ultrasound showed a heterogeneous mass within the right liver lobe which measured 11·8 cm; it had invaded the right portal vein (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed haemoglobin concentration of 9·1 g/dL with mean corpuscular volume of 72·1 fL, white cell count of 2·61  × 109 per L (normal 3·5–9·5), platelet count of 742  × 109 per L (normal 125–350), bilirubin concentration was 4·5 μmol/L, alanine aminotransferase was 41 units per L, gamma-glutamyl transferase was 168·8 units per L, albumin concentration was 18·6 g/L, and creatinine concentration was 52·1 μmol/L. Rapid tests for HIV and anti-hepatitis C antibody were negative but positive for HBsAg.
We diagnosed hepatocellular carcinoma, commenced regular morphine sulphate for pain relief, and referred the patient to the palliative care. He was allowed home after 3 days; 3 months after admission, he died from the effects of progressive malignant disease.
In sub-Saharan Africa, hepatocellular carcinoma is the cancer reported to have the second highest mortality among men and the fourth highest among women, according to the Global Cancer Observatory. Late diagnosis is common due to referral delay and initial care seeking from traditional healers. In southern Africa, hepatitis B virus infection is estimated to be the attributable cause of 29% of liver cancers with a median age of onset of 46 years.
In 2016, a strategic plan to reduce mortality from chronic hepatitis B virus by 2030 was approved at the World Health Assembly. However, modelling data show that without implementation of additional public health measures—including community-based screening and treatment programmes, birth dose vaccination rather than vaccination schedules starting at 6 weeks, and antenatal antiviral therapy for highly viraemic pregnant women—mortality will continue to rise beyond 2030 in sub-Saharan Africa.
The effective public health tools to tackle mortality from hepatitis B virus associated hepatocellular carcinoma in sub-Saharan Africa—delineated above—are available now. That patients—as illustrated by our case—continue to present late with hepatocellular carcinoma, when the prognosis is poor, demands awareness and action from both clinicians and policy makers alike (video).

A 69-year-old woman who was obese presented to our emergency department with breathlessness after episodic vomiting and diarrhoea that had started the night before. She also reported right-sided pleuritic chest pain radiating to the back. She had a medical history of hyperlipidaemia and recurrent urinary tract infections.On examination she was anxious, tachycardic, tachypnoeic, and hypoxic, initially requiring supplemental oxygen, which was given through a nasal cannula. Her lungs were clear on auscultation. Arterial blood gas showed combined metabolic and respiratory acidosis. A chest x-ray was initially read as clear except for bilateral pleural effusion (figure). We decided to intubate her because she had acute hypoxic hypercarbic respiratory failure. CT of her chest showed pneumomediastinum from the thoracic inlet to the diaphragmatic hiatus, right pneumothorax, large right pleural effusion, right subcutaneous emphysema, and complete collapse of the lower lobe of the right lung (figure). On closer retrospective review of the chest x-ray, the pneumomediastinum and right subcutaneous emphysema were visible (figure). Interestingly, the subcutaneous emphysema was not palpable on physical examination.
Oesophagoscopy with minimal air inflation showed severe oesophagitis with diffuse, circumferential, black, friable mucosa that spontaneously bled from the middle to the distal third—consistent with a diagnosis of acute oesophageal necrosis (figure). We also found a slit-like perforation measuring 20 mm in the distal third of the oesophagus and put in a stent; using video-assisted thoracoscopy, we explored and washed out the mediastinum. 30 days later, when the oesophageal stent was removed, the mucosa was pink and healed. After 3 months in hospital, the patient went home.
Acute oesophageal necrosis—also known as black oesophagus—is a rare but important finding. It is associated with a high mortality and perforation is a serious complication that may lead to mediastinitis and empyema. Because of rapid clinical deterioration—especially among patients with underlying comorbidities—awareness and prompt recognition of this condition are essential for timely intervention. Vigilant chest x-ray review for any hints of pneumomediastinum or pneumothorax in any patient with significant vomiting and chest pain is essential as, initially, such findings can be subtle even to the trained eye.

input:
An 8-year-old boy was referred to our centre for haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation. 2 years earlier he had been diagnosed with X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.The unrelated donor was 10 out of 10 HLA-matched; bone marrow was chosen as the graft source. The patient was given a conditioning regimen of busulfan, fludarabine, and thiotepa along with graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) prophylaxis based upon standard recommendations: ciclosporin, anti-T-lymphocyte globulin, and short-term methotrexate.
Neutrophil engraftment was achieved on day +14. However, the early post-haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation period was complicated by the development of peri-engraftment syndrome: the patient had a non-infectious fever, non-productive cough, and respiratory distress with moderate hypoxia that required oxygen support via a nasal cannula. Additionally, interstitial infiltrates were seen on a chest CT scan. He was treated with methylprednisolone, initially at a dose of 1 mg/kg per day and progressively tapering down over 2 weeks, with good response.
On day +39, the patient reported abdominal pain and watery diarrhoea—his stool output increased from 500 mL per day to a maximum of 2900 mL per day. Investigations for Clostridioides difficile, parasites, stool cultures, and viral DNA testing of samples of the patient's stool and blood—for cytomegalovirus, adenovirus, and rotavirus—were negative.
Abdominal ultrasound examination showed a thickened bowel wall in the jejunal and ileal region and free abdominal fluid; colour doppler imaging of the arterial blood flow in the superior mesenteric artery showed increased perfusion (figure).
Notably, endoscopic evaluation was contraindicated because of the patient's clinical state—he was febrile and physically moribund—with a severe thrombocytopenia of 5 × 109 platelets (normal 140–440).
We diagnosed the patient as having grade IV GVHD—skin 0, liver 0, and gut 4. Methylprednisolone was restarted at a dose of 2 mg/kg per day, but to no avail. We then moved to second-line therapy which included ruxolitinib and oral beclomethasone dipropionate. The patient's diarrhoea and abdominal pain gradually improved and by day +100 both had completely resolved; the abnormal ultrasound findings also resolved (figure). The patient was allowed home after 2 months; at follow-up he was fit and well.
Intestinal GVHD—along with opportunistic infections—remains a major cause of death in patients undergoing allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation; timely diagnosis is of crucial importance since any delay in the commencement of immunosuppressants may have dramatic consequences for the patient.
Even though endoscopy remains the gold standard for diagnosing GVHD, it is associated with the risk of major life-threatening complications when undertaken in such clinically vulnerable patients. Therefore, alternative radiological investigations—including a CT scan with intravenous and oral contrast, magnetic resonance enterography, PET-CT, and both standard and contrast-enhanced ultrasonography—need to be considered for diagnosing and assessing GVHD.
Notably, standard and contrast-enhanced ultrasonography combined with colour-coded and power doppler—as shown in this case—are valuable, time-saving, non-invasive and non-ionising, readily repeatable, and well tolerated investigations for the diagnosis, assessment, and follow-up of patients with intestinal GVHD (video).
target: Standard and contrast enhanced transabdominal ultrasonography, along with color-coded and power doppler emerged are not a valuable option for diagnosing GVHD.

An 83-year-old man was admitted to our hospital reporting a 3-week history of cough and exertional dyspnoea. At the time of admission, the patient was 4 weeks into a 6-week course of daptomycin and rifampicin because he had an infected prosthetic knee joint; he also had a history of pituitary hypoplasia and had not been vaccinated against SARS-CoV-2.On examination, he was afebrile, his vital signs were normal, and there was no sign of active infection in the prosthetic knee joint.
Laboratory investigations showed a long-standing lymphopenia of 0·7 × 109 cells per L (normal 1·5–4·0) and a raised C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 186·5mg/L (normal 0–5). The patient's eosinophil cell count was 0·3 × 109 per L (normal 0–0·4), haemoglobin concentration 97 g/L (normal 130–170), and platelet cell count was 322 × 109 per L (normal 150–400). RT-PCR of four consecutive nasopharyngeal swabs for SARS-CoV-2 were negative; routine sputum culture and sensitivity, tuberculosis work-up, respiratory viral screen, and HIV serology were all negative.
Chest imaging—both x-ray and CT—showed bilateral, predominantly peripheral pulmonary infiltrates (figure).
The patient was initially treated as presumed PCR-negative COVID-19 and the antibiotics were replaced with ceftriaxone; dexamethasone was not indicated because he was not hypoxic.
On day 7, due to persisting cough, a bronchoscopy was done; examination of the washings showed an eosinophilic infiltrate. A diagnosis of acute eosinophilic pneumonitis (AEP) was established through the modified Philit criteria: a respiratory illness of less than 1 month duration, pulmonary infiltrates on chest imaging, an eosinophilia of at least 25% in bronchoscopic washings, and the exclusion of other pulmonary eosinophilic diseases such as allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and vasculitis. We thought parasitic infections were unlikely to be the cause—given the absence of a peripheral blood eosinophilia or any history of travel to a country where such infections are endemic. Additionally, the patient had no occupational or lifestyle exposure risk factors. And finally, x-ray and CT findings were not suggestive of fungal infections or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody test was negative. The patient responded rapidly to high dose prednisolone and was allowed home 14 days after he was admitted. At follow-up 3 months later, the patient's chest x-ray was normal.
Common causes of AEP include inhaled toxins—such as smoking, inhalational drugs, and dust—medications, and parasitic and fungal infections. Daptomycin therapy is a well recognised cause of eosinophilic pneumonitis, and we believe this was the most likely cause in our case.
Notably, the patient's symptoms, biochemical, and radiological findings—including lymphopenia, raised CRP, and bilateral peripheral pulmonary infiltrates—pointed towards a diagnosis of PCR-negative COVID-19. Clinicians need to be on the look out for those subtle nuances that might indicate alternative diagnoses.

She had a medical history of well controlled hypertension, and had mechanic's hands (scaly, hyperkeratoic rash) and 3 out of 5 according to the Oxford scale for strength in deltoids and biceps.
Laboratory investigations found a creatine kinase concentration of 3193 IU/L (normal range 26–200 IU/L) and creatinine concentration of 90·2 μmol/L (normal range 35–106 μmol/L). Antinuclear antibodies were positive with a 1:160 titre (normal range <1:80) in a cytoplasmic pattern, anti-EJ antibody was positive (identified through immunoblotting), and a chest CT showed a fibrotic non-specific interstitial pneumonia pattern (figure A).
Considering the patient's presentation and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of anti-synthetase syndrome was made. She was treated with methylprednisolone (40 mg per day) and cyclosporine (50 mg twice per day) for five days, and monitored at regular intervals as an inpatient. Over 2 weeks after the initial treatment the patient's creatine kinase concentration decreased gradually; however, she began to show decreased urine output, her creatinine concentration increased to 600·3 μmol/L, her haemoglobin concentration dropped from 87 g/L to 73 g/L, and her platelet count gradually decreased from 266 × 109 per L to 78 × 109 per L. Furthermore, the patient developed abdominal pain with bloody stools 3 weeks after the initial treatment. Abdominal enhanced CT showed swelling of the small intestine wall, suggesting ischemic bowel disease (figure B). The patient had percutaneous renal biopsy, and the pathological results showed microthrombus formation in the glomerular capillary lumen, disintegration and shedding of tubular epithelial cells, and renal tubular cast formation (figure C–F), indicating thrombotic microangiopathy with acute renal tubular injury.
The patient continued glucocorticoid therapy but stopped cyclosporine (due to deteriorating kidney function and the risk of kidney damage caused by cyclosporine itself). Meanwhile, continuous renal replacement therapy, plasma exchange, and immunoglobulin infusion were performed, and rituximab was tried (2 × 500 mg intravenous infusions, each separated by 15 days) to treat both thrombotic microangiopathy and anti-synthetase syndrome. The patient's symptoms of ischemic bowel disease and changes in the blood system were improved; however, her impaired renal function did not recover and regular haemodialysis was performed during follow-up for 3 months.
Anti-synthetase syndrome is a subtype of idiopathic inflammatory myopathy, and has clinical features including interstitial lung disease, myositis, Raynaud's phenomenon, arthritis, mechanic's hands, and fever. Thrombotic microangiopathy rarely accompanies anti-synthetase syndrome; only about six cases of anti-synthetase syndrome with thrombotic microangiopathy have been reported, of which two cases had no or only mild kidney injury. However, the pathogenetic mechanisms that link anti-synthetase syndrome and thrombotic microangiopathy remain obscure. One hypothesis is that activation of the complement system might play a role in promoting anti-synthetase syndrome and thrombotic microangiopathy simultaneously. Other studies have suggested that, under certain circumstances, circulating autoantibodies in patients with autoimmune inflammatory muscle diseases (including anti-synthetase syndrome) might inhibit plasma von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease activity, which is another pathogenesis of thrombotic microangiopathy. Patients could need combination therapy to treat anti-synthetase syndrome with thrombotic microangiopathy, including plasma exchange, glucocorticoids, and immunosuppressive drugs. A 78-year-old man with primary central nervous system lymphoma was transferred to our cancer centre for further treatment. The patient had been diagnosed 3 months earlier after he presented to another hospital with back pain, numbness, and tingling in all extremities; he had two cycles of rituximab and high-dose methotrexate, which had produced a partial response. The patient had also been given dexamethasone for cerebral oedema; his medical history included type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and coronary artery disease. He was originally from a country with a high prevalence of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection.
The patient's Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status score ranged from 3 to 4 due to the aggressive cancer; we planned to give him two additional cycles of rituximab and high-dose methotrexate and continue dexamethasone.
2 months after admission—the patient had completed one rituximab combined with methotrexate cycle and started the second—treatment was discontinued due to worsening cognitive function and chemotherapy-related leukoencephalopathy; whole brain radiotherapy was then started. A week later the patient was allowed home to continue treatment as an outpatient.
4 weeks later, the patient was readmitted with nausea, anorexia, increased daytime somnolence, and elevated liver transaminase levels (figure). On examination he was lethargic, but we found no clinical findings—including scleral icterus or ascites—compatible with cirrhosis. Notably, baseline HBV serology tests using an ADVIA Centaur XP immunoassay system (Siemens Diagnostics, Tarrytown, NY, USA) had been done 2 months before chemotherapy was initiated at the previous hospital, with non-reactive hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis B core antibody (HBcAb) total results. He was not tested for hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs). However, on re-testing at our centre using an ARCHITECT analyser (Abbott Laboratories, Abbott Park, IL, USA) we found reactive HBsAg and hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) results but with a persistently non-reactive HBcAb total result; non-reactive anti-HBs; and the HBV-DNA level was 14 100 000 IU/mL, log10 7·15 IU/mL (COBAS HBV assay, Roche Molecular Systems), indicating HBV reactivation with hepatitis flare but without liver failure. FibroTest (Mayo Clinic Laboratories) findings were compatible with F4 fibrosis—but liver ultrasonography with elastography showed normal echogenicity. Tests for total and IgM antibody to hepatitis B core antigen (IgM anti-HBc), HBeAg, hepatitis D total antibody, hepatitis E RNA, herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 DNA, and cytomegalovirus DNA in blood were negative. The HBV genotype was B. No HBV polymerase, precore, or basal core promoter mutations were detected.Entecavir, 0·5 mg orally daily, was started, which produced a good virologic response (figure).
At follow-up 8 months later, the patient was receiving cancer treatment with zanubrutinib plus entecavir and his HBV DNA level was undetectable.
Seronegative occult HBV infection, if reactivated, can cause life-threatening disease in cancer patients; the infection can occur without finding traditional markers—including HBsAg and total anti-HBc, and anti-HBs. The significance and seriousness of the reactivation reinforces the importance of screening patients for HBsAg, HBcAb, and anti-HBs—and the need to be aware that high-level HBV viraemia and significant liver inflammation may occur in the absence of these serum markers, as occurred in our patient.
The prevalence of seronegative occult HBV infection ranges from less than 0·5% among US blood donors to 6% among blood donors from high-HBV-endemicity areas. The wide range may be explained using low-sensitivity assays not standardised or validated and by the lack of a standardised definition of seronegative occult HBV infection. The diagnosis of this condition requires a high degree of epidemiological and clinical suspicion.

input: A 65-year-old man with type 2 diabetes was admitted to the hospital with hyperosmolar hyperglycemia state. Two weeks before admission, the patient’s insulin dose had been increased owing to inadequate glycemic control. The physical exam was notable for confusion and sarcopenia. There were also rubbery, subcutaneous masses on either side of the umbilicus where the patient had been repeatedly administering insulin injections. Which of the following should be done to prevent this finding?
output:
Insulin injection site rotation

The image shows **lipohypertrophy** - the rubbery, subcutaneous masses visible on the abdomen around the umbilical area. This is a common complication of repeated insulin injections at the same site.

**Prevention:** Regular rotation of insulin injection sites

Lipohypertrophy occurs due to the local lipogenic (fat-promoting) effect of insulin when injected repeatedly into the same area. This condition can lead to:
- Erratic insulin absorption
- Poor glycemic control
- Need for higher insulin doses

Proper injection site rotation (using different areas of the abdomen, thighs, arms, and buttocks, and rotating within each area) is essential to prevent this complication.

output:
Duodenal lymphoid nodular hyperplasia (nodular lymphoid hyperplasia of the duodenum)

The endoscopic image shows multiple small, whitish-yellow, rounded nodules scattered throughout the duodenal mucosa, giving a characteristic "cobblestone" or "polypoid" appearance. This finding, in the context of a young patient with Giardia lamblia infection, is highly suggestive of nodular lymphoid hyperplasia (NLH).

NLH is commonly associated with:
- Giardia lamblia infection
- Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID)
- IgA deficiency
- Other immunodeficiency states

The association between giardiasis and nodular lymphoid hyperplasia is well-established, as the parasite can trigger a lymphoid proliferative response in the small intestinal mucosa.

A 14-year-old boy came to our clinic with lumps in his oral cavity. His mother informed us that the lesions had appeared spontaneously 13 years before. The boy had taken numerous drugs for the condition without effect. Another 8-year-old son had similar lesions. The patient was of North American Indian descent. Oral examination showed several papulonodular lesions on the cheek mucosa, lip mucosa, and tongue (figure). The lesions were painless to palpation, soft, of different diameter, and similar in colour to normal mucosa. The clinical diagnosis was focal epithelial hyperplasia (FEH), a rare benign condition caused by human papillomavirus subtype 13 or 32. An incisional biopsy was done. Microscopic analysis showed parakeratosis, acanthosis, epithelial hyperplasia, and koilocytic cells (figure), which confirmed FEH. The patient had therapy with CO2 laser ablation; however, it is not possible to predict when FEH lesions will recur or where new lesions will be seen.

A 6-month-old infant was brought to our hospital by his parents because they were concerned that the child's head had been getting progressively larger and that he had been refusing feeds. The parents also said that their child had a fever and was vomiting; his problems had been getting worse over the previous 2 months. The infant had no history suggestive of congenital heart disease or immunosuppression, and he had not received any vaccinations. He was born by normal vaginal delivery, and the pregnancy was uncomplicated. The child had reached all the normal developmental milestones for age until the current problems began. On examination he was conscious but moderately malnourished and healed boils were seen over his scalp. His anterior fontanelle was tense and full, and his occipitofrontal circumference was 47 cm—between the 98th and the 99th percentiles. He was febrile with an axillary temperature of 38·9°C. Examination of his eyes found them to have a persistent downward gaze—known as the sun-setting sign—and his pupils were 4 mm in diameter and sluggishly reactive to light (figure). He had muscle weakness in his left arm and left leg, with power recorded as 1/5.A full blood count found a haemoglobin concentration of 8 g/dL and a leucocytosis (12×109per μ per L). Serum concentrations of electrolytes, urea, and creatine were normal. HIV testing with rapid diagnostic kits was negative. A CT of the infant's brain showed a huge right frontoparietal lesion and a smaller right parieto-occipital lesion: a ring around the outside of both hypodense lesions was enhanced by contrast. There was substantial midline shift and effacement of the ipsilateral lateral ventricle, and compensatory dilatation of the contralateral occipital horn (figure).
We made a diagnosis of cerebral abscesses causing macrocephaly; the anaemia was corrected by a blood transfusion and the child's haemoglobin concentration was 12 g/dL when he went to the theatre.
During the operation we made burr holes in the right frontoparietal and parieto-occipital regions and drained 250 mL of purulent, yellowish fluid from both lesions; we irrigated the brain with normal saline and did intraoperative barbotage with ceftriaxone solution.
Microbiological cultures of the fluid grew Staphylococcus aureus that was sensitive to ceftriaxone: the infant was therefore commenced on ceftriaxone at a dose of 100 mg/kg per day, divided into two and given intravenously every 12 h for 6 weeks. We then changed the antibiotic to oral cefuroxime, which was given for a further 2 weeks. The infant remained in hospital during the entire time, firstly, to ensure compliance and, secondly, to reduce the possibility of recurrence. He made a very good recovery—the left hemiparesis resolved completely and all the features of raised intracranial pressure resolved. An ultrasound scan of the brain showed no residual abscess collection.
Brain abscesses in children are rare. Bacteria causing the infection include Klebsiella pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and group A S aureus: the relative frequencies of the different causative organisms vary by geographical location. Predisposing factors for a child developing a brain abscess include malnutrition, low socioeconomic class, HIV infection, congenital heart disease, and being immunocompromised. Early detection and appropriate surgical intervention—including drainage if possible, as in our case—followed by long-term antibiotic treatment can lead to a successful outcome. Importantly, children who have been treated for the initial infection need long-term follow-up to monitor for sequelae such as hearing and visual loss, epilepsy, and motor and behavioural problems. Age remains an important factor in predicting outcome—the younger the patient, the more likely a successful result.

input: A healthy 14-year-old boy presented with a 6-hour history of hoarseness and difficulty swallowing after accidentally swallowing a coin. On physical examination, the patient was breathing comfortably without stridor or drooling. Radiographs of the chest (left, posteroanterior view) and neck (right, lateral view) showed a rounded radiopaque foreign object situated vertically within the subglottis. Which of the following is NOT an indication for urgent removal for this diagnosis?
output:
Based on the radiographic images showing a coin lodged in the esophagus (appearing as a rounded radiopaque object oriented in the coronal plane on the PA view, which is characteristic of esophageal rather than tracheal foreign body), the diagnosis is:

**Esophageal foreign body (coin ingestion)**

Regarding indications for urgent removal, the following are typically considered urgent indications:
- Complete esophageal obstruction (inability to handle secretions/drooling)
- Airway compromise/respiratory distress
- Button battery ingestion
- Sharp objects
- Multiple magnets
- Signs of perforation
- Location at the cricopharyngeus/upper esophagus with symptoms

**NOT an indication for urgent removal:**

A 6-month-old infant was brought to our hospital by his parents because they were concerned that the child's head had been getting progressively larger and that he had been refusing feeds. The parents also said that their child had a fever and was vomiting; his problems had been getting worse over the previous 2 months. The infant had no history suggestive of congenital heart disease or immunosuppression, and he had not received any vaccinations. He was born by normal vaginal delivery, and the pregnancy was uncomplicated. The child had reached all the normal developmental milestones for age until the current problems began. On examination he was conscious but moderately malnourished and healed boils were seen over his scalp. His anterior fontanelle was tense and full, and his occipitofrontal circumference was 47 cm—between the 98th and the 99th percentiles. He was febrile with an axillary temperature of 38·9°C. Examination of his eyes found them to have a persistent downward gaze—known as the sun-setting sign—and his pupils were 4 mm in diameter and sluggishly reactive to light (figure). He had muscle weakness in his left arm and left leg, with power recorded as 1/5.A full blood count found a haemoglobin concentration of 8 g/dL and a leucocytosis (12×109per μ per L). Serum concentrations of electrolytes, urea, and creatine were normal. HIV testing with rapid diagnostic kits was negative. A CT of the infant's brain showed a huge right frontoparietal lesion and a smaller right parieto-occipital lesion: a ring around the outside of both hypodense lesions was enhanced by contrast. There was substantial midline shift and effacement of the ipsilateral lateral ventricle, and compensatory dilatation of the contralateral occipital horn (figure).
We made a diagnosis of cerebral abscesses causing macrocephaly; the anaemia was corrected by a blood transfusion and the child's haemoglobin concentration was 12 g/dL when he went to the theatre.
During the operation we made burr holes in the right frontoparietal and parieto-occipital regions and drained 250 mL of purulent, yellowish fluid from both lesions; we irrigated the brain with normal saline and did intraoperative barbotage with ceftriaxone solution.
Microbiological cultures of the fluid grew Staphylococcus aureus that was sensitive to ceftriaxone: the infant was therefore commenced on ceftriaxone at a dose of 100 mg/kg per day, divided into two and given intravenously every 12 h for 6 weeks. We then changed the antibiotic to oral cefuroxime, which was given for a further 2 weeks. The infant remained in hospital during the entire time, firstly, to ensure compliance and, secondly, to reduce the possibility of recurrence. He made a very good recovery—the left hemiparesis resolved completely and all the features of raised intracranial pressure resolved. An ultrasound scan of the brain showed no residual abscess collection.
Brain abscesses in children are rare. Bacteria causing the infection include Klebsiella pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and group A S aureus: the relative frequencies of the different causative organisms vary by geographical location. Predisposing factors for a child developing a brain abscess include malnutrition, low socioeconomic class, HIV infection, congenital heart disease, and being immunocompromised. Early detection and appropriate surgical intervention—including drainage if possible, as in our case—followed by long-term antibiotic treatment can lead to a successful outcome. Importantly, children who have been treated for the initial infection need long-term follow-up to monitor for sequelae such as hearing and visual loss, epilepsy, and motor and behavioural problems. Age remains an important factor in predicting outcome—the younger the patient, the more likely a successful result.

input: A healthy 14-year-old boy presented with a 6-hour history of hoarseness and difficulty swallowing after accidentally swallowing a coin. On physical examination, the patient was breathing comfortably without stridor or drooling. Radiographs of the chest (left, posteroanterior view) and neck (right, lateral view) showed a rounded radiopaque foreign object situated vertically within the subglottis. Which of the following is NOT an indication for urgent removal for this diagnosis?
output:
Looking at the radiographs, I can see a coin lodged in the esophagus. The key finding is that on the PA chest view, the coin appears oriented in the coronal plane (showing its full circular face), and on the lateral neck view, it appears as a thin line. This orientation pattern indicates **esophageal foreign body** (coins in the esophagus orient coronally, appearing round on AP view).

However, the question states the object is "within the subglottis," which would indicate an **airway foreign body**.

**Indications for URGENT removal of esophageal foreign bodies include:**
1. Complete esophageal obstruction (inability to handle secretions/drooling)
2. Airway compromise/respiratory distress
3. Button/disc batteries (risk of caustic injury)
4. Sharp objects
5. Multiple magnets
6. Signs of perforation or mediastinitis
7. Foreign body in esophagus >24 hours
8. Location at cricopharyngeus/upper esophagus with symptoms

**NOT an indication for urgent removal:**
- **Asymptomatic patient with a blunt object (like a coin) in the mid-to-lower esophagus for less than 24 hours**

In this case, since the patient is:
- Breathing comfortably
- No stridor
- No drooling
- Coin (blunt object)
- Duration only 6 hours

The answer to "which is NOT an indication for urgent removal" would be:

**Asymptomatic presentation with a smooth/blunt foreign body present for less than 24 hours** - this patient could potentially be observed for spontaneous passage rather than requiring urgent intervention, though given the location and symptoms (hoarseness, dysphagia), intervention would still be warranted.

Radiographs of the chest (left, posteroanterior view) and neck (right, lateral view) showed a rounded radiopaque foreign object situated vertically within the subglottis. Which of the following is NOT an indication for urgent removal for this diagnosis?
output:
Looking at the radiographs, I can see a coin lodged in the **esophagus** (not the airway). Key findings:

- **Posteroanterior view**: The coin appears oriented in the coronal plane (seen as a circle/oval)
- **Lateral view**: The coin is seen edge-on

This orientation (coronal plane on AP view) is characteristic of an **esophageal foreign body**, as the esophagus is naturally flattened anteroposteriorly. A coin in the trachea would typically orient in the sagittal plane (seen edge-on on AP view).

## Indications for URGENT removal of esophageal foreign bodies include:

1. **Complete esophageal obstruction** (unable to handle secretions/drooling)
2. **Airway compromise** (stridor, respiratory distress)
3. **Button/disc batteries** (risk of rapid mucosal injury)
4. **Sharp objects** (risk of perforation)
5. **Multiple magnets** (risk of pressure necrosis)
6. **Objects lodged >24 hours** (increased complication risk)
7. **Signs of complications** (fever, chest pain suggesting perforation)

## NOT an indication for urgent removal:

**Asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic patient with a blunt object (like a coin) lodged for <24 hours**

In this case, despite the 6-hour history with hoarseness and dysphagia, the patient is:
- Breathing comfortably
- No stridor
- No drooling

A **coin** (blunt, non-caustic object) in a **stable patient** without complete obstruction can be observed for **12-24 hours** as many will pass spontaneously, though removal within 24 hours is generally recommended.

**Answer: Asymptomatic presentation with a smooth/blunt object and duration <24 hours is NOT an indication for urgent (emergent) removal.**

An 85-year-old Gujarati woman with a 1-day history of confusion, left-sided weakness, and slurred speech attended our hospital. She had a history of headaches, which had been extensively investigated for 2 years from 2013. She also had hypertension. She had no history of recent travel.On examination, she was afebrile. She had a dense left hemiparesis; cranial nerves, visual fields, and fundoscopy examinations were normal. She was also in atrial fibrillation.
A CT scan of the patient's brain showed multiple cortical and subcortical, hypodense lesions; an MRI showed the lesions to be ring-enhancing, with surrounding vasogenic oedema (figure). A CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis found no abnormalities and a transthoracic echo was normal.
Blood investigations found her haemoglobin concentration was 12·4 g/dL (normal range 12·0–15·5); her white cell count was 9·4 × 109 per L (normal range 4·3 × 109–10·8 × 109); neutrophil count was 7·9 × 109 per L (normal range 1·5 × 109–8 × 109); lymphocyte count was 0·7 × 109 per L (normal range 1·0 × 109–4·8 × 109); C-reactive protein concentration was 4·6 mg/L (normal range <3); and eosinophil count was 0·1 × 109 per L (normal range <0·45 × 109). Blood cultures were negative. HIV, syphilis, and Brucella spp serology were negative. An autoimmune screen was negative and serum immunoglobulins were not raised.
A lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 22 cm water (normal range 10–25), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was clear, with 98% lymphocytes (60 cells per μL; normal range 0–5), a normal glucose concentration (3·1 mg/L; normal range 2·8–4·2), and a total protein concentration of 0·66 g/L (normal 0·15–0·45). GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra (Xpert Ultra; Cepheid, Sunnyvale, CA, USA) of the CSF—for diagnosis of tuberculous meningitis—was negative. However, we still suspected the diagnosis to be tuberculous meningoencephalitis because of the patient's ethnicity, and we started empirical treatment with rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, moxifloxacin, and prednisolone.
The patient's condition deteriorated and on day 3 of the admission, she had tonic–clonic seizures, which were initially controlled with lorazepam and levetiracetam. However, her Glasgow Coma Scale steadily dropped to 4 by the afternoon; she had an extensor response to pain stimuli, tachypnoea, pinpoint pupils, and absent doll's head and corneal reflexes. An urgent meeting between the family and clinicians was held; a consensus was made to stop active treatment—including a decision not to carry out a brain biopsy—and to keep the patient comfortable. She died 11 days after admission. A post-mortem examination found multiple haemorrhagic lesions in the brain (figure). Histopathology showed large amoebic cysts in the perivascular spaces and blood vessel lumens (figure). PCR for brain amoebae—Acanthamoeba spp, Naegleria fowleri, and Balamuthia mandrillaris—on formalin-fixed paraffin embedded tissue was negative. However, colleagues with expertise in parasitology from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, USA, using both real-time PCR and conventional genotyping PCR of the samples, were able to make a positive diagnosis for B mandrillaris (appendix). The family was informed.
Amoebic encephalitis is a difficult diagnosis to confirm and may need both diagnostic real-time PCR and conventional genotyping PCR. Often a definitive diagnosis can only be made by brain biopsy or post-mortem examination. B mandrillaris was first isolated in 1986 from the brain tissue of a mandrill. It causes serious cutaneous infections and encephalitis and is fatal in more than 98% of patients (video).
