A 34-year-old man was brought to our Emergency Department after a truck ran over the right side of his body while he was out walking. He had no medical history.On examination, the patient's vital signs were stable; he had tenderness over his right shoulder, mild tenderness and bruising over the right hip, and abrasions over the right side of his arm, chest, abdomen, and right flank. His pelvis was stable, and movements of the right hip joint were unaffected.
Laboratory investigations were within normal range. No fractures were seen on x-rays of the patient's chest, pelvis, right shoulder, and right femur. A whole-body CT scan showed subcutaneous haematomas about 3·5 cm × 3·0 cm in the right infra-axillary region, right lateral abdominal wall, and pelvis.
We admitted the patient under the trauma service; an MRI of his right shoulder showed an acute contusion of the right supraspinatus muscle and right acromioclavicular joint. The patient was allowed home after an orthopaedic review with a plan of conservative treatment: analgesia and outpatient physiotherapy.
At follow-up with his general practitioner, 3 weeks later, the patient had an ill-defined soft, fluctuant swelling over his right flank and a fluctuant, non-tender swelling around the right hip with no abnormalities of the overlying skin.
At further assessment, 5 weeks after the accident, the swelling over the patient's right flank had resolved, but the one over his right hip area had grown larger. An MRI of the right hip showed a large 14 cm × 9·5 cm × 26 cm fluid signal collection with multiple fat locules within the deep subcutaneous tissue of the right posterolateral proximal thigh and hip, immediately superficial to the intact deep fascia (figure). The findings were consistent with a diagnosis of a Morel-Lavallée lesion.
The patient underwent open debridement; a mixture of blood and serous fluid was drained from the lesion and multiple pseudo-polyps, that had formed as a result of fat necrosis, were excised along with the capsule of the cavity. The cavity was washed out and the incision was closed.
The patient was allowed home. At postoperative follow-up in the trauma clinic, 4 weeks later, the lesion had completely resolved.
A Morel-Lavallée lesion is a rare, closed, internal degloving soft-tissue injury usually resulting from trauma. Lesions can present acutely after the trauma or they can develop a few days or weeks after the injury; they are often missed initially—as in our case. They develop by shearing forces which lead to separation of the skin and subcutaneous tissues from the underlying fascia, leading to fluid accumulation in the perifascial space.
In approximately 8% of cases, Morel-Lavallée lesions are associated with underlying pelvic or acetabular fractures—although the true incidence may be higher in such patients. When the lesion is small, it may be overlooked. Additionally, Morel-Lavallée lesions are sometimes misdiagnosed as a post-traumatic muscle contusion, haematomas, or myositis ossificans. Early recognition of the condition prevents the development of complications such as infections or skin necrosis. MRI is the investigation of choice, aiding diagnosis, and guiding management.

A 52-year-old woman with a 10-day history of a fever and who had, for the past 4 days, an impaired level of consciousness attended our hospital.She had a medical history of autoimmune encephalitis and urinary tract infections.
On examination we found her to be unwell, with a respiratory rate of 20 breaths per min, pulse rate of 103 beats per min, a temperature of 38·11°C, blood oxygen saturation of 95%, and a blood pressure of 136/93 mm Hg.
A chest CT showed inflammation in both lungs and the patient was then intubated using an endotracheal tube.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised white blood cell count of 14·20 × 109 per L (normal 4·5–11·0); absolute neutrophil count was 13·83 × 109 per L (normal 1·8–7·5) with a percentage of 97·3%.
Sequencing of a strain isolated from the patient's sputum showed that she had a lung infection caused by the Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC)-producing KPC-2 strain.
We commenced treatment with antibacterial drugs: polymyxin B plus the cefoperazone-sulbactam combination for 8 days, followed by tigecycline plus fosfomycin for 2 days, and then ceftazidime-avibactam for 21 days. However, 3 days after stopping the ceftazidime-avibactam combination and replacing it with fosfomycin monotherapy, the patient's temperature increased again. Further laboratory investigations showed a white blood cell count of 10·46 × 109 per L, with an absolute neutrophil count of 8·63 × 109 per L; neutrophils were 82·4%.
Carbapenem-resistant K pneumoniae was still cultured from a sample of the patient's sputum.
We then re-sequenced the bacteria which showed that one of the genes encoding carbapenemases—the KPC-2 genotype—had evolved, in vivo, from blaKPC-2 to blaKPC-76 through a 7-amino acid tandem repeat, between amino acids 262 and 268 (262V-268N dup), and a D179Y substitution mutation. We presumed the change had resulted in the treatment failure.
Additionally, antimicrobial susceptibility testing indicated that the K pneumoniae had changed its antimicrobial susceptibility profile: initially it had the characteristic growth of classic KPC-2 (figure), which is susceptible to the ceftazidime-avibactam and aztreonam-avibactam combinations; and after 3 weeks, the profile had changed to the New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase-producing K pneumoniae, which is resistant to the ceftazidime-avibactam combination but susceptible to aztreonam-avibactam (figure).
The patient was then given the ceftazidime-avibactam combination plus amikacin, and then was switched to tigecycline plus meropenem; her symptoms improved, and her vital signs stabilised. She was then transferred to a rehabilitation facility for further treatment.
At the molecular level, nucleotide deletions, mutations, insertions, and tandem repeats are the mechanisms most commonly responsible for bacterial resistance to ceftazidime-avibactam.
The newer antibiotic combinations, such as carbapenem, meropenem, and the cyclic boronic acid β-lactamase inhibitor, vaborbactam, can be considered as salvage therapies for the treatment of infections caused by emerging strains with novel KPC-variants—although these agents have not yet been marketed for clinical use in many countries.
output: Ceftazidime-avibactam resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae infection due to in vivo evolution of KPC-2 to KPC-76

A 27-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 4-month history of bilateral frontal headache, irritability, frontal lobe signs, bilateral proptosis, and nasal obstruction. He had no other signs or symptoms of a systemic illness. Rhinoscopy showed a soft tissue mass obstructing both nasal airways. A CT scan of his head showed hyperdense lesions involving both the paranasal sinuses (figure), with expansions into the frontal interdiploë spaces, and some calcification (figure). An MRI scan of the brain showed a soft tissue mass extending along the anterior cranial fossa floor up to the sellar and parasellar regions (figure). Endoscopic biopsy was inconclusive; however, because of raised intracranial pressure, the patient was taken to surgery for craniotomy and excision of the lesion.During the operation, an extradural grey-coloured, foul smelling, soft tissue mass was seen carpeting the cranial fossa floor over both frontal lobes and extending up into the air sinuses. The extradural mass, which was found to be exerting pressure on the brain by compressing the frontal lobes without any macroscopic invasion of the dura, was excised completely. The intracranial pressure was reduced on completion of the operation.
Histopathological examination of the lesion showed septate fungal hyphae most consistent with Aspergillus spp.
In the immediate postoperative period, the patient was conscious and had no additional neurological deficits; he was also started on voriconazole. However, 24 h post-operatively, the patient suddenly became unresponsive and needed mechanical ventilation. He remained unconscious and on the fourth day after the operation, he developed diffuse ischaemic changes—possible global ischaemia—throughout the brain and died.
Unexpected deaths have been widely reported in cases of intracranial aspergillosis, but sudden deterioration on the first postoperative day is unusual. Systemic antifungal chemotherapy should be started prior to any surgical intervention. Such clinical and radiological presentations will, in our opinion, continue taking even the most experienced clinicians by surprise.

A 74-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of lower abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. A plain-film radiograph of the abdomen showed marked dilatation of bowel loops and abrupt termination of gas within the descending colon, referred to as a colon cutoff sign. The colon cutoff sign is classically described in association with which disease process?
output:
Acute pancreatitis

The colon cutoff sign is classically associated with **acute pancreatitis**. This radiographic finding describes the abrupt termination of colonic gas, typically at the splenic flexure, due to localized spasm or inflammation of the colon adjacent to an inflamed pancreas. The inflammatory process causes reflex ileus and spasm of the colon at this anatomic location where the pancreatic tail lies in close proximity to the splenic flexure of the colon.

The colon cutoff sign is classically described in association with which disease process?
output:
Acute pancreatitis

The colon cutoff sign is classically associated with **acute pancreatitis**. This radiographic finding occurs when inflammation from the pancreas spreads to the adjacent transverse colon and splenic flexure region, causing localized ileus and spasm. This results in gaseous distension of the colon proximal to the splenic flexure with an abrupt absence of gas distally, creating the characteristic "cutoff" appearance.

However, it should be noted that while this sign is classically taught in association with pancreatitis, in clinical practice it can also be seen with other conditions causing colonic obstruction or ileus, including colonic malignancy, volvulus, or other causes of mechanical obstruction.

A 53-year-old man was referred to the dermatology clinic with a 20-year history of a generalised, pruritic rash—with features of both psoriasis vulgaris and atopic dermatitis—and an 8-year history of progressive arthritis, diagnosed as polyarticular gout, that had recently affected his ability to walk.The patient had been prescribed topical steroids and allopurinol with little improvement to his skin or joint disease.
On examination he was generally well but confined to a gurney because of his arthritis. He had ill-defined facial erythema and erythematous scaly plaques involving approximately 30% of the body surface area of his trunk and extremities (figure; appendix). He also had tophaceous nodules and flexion deformities bilaterally in both his metacarpophalangeal and proximal inter-phalangeal joints.
While the patient's thin, scaly lesions resembled an eczematous dermatitis, the moderate demarcation of some plaques suggested psoriatic skin disease, so he was initiated on the tumour necrosis factor-α (TNFα) inhibitor adalimumab; no improvement was noted at 5 months and it was stopped (appendix).
Histopathological examination of a sample of a skin biopsy—with the hope of clarifying the diagnosis—showed the spongiotic pattern of an eczematous dermatitis (appendix). The anti-interleukin-4 receptor (IL-4R) α antibody, dupilumab—approved for eczema in the form of atopic dermatitis—was prescribed which, after 5 months, failed to show any clinical improvement.
To gain further understanding of our patient's disease, a single-cell RNA sequencing profile of his skin-resident T cells was performed—part of an ongoing molecular study of complex cases of skin disease (appendix). The skin T-cell transcriptomes closely resembled those of classic psoriasis, rather than atopic dermatitis (one-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test, W=56, p=0·0002; figure); they also showed elevated IL-23 pathway transcripts which included Chimerin 1 and Cathepsin H. Therefore, the patient was initiated on the IL-23 inhibitor, tildrakizumab, considered to be more specific for the treatment of psoriasis. output:
Butterfly vertebra (congenital vertebral anomaly)

The imaging shows a sagittal cleft vertebra, also known as a butterfly vertebra, which is a congenital vertebral anomaly resulting from failure of fusion of the lateral chondrification centers during embryonic development. This creates the characteristic appearance of two hemivertebrae separated by a midline cleft, resembling a butterfly on coronal imaging. It is typically an incidental finding and is usually asymptomatic, as in this case where the patient presented with unrelated respiratory symptoms.

A 21-year-old woman presented to our hospital for the first time with a history of seizures. The patient's mother had witnessed the fits and described them as lasting approximately 10 min, causing a loss of consciousness, and incontinence of urine—compatible with a tonic-clonic seizure.She had no significant medical or family history and was not taking any medication.
On examination the patient was afebrile, her blood pressure was 201/127 mm Hg, and she was drowsy. Direct fundoscopy showed no abnormal findings.
Laboratory investigations showed serum potassium concentration was 2·2 mmol/L (normal 3·5–5·1) and bicarbonate was 35 mmol/L (normal 21–31); serum creatinine concentration was normal. A screen for drugs of abuse was negative.
Chest-x ray, brain MRI, electroencephalogram, and doppler examination of the patient's renal arteries were all normal. The patient was admitted, and during her 4 day stay no further seizures were seen. Her blood pressure was slowly lowered using intravenous labetalol given at a dose of 1 mg per min; she was later started on oral amlodipine 10 mg, clonidine 0·2 mg daily, and carvedilol 12·5 mg twice a day. She continued with these medications and oral potassium chloride after leaving the hospital.
Further investigations for causes of secondary hypertension showed normal concentrations of free plasma metanephrines, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, androstenedione, dehydroepiandrosterone, dehydroepiandrosterone sulphate, and 24 h urine cortisol and creatinine. Plasma renin activity ranged from 24·48 to 30·86 μg/L per h (reference range 0·25–5·82), and serum aldosterone ranged from 1·02 to 1·39 nmol/L (reference range 0·03–0·89). An abdominal CT scan showed a solitary 11 mm central kidney mass measuring 88 Hounsfield units—arterial and venous phases—which was too dense to be a benign cyst (figure). Selective renal venous sampling demonstrated a left to right renin ratio of 1·3.
The patient underwent a partial left nephrectomy and examination after removal showed a well circumscribed, variegated, and orange to red nodule, measuring 1·6 cm × 1·5 cm × 1·3 cm surrounded by normal renal parenchyma (figure). Histological examination of a sample of the nodule showed sheets of round to oval uniform cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm (figure) and immunostaining for renin was strongly positive (figure). The diagnosis was a juxtaglomerular tumour—also known as a reninoma.
Postoperatively, the patient's blood pressure was 132/93 mm Hg, plasma renin activity ranged between 2·9 and 0·57, and serum aldosterone was 0·44 and 0·11 at 1 and 6 h, respectively. 1 h after surgery, blood pressure remained at 132/93 mm Hg without any medications. 4 weeks postoperatively, the blood pressure was 113/76 mm Hg off all medications; 16 months later, blood pressure and electrolytes remained normal. The patient was urged to check her blood pressure at regular intervals in the future and to report any persistent elevations.
Renal cell carcinomas may present with hypertension, hypokalaemia, and raised plasma renin concentrations—similarly to the presentation of the benign nodule found in our patient—and therefore need to be excluded by looking specifically for radiographic features of metastasis on imaging.
An extensive and timely work-up of secondary causes of hypertension in young people is paramount—particularly those with severe rises in blood pressure; the diagnosis and removal of a reninoma—as in this case—may save patients from a lifetime of antihypertensive medication.

The differential diagnosis of transient monocular vision loss (TMVL), based on clinical history alone, is a common clinical problem. A 66-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of recurrent right TMVL. He had more than 15 episodes without provocation. He described multiple islands of visual loss that coalesced to complete monocular blindness—persisting for several minutes—followed by recovery in a reverse manner. While venous access was being obtained for fluorescein angiography (FA), the patient reported onset of an attack. The examination was thus fortuitously done during vision loss.Normally, following intravenous injection, the dye passes through the short posterior ciliary arteries and appears in the optic disc and choroid within 8–12 s, depending on the age, cardiovascular status of the patient, and speed of dye injection. The arterial retinal circulation appears 11–18 s after injection. However, in our patient, FA of the right eye showed slightly delayed filling of the central retinal artery and severely delayed filling of the nasal choroid and prelaminar region of the optic disc (figure). The circulation of the left eye was normal. Examination 1 week later confirmed retinal circulation was normal between attacks (figure). A diagnosis of vasospasm was made and after treatment with nifedipine 5 mg twice a day, the attacks ceased. The patient remained attack free at 8 months' follow-up.

Further, it has been speculated that the reticulated, patchy pattern of TMVL corresponds to interruption of the choroidal circulation—related to its lobular arrangement. This will very rarely occur due to thromboembolism because of the extensive anastomoses between the posterior ciliary arteries supplying the choroid. However, whereas vasospasm of the central retinal artery has been directly observed, choroidal perfusion abnormalities can usually only be identified by FA, and no photographic evidence for this assertion has been published. Our Clinical Picture provides the first direct confirmation for the proposed theory that the reticulated pattern of TMVL is a signature of transient ischaemia of the choroidal lobular circulation. Clearly, such cases should be managed as vasospasm.
